questions.text:
A newly established hotel Gokwe Villa has approached you as a web developer. Construct a website for the hotel. The website has only one page. Create a form to allow users to enter customer details and select a room. The form must display:
• customer details
• details of the room (executive, single or double)
• cost of the room per day
• the total cost
Users must be able to enter the start date and check out date. Users must be able to select a room from the drop down list. Users must not be able to edit other fields.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Award marks for:
• Valid HTML page structure for Gokwe Villa hotel website (1 mark).
• Hotel name/branding visible on the page (1 mark).
• Form with customer detail fields (e.g. Name, ID/Passport) – at least 2 fields (2 marks).
• Start date input field (1 mark).
• Check-out date input field (1 mark).
• Drop-down list (<select>) for room type: executive, single, double (2 marks).
• Cost per day field displayed as read-only/disabled (1 mark).
• Total cost field displayed as read-only/disabled (1 mark).
• JavaScript or server-side logic to calculate total cost based on room selection and dates (3 marks).
• readonly or disabled attribute correctly applied to non-editable fields (2 marks).
• Room costs defined for each type (1 mark).
• Submit/Book button present (1 mark).
• Overall presentation and usability of the page (2 marks).
(Award up to 20 marks.)

questions.text:
(a) The following section of pseudocode inputs 100 numbers and outputs the largest positive and largest negative number. There are some errors in the pseudocode.
1. Input number
2. neg = number: pos = number
3. For x = 0 to 100
4. Input number
5. If number > pos then number = pos
6. If number < neg then number = neg
7. x = x + 1
8. Next x
9. Output pos, neg
Correct the errors and develop a program for the pseudocode.

(b) Develop a program that processes invoices for a company selling a variety of products. It should prompt the user to enter the unit cost of the product, how many were sold and the date the invoice was supposed to be paid. Use two functions, the first one calculates and returns the basic cost of the invoice including VAT (15%) and the second function reduces the basic cost by 10% if the invoice has been paid on time.

(c) Develop a program for a particular university. Students on a course take three module exams. Students can have two attempts at each exam module and the best result counts. Declare a class called student that stores the student's ID, name and three exam marks (out of 100). If the best mark for a given module is the student's second attempt, store the second attempt mark, otherwise keep the first mark. The program should output how many modules the student passed. A pass mark is 50 and above. Determining the number of passes should be one of the class' methods.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Errors identified and corrected:
• Line 3: 'For x = 0 to 100' should be 'For x = 1 to 99' (loop runs 100 times after initial input, so 1 to 99 giving 99 additional inputs = 100 total; OR For x = 1 to 100 with line 1 removed).
• Line 5: 'number = pos' should be 'pos = number' (assign number to pos when larger).
• Line 6: 'number = neg' should be 'neg = number' (assign number to neg when smaller).
• Line 7: 'x = x + 1' is redundant/error in a FOR loop (remove or it is automatically incremented).
Corrected pseudocode:
1. Input number
2. neg = number; pos = number
3. For x = 1 to 99
4.   Input number
5.   If number > pos then pos = number
6.   If number < neg then neg = number
7. Next x
8. Output pos, neg
Award marks for: each error identified (1 mark each = 4 marks), working program (6 marks).

(b) Award marks for:
• Prompting for unit cost (1 mark), quantity sold (1 mark), due date (1 mark).
• Function 1: calculates basic cost = unit cost × quantity (2 marks); adds VAT: total = basic × 1.15 (2 marks); returns value (1 mark).
• Function 2: accepts basic cost and payment date (1 mark); compares payment date to due date (2 marks); reduces by 10% if paid on time: discounted = basic × 0.90 (2 marks); returns value (1 mark).
• Correct function calls and output of final invoice amount (3 marks).
• Program compiles and runs correctly (3 marks). (Up to 20 marks.)

(c) Award marks for:

• Constructor/initialisation method (1 mark).

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Normalisation to 2NF:

Step 1 – First Normal Form (1NF): Remove repeating groups. Split multi-valued 'Category' field so each row has one category. Identify primary key: composite key (MemberID, MovieRented) or introduce MovieID.

Step 2 – Second Normal Form (2NF): Remove partial dependencies. Since all non-key attributes depend on MemberID alone, split into two tables:

Member Table (MemberID, Title, FullName, Address)
  Primary Key: MemberID

Rental Table (RentalID, MemberID, MovieRented, Category)
  Primary Key: RentalID; Foreign Key: MemberID references Member(MemberID)

Award marks for: correct identification of repeating groups/1NF (3 marks); correct identification of partial dependencies (3 marks); correctly structured Member table with PK (3 marks); correctly structured Rental/Movie table with PK and FK (3 marks); correct 2NF explanation (2 marks). (Up to 14 marks.)

(b)(i) Primary Key: Student-ID (e.g. 4241).
SQL to create table:
CREATE TABLE Sport (
  StudentID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  FName VARCHAR(50),
  Surname VARCHAR(50),
  Sport VARCHAR(50),
  Venue VARCHAR(50)
);
Award: PK identified (1 mark), CREATE TABLE syntax (1 mark), correct fields/data types (1 mark), screenshot of table (1 mark). (4 marks.)

(b)(ii)
SELECT * FROM Sport WHERE Sport = 'cricket';
Expected results: Sibo Nare, Layla Tanguni, Sindiso Moyo.

(OR WHERE StudentID = 4858)
Award: correct DELETE syntax (1 mark), correct WHERE condition (1 mark), record removed confirmed (1 mark), screenshot (1 mark). (4 marks.)

(b)(iv)
INSERT INTO Sport VALUES (4748, 'Kenneth', 'Shawa', 'soccer', 'Gweru');
Award: correct INSERT syntax (1 mark), correct values (1 mark), record visible in table (1 mark), screenshot (1 mark). (4 marks.)

questions.topic: Sport Law, Ethics and Management Principles
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any two valid provisions e.g.: Every citizen has the right to participate in sport; the State must promote sport participation; sport participation shall not be discriminated against on grounds of race, gender, age, etc. [1 mark each, max 2]

(b) Any three valid legal duties e.g.: Duty of care to participants; ensuring compliance with sport regulations/by-laws; maintaining safe facilities; upholding athletes' rights; ensuring contracts are honoured; preventing discrimination. [1 mark each, max 3]

(c) Any three processes e.g.:
1. Negotiation – parties in dispute discuss and attempt to resolve the matter amicably without a third party.
2. Mediation – a neutral third party (mediator) assists disputing parties to reach a mutual agreement.
3. Arbitration – an arbitrator hears both sides and makes a binding decision.
4. Litigation – the dispute is taken to a court of law for a legal ruling.
[2 marks each, max 6]

(d) Contents of a code of conduct: statement of purpose/values; expected behaviour of members; prohibited conduct; disciplinary procedures; reporting mechanisms; anti-discrimination clauses; confidentiality; consequences for violations. [1 mark per valid point, max 4]

(e) Sportsmanship: the ethical and fair conduct demonstrated by athletes, officials and supporters in sport, characterised by respect for opponents, adherence to rules, graciousness in victory and defeat, and integrity. [2 marks for a complete, accurate definition]

(f) Any three principles e.g.: Unity of command; division of labour/specialisation; planning; accountability; transparency; integrity; fairness; teamwork; leadership. [1 mark each, max 3]

questions.topic: Sport Communication, Management Principles and Human Resources
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any five ways e.g.: Use of social media platforms; regular team meetings/briefings; clear notice boards; use of official memoranda/circulars; open-door management policy; use of modern communication technology (email, apps); training in communication skills; feedback mechanisms; regular newsletters. [1 mark each, max 5]

(b)
(i) Planning – the process of setting goals and objectives and determining the best course of action to achieve them; involves identifying resources, timelines and responsibilities. [2 marks]
(ii) Forecasting – the process of predicting future events, trends or outcomes in sport (e.g., budget needs, participant numbers, performance targets) to guide decision-making. [2 marks]
(iii) Organizing – the process of arranging resources (human, financial, physical) and tasks in a structured way to achieve the organisation's goals efficiently. [2 marks]

(c) Any four ways e.g.: Salary increments/bonuses; promotions; recognition/awards; provision of good working conditions; training and development opportunities; flexible working hours; team-building activities; provision of sport equipment. [1 mark each, max 4]

(d) Any two strategies e.g.: Team-building activities/retreats; conflict resolution mechanisms; open and transparent communication channels; equal treatment and fairness in roles/responsibilities; shared vision and goals. [1 mark each, max 2]

(e) Justification (any three valid points): A skilled and motivated workforce increases productivity; staff development reduces turnover; investing in human capital improves performance and service delivery; a cohesive workforce attracts sponsors and partners; staff training improves professional standards of the organisation. [1 mark each, max 3]

questions.topic: Sport Management Skills, Risk, Marketing and Advertising
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any four skills e.g.: Leadership skills; communication skills; financial management skills; conflict resolution skills; strategic planning skills; decision-making skills; time management; interpersonal/people management skills; technical sport knowledge. [1 mark each, max 4]

(b) Main considerations e.g.: Relevant qualifications and experience; leadership and management competencies; knowledge of sport administration; integrity and ethical standing; availability and commitment; references/background checks; salary expectations vs budget. [1 mark each, max 3]

(c) Risk in sport management: the probability or likelihood of an event occurring that may result in harm, injury, financial loss, reputational damage or failure to achieve organisational objectives. [2 marks for a complete definition]

(d) Role of marketing: promotes the organisation's brand/image; attracts sponsors and funding; increases event attendance/fan base; generates revenue through merchandise and ticket sales; builds community engagement; creates awareness of sport programmes; identifies target audiences and their needs. [1 mark each, max 5]

(e) Advertising: a paid, non-personal form of communication used to promote sport products, services, events or organisations to a target audience through various media channels (TV, radio, print, social media, etc.). [2 marks for a complete definition]

(f) Ways to protect local sports products: patenting/trademarking local sport brands; government policy support/legislation; import tariffs on competing foreign products; promoting 'buy local' campaigns; sport associations endorsing local products; partnering with local manufacturers; labelling and certification of local products. [1 mark each, max 4]

questions.topic: Gamesmanship, Fair Play, Legal Duties, Cheating and Doping
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Gamesmanship: the use of dubious, unsporting or borderline legal methods/tactics to gain an advantage over an opponent without technically breaking the rules; prioritising winning over fair play. [2 marks for a complete, accurate definition]

(b) Fair-play principle: the concept that all participants in sport should compete honestly, with respect for opponents and officials, adhering strictly to the rules of the game, and accepting results graciously; it encompasses equality, integrity and respect in sport. [2 marks]

(c) Any four legal duties with Zimbabwean examples e.g.:
1. Duty of care – e.g., ZIFA ensuring safe pitches for players in the PSL.
2. Ensuring compliance with sport regulations – e.g., ZASU ensuring university sport follows national federation rules.
3. Upholding anti-doping regulations – e.g., SRC ensuring athletes comply with WADA/ZADA regulations.
4. Contractual obligations – e.g., sport administrators honouring player contracts under Zimbabwe Labour Act.
5. Child protection – e.g., school sport administrators adhering to MoPSE child protection policies.
[1 mark each, max 4 — must reference Zimbabwean context]

(d) Ways of reducing cheating in Zimbabwean school sports (any six points at 1 mark each):
- Strict enforcement of rules by officials/referees
- Use of qualified and independent match officials
- Anti-cheating education in the curriculum
- Schools adopting strong codes of conduct
- Disqualification and banning of repeat offenders
- Parental and teacher monitoring
- Transparent scoring and result recording systems
- Rewarding fair play with awards/recognition
[1 mark each, max 6]

(e) Implications of doping in sport (any six points at 1 mark each):
- Health risks/long-term physical harm to athletes
- Bans and suspensions from competition
- Stripping of medals, titles and records
- Legal consequences/criminal prosecution
- Reputational damage to the athlete and country
- Loss of sponsorships and endorsements
- Psychological impact on the athlete
- Undermines the integrity and credibility of sport
[1 mark each, max 6]

questions.topic: Sportsmanship, Gamesmanship, Code of Conduct and Contracts

- Sportsmanship refers to ethical, fair and respectful conduct in sport; gamesmanship refers to the use of cunning, borderline or unsporting tactics to win.
- Sportsmanship upholds the spirit of the game; gamesmanship exploits loopholes in rules.
- A sportsman respects the opponent; a gamesman may deliberately distract or psyche out opponents.
- Sportsmanship promotes integrity; gamesmanship prioritises victory at almost any cost.
- Sportsmanship is universally admired and encouraged; gamesmanship is frowned upon though not always illegal.
- Example of sportsmanship: helping an injured opponent; Example of gamesmanship: time-wasting tactics.

questions.text:
Read the following case study and answer all the questions.

On 1 May 2025, the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (MoPSE) in Zimbabwe, launched an inaugural Indigenous games Festival at Paruzevha resort in Mashonaland East province. The event marked a decorated Africa day celebration. Learners from both the primary school level and the secondary school level converged at the heritage-decorated venue. School buses and trucks travelled from as far as Masvingo province to showcase their respective talents in indigenous games. Accredited media houses covered the event. Local leadership including chiefs, councillors and other government officials graced the event. Among the games that were showcased are tsoro, nhodo, mbakumba, mafurawu, rock climbing and many others. Learners also had an opportunity to participate in adventure games like horse-riding, canoeing and zip-lining. Stakeholders like the National Association for School Heads (NASH), Lobels bread, AWANA, Eversharp and many others were also present.

[Award 1 mark per valid point; must demonstrate critical analysis for full marks, max 4]

(d) Processes involved in sport event hosting [10 marks — award 1–2 marks per well-explained process, up to 10]:
1. Conceptualisation/Planning – defining the purpose, goals and scope of the event (e.g., MoPSE deciding to launch an indigenous games festival).
2. Budgeting – estimating and allocating financial resources for all aspects of the event (transport, venue, equipment, catering, etc.).
3. Venue selection and preparation – choosing and setting up an appropriate venue (e.g., Paruzevha resort was selected and heritage-decorated).
4. Stakeholder engagement – identifying and involving key stakeholders such as sponsors (Lobels, AWANA, Eversharp), government officials, chiefs and NASH.
5. Participant/Team registration – coordinating participation of schools, ensuring transport arrangements (buses and trucks from Masvingo province).
6. Media accreditation and communication – inviting and managing accredited media houses to cover the event.
7. Safety and risk management – ensuring participant safety especially for adventure activities (horse-riding, canoeing, zip-lining).
8. Event execution/coordination – managing the running of all activities, games and programmes on the day of the event.
9. Monitoring and evaluation – assessing the success of the event against its objectives, gathering feedback from participants and stakeholders.
10. Post-event reporting – documenting outcomes, financial reconciliation and lessons learnt for future events.
[1 mark per valid, explained process; max 10]

questions.text: Discuss the importance of management principles in a sport organisation.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for full marks:
• Definition of management principles (e.g. Fayol's 14 principles: division of work, authority, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest, remuneration, centralisation, scalar chain, order, equity, stability, initiative, esprit de corps).
• Application of each principle to a sport organisation context (e.g. a national federation, sports club, or sports ministry).
• Planning: setting strategic goals, season plans, budgets.
• Organising: structuring departments (marketing, finance, coaching, HR).
• Leading/Directing: motivating staff, coaches, and athletes toward organisational goals.
• Controlling: monitoring performance, financial audits, performance appraisals.
• Coordination: ensuring all departments work in harmony for smooth event delivery and athlete management.
• Accountability and transparency in governance.
• Improved resource utilisation (human, financial, physical).
• Enhanced athlete performance outcomes through structured management.
• Conclusion: Management principles provide a framework for efficiency, effectiveness and sustainability of sport organisations.

questions.text: Assess the historical development of sport from colonial to post-colonial period in Zimbabwe.
questions.topic: Historical Development of Sport in Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for full marks:
• Colonial Period (pre-1980): Introduction of Western sports (cricket, rugby, golf, tennis, horse racing) by European settlers; sport used as a tool of racial segregation — separate facilities, leagues and competitions for Black and White Zimbabweans; indigenous games marginalised; sport administered by racially exclusive bodies.
• Role of sport in nationalist/liberation struggle: sport used to build solidarity and morale among liberation movements.
• Post-Independence (1980 onwards): Racial integration of sporting bodies and facilities; Zimbabwe rejoined international sport (e.g. ICC, FIFA); formation of the Zimbabwe Sports Council and later Zimbabwe Olympic Committee.
• Government policy interventions: National Sports Policy, establishment of the Zimbabwe Sports Commission (2000s), construction of national stadiums and recreation centres.
• Development of mass participation programmes and school sport.
• Emergence of indigenous/traditional sport and games promotion.
• Challenges: funding shortfalls, brain drain of athletes and coaches, political interference in sport administration.
• Recent developments: professionalisation of local leagues (PSL in football), successes on the continental and global stage.
• Critical assessment of progress made and gaps remaining in transformation.

questions.text: Evaluate measures that the Zimbabwean government employed to promote gender equity in sport.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for full marks:
• Definition of gender equity in sport — fair and equal access, resources and opportunities for all genders.
• Legislative framework: Gender and Women Advancement Act; Constitution of Zimbabwe 2013 (Section 56 — equality and non-discrimination; Section 80 — rights of women); National Gender Policy.
• Zimbabwe Sports Commission Act — provisions for inclusive participation.
• Establishment of women's leagues and national teams (e.g. Zimbabwe Women's National Football team — Mighty Warriors; women's cricket, netball).
• Funding and scholarships directed at female athletes.
• Awareness campaigns and advocacy by Zimbabwe Olympic Committee and national federations.
• School sport programmes encouraging girls' participation.
• Appointment of women to sport administrative and leadership roles.
• International obligations: compliance with IOC Gender Equality norms and WADA policies.
• Evaluation: positive strides in women's football and netball; persistent challenges — lower funding for women's sport, media under-representation, cultural/societal barriers.
• Conclusion: Government measures have yielded partial success; sustained political will and funding are needed.

questions.text: Discuss the process of resolving sport related disputes in a sport code of your choice.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for full marks (candidate must cite a specific sport code, e.g. football/ZIFA):
• Definition of sport disputes: eligibility disputes, disciplinary offences, contractual disputes, doping violations, selection disputes.
• Internal dispute resolution mechanisms: club/federation disciplinary committee hearings; appeals to the national federation board (e.g. ZIFA Appeals Committee for football).
• Mediation and arbitration within the federation.
• Role of the Zimbabwe Sports Commission as an oversight body.
• Regional bodies: e.g. COSAFA for Southern African football disputes.
• International bodies: Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in Lausanne — final arbitral body for international sport disputes.
• FIFA Dispute Resolution Chamber (DRC) for contractual disputes between players and clubs.
• Principles of natural justice applied throughout: right to be heard, right to an independent tribunal, right to appeal.
• Doping disputes handled via WADA/NADA processes and the Anti-Doping Tribunal.
• Steps: complaint lodged → investigation → hearing → decision → appeal → external arbitration if needed.
• Importance of clear, codified rules and transparent processes in maintaining integrity of the sport.
• Conclusion: Effective dispute resolution protects athletes' rights and upholds the credibility of the sport.

questions.text: Evaluate the principles of doping in sports.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for full marks:
• Definition of doping: use of prohibited substances or methods to enhance athletic performance.
• The World Anti-Doping Code (WADC) and WADA's role in setting global anti-doping standards.
• The three criteria for a substance/method to be prohibited (presence on WADA Prohibited List): (1) performance-enhancing potential, (2) health risk to the athlete, (3) violation of the spirit of sport.
• Spirit of sport principles: ethics, fair play, honesty, health, excellence, character, education, fun, teamwork, dedication, respect for rules and laws, respect for self and other participants, courage, community and solidarity.
• Categories of prohibited substances: anabolic steroids, peptide hormones (EPO, HGH), beta-2 agonists, diuretics, stimulants, narcotics, cannabinoids, glucocorticoids, beta-blockers.
• Prohibited methods: blood doping, gene doping, manipulation of blood and blood components.
• The strict liability principle: athlete is responsible regardless of intent.
• Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs).
• Anti-doping violations and sanctions: 4-year ban for intentional doping, 2-year ban for first violation.
• Health consequences: cardiovascular damage, hormonal imbalances, psychological effects, liver damage.
• Ethical dimension: undermines fair competition, violates integrity of sport.
• Role of NADA Zimbabwe and ZCAS (Zimbabwe Constitutional Anti-Doping Agency).
• Evaluation: WADA framework has strengthened anti-doping efforts but challenges remain (sophisticated masking agents, out-of-competition testing gaps).
• Conclusion: Strong governance, education and testing are essential to protect clean sport.

questions.text: Examine the importance of patenting sport products in Zimbabwe.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for full marks:
• Definition of a patent: an exclusive right granted for an invention (product or process) that provides a new way of doing something or offers a new technical solution to a problem.
• Legal framework in Zimbabwe: Patents Act [Chapter 26:03]; Zimbabwe Intellectual Property Office (ZIPO).
• Importance of patenting sport products:
  – Protection of innovation: inventors/designers of sporting equipment (e.g. specialised footwear, training devices, timing systems) gain exclusive rights, preventing copying.
  – Revenue generation: patent holders can license products, earning royalties and fostering commercialisation of sport technology.
  – Competitive advantage: sport organisations and companies can differentiate their products in the market.
  – Encouragement of R&D investment: legal protection motivates further innovation in sport science and technology.
  – Prevention of counterfeit products that may be unsafe for athletes.
  – Contribution to national economy: local sport product manufacturing stimulates employment and GDP.
  – Technology transfer: patents can facilitate licensing agreements with international sport companies, bringing modern technology to Zimbabwe.
  – Protection of indigenous sport equipment and traditional games inventions.
• Challenges: cost of patent registration, lengthy process, lack of awareness among sport entrepreneurs, limited enforcement capacity.
• Conclusion: Patenting is vital for fostering a sustainable, innovative sport industry in Zimbabwe.

questions.text: Analyse the differences between sport and recreation citing examples.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for full marks:
• Definitions:
  – Sport: a structured, competitive physical activity governed by rules, with defined winners and losers, often involving formal training and organised events (e.g. football, athletics, swimming).
  – Recreation: leisure activities undertaken voluntarily for enjoyment, relaxation or personal well-being, not necessarily competitive or rule-governed (e.g. hiking, casual swimming, family picnics, gardening).
• Key differences:
  1. Competition: Sport is inherently competitive; recreation is primarily for enjoyment without competitive outcomes.
  2. Structure/Rules: Sport has standardised rules and governing bodies (e.g. FIFA for football); recreation may be loosely structured.
  3. Objectives: Sport aims at performance excellence, winning, and records; recreation aims at relaxation, health and social interaction.
  4. Governance: Sport is regulated by national and international federations; recreation has minimal formal governance.
  5. Professionalism: Sport can be professional with monetary rewards; recreation is non-professional.
  6. Training and preparation: Sport requires systematic training schedules; recreation does not demand rigorous preparation.
  7. Spectatorship and media: Sport attracts large audiences and media coverage; recreation is largely private.
  8. Time commitment: Sport requires regular, structured time; recreation is flexible.
• Examples in Zimbabwe: Sport — Premier Soccer League matches, Zimbabwe cricket internationals; Recreation — fishing at Lake Kariba, community aerobics sessions, nature walks in national parks.
• Overlapping area: Physical activity can serve both sport and recreational purposes (e.g. a casual tennis game among friends).
• Conclusion: While sport and recreation share physical activity as a common element, they differ fundamentally in purpose, structure and outcomes.

questions.text: Examine the benefits of hosting a sport event in a Zimbabwean rural area.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for full marks:
• Economic benefits: Injection of income into local economy through tourism, accommodation, food vendors and transport; employment creation (event staff, security, catering); stimulation of local businesses and markets.
• Infrastructure development: Justification for government/private investment in roads, stadia, water and sanitation facilities, telecommunications — leaving a lasting legacy for the community.
• Social cohesion: Brings together diverse communities, promotes unity, reduces social divisions; strengthens community identity and pride.
• Health and wellness: Encourages physical activity participation among rural residents; promotes healthy lifestyles and reduces non-communicable diseases.
• Youth development and talent identification: Platform for rural athletes to be scouted by coaches and selectors; discourages substance abuse by keeping youth engaged.
• Cultural promotion: Opportunity to showcase indigenous culture, music, dance and traditional sports alongside the main event.
• Educational value: Exposes rural communities to sport management, volunteerism and organisational skills.
• Increased visibility of rural areas: Media coverage during the event raises the profile of the rural community, attracting future investment.
• Government decentralisation goals: Supports national policy of taking services and development to rural communities.
• Challenges (for balanced evaluation): Limited existing infrastructure, logistical difficulties, funding constraints, security, lack of accommodation capacity.
• Conclusion: Hosting sport events in rural Zimbabwe can be a powerful catalyst for holistic community development when properly planned and resourced.

title: Theatre Arts And Film Studies A-Level 2025 Paper 2
subject: Theatre Arts And Film Studies

questions.text:
Answer either 1(a) or 1(b).

(a) Discuss the use of camera techniques in improving the visual quality of historical films in Zimbabwe.

(b) Analyse the role of Applied theatre in promoting enterprise.

subParts.text: Discuss the use of camera techniques in improving the visual quality of historical films in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Analyse the role of Applied theatre in promoting enterprise.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
Answer EITHER (a) OR (b):

(a) Camera Techniques in Historical Films (Zimbabwe):
• Shot types: wide/establishing shots used to capture historical landscapes and settings (e.g. Great Zimbabwe ruins, colonial-era architecture); close-ups to convey emotion and authenticity of period characters.
• Camera angles: low angles to portray powerful historical figures (kings, chiefs); high angles to show vulnerability of colonised peoples or vast historical landscapes.
• Camera movement: tracking/dolly shots to follow historical processions or battles; handheld camera for a documentary/realistic feel; crane shots for epic battle scenes.
• Lighting techniques: natural/soft lighting to recreate authentic period atmosphere; chiaroscuro (contrast of light and dark) to reflect historical drama.
• Colour grading/filter use: sepia or desaturated tones to evoke the past; vibrant colours for pre-colonial cultural scenes.
• Framing and composition: rule of thirds, depth of field to separate subject from historically significant backgrounds.
• Use of slow motion/time-lapse to dramatise key historical moments.
• Continuity editing and matching shots to maintain visual coherence in historical narratives.
Mark scheme: Award up to 25 marks for a well-structured discussion identifying at least 5 techniques with clear explanation of how each improves visual quality in a Zimbabwean historical film context, supported by examples.

(b) Role of Applied Theatre in Promoting Enterprise:
• Definition of Applied Theatre: theatre used in non-traditional settings for social, educational and community purposes.
• Forum Theatre (Boal): engages communities to problem-solve, encouraging entrepreneurial thinking and identifying business opportunities.
• Theatre-in-Education (TIE): used in schools/workplaces to teach enterprise skills such as financial literacy, negotiation, marketing.
• Role-play and simulation: participants rehearse business scenarios (pitching ideas, managing conflict, customer service), building practical enterprise skills.
• Community-based theatre: raises awareness of small business opportunities (SMEs, cooperatives) and challenges affecting local economies.
• Theatre as a platform for showcasing and marketing local products and cultural industries, generating income.
• Building soft skills: communication, confidence, teamwork, creativity — all essential for enterprise.
• Fundraising productions that demonstrate viable arts-based enterprise models.
Mark scheme: Award up to 25 marks for a well-structured analysis identifying at least 5 roles with supporting argument and practical examples.

questions.text: How can a script writer incorporate cultural heritage in a script.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for awarding marks:
• Use of indigenous languages, proverbs, idioms and oral literature (e.g. Shona/Ndebele sayings) within dialogue to reflect authentic cultural heritage.
• Incorporation of traditional ceremonies, rituals and rites of passage (e.g. lobola, bira, initiation ceremonies) as plot devices or thematic elements.
• Characters drawn from cultural archetypes — elders, spirit mediums, chiefs — representing traditional values and authority structures.
• Setting: depicting historical or rural Zimbabwean environments that reflect pre-colonial or traditional ways of life.
• Storylines based on oral tradition: folk tales, myths, legends and historical narratives passed down through generations.
• Use of traditional music, dance and performance styles written into stage/screen directions.
• Themes reflecting cultural values: Ubuntu/hunhu (communalism), respect for elders, land and ancestral connection.
• Conflict arising from tension between modernity and tradition, reflecting the lived cultural reality of Zimbabwean communities.
• Use of traditional artefacts, costumes and food as props/settings described in stage directions.
• Research and consultation with cultural custodians (chiefs, n'angas, elders) to ensure authenticity.
Mark scheme: Award up to 25 marks for a well-structured response covering at least 5 methods with explanation and relevant examples from Zimbabwean cultural heritage.

questions.text: How can cultural values be highlighted through technical design in theatre productions.
questions.topic: Technical Design / Cultural Values in Theatre
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for awarding marks:
• Set design: use of traditional hut structures (rondavels), kraals, village layouts and symbolic objects (totems, ancestral artefacts) to visually communicate cultural identity and values.
• Costume design: use of traditional attire (animal skins, beadwork, nguo/chiremba, headgear) to distinguish cultural roles, status and identity; symbolism in colour choices.
• Lighting design: use of warm, firelight-inspired tones to evoke traditional evening gatherings (dare/indaba); use of colour symbolism (red for danger/spirituality, white for purity/ancestors).
• Sound design: incorporation of traditional instruments (mbira, ngoma drums, hosho) and oral soundscapes to establish cultural atmosphere and emotional tone.
• Props: culturally significant objects (clay pots, traditional weapons, baskets) used to reinforce values of craftsmanship, communal living and heritage.
• Make-up and body decoration: traditional face paint and body art used to signify cultural roles (warriors, spirit mediums, brides).
• Space and staging: use of circular staging (in-the-round) to mirror traditional community gathering spaces (dare), reinforcing communal values.
• Projection/multimedia: images of traditional art (cave paintings, Zimbabwe bird) projected to contextualise cultural setting.
Mark scheme: Award up to 25 marks for a well-structured response identifying at least 5 technical design elements with clear explanation of how each highlights specific cultural values, supported by examples.

questions.text: Justify the choice of graphic design elements in creating animation characteristics of traditional Zimbabwean folk tales.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for awarding marks:
• Colour palette: justification for using earthy tones (ochre, brown, green) to reflect the natural African environment of folk tales; bold, bright colours for magical or supernatural elements.
• Character design: animal characters (hare/tsuro, lion/shumba, tortoise/kamba) styled with recognisable Zimbabwean cultural features, traditional patterns and body markings to reflect cultural authenticity.
• Typography: use of indigenous scripts or stylised fonts inspired by traditional Zimbabwean art (e.g. Zimbabwe ruins motifs) to reinforce cultural identity in titles and captions.
• Background/environment design: savannah landscapes, village settings, rivers and mountains characteristic of Zimbabwean geography to ground stories in authentic settings.
• Pattern and texture: incorporation of traditional Zimbabwean geometric patterns (from pottery, basketry, stone carving) as textures for clothing, environments and borders.
• Line and shape: use of bold, flowing lines inspired by Zimbabwean cave art and traditional sculpture to define characters and scenes.
• Movement/animation style: fluid, rhythmic movement inspired by traditional dance forms (mbira music rhythm, drumming beats) to animate characters.
• Symbolism: inclusion of totems, ancestral symbols and culturally significant motifs to maintain the moral and spiritual dimension of folk tales.
• Layout and composition: visual storytelling techniques consistent with the oral tradition (sequential, episodic panel design).
Mark scheme: Award up to 25 marks for a well-argued justification covering at least 5 graphic design elements with clear links to characteristics of traditional Zimbabwean folk tales.

questions.text: Analyse the contribution of theatre in employment creation in Zimbabwe.
questions.topic: Theatre and Employment / Theatre Industry in Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for awarding marks:
• Direct employment: actors, directors, playwrights, stage managers, lighting and sound technicians, costume designers, set builders, make-up artists, choreographers.
• Indirect employment: venue/theatre management and administration staff, ticket sales/box office, marketing and public relations, catering and hospitality at events.
• Theatre education: employment of teachers, trainers and facilitators in schools, colleges, drama schools and community arts centres.
• Theatre festivals: National Arts Merit Awards (NAMA), Harare International Festival of the Arts (HIFA) — create seasonal employment for performers, crew, security, vendors.
• Film and television industry linked employment: screen actors, film crew, post-production editors, cinematographers stimulated by theatre training.
• Community and Applied Theatre: NGOs and development organisations employ theatre practitioners for health campaigns (HIV/AIDS awareness, etc.), creating a development theatre sector.
• Entrepreneurship: theatre provides opportunities for self-employment in areas such as event management, costume hire, props rental, set construction.
• Cultural tourism: theatre and traditional performance attract tourists, generating employment in hospitality and related sectors.
• Music and dance ensembles linked to theatre create additional employment.
• Challenges: limited government funding, brain drain, informal sector dominance — awareness of challenges earns credit when balanced with contributions.
Mark scheme: Award up to 25 marks for a well-structured analysis identifying at least 5 distinct areas of employment contribution with supporting argument and Zimbabwean examples.

questions.text: Describe the key stages involved in the preparation of a Theatre Arts festival.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Key points for awarding marks:
• Conceptualisation and planning: defining the festival's theme, objectives, target audience and scale; forming an organising committee with clearly defined roles.
• Budgeting and fundraising: preparing a detailed budget covering venue hire, marketing, travel, accommodation, technical equipment, adjudicators' fees; sourcing sponsorship, grants (e.g. NACZ, NAC) and ticket revenue.
• Call for entries / adjudication criteria: advertising the festival, setting entry deadlines, establishing categories (drama, dance, music, poetry), setting adjudication criteria and appointing qualified adjudicators.
• Venue selection and preparation: choosing an appropriate venue (theatre, school hall, outdoor space); arranging technical setup — stage, lighting, sound, seating.
• Programming and scheduling: drawing up the festival programme/schedule; allocating rehearsal/performance slots to participating groups; managing timing.
• Marketing and publicity: designing promotional materials (posters, flyers, social media campaigns); engaging media (radio, TV, newspapers); community outreach.
• Rehearsals and technical run-throughs: coordinating technical rehearsals with participating groups; sound checks, lighting checks, stage management briefings.
• Health, safety and logistics: risk assessment; first aid provision; transport and accommodation arrangements for travelling participants.
• Festival execution: front-of-house management (ushers, ticketing), stage management, MC/compère, adjudication sessions, awards ceremony.
• Post-festival evaluation: debrief with organising committee; collecting feedback from participants and audience; financial reconciliation; report writing for sponsors/funders.
Mark scheme: Award up to 25 marks for a well-structured response clearly describing at least 5 key stages in logical sequence, with sufficient detail for each stage.

Prie Ltd manufactures local sewing machines. The following summarised profit statement for the year ended 31 October 2025 is provided as follows.
$ $

         94 500

Additional information
1. The current selling price per unit is $100.
2. Included in the total overheads figure are fixed production costs of $11 000.
3. For the year ending 31 October 2026, the following changes are to be effected;
   - sales agents are to be employed at a total annual sales commission of $15 000. This is expected to increase sales revenue by 40%,
   - fixed overheads are to increase by 25%.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Forecast Profit Statement (Marginal Costing) – Year ending 31 October 2026:

Step 1 – 2025 figures:
Units sold = $170 000 ÷ $100 = 1 700 units.
Direct materials per unit = $51 000 ÷ 1 700 = $30.
Direct labour per unit = $25 500 ÷ 1 700 = $15.
Variable overheads = Total overheads $18 000 – Fixed overheads $11 000 = $7 000. Variable OH per unit = $7 000 ÷ 1 700 = $4.118 ≈ $4.12.
Total variable cost per unit = $30 + $15 + $4.12 = $49.12.

Step 2 – 2026 forecasts:
Sales revenue increase 40%: $170 000 × 1.4 = $238 000.
Units sold = $238 000 ÷ $100 = 2 380 units.
Fixed overheads increase 25%: $11 000 × 1.25 = $13 750.
Sales commission (new fixed cost): $15 000.
Total fixed costs 2026 = $13 750 + $15 000 = $28 750.
Variable costs per unit remain: $30 + $15 + $4.12 = $49.12.
Total variable costs = 2 380 × $49.12 = $116 906.

Forecast Profit Statement (Marginal Costing) – Year ending 31 October 2026:
Sales (2 380 × $100)                  $238 000
Less Variable costs:
  Direct materials (2 380 × $30)       $71 400
  Direct labour (2 380 × $15)          $35 700
  Variable overheads (2 380 × $4.12)   $9 806
Total variable costs                  ($116 906)
Contribution                           $121 094
Less Fixed costs:
  Fixed production overheads           $13 750
  Sales commission                     $15 000
Total fixed costs                      ($28 750)
Net profit                             $92 344

(b)(i) Break-Even Point in Units:
Contribution per unit (CPU) = Selling price – Variable cost per unit = $100 – $49.12 = $50.88.

2025 (previous):
Fixed costs = $11 000.
BEP = $11 000 ÷ $50.88 = 216.2 ≈ 216 units (or 217 units).

2026 (forecast):
Fixed costs = $28 750.
BEP = $28 750 ÷ $50.88 = 564.9 ≈ 565 units.

(b)(ii) Margin of Safety in Units:
2025 (previous):
Actual sales 1 700 units – BEP 216 units = 1 484 units.

2026 (forecast):
Forecast sales 2 380 units – BEP 565 units = 1 815 units.

(c) Three differences between marginal costing and absorption costing:
1. Treatment of fixed overheads: Under marginal costing, fixed production overheads are treated as period costs and charged in full to the income statement in the period they are incurred. Under absorption costing, fixed overheads are absorbed into the cost of production and included in closing inventory valuations.
2. Inventory valuation: Marginal costing values closing inventory at variable (marginal) cost only. Absorption costing values closing inventory at full production cost (including a share of fixed overheads), resulting in higher inventory values.
3. Profit reported: When inventory levels change (increase or decrease), the two methods report different profits. Absorption costing reports higher profit than marginal costing when inventory levels rise (because some fixed costs are deferred in inventory), and lower profit when inventory levels fall. Marginal costing profit is unaffected by changes in inventory levels in relation to fixed cost treatment.

(d) One limitation of CVP/break-even analysis:
It assumes that all costs can be clearly classified as either fixed or variable, and that selling price and variable costs per unit remain constant throughout the relevant range, which may not hold true in practice.

questions.text: Evaluate the contribution of archaeology and linguistics in the reconstruction of Zimbabwe's colonial past.
questions.topic: Historical Sources and Reconstruction of Zimbabwe's Past
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Award marks for a balanced evaluation of both archaeology and linguistics as sources for reconstructing Zimbabwe's pre-colonial past.

Archaeology:
- Archaeological excavations (e.g., Great Zimbabwe, Khami ruins) provide material evidence of settlement patterns, trade, and social organisation.
- Artefacts such as pottery, tools, and trade goods (Chinese ceramics, glass beads) reveal economic and cultural connections.
- Radiocarbon dating and stratigraphy help establish chronologies.
- Limitation: archaeology is silent on names, languages, and specific events; subject to bias in interpretation.

Linguistics:
- Comparative Bantu linguistics helps trace migration routes and population movements (e.g., spread of Shona dialects).
- Place names (toponymy) and clan names preserve historical memory.
- Oral traditions encoded in language reveal social structures and beliefs.
- Limitation: language change over time makes reconstruction speculative; not always reliable for precise dating.

Conclusion: Both sources are complementary and indispensable; neither alone gives a complete picture. Together they help reconstruct political, social, and economic history that written records omit for the pre-colonial period. Award up to 5 marks for evaluation/conclusion.

questions.text: Although the San were regarded as backward, they lived far ahead of their times. Discuss.
questions.topic: The San People — Society, Culture and Way of Life
questions.aiModelAnswer:
The question requires candidates to challenge the negative stereotype of the San and demonstrate their advanced qualities relative to modern values.

Arguments supporting 'ahead of their times':
- Ecological sustainability: hunter-gatherer lifestyle had a minimal carbon footprint and preserved biodiversity — aligns with modern environmentalism.
- Gender equality: San women had significant say in band decisions and resource allocation.
- Egalitarianism: no rigid class/hierarchy; resources shared communally — resonates with modern social justice ideals.
- Medical knowledge: extensive knowledge of medicinal plants used to treat illness.
- Rock art: sophisticated artistic expression conveying spiritual beliefs, recording history.
- Conflict resolution: bands resolved disputes through discussion and movement rather than warfare.
- Democratic decision-making: consensus-based governance anticipates modern democratic ideals.

Counter-arguments (why they were regarded as 'backward'):
- No permanent settlements, no written language, no metal use.
- Dismissed by settler/colonial observers as primitive.

Conclusion: The San's sustainable, egalitarian, and knowledge-rich lifestyle reflects values that contemporary society is only now catching up with, justifying the assertion. Award up to 5 marks for quality of discussion/conclusion.

questions.text: To what extent did economic factors contribute to the rise of Mapungubwe state?
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must weigh economic factors against other factors in the rise of Mapungubwe (c. 900–1300 CE).

Economic factors (main focus):
- Control of gold and ivory trade routes between the interior and the East African coast (Swahili traders).
- Agricultural surplus from the fertile Limpopo valley enabled population growth and social stratification.
- Cattle wealth as a symbol of status and medium of exchange.
- Trade in glass beads and other imported goods indicated participation in the Indian Ocean trade network.
- Economic surplus allowed ruling class to consolidate power and sponsor craft specialisation.

Other factors:
- Political/military: strong centralised leadership and control over subordinate chiefdoms.
- Environmental/geographical: strategic location at the confluence of the Limpopo and Shashe rivers provided water, fertile land, and natural defence.
- Religious/ideological: divine kingship ideology legitimised the ruler's authority.
- Social: class differentiation and hierarchy reinforced state structures.

Conclusion: Economic factors, especially trade and agricultural surplus, were the primary drivers, but the rise of Mapungubwe was also shaped by geography, political organisation, and ideology. A fully argued response should show that economic factors were necessary but not sufficient alone. Award up to 5 marks for extent/conclusion.

questions.text: Succession disputes were a persistent problem in the Rozvi State. Propose, in essay form, measures that could have been used by the Rozvi people to ensure a smooth takeover of power in the State.
questions.topic: Rozvi State — Governance and Succession (Problem Solving)
questions.aiModelAnswer:
This is a problem-solving question. Candidates must propose practical, historically grounded measures.

Key proposals (award marks for any well-argued relevant point):
1. Codification of succession rules: Establish a clear, widely known and accepted law (e.g., primogeniture or matrilineal descent) to remove ambiguity.
2. Establishment of a regency council: A council of elders/chiefs to govern during interregnum and oversee transition.
3. Early designation of heir: The Mambo (king) should publicly name and groom a successor during his lifetime.
4. Role of the spirit mediums (mhondoro): Formalise the role of spirit mediums as neutral arbiters to validate the chosen successor.
5. Decentralisation of power: Reduce the stakes of central succession by giving provincial chiefs more autonomy, making the throne less of a 'winner-takes-all' prize.
6. Political marriages and alliances: Forge alliances between rival clans through marriage to reduce likelihood of armed disputes.
7. Education/training of heirs: Structured preparation of the designated heir in governance and military matters.
8. Constitutional checks: An advisory council with power to ratify or reject a claimant.

Conclusion: A combination of legal clarity, institutional oversight, and cultural legitimacy would have minimised succession conflicts. Award up to 5 marks for quality of proposals and conclusion.

questions.text: The Portuguese destabilized the Mutapa State. In essay form, suggest measures that could have been employed by Mutapa leaders to control Portuguese activities.
questions.topic: Mutapa State and Portuguese Interference (Problem Solving)
questions.aiModelAnswer:
This is a problem-solving question. Candidates must suggest realistic measures Mutapa leaders could have taken.

Key suggestions:
1. Military modernisation: Acquire firearms and military technology to counter Portuguese military superiority; form alliances with neighbouring states against the Portuguese.
2. Expulsion/restriction of Portuguese traders: Issue decrees limiting Portuguese access to the interior and the gold trade (as Mutapa Gatsi Rusere partially did).
3. Diplomatic alliances: Seek alliances with other African or Arab powers (e.g., Swahili merchants or the Rozvi) to counterbalance Portuguese influence.
4. Control of the prazo system: Prevent Portuguese settlers from acquiring land grants (prazos) by strengthening land tenure laws.
5. Limit missionary access: Restrict or expel Jesuit missionaries who were seen as agents of political destabilisation.
6. Strengthen central authority: Reduce internal rivalries that the Portuguese exploited by intervening in succession disputes.
7. Develop alternative trade routes: Reduce economic dependence on Portuguese-controlled trade by establishing direct links with Indian Ocean merchants.
8. Intelligence networks: Develop informants to monitor and anticipate Portuguese movements and plans.

Conclusion: A multi-pronged approach combining military, diplomatic, and economic strategies would have been most effective. Credit well-argued, realistic proposals.

questions.text: How far did Africans benefit from missionary activities in Zimbabwe between 1850 and 1900?
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must assess the extent of African benefits and weigh them against drawbacks.

Benefits:
- Education: Missionaries established schools (e.g., Hope Fountain, Inyati, Chishawasha) providing literacy and numeracy that later enabled Africans to engage with the colonial system.
- Healthcare: Mission hospitals and clinics reduced mortality from diseases like smallpox.
- Translation: Missionaries translated the Bible into African languages, preserving and formalising local languages.
- Advocacy: Some missionaries (e.g., John Mackenzie) spoke out against the worst colonial abuses.
- New skills: Carpentry, printing, and other vocational skills were taught at missions.
- Protection: Mission stations occasionally offered refuge during times of conflict.

Limitations / negative aspects:
- Cultural destruction: Missionaries condemned African religion, customs (lobola, polygamy, initiation), and traditional governance.
- Land alienation: Missions acquired large tracts of land, displacing communities.
- Ideological tool of colonialism: Missionaries prepared Africans to accept colonial rule ('softening' resistance).
- Education was limited and designed to produce subordinate labour, not independent thinkers.
- Undermined African political authority and social cohesion.

Conclusion: Africans benefited in education, health, and skills, but benefits were limited and often served colonial interests more than African ones. The extent of benefit was therefore partial. Award up to 5 marks for evaluative conclusion.

questions.text: Cecil John Rhodes was instrumental in the colonization of Zimbabwe. How valid is this assertion?
questions.topic: Colonisation of Zimbabwe — Role of Cecil John Rhodes
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must assess the validity of Rhodes's role while acknowledging other factors.

Arguments supporting the assertion:
- Rhodes founded the British South Africa Company (BSAC) in 1889, which obtained the Rudd Concession (1888) from Lobengula through deception.
- He personally funded and organised the Pioneer Column (1890) that colonised Mashonaland.
- He used political connections (British government, Cape Colony) to obtain the Royal Charter legitimising BSAC rule.
- He had a clear expansionist 'Cape to Cairo' vision that drove colonisation northward.
- He was Prime Minister of the Cape Colony and used that position to advance colonisation.

Limitations of the assertion (other factors):
- British imperial policy and demand for new markets/resources drove colonisation beyond any individual.
- The role of the British government and Colonial Office was crucial.
- Leander Starr Jameson and other BSAC officials executed the practical colonisation.
- The discovery of gold in the Witwatersrand redirected attention; Zimbabwe was partly colonised on speculation of gold.
- European scramble for Africa created the broader context.
- Lobengula's advisers' misunderstanding of the Rudd Concession also played a role.

Conclusion: Rhodes was a critical individual agent, but colonisation was also driven by broader imperial forces. The assertion is largely valid but overstates individual agency. Award marks for balanced analysis.

questions.text: Assess the impact of the Anglo-Ndebele war of 1893 to 1894 on Africans.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates should assess both the immediate and long-term impacts, and consider different African groups (Ndebele, Shona, others).

Negative impacts:
- Destruction of the Ndebele state: The kingdom of Lobengula was dismantled; Lobengula fled and died in 1894.
- Land dispossession: Ndebele land was seized by BSAC settlers; 'loot committees' distributed cattle and land to white settlers.
- Cattle confiscation: The Ndebele's main source of wealth (cattle) was taken, destroying their economic base.
- Loss of political independence: Ndebele lost their centralised political structures and became subjects of colonial rule.
- Population displacement: Many Ndebele were displaced into Native Reserves.
- Loss of life: Significant Ndebele casualties in battle due to Maxim gun superiority.
- Psychological trauma: Defeat shattered Ndebele pride and sense of invincibility.

Relative benefits (limited):
- Some Shona groups who had suffered Ndebele raids experienced temporary relief from raids.
- A few collaborators received short-term rewards.

Long-term:
- The defeat was a catalyst for the First Chimurenga/Umvukela uprising (1896–97) as Africans sought to reverse colonial gains.

Conclusion: The war was overwhelmingly negative for Africans, particularly the Ndebele, leading to political, economic, and social subjugation. Award up to 5 marks for evaluative conclusion.

questions.text: Assess the effectiveness of various measures taken by Africans to resist exploitation in settler mines and farms since 1900.
questions.topic: African Resistance to Settler Exploitation — Mines and Farms
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must identify the measures and assess how effective each was.

Measures and their effectiveness:
1. Desertion/absenteeism: Workers absconded from mines and farms — partially effective as it disrupted labour supply but led to harsher pass laws.
2. Strikes: E.g., the 1945 General Strike and 1948 Railway Workers' Strike — showed collective power but were suppressed by colonial authorities.
3. Go-slows and sabotage: Reducing work pace or damaging equipment — difficult to prove, offered some leverage.
4. Formation of trade unions: ICU (Industrial and Commercial Workers' Union) in the 1920s, RICU — gave workers an organised voice but were restricted by legislation (e.g., Industrial Conciliation Act excluded Africans).
5. Political organisations: ANC (Rhodesian), NDP, ZAPU, ZANU — escalated resistance to the political level, eventually successful via liberation war.
6. Arson and stock theft: Direct economic sabotage of settler farms.
7. Migration: Moving to urban areas or neighbouring territories to escape exploitative conditions.

Limitations on effectiveness:
- Repressive colonial legislation (Masters and Servants Act, pass laws, LOMA).
- Lack of unity and organisation in early years.
- Military and police suppression of any significant resistance.

Conclusion: Measures were largely ineffective in the short term due to colonial repression, but cumulatively they built a culture of resistance that contributed to eventual independence. Award marks for assessment of effectiveness.

questions.text: The African reserves were unfit for human settlement. Recommend, in essay form, measures that could have been taken by settlers to ensure fair treatment of Africans.
questions.topic: African Reserves and Land Apportionment (Problem Solving)
questions.aiModelAnswer:
This is a problem-solving question. Candidates must recommend realistic measures.

Key recommendations:
1. Equitable land distribution: Allocate land based on population size and agricultural potential rather than race; repeal the Land Apportionment Act (1930) and Land Tenure Act (1969).
2. Infrastructure investment: Build roads, irrigation systems, dip tanks, and storage facilities in reserve areas to make them agriculturally viable.
3. Agricultural extension services: Provide African farmers with technical support, improved seeds, fertilisers, and access to markets.
4. Fair wages and labour conditions: Improve wages on settler farms/mines so that Africans could afford to develop their own land.
5. Land quality assessment: Conduct impartial surveys and allocate land of comparable fertility to all racial groups.
6. Access to credit: Provide African farmers with loans to purchase inputs and improve productivity (comparable to facilities available to white farmers).
7. Education and training: Establish agricultural colleges and vocational training for Africans.
8. Legal protections: Enact legislation protecting African land rights and preventing further dispossession.
9. Removal of racial restrictions: Abolish the colour bar in agriculture, allowing Africans to grow and sell cash crops freely.

Conclusion: A combination of legal reform, investment, and equitable resource allocation was necessary for fair treatment. Credit creative, well-argued proposals.

questions.text: Compare the extent to which Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland benefitted from the Federation (1953 to 1963).
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must compare benefits for Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland with balanced analysis.

Southern Rhodesia's benefits:
- Gained access to Northern Rhodesia's copper revenues which funded infrastructure (Kariba Dam, roads, railways).
- Southern Rhodesia dominated the Federal government and Parliament, shaping policy in its favour.
- Expanded manufacturing base as the Federation's industrial hub.
- Access to labour from Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia for mines and farms.
- Greater international recognition and political leverage.

Nyasaland's (limited) benefits:
- Some infrastructure development (roads, schools, hospitals) funded from Federal revenues.
- Small educated elite gained access to Federal civil service jobs.
- Limited improvement in healthcare and education infrastructure.

Nyasaland's disadvantages (indicating limited benefit):
- Economically the poorest territory; revenues flowed to Southern Rhodesia rather than back to Nyasaland.
- Nyasaland was regarded primarily as a labour reserve.
- African political rights were suppressed under Federation.
- Dr Hastings Banda led strong nationalist opposition (1959 State of Emergency declared).
- Nyasaland received the least Federal investment proportionally.

Comparison conclusion: Southern Rhodesia benefitted enormously and disproportionately; Nyasaland gained relatively little and was largely exploited as a labour pool. The Federation was fundamentally unequal in its distribution of benefits. Award up to 5 marks for quality of comparison and conclusion.

questions.text: Peasants played the most significant role in the liberation struggle in Zimbabwe. How far true is this assertion?
questions.topic: Zimbabwe Liberation Struggle — Role of Peasants
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must assess the peasants' role and weigh it against other contributors.

Arguments supporting the assertion:
- Peasants provided food, shelter, and intelligence to freedom fighters (guerrillas/vacomrades).
- Mao Zedong's theory of protracted war (which ZANLA adopted) placed peasants at the centre — 'fish in the sea'.
- Rural masses provided recruits for both ZANLA and ZIPRA.
- Spirit mediums (mhondoro) mobilised rural communities and legitimised the struggle.
- Peasants' land grievances (removal to reserves, dispossession) were the ideological engine of the struggle.
- They endured brutal collective punishments (protected villages/keeps) yet continued to support guerrillas.

Limitations — other significant roles:
- Political leaders (Mugabe, Nkomo, Tongogara): Strategic and diplomatic leadership.
- ZANLA and ZIPRA guerrillas: Conducted actual military operations.
- Frontline States (Mozambique, Zambia, Tanzania, Botswana): Provided bases, logistics, and diplomatic support.
- OAU and international solidarity: Financial and material support.
- Urban workers and students: Supported the struggle through strikes, demonstrations, and recruitment.
- Church leaders and intellectuals: Moral and ideological support.

Conclusion: Peasants were indispensable and arguably the backbone of the rural guerrilla war, but the struggle required the combined efforts of military commanders, political leaders, diaspora, and frontline states. The assertion is largely true but needs qualification. Award marks for balanced argument.

questions.text: Economic Structural Adjustment Programme (ESAP) caused unemployment in Zimbabwe between 1990 and 2000. Propose, in essay form, measures the Zimbabwe Government could have taken to correct the negative effects of Economic Structural Adjustment Programme (ESAP).
questions.topic: ESAP and its Economic Effects on Zimbabwe (Problem Solving)
questions.aiModelAnswer:
This is a problem-solving question. Candidates must propose well-reasoned corrective measures.

Key proposals:
1. Social safety nets: Establish robust unemployment benefits, food subsidies, and welfare programmes (the Social Dimensions of Adjustment — SDA fund was inadequate; a stronger version was needed).
2. Retraining and skills development: Fund vocational training centres to retrain retrenched workers for new industries.
3. Support for SMEs: Provide micro-credit, tax incentives, and business development support to encourage small and medium enterprise growth as an employment buffer.
4. Phased liberalisation: Slow down the pace of privatisation and tariff removal to allow local industries time to adjust and remain competitive.
5. Investment in public works: Launch government-funded infrastructure projects (roads, schools, hospitals) as labour-intensive employment schemes.
6. Agricultural support: Invest in smallholder agriculture to absorb retrenched urban workers returning to rural areas.
7. Negotiate with IFIs: Renegotiate ESAP conditionalities with the IMF/World Bank to include more pro-poor protections.
8. Industrial policy: Retain selective protection for strategic industries rather than blanket liberalisation.
9. Strengthening labour laws: Amend labour legislation to limit mass retrenchments and require adequate severance packages.

Conclusion: A human-centred adjustment programme balancing economic reform with social protection was essential. Credit creative, well-argued proposals.

questions.text: How successful was Comrade Robert Mugabe in addressing land imbalances in post-independence Zimbabwe?
questions.topic: Land Reform in Post-Independence Zimbabwe — Mugabe's Role
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must assess Mugabe's land reform efforts across different phases.

Successes:
- Willing-seller willing-buyer model (1980–1990): Resettled approximately 70,000 families on 3.5 million hectares; addressed some of the most extreme land imbalances.
- Land Acquisition Act (1992): Gave government power to compulsorily acquire land, signalling stronger intent.
- Fast Track Land Reform Programme (FTLRP, 2000–2002): Redistributed over 11 million hectares to approximately 300,000 black Zimbabwean families — the largest redistribution in post-colonial Africa.
- Addressed the historical injustice of colonial land dispossession symbolically and materially.
- Empowered many landless Africans with access to productive land.

Failures/Limitations:
- Early phase (1980s): Too slow and dependent on British funding that was not consistently provided; Lancaster House restrictions limited redistribution.
- FTLRP was chaotic, violent, and poorly planned — white farm invasions led to loss of life and destruction of infrastructure.
- Commercial agriculture collapsed: Zimbabwe went from a food exporter to requiring food aid.
- Many beneficiaries lacked capital, equipment, and skills to productively use allocated land.
- Economic collapse (hyperinflation, unemployment) followed, partly due to agricultural disruption.
- Cronyism: Land was distributed to political cronies (chefs) rather than genuinely landless peasants.
- International isolation and sanctions followed.

Conclusion: Mugabe had partial success in redistributing land (especially quantitatively) but the manner of redistribution caused severe economic and social harm. Success was symbolic but practically limited. Award marks for balanced assessment.

questions.text: "The Zimbabwe Land Reform Programme of 2000 had many unintended consequences." Discuss.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must identify and discuss both intended and unintended consequences.

Intended consequences (for context):
- Redistribution of land from white commercial farmers to black Zimbabweans.
- Correction of colonial land imbalances.
- Empowerment of landless peasants.

Unintended consequences (main focus):
Economic:
- Collapse of commercial agriculture: Zimbabwe transformed from 'breadbasket of Africa' to food insecure nation requiring international food aid.
- Hyperinflation: Agricultural collapse contributed to economic meltdown and world-record hyperinflation (2007–2009).
- Unemployment surge: Farm workers (mostly black Zimbabweans) lost jobs — estimated 350,000+ farm workers displaced.
- Capital flight: White farmers took capital, expertise, and equipment, gutting agricultural productivity.
- Foreign currency shortages: Loss of tobacco and other export earnings devastated foreign reserves.

Social:
- Farm worker displacement: Black farm labourers became the unintended victims — losing homes, schools, clinics on farms.
- Violence and human rights abuses: Farm invasions led to deaths, assaults, and displacement of white farmers and their workers.
- Brain drain: Skilled Zimbabweans emigrated en masse (diaspora grew to millions).

Political:
- International isolation: Western sanctions (ZIDERA, EU sanctions) followed, worsening the economic crisis.
- Cronyism: Land going to political elite rather than poor peasants undermined stated objectives.

Conclusion: While intended to correct historical injustice, the Land Reform Programme triggered a cascade of unintended consequences that severely damaged Zimbabwe's economy and society. Award marks for depth and range of discussion.

questions.text: How far does the concept of Devolution as enshrined in Chapter 14 of the Constitution of Zimbabwe, seek to reduce conflict between central and local government?
questions.topic: Devolution and Constitutional Governance in Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates must analyse the provisions of Chapter 14 and assess the extent to which devolution reduces central-local government conflict.

How devolution seeks to reduce conflict:
- Chapter 14 (Sections 264–278) establishes Provincial and Metropolitan Councils and empowers local authorities with defined functions.
- Decentralisation of power: Local councils are given authority over local governance, development planning, and resource allocation — reducing the need to refer everything to central government.
- Revenue sharing: The Constitution provides for transfer of resources from central to local government, reducing financial dependency conflicts.
- Democratic accountability: Elected local representatives give communities a direct voice, reducing grievances about being ignored by central government.
- Recognition of local identity: Provincial autonomy respects regional differences and reduces the feeling of central imposition.
- Section 264 explicitly states that devolution must 'ensure democratic governance at all levels of government.'

Limitations — how far it reduces conflict:
- Implementation gap: The Constitution's devolution provisions have not been fully implemented; central government has retained control over key resources and appointments.
- Fiscal devolution is incomplete: Local authorities remain financially dependent on central government transfers, which are often withheld.
- Political interference: Central government (ruling party) continues to interfere in local government affairs, especially in opposition-controlled urban councils.
- Ambiguity: Overlapping mandates between central ministries and local authorities create rather than reduce conflict.
- Urban-rural divide: Urban councils (often opposition-controlled) face greater conflict with central government than rural councils.

Conclusion: Chapter 14 provides a strong constitutional framework for reducing central-local conflict, but weak implementation means conflict persists. The concept is sound but the practice falls short. Award marks for use of constitutional knowledge and balanced evaluation.

questions.text:
1. (a) Explain the significance of the following water properties:
(i) specific heat capacity,
(ii) universal solvent.
(b) State any three importance of osmosis in plant growth.
(c) Describe any three effects of water stress in photosynthesis.

subParts.text: Explain the significance of the following water property: specific heat capacity.
subParts.label: (a)(i)

subParts.text: Explain the significance of the following water property: universal solvent.
subParts.label: (a)(ii)

subParts.text: State any three importance of osmosis in plant growth.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Describe any three effects of water stress in photosynthesis.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Specific heat capacity – Water has a high specific heat capacity, meaning it absorbs/releases large amounts of heat energy with little change in temperature. This stabilises plant cell temperatures and moderates the microclimate around plants, preventing heat damage to cells and enzymes. [1 mark each for stating what it means and why it matters, max 2]

(a)(ii) Universal solvent – Water dissolves a wide range of ionic and polar substances (minerals, gases, sugars). This allows nutrients to be absorbed from the soil and transported in the xylem/phloem, and for biochemical reactions to take place in an aqueous medium. [1 mark each for explanation and significance, max 2]

(b) Any THREE of:
• Osmosis maintains cell turgor pressure, giving structural support to non-woody plant parts.
• It drives the uptake of water from the soil into root hair cells (from high to low water potential).
• It regulates stomatal opening and closing via guard cell turgor.
• It facilitates the movement of water up the plant through osmotic gradients.
[1 mark per valid point, max 3]

(c) Any THREE of:
• Stomata close to reduce water loss, limiting CO₂ entry and reducing the rate of photosynthesis.
• Reduced leaf water content causes wilting, decreasing the leaf area available to capture light.
• Water is a raw material (reactant) in the light-dependent reactions (photolysis); its shortage reduces production of ATP and NADPH.
• Water stress disrupts chloroplast structure and degrades chlorophyll, lowering light absorption.
• Reduced turgor leads to reduced cell expansion and overall decreased metabolic activity.
[1 mark per valid point, max 3]

(a)(ii) Floriculture – the study of flower/ornamental plant production; important for the production of cut flowers, potted plants and seeds for aesthetic, commercial and export purposes, contributing to national income. [1 mark]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any FOUR of the following symptoms (1 mark each):
• Root galls/knots (swollen, knotted roots) due to root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.).
• Stunted/poor plant growth and yellowing (chlorosis) of leaves.
• Wilting of plants even when soil moisture is adequate.
• Lesions/discolouration on roots (root rot/necrosis).
• Reduction in root mass/fibrous roots, leading to poor nutrient and water uptake.
• Above-ground symptoms resembling nutrient deficiency.

(b) Suggested model answers for table cells:
(i) Name of pest with mandibles: Locusts / Grasshoppers / Caterpillars (chewing insects)
(ii) Description: Insects with chewing mouthparts (mandibles) used to bite and chew plant tissue.
(iii) Effect: Defoliation / removal of leaf tissue, leading to reduced photosynthesis and crop yield.
(iv) Effect of pest with mandibles on plant: Chewing and skeletonising of leaves, defoliation, stem damage.
(v) Description of American bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera): Larva (caterpillar) of a moth; greenish-yellow to brown with stripes; bores into fruits, flowers and pods.
(vi) Effect of American bollworm: Bores into fruits/bolls/pods causing internal feeding damage; secondary rots; severe crop losses; destruction of reproductive parts.
[1 mark per correct cell, max 6]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Evaluation of terracotta for flower pots (award marks for advantages AND disadvantages/limitations; up to 5 marks):
Advantages:
• Terracotta is porous, allowing air and moisture exchange, promoting healthy root development.
• Readily available natural clay material, making pots affordable and easy to produce locally.
• Heavy and stable, reducing risk of pots tipping over.
• Aesthetically appealing, natural appearance suited to ornamental use.
• Excellent thermal properties — moderates soil temperature changes.
Disadvantages/Limitations:
• Fragile and breaks easily.
• Heavy and difficult to transport in large quantities.
• Porous nature means rapid drying — frequent watering required.
• In the 19th century, limited precision in pot sizing/standardisation.
• Over time, salt deposits from irrigation water build up on surfaces.
[Award 1 mark per valid evaluative point, balanced evaluation rewarded, max 5]

(b) Any TWO of:
• Waterlogging leads to oxygen deprivation in the root zone (anaerobic conditions), causing root rot.
• Promotes growth of fungal pathogens (e.g. Phytophthora) leading to disease.
• Leaching of nutrients from the growing medium.
• Wilting/yellowing of leaves due to root damage.
[1 mark each, max 2]

(c) Any THREE of the following (1 mark each):
• Flowers have highest water content/turgor in the morning before transpiration causes wilting.
• Cooler temperatures in the morning slow respiration and extend vase life.
• Stomata are closed/less open in the morning, reducing water loss after cutting.
• Reduced bacterial activity in cool morning temperatures, minimising stem-end contamination.
• Flowers harvested in the morning have higher sugar (carbohydrate) reserves stored overnight.
