questions.diagramNote: A diagram/figure showing three different soil structures labelled A, B and C, representing different aggregate/structure types found in Zimbabwean communal farming soils.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) The three soil structures commonly illustrated in Zimbabwean soil science (1 mark each):
• A – Granular/Crumb structure (rounded aggregates, common in topsoil/A-horizon).
• B – Blocky structure (angular or sub-angular blocks; common in subsoils).
• C – Platy/Prismatic/Columnar structure (flat horizontal layers or vertical columns).
[Award 1 mark per correctly identified structure matching the figure; accept other standard structures such as single-grain or massive if consistent with diagram.]

(b)(i) Soil colour (2 marks):
• Dark/black colour indicates high organic matter/humus content, associated with good fertility and moisture retention.
• Red/yellow colour indicates iron oxide presence, suggesting well-aerated, well-drained soils.
• Grey/blue colour (gleying) indicates waterlogging/poor drainage (anaerobic conditions), unfavourable for most horticultural crops.
[1 mark per valid point, max 2]

(b)(ii) Soil texture (2 marks):
• Determines water-holding capacity — clay soils hold more water; sandy soils drain quickly.
• Influences aeration — sandy soils are better aerated, suitable for root crops; clay soils may become waterlogged.
• Affects nutrient retention — finer-textured soils have more surface area and higher CEC, retaining more nutrients for plant uptake.
• Loamy soils (mix of sand, silt, clay) are ideal for most horticultural crops.
[1 mark per valid point, max 2]

(b)(iii) Soil structure (3 marks):
• Good granular/crumb structure creates macropores and micropores allowing adequate aeration and water infiltration while retaining moisture — ideal for root development.
• Stable soil aggregates reduce erosion and surface crusting, maintaining good seedbed conditions.
• Good structure facilitates root penetration and expansion, supporting plant anchorage and nutrient uptake.
• Poor/platy or compacted structure restricts drainage, causing waterlogging and root diseases.
[1 mark per valid point, max 3]

questions.text:
7. (a) Discuss the constraints faced by small holder horticultural farmers in Zimbabwe. [10]
(b) Evaluate the development of horticulture in Zimbabwe. [10]

questions.topic: Smallholder horticulture and development of horticulture in Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Constraints faced by smallholder horticultural farmers in Zimbabwe (10 marks — award marks for discussion of each constraint with explanation; up to 2 marks per well-discussed point):
• Financial constraints – limited access to capital and credit; high cost of inputs (seeds, fertilisers, agro-chemicals); most smallholders cannot afford irrigation equipment.
• Water/irrigation challenges – erratic rainfall; limited access to reliable irrigation water; high cost of irrigation infrastructure.
• Poor infrastructure – poor road networks increase transport costs and post-harvest losses; limited cold chain facilities.
• Land tenure insecurity – lack of formal land rights limits investment in perennial crops and improvements.
• Limited technical knowledge/skills – inadequate extension services; low adoption of good agricultural practices (GAP).
• Pest and disease problems – limited access to agro-chemicals; poor pest management knowledge leads to high crop losses.
• Market access challenges – exploitation by middlemen; lack of market information; stiff competition from large commercial farmers and imports.
• Climate change – increasingly unpredictable weather, droughts, floods affecting production.
• Post-harvest losses – lack of storage and refrigeration; poor packaging and handling.
• Limited value addition – most produce sold fresh with no processing, limiting income.
[Award up to 10 marks for well-discussed, relevant constraints.]

(b) Evaluation of the development of horticulture in Zimbabwe (10 marks):
Positive developments:
• Zimbabwe has a well-established commercial horticulture sector producing flowers (roses, carnations), vegetables and fruits for export (EU markets).
• Introduction of new crop varieties and technologies improving yields and quality.
• Growth of cut flower industry especially in Mazowe and Harare areas.
• Government policy support through ZACP and Horticulture promotion programmes.
• Expansion of smallholder horticulture through irrigation schemes.
• Contribution to employment and foreign currency earnings.
Challenges/Negative aspects:
• Decline of large-scale commercial horticulture following Fast Track Land Reform (2000), disruption of established farms.
• Loss of export markets due to trade sanctions and quality inconsistencies.
• Economic instability affecting investment in the sector.
• Deteriorating infrastructure (cold chain, roads, power supply).
• Brain drain — loss of skilled horticulturists.
Overall evaluation: Despite significant challenges, horticulture remains a vital sector with growth potential if infrastructure, finance and market access constraints are addressed.
[Award marks for factual accuracy, balanced evaluation of positives and negatives, and conclusion; max 10 marks.]

(a) light, [5]

(d) soil. [5]

questions.topic: Environmental factors affecting indigenous flower production
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidate must name an indigenous flower e.g. African Violet (Saintpaulia), Agapanthus, Strelitzia (Bird of Paradise), Protea, Gloriosa lily, or another recognised Zimbabwean indigenous flower. Award 1 mark for naming the flower.

(a) Light (max 5 marks):
• Light is necessary for photosynthesis — insufficient light reduces carbohydrate production and weakens the plant.
• Day length (photoperiod) affects flowering — many indigenous flowers are short-day or long-day plants; incorrect photoperiod delays/inhibits flowering.
• Light intensity affects stem elongation — low light causes etiolation (spindly growth).
• High light intensity can cause scorching/bleaching of petals/leaves.
• Optimal light enhances flower colour and quality.

(b) Humidity (max 5 marks):
• High humidity reduces transpiration and can lead to fungal diseases (e.g. Botrytis — grey mould) on petals and leaves.
• Low humidity increases transpiration, causing wilting and bud drop.
• Optimal humidity maintains turgidity of flowers and prolongs vase life.
• High humidity during storage causes rotting of cut flowers.
• Humidity affects pollen viability and pollination success.

(c) Temperature (max 5 marks):
• Optimal temperature range promotes active growth, flowering and metabolic processes.
• Very high temperatures accelerate respiration, depleting carbohydrate reserves and shortening flower life.
• Low/chilling temperatures can damage tropical indigenous flowers, causing tissue discolouration and death.
• Vernalisation (exposure to cold) may be required to initiate flowering in some species.
• Temperature fluctuations affect stomatal function and water balance.

(d) Soil (max 5 marks):
• Soil pH affects nutrient availability — most indigenous flowers prefer slightly acidic to neutral soils (pH 6–7).
• Well-drained, loamy soils with good organic matter are ideal for root development.
• Soil fertility (N, P, K and micronutrients) directly affects growth, foliage quality and flower production.
• Waterlogged soils cause root rot; drought-prone sandy soils require irrigation.
• Soil texture and structure affect aeration and root penetration.
[Award up to 5 marks per section for well-explained, relevant points.]

(i) handling agro-chemicals, [5]
(ii) storing agro-chemicals, [5]
(iii) disposing agro-chemical containers. [5]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Environmental hazards of agro-chemicals (max 5 marks; 1 mark per valid hazard explained):
• Water pollution – leaching/runoff of pesticides/fertilisers contaminates rivers, lakes and groundwater, harming aquatic life and making water unsafe for human/animal consumption.
• Soil contamination – accumulation of persistent chemicals degrades soil biota, reducing soil fertility and disrupting nutrient cycles.
• Air pollution – volatilisation and spray drift of agro-chemicals contaminates air, harming non-target organisms and causing human health problems.
• Destruction of biodiversity – non-selective pesticides kill beneficial insects (pollinators, natural predators), birds, and other non-target organisms.
• Bioaccumulation/biomagnification – persistent organochlorine chemicals accumulate in the food chain, causing toxicity in top predators.
• Resistance development – overuse leads to resistant pest/weed populations, requiring more chemicals and creating a cycle of environmental damage.

(b)(i) Safety precautions when handling agro-chemicals (max 5 marks):
• Always read and follow label instructions before use.
• Wear appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): gloves, mask/respirator, goggles, overalls, boots.
• Do not eat, drink, or smoke while handling chemicals.
• Mix chemicals in a well-ventilated area, preferably outdoors.
• Avoid skin contact and inhalation; wash hands and exposed skin thoroughly after use.
• Use correct dosages and calibrated equipment to avoid over-application.
• Keep children and animals away from the application area.

(b)(ii) Safety precautions when storing agro-chemicals (max 5 marks):
• Store in a dedicated, locked, well-ventilated chemical store away from living areas and food stores.
• Keep in original labelled containers; never transfer to food/drink containers.
• Store separately from seeds, fertilisers, and food items.
• Ensure containers are tightly sealed and upright to prevent leaks/spills.
• Keep out of reach of children and animals.
• Maintain an up-to-date inventory/register of chemicals stored.
• Store flammable chemicals away from heat sources and flames.

(b)(iii) Safety precautions when disposing of agro-chemical containers (max 5 marks):
• Triple rinse empty containers with water; add rinsate to spray tank — do not pour down drains or into water bodies.
• Puncture/crush containers to prevent re-use for food/water storage.
• Do not burn plastic containers as toxic fumes are released; burning metal containers at designated sites may be acceptable.
• Bury rinsed containers in a pit at an approved waste disposal site, away from water sources.
• Follow local/national regulations and manufacturer instructions on container disposal.
• Never leave empty containers in the open where children or animals may access them.
• Return containers to registered collection/disposal schemes where available.

10. (a) Discuss the management practices carried out on the establishment of turf grass in the school environment. [10]
(b) Assess the need of analysing a given area in landscape design. [10]

subParts.text: Discuss the management practices carried out on the establishment of turf grass in the school environment.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Assess the need of analysing a given area in landscape design.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Turf grass management and landscape design
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Management practices for establishing turf grass in a school environment (10 marks; up to 2 marks per well-discussed practice):
• Site preparation – clearing the area of weeds, debris and stones; tilling/raking to a fine tilth to create a good seedbed; levelling to prevent waterlogging.
• Soil improvement – incorporation of organic matter/compost to improve soil fertility and structure; liming if soil is too acidic.
• Species/cultivar selection – choose appropriate turfgrass species suited to Zimbabwe's climate (e.g. Kikuyu grass, Buffalo grass, Bermuda grass) and school use (wear tolerance, low maintenance).
• Planting method – seeding, turfing (laying sod), sprigging or plugging; ensure good soil-to-grass contact; roll after laying turf.
• Fertiliser application – apply a starter fertiliser (high phosphorus) at establishment to promote root development.
• Irrigation – regular watering during establishment especially in dry season; avoid waterlogging.
• Weed control – pre-emergent herbicides before planting or hand-weeding post-establishment; avoid competition from weeds.
• Mowing – begin mowing when grass reaches required height (first mow at about 7–8 cm); regular mowing encourages lateral spread and dense sward.
• Pest and disease management – monitor for grubs, armyworms, fungal diseases; apply appropriate treatments.
• Traffic management – restrict foot traffic on newly established turf until fully rooted; use pathways to reduce wear.
[Award up to 10 marks.]

(b) Assessment of the need to analyse a given area in landscape design (10 marks; up to 2 marks per well-assessed point):
• Site analysis (inventory) identifies existing features — topography, soil type, drainage, existing vegetation, structures — that determine what can be planted and where.
• Climate/microclimate analysis (sun path, prevailing winds, frost pockets) ensures appropriate plant selection and placement for survival and aesthetic effect.
• Soil analysis determines pH, fertility and drainage characteristics, guiding soil amendments and plant species selection.
• Understanding the client's needs/functional requirements (play areas, pathways, seating, aesthetic preferences) ensures the design is fit for purpose.
• Analysis of views and vistas helps position plants and structures to enhance or screen views.
• Assessment of existing utilities (underground pipes, overhead cables) prevents costly damage during construction.
• Zoning analysis (sun/shade areas, wet/dry areas) allows optimal placement of plants and hardscape features.
• Legal/regulatory considerations (building lines, heritage trees) must be identified to ensure compliance.
• Budget and maintenance requirements analysis ensures the design is economically feasible and sustainable long-term.
• Without thorough area analysis, design errors lead to plant failure, poor aesthetics, safety hazards and wasted resources.
[Award up to 10 marks for well-assessed, relevant points with conclusion.]

Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

ABC ENTERPRISE

ABC Enterprise is a partnership business owned by Ayanda, Ben and Caro, providing catering services. The business is located in the busy township of Katanga in Norton. Its non-current assets include an industrial stove, Isuzu D Max truck and a freezer. The business was operating successfully providing the best catering services in the area. As a result, it managed to withstand competition from other businesses. Due to economic hardships and changes in the business operations, ABC enterprise lost its viability. The enterprise's expenses were exceeding its Income. The demand for catering services decreased coupled with a rise in stock holding costs. The partners agreed to dissolve the business and engage an accountant to help them manage the disposal of assets so that they distribute profit accordingly.

The following information of Non-Current Assets was provided.

Asset | Cost $ | Estimated Residual values $ | Life expectancy Number of years
ISUZU D MAX | 40 000 | 10 000 | 3
Freezer | 20 000 | 10 000 | 5
Industrial stove | 10 000 | 1 000 | 3

subParts.text: Define the term non-current assets in the case study.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Calculate the annual depreciation for each asset.
subParts.label: (b)(i)

subParts.text: Outline the benefits of depreciating non-current assets to ABC enterprise.
subParts.label: (b)(ii)

subParts.text: Explain any three stock holding costs that ABC enterprise may be incurring.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Evaluate the advantages of operating as a partnership business.
subParts.label: (d)

questions.diagramNote: Table of non-current assets showing Cost, Estimated Residual Values, and Life Expectancy for ISUZU D MAX, Freezer, and Industrial Stove.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Non-current assets are long-term assets owned by a business that are not intended to be converted into cash within one year / used over more than one accounting period. In the context of ABC Enterprise, these include the industrial stove, Isuzu D Max truck, and freezer — assets used in the delivery of catering services over multiple years. [1 mark for definition, 1 mark for application to context, 1 mark for elaboration/example.]

(b)(i) Using Straight-Line Depreciation formula: Annual Depreciation = (Cost − Residual Value) / Useful Life
- ISUZU D MAX: (40,000 − 10,000) / 3 = $10,000 per year
- Freezer: (20,000 − 10,000) / 5 = $2,000 per year
- Industrial Stove: (10,000 − 1,000) / 3 = $3,000 per year
[1 mark per correct calculation, 3 marks total.]

(b)(ii) Benefits of depreciation to ABC Enterprise:
- Ensures assets are recorded at accurate/realistic values on the balance sheet (matching principle).
- Helps the business set aside funds to replace assets in future (provision for replacement).
- Reduces taxable profit as depreciation is treated as an expense, lowering tax liability.
[1 mark per valid benefit, up to 3 marks.]

(c) Three stock holding costs:
1. Storage/warehousing costs – ABC Enterprise incurs costs for renting or maintaining space to store perishable catering stock such as food and beverages.
2. Insurance costs – The business must insure its stock against theft, fire, or spoilage, adding to holding costs.
3. Deterioration/wastage costs – Perishable food items may spoil over time, leading to losses from stock that cannot be used.
(Other valid answers: opportunity cost of capital tied up in stock, security costs, handling costs.)
[2 marks per explanation — 1 mark for identifying the cost + 1 mark for elaboration, up to 6 marks.]

(d) Evaluation of advantages of operating as a partnership:
Advantages:
- Shared capital: Partners pool financial resources, allowing the business to access more capital than a sole trader — enables ABC Enterprise to purchase expensive assets like the Isuzu D Max.
- Shared responsibility/workload: Tasks and decision-making are divided among Ayanda, Ben and Caro, reducing individual burden and bringing diverse skills.
- Shared risk: Financial losses and liabilities are distributed among partners, reducing individual exposure.
- Continuity and specialisation: Different partners can specialise in different aspects (e.g., cooking, finance, logistics).
Limitations (for evaluation):
- Unlimited liability: In a general partnership, partners are personally liable for business debts — risky when ABC Enterprise became insolvent.
- Profit sharing: Profits must be shared among all three partners, reducing individual earnings.
- Potential for conflict: Disagreements among Ayanda, Ben, and Caro over business decisions could slow down operations.
- Lack of continuity: Dissolution requires unanimous agreement and can be complicated.
Conclusion: While partnerships offer significant advantages in terms of resource pooling and shared risk, the unlimited liability and potential for disputes can be serious drawbacks, as demonstrated by ABC Enterprise's dissolution. The value of a partnership depends on the nature of the business and the strength of the partnership agreement.
[Up to 10 marks: 4–5 marks for well-explained advantages, 3–4 marks for limitations/evaluation, 1–2 marks for a balanced conclusion.]

questions.text:
(a) Justify the reasons for starting a business. [10]
(b) Assess the significance of using Net Present Value (NPV) as an investment appraisal technique. [15]

subParts.text: Justify the reasons for starting a business.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Assess the significance of using Net Present Value (NPV) as an investment appraisal technique.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Reasons for starting a business (justified):
- Profit motive: Entrepreneurs start businesses to earn profit and improve their standard of living — this is a primary financial incentive.
- Independence/autonomy: Owning a business provides freedom to make one's own decisions without being subject to an employer.
- Identify a gap in the market: An entrepreneur may recognise an unmet consumer need and start a business to fulfil it.
- Social enterprise/community benefit: Some businesses are started to provide social value, such as employment creation or supplying essential services.
- Innovation: To commercialise a new idea, product, or technology.
- Following a passion or hobby: Turning personal interests into a business venture.
- Job creation: Starting a business creates employment for oneself and others, contributing to economic development.
[Up to 10 marks: 2 marks per well-justified reason — 1 mark for stating + 1 mark for justification/elaboration. Award up to 5 well-developed reasons.]

(b) Assessment of NPV as an investment appraisal technique:
Significance/Advantages:
- Takes into account the time value of money by discounting future cash flows, giving a more accurate picture of an investment's true value.
- Considers all cash flows over the entire life of a project, not just the payback period.
- Provides a clear decision rule: if NPV > 0, the project adds value; if NPV < 0, it destroys value.
- Allows comparison between mutually exclusive projects on a common basis.
- Accounts for risk through the choice of discount rate — a higher rate can reflect higher risk.
Limitations:
- Requires an accurate discount rate, which is difficult to determine and can significantly affect the outcome.
- Complex to calculate compared to simpler methods like Payback Period.
- Relies on estimated future cash flows which may be inaccurate — garbage in, garbage out.
- Does not account for non-financial factors such as employee morale, brand image, or environmental impact.
- May not be suitable for businesses with limited financial expertise.
Conclusion: NPV is arguably the most theoretically sound investment appraisal method as it accounts for the time value of money and total returns. However, its reliability is heavily dependent on the accuracy of cash flow forecasts and the appropriateness of the discount rate. Businesses should use NPV alongside other techniques (e.g., Payback Period, ARR) for more well-rounded investment decisions.
[Up to 15 marks: 5–6 marks for significance, 5–6 marks for limitations, 2–3 marks for a well-reasoned conclusion/judgement.]

questions.text:
(a) Explain the benefits of producing a business plan to a new business. [10]
(b) To what extent is a matrix organisational structure useful to an expanding business. [15]

subParts.text: Explain the benefits of producing a business plan to a new business.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: To what extent is a matrix organisational structure useful to an expanding business.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Benefits of a business plan to a new business:
- Securing finance: Banks and investors require a business plan before granting loans or investment; it demonstrates viability and reduces perceived risk.
- Sets clear objectives and direction: Gives the business a roadmap of goals and how to achieve them, keeping founders focused.
- Identifies potential risks and challenges: Forces the entrepreneur to think ahead and prepare contingency plans.
- Guides decision-making: Acts as a reference point for strategic and operational decisions.
- Helps in resource allocation: Clarifies what human, financial, and physical resources are needed and when.
- Benchmarking and monitoring performance: Provides targets against which actual performance can be measured.
[Up to 10 marks: 2 marks per well-explained benefit — 1 mark for identifying + 1 mark for explanation. Up to 5 benefits.]

(b) Usefulness of a matrix organisational structure to an expanding business:
Advantages:
- Combines functional and project-based structures, allowing specialists from different departments to collaborate on specific projects — ideal for expansion into new markets or product lines.
- Encourages cross-functional communication and information sharing, improving innovation.
- Flexible and adaptable: Resources can be reallocated between projects as the business grows and priorities change.
- Employees develop broader skills by working across departments, creating a more versatile workforce.
- Suitable for large, complex organisations where multiple projects run simultaneously.
Limitations:
- Dual authority (two bosses) can create confusion, role conflict, and unclear accountability.
- Can lead to power struggles between functional managers and project managers.
- More expensive to manage due to increased coordination requirements.
- May cause communication overload in a rapidly expanding business.
- Requires highly skilled and adaptable employees, which may not always be available.
Conclusion: A matrix structure can be highly useful to an expanding business, particularly where projects require multi-disciplinary teams and flexibility. However, its success depends on clear communication channels, well-defined roles, and a strong management culture. For businesses expanding rapidly, the complexity introduced by a matrix structure may outweigh its benefits unless properly managed.
[Up to 15 marks: 5–6 marks for advantages, 5–6 marks for limitations/counterarguments, 2–3 marks for evaluative conclusion.]

questions.text:
(a) Explain the purpose of communication to an organisation of your choice. [10]
(b) Assess the usefulness of Critical Path Analysis to a construction company. [15]

subParts.text: Explain the purpose of communication to an organisation of your choice.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Assess the usefulness of Critical Path Analysis to a construction company.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Purpose of communication to an organisation:
(Credit any relevant organisation, e.g., a hospital, school, manufacturing firm.)
- Coordination: Ensures all departments and employees work towards the same organisational goals — e.g., a construction company communicates project timelines to all teams.
- Decision-making: Management needs accurate information from all levels to make informed decisions.
- Motivation: Effective communication of targets, feedback, and recognition boosts employee morale and productivity.
- Instruction and direction: Managers convey tasks, policies, and procedures to employees, ensuring work is done correctly.
- Customer relations: External communication builds and maintains relationships with clients, suppliers, and stakeholders.
- Conflict resolution: Open communication channels help address and resolve disputes quickly.
[Up to 10 marks: 2 marks per well-explained purpose — 1 mark identifying + 1 mark explanation with organisational context.]

(b) Usefulness of Critical Path Analysis (CPA) to a construction company:
Advantages:
- Identifies the critical path — the sequence of tasks that determines the minimum project duration, helping the company complete buildings on schedule.
- Highlights float time (slack) for non-critical tasks, allowing flexible reallocation of resources without delaying the overall project.
- Aids in resource planning: the company can schedule labour, materials, and equipment efficiently, reducing idle time and costs.
- Useful for complex projects with multiple interdependent activities (e.g., foundations must be completed before walls are built).
- Provides a visual project timeline that aids communication between site managers, contractors, and clients.
- Enables monitoring and control — deviations from the plan can be quickly identified and corrected.
Limitations:
- Time-consuming and complex to construct for large projects with hundreds of activities.
- Based on estimated activity durations which may be inaccurate due to weather delays, supply chain disruptions, etc.
- Does not account for resource constraints — a task may be on the non-critical path but still require the same workers as a critical task.
- Requires skilled personnel to construct and interpret the network diagram correctly.
- Constantly needs updating as conditions change on a construction site.
Conclusion: CPA is highly useful to a construction company due to the complex, interdependent nature of construction activities and the high cost of delays. However, its effectiveness depends on the accuracy of time estimates and the capability of management to maintain and adapt the plan throughout the project.
[Up to 15 marks: 5–6 marks for advantages, 5–6 marks for limitations, 2–3 marks for evaluative conclusion.]

questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of marketing research to a business entering foreign markets.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Usefulness of marketing research to a business entering foreign markets:

Advantages/Arguments for usefulness:
- Identifies consumer needs and preferences in the target foreign market — cultural differences mean that products successful domestically may require adaptation (e.g., different tastes, packaging requirements).
- Assesses market size and potential demand, helping the business decide whether entry is financially viable.
- Identifies competitors already operating in the foreign market, enabling the business to develop a competitive strategy.
- Reduces risk and uncertainty by providing data-driven insights before committing significant investment to a new market.
- Helps identify legal, regulatory, and cultural barriers to entry — critical for compliance and brand positioning.
- Aids in pricing strategy by revealing consumer income levels, willingness to pay, and competitor pricing in the foreign market.
- Supports the selection of the most appropriate market entry mode (e.g., joint venture, licensing, direct export).

Limitations/Arguments against over-reliance:
- Expensive and time-consuming, particularly primary research conducted in foreign markets (requires translation, local fieldwork, etc.).
- Secondary data may be outdated, incomplete, or unreliable in some developing countries.
- Cultural bias: researchers may misinterpret foreign consumer behaviour through their own cultural lens.
- Market conditions can change rapidly — research findings may become obsolete before the business enters the market.
- Does not guarantee success; even well-researched market entries can fail due to unforeseen political, economic, or social changes.

Conclusion: Marketing research is highly valuable to a business entering foreign markets as it significantly reduces the risk of failure and improves the quality of strategic decisions. However, it must be recognised as a tool to inform, not guarantee, success. Its value is greatest when combined with local expertise and a flexible market entry strategy.
[Up to 25 marks: 8–10 marks for advantages, 8–10 marks for limitations, 4–5 marks for a well-reasoned evaluative conclusion.]

questions.text:
(a) Examine ways a business can use to increase capacity utilisation. [10]
(b) Evaluate the appropriateness of vertical communication to the success of a business. [15]

subParts.text: Examine ways a business can use to increase capacity utilisation.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Evaluate the appropriateness of vertical communication to the success of a business.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Ways to increase capacity utilisation:
- Subcontracting excess work in reverse — bring back previously outsourced work in-house to fill idle capacity.
- Reduce the workforce or shift patterns — match staffing levels to actual output needs, reducing fixed costs per unit.
- Increase marketing and promotional activities to stimulate demand and fill spare capacity.
- Diversify product range — use existing machinery and labour to produce new products to fill idle capacity.
- Offer competitive pricing/discounts to attract more customers and increase output volumes.
- Use flexible manufacturing systems to switch between products quickly and respond to demand changes.
- Enter new markets (domestic or international) to increase sales volume.
- Accept subcontracting work from other businesses to utilise spare machinery and labour.
[Up to 10 marks: 2 marks per well-examined way — 1 mark for identifying + 1 mark for explanation. Up to 5 well-developed ways.]

(b) Evaluation of vertical communication to business success:
Vertical communication includes both downward (management to employees) and upward (employees to management) communication.

Advantages:
- Downward communication ensures that strategic goals, policies, and instructions are clearly conveyed to employees, maintaining organisational direction and discipline.
- Upward communication allows employees to report problems, provide feedback, and share innovative ideas — improving decision-making quality at management level.
- Maintains the chain of command and establishes clear authority, which is important in large organisations.
- Keeps employees informed about organisational changes, reducing uncertainty and resistance.
- Supports performance management — managers can communicate targets, appraisals, and disciplinary matters formally.

Limitations:
- Slow: Information passing through multiple levels of hierarchy can be delayed — critical in fast-changing business environments.
- Distortion: Messages may be filtered or altered as they pass through layers of management (the 'grapevine' effect).
- Can stifle creativity and innovation if employees feel their upward communication is ignored.
- Overemphasis on vertical communication may reduce horizontal/lateral collaboration between departments.
- In flat organisations, vertical communication may be less relevant as fewer hierarchical layers exist.

Conclusion: Vertical communication is essential for maintaining order, direction, and accountability in a business, particularly in large hierarchical organisations. However, relying solely on vertical channels can slow responsiveness and suppress employee initiative. The most successful businesses balance vertical and horizontal communication to maximise both control and collaboration.
[Up to 15 marks: 5–6 marks for advantages, 5–6 marks for limitations, 2–3 marks for evaluative conclusion.]

questions.text:
(a) Justify the significance of an organisational structure to a business. [10]
(b) Assess the appropriateness of Just In Time (JIT) method of stock holding to a food outlet. [15]

subParts.text: Justify the significance of an organisational structure to a business.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Assess the appropriateness of Just In Time (JIT) method of stock holding to a food outlet.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Significance of organisational structure (justified):
- Defines roles and responsibilities: Employees know what is expected of them, reducing confusion and duplication of effort.
- Establishes the chain of command and lines of authority, ensuring accountability at every level.
- Facilitates coordination and communication between departments, improving operational efficiency.
- Enables delegation: A clear structure allows managers to delegate tasks appropriately, freeing up senior management for strategic decisions.
- Supports growth and expansion: As a business grows, a defined structure helps manage increased complexity and larger workforces.
- Aids in decision-making by clarifying who has the authority to make specific types of decisions.
- Influences organisational culture and employee behaviour — a flat structure promotes collaboration while a tall structure enforces formality.
[Up to 10 marks: 2 marks per justified significance — 1 mark for point + 1 mark for justification. Up to 5 well-developed points.]

(b) Appropriateness of JIT to a food outlet:
JIT involves receiving stock only as and when it is needed for production/sale, holding minimal inventory.

Advantages for a food outlet:
- Reduces storage costs — a food outlet has limited refrigeration/storage space, so holding minimal stock is practical.
- Minimises wastage of perishable goods — food items have short shelf lives, so ordering only what is needed reduces spoilage.
- Frees up cash flow — capital is not tied up in large stock holdings, which is vital for small food businesses.
- Ensures freshness of ingredients, improving food quality and customer satisfaction.

Limitations for a food outlet:
- Relies on highly reliable suppliers — if a supplier fails to deliver on time, the food outlet may run out of key ingredients and lose sales.
- In Zimbabwe's context, supply chain disruptions (transport issues, supplier shortages) make JIT risky.
- Increases administrative burden of frequent small orders and supplier management.
- Vulnerable to sudden spikes in demand (e.g., public holidays, events) where insufficient stock leads to lost revenue.
- Requires strong supplier relationships and sophisticated inventory management systems which small food outlets may lack.

Conclusion: JIT can be highly appropriate for a food outlet due to the perishable nature of food and the importance of freshness. However, in an environment with unreliable supply chains, it carries significant risk. A hybrid approach — maintaining a small buffer stock of key non-perishable items while using JIT for fresh produce — may be more practical.
[Up to 15 marks: 5–6 marks for advantages, 5–6 marks for limitations, 2–3 marks for evaluative conclusion.]

questions.text: Evaluate the importance of Information Communication Technology (ICT) to the Human Resource department of a business.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Importance of ICT to the Human Resource (HR) department:

Advantages/Importance:
- Recruitment and selection: Online job portals, applicant tracking systems (ATS), and video interviews widen the talent pool and speed up recruitment processes.
- Employee records management: HR information systems (HRIS) allow accurate, secure, and easily retrievable storage of employee data (contracts, payroll, performance records).
- Payroll processing: Automated payroll software reduces errors, ensures timely payment, and maintains compliance with tax/labour regulations.
- Training and development: E-learning platforms and virtual training modules allow flexible, cost-effective employee development without geographical constraints.
- Performance management: Digital performance appraisal tools allow continuous monitoring, goal-setting, and feedback between managers and employees.
- Communication: Email, intranets, and collaboration tools (e.g., Microsoft Teams) improve internal HR communication across departments and locations.
- Data analytics: HR can analyse workforce data to identify trends such as high turnover rates, skills gaps, and absenteeism, enabling proactive HR planning.

Limitations:
- High initial cost of implementing ICT systems, which can be prohibitive for smaller businesses.
- Risk of data breaches and cybersecurity threats — employee personal data is sensitive and must be protected.
- Requires ongoing staff training to use new systems effectively, adding cost and time.
- Over-reliance on technology may depersonalise HR functions — employee relations and motivation require a human touch.
- System failures or downtime can disrupt critical HR functions such as payroll processing.
- In Zimbabwe, unreliable internet connectivity and power outages can limit the effectiveness of ICT-based HR systems.

Conclusion: ICT is critically important to the HR department as it enhances efficiency, accuracy, and strategic capability across all core HR functions. However, its value is contingent on reliable infrastructure, adequate training, and robust data security measures. Businesses must balance technological adoption with maintaining the human element that is central to effective people management.
[Up to 25 marks: 9–10 marks for importance/advantages, 9–10 marks for limitations, 4–5 marks for evaluative conclusion.]

questions.text:
(a) Analyse the benefits of effective management of working capital to a business. [10]
(b) Discuss the importance of economic integration to businesses in your country. [15]

subParts.text: Analyse the benefits of effective management of working capital to a business.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Discuss the importance of economic integration to businesses in your country.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Benefits of effective working capital management:
Working capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities
- Ensures liquidity: The business can meet its short-term obligations (wages, supplier payments, utilities) on time, avoiding insolvency.
- Improves relationships with suppliers and creditors: Timely payments secure better credit terms, discounts, and reliable supply chains.
- Reduces the need for expensive short-term borrowing (overdrafts/loans), lowering interest costs.
- Enables the business to take advantage of bulk purchase discounts when it has sufficient cash/stock levels.
- Supports business continuity and operational efficiency by ensuring uninterrupted production/service delivery.
- Signals financial health to investors and lenders, improving access to long-term finance.
- Allows strategic flexibility — surplus working capital can be invested in growth opportunities.
[Up to 10 marks: 2 marks per well-analysed benefit. Up to 5 benefits.]

(b) Importance of economic integration to businesses in Zimbabwe:
Economic integration refers to agreements between countries to reduce trade barriers (e.g., SADC, COMESA, AfCFTA).

Importance:
- Access to larger markets: Zimbabwean businesses can export to member states with reduced tariffs, increasing sales volumes and revenue.
- Economies of scale: Higher export volumes allow businesses to produce more efficiently, reducing unit costs.
- Increased competition: Exposure to foreign competitors forces local businesses to innovate and improve quality to remain competitive.
- Attraction of foreign direct investment (FDI): Regional integration makes Zimbabwe a more attractive investment destination as investors gain access to a larger regional market.
- Access to raw materials and intermediate goods: Businesses can import inputs from regional partners at lower tariff costs, reducing production costs.
- Technology and knowledge transfer: Integration promotes sharing of best practices and technology among member states.

Limitations/Challenges:
- Increased competition may harm domestic industries that are not competitive enough to survive against regional rivals.
- Revenue loss for government from reduced tariffs, which may lead to reduced public spending.
- Dependence on regional trading partners makes Zimbabwean businesses vulnerable to economic shocks in those countries.

Conclusion: Economic integration offers significant opportunities for Zimbabwean businesses through market expansion, cost reduction, and investment attraction. However, it requires businesses to be competitive and adaptable to thrive in a more open regional economy.
[Up to 15 marks: 5–6 marks for advantages, 4–5 marks for limitations/challenges, 2–3 marks for conclusion.]

questions.text:
(a) Explain the importance of the Ansoff Matrix in designing marketing strategies. [10]
(b) To what extent are multinational companies (MNCs) significant to Zimbabwe. [15]

subParts.text: Explain the importance of the Ansoff Matrix in designing marketing strategies.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: To what extent are multinational companies (MNCs) significant to Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Importance of the Ansoff Matrix in designing marketing strategies:
The Ansoff Matrix is a strategic planning tool with four growth strategies: Market Penetration, Market Development, Product Development, and Diversification.
- Provides a clear framework: Helps businesses systematically evaluate different growth options based on existing/new products and existing/new markets.
- Market Penetration: Encourages businesses to increase market share with existing products in existing markets through competitive pricing or promotions — lower risk strategy.
- Market Development: Guides businesses to enter new markets (geographic or demographic) with existing products — useful for businesses looking to internationalise.
- Product Development: Encourages innovation by developing new products for existing customers, maintaining competitiveness and loyalty.
- Diversification: Identifies opportunities for growth in entirely new markets with new products — highest risk but potentially highest reward.
- Risk assessment: The matrix helps businesses assess the relative risk of each strategy, guiding resource allocation and risk management.
- Supports strategic alignment: Ensures marketing strategies align with overall corporate objectives and capabilities.
[Up to 10 marks: 2 marks per well-explained point. Up to 5 points.]

(b) Significance of MNCs to Zimbabwe:
Significance/Advantages:
- Job creation: MNCs employ local Zimbabweans, reducing unemployment and raising living standards (e.g., Unilever, Econet-linked firms).
- Foreign Direct Investment (FDI): MNCs bring capital into Zimbabwe, funding infrastructure, production facilities, and services.
- Technology and skills transfer: Local employees gain access to advanced technology and management practices, improving human capital.
- Tax revenues: MNCs contribute to government revenues through corporate taxes, which fund public services.
- Backward linkages: MNCs source inputs from local suppliers, stimulating growth in related domestic industries.
- Improved access to goods and services: MNCs introduce new products and international standards of quality to Zimbabwean consumers.

Limitations/Counterarguments:
- Profit repatriation: MNCs send profits back to their home countries rather than reinvesting in Zimbabwe, limiting local economic benefit.
- Crowding out local businesses: MNCs' economies of scale and brand power can drive smaller local competitors out of business.
- Exploitation of resources: MNCs may extract natural resources without adequate compensation or environmental responsibility.
- Limited local ownership and control: Strategic decisions are made in foreign headquarters with little regard for Zimbabwe's specific developmental needs.
- Transfer pricing: MNCs may manipulate internal pricing to minimise tax obligations in Zimbabwe.

Conclusion: MNCs are significant to Zimbabwe primarily through FDI, employment, and technology transfer, which are vital for a developing economy. However, their overall impact must be carefully managed through regulatory frameworks that ensure profit retention, environmental compliance, and local industry protection. Their significance is considerable but not unconditionally positive.
[Up to 15 marks: 5–6 marks for significance/advantages, 5–6 marks for limitations, 2–3 marks for evaluative conclusion with judgement.]

questions.text:
NGANEA NA MANWELEDZO
Vhalani nganea i tevhelaho ni konou fhindula mbudziso.

Zimbabwe ndi ḽiṅwe ḽa mashango a na tshaka dzo fhambanaho dza vhathu. Dziṅwe dza dzitshaka dzenedzi ndi Vhasuthu, Vhakalanga, Vhandevhele, Vhashona na Vhavenḓa. Tshaka dzenedzi dzi na kutshilele kwadzo nga u fhambana hadzo. Vhavenḓa ndi vhathu vhane vha alusa vhana vhavho nga nḓila ya mvelele. Lushaka ulu lu shumisa maambele, mirero na ngano vhukati ha zwiṅwe, nga nḓila ya u tou anetshela. Maambele, mirero na ngano zwi dzhielwa nṱha nga Vhavenḓa. Zwi anzela u shumiswa kha u fhaṱa vhuthu ha miraḓo ya lushaka ulu. Vhahulwane na vhaṱuku vha tshila vho ḓitika ngazwo. Hu na mirero na maambele ane a shumiswa sa zwihali zwa u kaidza nyito dzo bvaho nḓilani. Izwi zwi thusa vhaṱuku uri vha aluwe vha tshi thetshelesa, vha ṱhonifha, vha ḓifara zwavhuḓi khathihi na u konḓelela nyimele dzo fhambanaho kha vhutshilo. Mirero na maambele zwi shuma sa mapholisa ngauri zwi a kona u kaidza muthu naho hu si na ane a mu humbudza ngazwo. U wana muthu a tshi ḓikaidza nga ene muṋe. Na musi vhana vhe vhoṱhe vhabebi vha si ho tsini, mirero na maambele zwi a vha humisela nḓilani. Ngano dza Vhavenḓa na dzone ndi dza ndeme. Ndi tshihali tshine vha tshi shumisa kha u lela vhana. U wana vhomakhulu vho tou mbaa! nga madekwana thungo ha tshivhaswo. Muḓuhulu muṅwe na muṅwe o tou ṅoo! makhulu vha tshi khou anetshela. Ngano idzi u wana hu dzone dzine dza ṋea ngeletshedzo na u kaidza vhathu. Dzone dzi bvisela khagala masiandoita a u sa thetshelesa. Dzi dovha hafhu dza bvukulula nḓila dzavhuḓi dza kutshilele. Ngauralo ndi zwa ndeme uri maambele, mirero na ngano zwi tsireledzwe uri zwi si ngalangale. Izwi zwi nga itwa nga u tou zwi ṅwala zwa rekhodiwa nga mitshini ya thekhinoḽodzhi.

MBUDZISO
(a) Shango ḽo buliwaho kha nganea ḽi na tshaka dzo fhambanaho ndi ḽifhio?
(b) Bulani nḓila nthihi ine Vhavenḓa vha i shumisa kha u kaidza vhana?
(c) Ndi ngani kha nganea mirero yo fanyiswa sa mapholisa?
(d) Maipfi ane a ri 'O tou ṅoo!' kha nganea a amba mini?
(e) U ya nga ha nganea, maambele, mirero na ngano zwi nga tsireledzwa hani uri zwi si ngalangale?

PFUFHIFHADZO/MANWELEDZO
(f) Nga maipfi a sa fhiriho a furathi, pfufhifhadzani nganea ye na vhala ni tshi bvisela khagala ndeme ya u gudisa vhana mirero, maambele na ngano.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any two ways of enterprising (1 mark each):
• Starting a new business / self-employment
• Innovation — introducing new products or services
• Social enterprise / community-based initiative
• Franchising an existing business concept
• Taking calculated risks to exploit a market opportunity

(b) Benefits of enterprising to the economy (up to 4 marks; 1 mark per explained point):
• Job creation — new enterprises employ workers, reducing unemployment and increasing household incomes.
• GDP growth — productive enterprises add to national output, raising GDP.
• Tax revenue — profitable businesses pay taxes, funding public services.
• Innovation & competitiveness — entrepreneurs introduce new products/processes, improving efficiency and international competitiveness.
• Import substitution / export earnings — local enterprises can reduce reliance on imports or earn foreign currency through exports.
• Improved living standards — wider availability of goods and services at competitive prices benefits consumers.

questions.text: Describe two components of a business plan.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Award 1 mark for identifying the component and 1 mark for a correct description (×2):
• Executive Summary — a brief overview of the entire business plan, covering the business idea, objectives, and key financial highlights.
• Market Analysis / Market Research — an examination of the target market, customer profile, competitors, and demand trends to justify the business opportunity.
• Marketing Plan / Marketing Mix — outlines how the business will promote, price, and distribute its products to reach target customers.
• Financial Plan / Projections — includes projected income statements, cash flow forecasts, and break-even analysis showing financial viability.
• Operations Plan — describes production processes, equipment, location, and supply chain arrangements.
• Organisational Structure — details management roles, staffing requirements, and lines of responsibility.

questions.text:
(a) Explain the term gearing.
(b) Distinguish between debt and equity finance.

subParts.text: Explain the term gearing.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Distinguish between debt and equity finance.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Gearing (up to 4 marks):
• Gearing refers to the proportion of a business's capital that is financed by long-term debt (borrowings) compared to equity (shareholders' funds).
• It is calculated as: Gearing ratio = (Long-term debt / Capital employed) × 100.
• A highly geared business has a large proportion of debt relative to equity, meaning it faces higher interest obligations and greater financial risk.
• A low-geared business relies more on equity, making it less vulnerable to interest rate changes but potentially limiting returns to shareholders.

(b) Distinguishing debt from equity finance (up to 4 marks; 2 marks per clear distinction):
• Debt finance (e.g. bank loans, debentures) must be repaid with interest; equity finance (e.g. share capital, retained profits) does not have to be repaid and carries no fixed interest charge.
• Debt providers (creditors) have a legal claim over assets if the business cannot repay; equity holders (shareholders) bear the residual risk but enjoy unlimited upside through dividends and capital growth.
• Debt interest is tax-deductible, reducing the net cost to the business; dividends paid to equity holders are not tax-deductible.
• Equity financing does not increase financial risk in the same way as debt, but issuing new shares may dilute existing ownership.

(a) business entity,
(b) money measurement.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Business Entity (2 marks):
• The business is treated as a separate legal/accounting entity from its owner(s). (1 mark)
• Therefore, the owner's personal transactions and assets are kept separate from the business's financial records — only transactions relating to the business are recorded in its accounts. (1 mark)

(b) Money Measurement (2 marks):
• Only transactions that can be expressed in monetary (financial) terms are recorded in the accounts. (1 mark)
• Non-monetary factors such as employee morale, brand reputation, or management skill are not recorded in the financial statements because they cannot be objectively measured in money. (1 mark)

questions.text: Analyse the benefits of batch production to a business enterprise.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Award up to 4 marks for analysed points (identification + explanation + impact):
• Economies of scale — producing items in batches allows the business to buy raw materials in bulk, reducing unit costs and improving profit margins.
• Flexibility — the business can switch between different batches (e.g. different product variants) to respond to changing customer demand without major retooling costs.
• Improved quality control — each batch can be inspected before the next stage of production, reducing the risk of large-scale defects reaching customers.
• Efficient use of machinery and labour — workers and equipment can be dedicated to one batch at a time, reducing idle time compared to job production.
• Suitable for moderate demand — balances the cost advantages of mass production with the customisation benefits of job production, making it viable for medium-sized markets.

questions.text: Explain two marketing mix variables.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Award 1 mark for identifying the variable and 1 mark for a correct explanation (×2). Any two from:
• Product — the good or service offered to customers, including its features, quality, design, branding, and packaging, designed to meet customer needs and differentiate it from competitors.
• Price — the amount charged to customers; must reflect costs, competitor pricing, and perceived value, and influences demand and revenue.
• Place (Distribution) — how and where the product is made available to customers (e.g. retail outlets, online, direct delivery), ensuring convenience and accessibility.
• Promotion — all communication activities used to inform and persuade customers (e.g. advertising, sales promotions, social media, public relations).
• People — the staff who interact with customers; their skills and attitude affect customer experience and satisfaction.
• Process — the systems and procedures used to deliver the product/service efficiently.
• Physical Evidence — tangible cues (e.g. premises, packaging, uniforms) that reassure customers about service quality.

questions.text: Discuss the benefits of decision trees to a business enterprise.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Award marks for identified benefits with discussion of impact/limitation (up to 4 marks):
• Quantitative basis for decisions — decision trees assign probabilities and expected monetary values (EMVs) to outcomes, giving managers an objective, numerical framework rather than relying on intuition.
• Clarity and visualisation — the tree diagram clearly maps all possible options and outcomes, helping managers see the full range of choices and their consequences.
• Risk assessment — by incorporating probabilities, the tool highlights the likelihood of different outcomes, enabling the business to choose the option with the best risk-adjusted return.
• Comparison of alternatives — multiple options can be evaluated side by side using EMV, making it easier to select the most financially sound decision.
• Limitation/balance: decision trees rely on accurate probability estimates; if these are subjective or wrong, the output is unreliable, and the tool ignores qualitative factors such as staff morale or ethical concerns.

questions.text: Evaluate the importance of being ethical to a soft drink producer.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Award marks for balanced evaluation (benefits + limitations/challenges) with specific application to a soft drink producer:

Benefits of being ethical:
• Enhanced brand reputation — ethical practices (e.g. honest labelling, no misleading health claims) build consumer trust and loyalty, supporting long-term sales.
• Attracting and retaining talent — employees prefer to work for ethical employers, reducing recruitment and training costs.
• Regulatory compliance / avoiding fines — adhering to food safety, environmental, and advertising standards avoids costly legal penalties and product recalls.
• Investor confidence — ethical businesses attract socially responsible investors (ESG), potentially lowering the cost of capital.
• Sustainability — responsible sourcing of ingredients (e.g. water, sugar) and reducing plastic waste protects long-term input supplies and reduces environmental levies.

Limitations/challenges:
• Higher costs — ethical sourcing, fair wages, and eco-friendly packaging increase production costs, potentially reducing competitiveness on price.
• Short-term profit reduction — ethical decisions may sacrifice immediate profit for long-term reputation gains.
• Subjectivity — what is considered ethical varies across markets and cultures, making consistent application difficult.

Conclusion: Overall, being ethical is important for long-term sustainability and brand value, but the business must balance ethical costs against competitive pressures to remain viable.

questions.text:
Case Study 1 – Green Earth Farm

Green Earth Farm is a leading vegetable producer in Gokwe. The enterprise's main objective is to increase sales and market share in the competitive fresh produce market. With over 20 years of experience, the enterprise has built a reputation for delivering high-quality, fresh vegetables to supermarkets and restaurants nationwide. The enterprise's marketing strategy focuses on exploiting unique selling points of vegetables, emphasizing their refreshing qualities, nutritional benefits, and versatility in various recipes. Despite the growing demand for healthy and sustainable food options, Green Farm is facing a marketing challenge of low brand awareness and commodity perception hence the need for market research. By leveraging social media campaigns, influence partnership, content marketing and trade promotions, the enterprise increased brand awareness, maintained a consistent revenue stream and positioned their vegetables as a premium product. To support the marketing efforts, Green Earth Farm's accounting team provided the following financial information:

Income Statement
Revenue: 1 000 000 zig
Cost of Goods Sold: 600 000 zig
Marketing Expenses: 150 000 zig
Gross Profit: 400 000 zig

(a) Define unique selling point.
(b) Describe three methods which can be used by Green Earth Farm to promote its products.
(c) Using information from the case study, calculate (i) net profit, (ii) net profit margin.
(d) Evaluate two methods which can be used by Green Earth Farm to use resources sustainably.
(e) Discuss the usefulness of an Income Statement to Green Earth Farm.

subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Describe three methods which can be used by Green Earth Farm to promote its products.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Using information from the case study, calculate (i) net profit, (ii) net profit margin.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Unique Selling Point (2 marks):
• A unique selling point (USP) is a feature or characteristic that distinguishes a product or business from its competitors (1 mark) and gives customers a specific reason to choose it over alternatives (1 mark). E.g. Green Earth Farm's vegetables' nutritional benefits and freshness.

(b) Three promotional methods (2 marks each = 6 marks; 1 mark identify + 1 mark describe):
• Social media campaigns — using platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, or X (Twitter) to post content about the vegetables' quality and nutritional benefits, reaching a wide audience at relatively low cost.
• Trade promotions — offering discounts, bulk-buy deals, or point-of-sale displays to supermarkets and restaurants to incentivise stocking and featuring Green Earth Farm's vegetables.
• Influencer partnerships — collaborating with food bloggers or nutritionists who promote the vegetables to their followers, leveraging their credibility and reach.
• Content marketing — creating recipes, nutritional guides, or videos featuring the vegetables, educating consumers and building brand awareness online.
• Direct selling / sampling — offering free samples at supermarkets or food fairs to allow customers to taste the quality directly.

(c) Financial calculations (4 marks):
(i) Net Profit:
Gross Profit = Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold = 1 000 000 − 600 000 = 400 000 zig ✓
Net Profit = Gross Profit − Marketing Expenses = 400 000 − 150 000 = 250 000 zig ✓ (2 marks)

(ii) Net Profit Margin:
Net Profit Margin = (Net Profit / Revenue) × 100
= (250 000 / 1 000 000) × 100 = 25% ✓ (2 marks; award 1 mark for correct formula, 1 mark for correct answer)

(d) Evaluate two sustainable resource-use methods (10 marks; up to 5 marks per method — identify, explain, benefit, limitation, conclusion):
Method 1 — Crop Rotation:
• Involves alternating the types of vegetables grown on a given piece of land each season.
• Benefit: Maintains soil fertility and reduces the need for chemical fertilisers, lowering input costs and protecting long-term productivity.
• Limitation: Requires careful planning and may temporarily reduce output of high-demand crops, affecting revenue.
• Evaluation: Effective for long-term land sustainability but needs agronomic expertise.

Method 2 — Water Conservation / Irrigation Management (e.g. drip irrigation):
• Uses targeted water delivery systems to minimise water wastage in vegetable production.
• Benefit: Reduces water consumption and costs, and protects against water scarcity — important in Gokwe's climate.
• Limitation: High initial capital investment in irrigation infrastructure may strain cash flow.
• Evaluation: Highly appropriate given the agricultural context; long-term savings outweigh initial costs, supporting both profitability and sustainability.

Other acceptable methods: composting, use of renewable energy, integrated pest management, reducing packaging waste.

(e) Discuss the usefulness of an Income Statement to Green Earth Farm (8 marks):
Usefulness:
• Measures profitability — shows gross profit (400 000 zig) and net profit (250 000 zig), enabling management to assess whether the business is generating sufficient returns.
• Performance benchmarking — allows comparison of current performance against previous periods or competitors to identify trends (e.g. whether marketing spend is improving revenue).
• Decision-making tool — reveals the impact of marketing expenses (150 000 zig) on profit, helping managers decide whether to increase or reduce promotional spending.
• Stakeholder communication — lenders, investors, and suppliers use the income statement to assess financial health and creditworthiness, supporting Green Earth Farm's ability to raise finance.
• Identifies cost control opportunities — by highlighting COGS (600 000 zig) as 60% of revenue, management can investigate ways to reduce production costs.

Limitations:
• Historical data only — the income statement reflects past performance and may not predict future profitability in a volatile fresh-produce market.
• Does not show cash position — a profitable business can still face cash flow problems (accruals vs. cash); a cash flow statement is also needed.
• Excludes non-financial information — does not capture brand strength, customer loyalty, or employee productivity, which also affect long-term performance.

Conclusion: The income statement is a vital financial tool for Green Earth Farm, providing key profitability data for management decisions, but it should be used alongside other financial statements (balance sheet, cash flow) for a complete picture.

questions.text:
Case Study 2 – Sports Apparel Manufacturers

Pfeka Afro Sports Co enterprise is a leading manufacturer of sport kits and sportswear in Harare. The enterprise is also investing in a new sporting ground development project to cater for the growing demand for sports and recreational activities in the community. The manager has drawn a business plan for the project. There was an increase in demand for high quality sports facilities due to globalisation. Pfeka Afro Sports Co also navigates the globalized markets to attract top-tier sports events and teams. The new sporting ground development project offers a compelling opportunity for Pfeka Afro Sports Co to create a state-of-the-art sports facility. Apparently, key stakeholders including the local community, sports teams and the government, which are providing funding and support were also involved in sporting ground development. The project faces moderate competition from existing sport facilities, with buyers having moderate bargaining power due to several options available. However, the threat of new entrants is moderate, as high initial investment is required, and suppliers have low bargaining power due to numerous options.

(a) Define the term stakeholders.
(b) Explain the effects of globalisation to Pfeka Afro Sports company.
(c) Describe three sources of finance that are available to Pfeka Afro Sports company.
(d) Assess the benefits of Porter's five forces model to Pfeka Afro Sports company.
(e) Evaluate the importance of human resource planning to Pfeka Afro Sports company.
