questions.topic: Stakeholders, Globalisation, Finance, Strategic Analysis, HRM
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Stakeholders (2 marks):
• Stakeholders are individuals or groups who have an interest in, or are affected by, the activities and decisions of a business (1 mark).
• Examples relevant to Pfeka Afro Sports Co include the local community, sports teams, the government, employees, and suppliers (1 mark for valid example).

(b) Effects of globalisation on Pfeka Afro Sports Co (up to 4 marks; 1 mark per explained effect):
• Access to larger markets — globalisation enables Pfeka Afro Sports Co to attract top-tier international sports events and teams, increasing revenue opportunities beyond the domestic market.
• Increased competition — global brands entering the Zimbabwean sportswear/sports facilities market intensify competition, putting pressure on pricing and quality.
• Access to international investment/funding — globalisation opens doors to foreign direct investment and sponsorship from multinational companies, supporting the sporting ground project.
• Technology transfer — exposure to global best practices in sports facility design and management improves operational standards.
• Supply chain benefits — global sourcing of materials (e.g. synthetic fabrics, equipment) may reduce input costs if international suppliers offer better prices.

(c) Three sources of finance (2 marks each = 6 marks; 1 mark identify + 1 mark describe):
• Government grants/funding — the case study notes the government is providing funding and support; grants do not require repayment and reduce financial risk.
• Bank loans — Pfeka Afro Sports Co can borrow a lump sum from a commercial bank, repaid with interest over an agreed period; suitable for large capital projects like the sporting ground.
• Share capital / equity financing — issuing shares to investors raises capital without repayment obligations; shareholders receive dividends from profits.
• Retained profits — reinvesting profits generated from sportswear manufacturing into the new project; no interest cost but reduces funds available for other uses.
• Community/sponsorship funding — local community organisations or corporate sponsors contribute funds in exchange for naming rights or promotional benefits.

(d) Assess the benefits of Porter's Five Forces model to Pfeka Afro Sports Co (8 marks):
Benefits:
• Competitive rivalry analysis — the model reveals that Pfeka faces moderate competition from existing sports facilities, helping management understand the intensity of competition and plan differentiation strategies (e.g. state-of-the-art facilities).
• Threat of new entrants — identifying that high initial investment creates a moderate barrier to entry assures Pfeka that new competitors will not easily enter, justifying the capital investment.
• Buyer bargaining power — understanding that buyers have moderate bargaining power (due to alternative facilities) guides Pfeka to improve service quality and pricing strategy to retain customers.
• Supplier bargaining power — low supplier bargaining power (many supplier options) means Pfeka can negotiate favourable terms, reducing costs.
• Threat of substitutes — the model prompts Pfeka to consider alternative recreational activities that could reduce demand for its facility, encouraging innovation in offerings.
• Strategic planning tool — overall, the model provides a structured framework for analysing the competitive environment, informing the business plan for the sporting ground project.

Limitations:
• Static analysis — Porter's model is a snapshot; the sports and entertainment industry changes rapidly due to technology and consumer trends.
• Does not address internal capabilities — focuses on external forces, ignoring Pfeka's own strengths and weaknesses (better addressed by SWOT).
• Oversimplification — assigning forces as 'moderate' or 'low' may miss nuances in a complex market.

Conclusion: Porter's Five Forces is a valuable strategic tool for Pfeka Afro Sports Co, especially in evaluating the viability of the sporting ground project, but should be complemented with internal analysis tools.

(e) Evaluate the importance of human resource planning (HRP) to Pfeka Afro Sports Co (10 marks):
Importance of HRP:
• Ensures adequate staffing — with a new sporting ground project, HRP identifies the number and types of staff needed (e.g. facility managers, groundskeepers, coaches), preventing understaffing that could delay the project or reduce service quality.
• Skill gap identification — HRP reveals if current employees lack skills needed for the new facility (e.g. sports event management), enabling targeted recruitment or training.
• Cost management — planning ahead avoids expensive last-minute recruitment; training existing staff is often cheaper than hiring new specialists, protecting profitability.
• Succession planning — as a growing enterprise, HRP ensures leadership continuity by identifying and developing future managers, reducing operational disruption.
• Alignment with business objectives — HRP ensures the workforce is aligned with Pfeka's strategic goals (attracting top-tier sports events), integrating HR strategy with business planning.
• Legal compliance — planning ensures staffing levels meet labour law requirements (e.g. health and safety staffing ratios for sports facilities).

Limitations/Challenges:
• Uncertainty — demand for the sporting ground may fluctuate due to economic conditions or competition, making precise workforce forecasting difficult.
• Cost of planning — conducting detailed HRP (surveys, audits, forecasts) takes time and money, which may strain resources in a growing enterprise.
• Rapid change — globalisation and technology change skill requirements quickly, making long-term HR plans potentially outdated.

Conclusion: HRP is critically important for Pfeka Afro Sports Co, particularly as it expands into sports facility management, an area requiring specialised skills. The benefits of proper workforce planning outweigh the costs, as inadequate staffing could jeopardise both the project's delivery and the enterprise's reputation. However, HRP must be regularly reviewed to remain relevant in a dynamic, globalised market.

questions.text:
A landscape design principle that creates proportionality among design elements is
A scale.
B unity.
C balance.
D focalization.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – scale. Scale refers to the proportional relationship between design elements and their surroundings, ensuring proportionality among elements in a landscape design.

questions.text:
In old civilization, ornamental gardens were cultivated by
A royalty and the wealthy.
B landlords and peasants.
C peasants and commercial farmers.
D commercial farmers and small holder farmers.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – royalty and the wealthy. Historically, ornamental gardens were a luxury afforded only by royalty and the wealthy, who had the resources and land to maintain them.

questions.text:
Select the greatest factor that affects horticultural production.
A wind
B light
C rainfall
D temperature
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – rainfall. Rainfall is generally considered the greatest/most limiting factor affecting horticultural production, as water availability directly controls plant growth, yield, and the viability of production enterprises.

questions.text:
Choose a socio-economic importance of horticulture.
A beautification
B nutritional value
C therapeutic value
D employment creation
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – employment creation. Employment creation is a socio-economic benefit of horticulture. Beautification, nutritional value, and therapeutic value are social/health benefits rather than economic ones.

questions.text:
Select horticultural equipment used in the processing of horticultural products.
A Driers
B Planters
C Dusting machines
D Combine harvesters
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Driers. Driers are used in the processing/post-harvest handling of horticultural products (e.g., drying fruits, vegetables, herbs). Planters, dusting machines, and combine harvesters are field/production equipment.

questions.text:
The ability of a plant cell to regenerate the whole plant is termed as
A germination.
B propagation.
C totipotency.
D layering.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – totipotency. Totipotency is the inherent ability of a single plant cell to regenerate into a complete, whole plant organism, forming the basis of tissue culture techniques.

questions.text:
Choose an advantage of tissue culture.
A Production of exact copies of plants
B Unwanted traits will be produced
C Produce varied types of fruits
D Delayed maturation of plants
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Production of exact copies of plants. Tissue culture produces genetically identical (clonal) copies of the parent plant, ensuring uniformity of desirable traits.

questions.text:
Identify a method commonly used in propagating oranges in Zimbabwe.
A sucker
B cutting
C layering
D budding
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – budding. Budding (specifically T-budding) is the most commonly used commercial method for propagating oranges and other citrus in Zimbabwe, as it maintains varietal characteristics and promotes early bearing.

questions.text:
The Kreb's cycle occurs in the
A matrix.
B cristae.
C cytoplasm.
D mitochondria.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – matrix. The Krebs (citric acid) cycle specifically occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Note: While option D (mitochondria) is the organelle, the more precise answer is A (matrix), which is the specific location within the mitochondria where the cycle takes place.

questions.text:
An apical meristem is formed from
A lateral, intercalary and subapical.
B dermal, vascular and ground stem.
C calyptrogens, periblemium and plerone.
D protoderm, procambium and ground stem.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – calyptrogens, periblemium and plerone. The apical meristem is organised into three histogen layers: calyptrogen (gives rise to root cap), periblem (gives rise to cortex), and plerome (gives rise to the stele/vascular tissue).

questions.text:
How has climate change impacted small holder horticultural production in Zimbabwe?
A increased yield per unit area
B reduced the return per dollar invested
C increased the return per dollar invested
D reduced demand for horticultural produce
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – reduced the return per dollar invested. Climate change (erratic rainfall, droughts, flooding, temperature extremes) has increased production costs and reduced yields for smallholder farmers in Zimbabwe, thereby reducing the return per dollar invested.

questions.text:
Which irrigation system is used in the horticultural industry for frost protection?
A drip irrigation
B flood irrigation
C trickle irrigation
D sprinkler irrigation
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – sprinkler irrigation. Sprinkler irrigation is used for frost protection because water releases latent heat as it freezes on plant surfaces, maintaining the temperature around the plant tissue just above freezing point.

questions.text:
What is the effect of low soil pH on the following plant nutrients?
           Ca, Mg concentration    Fe, Mn concentration
A         Increase                        Decrease
B         Increase                        Increase
C         Decrease                       Increase
D         Decrease                       Decrease
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Ca, Mg concentration: Decrease; Fe, Mn concentration: Increase. At low (acidic) pH, Ca and Mg become less available (leached/displaced), while Fe and Mn become more soluble and available, sometimes to toxic levels.

questions.text:
How does soil compaction affect the following properties?
           Bulk density    Pore space
A         increase           decrease
B         decrease          decrease
C         increase           increase
D         decrease          increase
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Bulk density: increase; Pore space: decrease. Soil compaction forces soil particles closer together, increasing bulk density and reducing pore space (both macro and micro pores are reduced).

questions.text:
Air currents may accelerate the rate of transpiration by
A increasing humidity.
B raising the temperature.
C increasing CO2 concentration.
D preventing water vapour accumulation.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – preventing water vapour accumulation. Air currents remove water vapour from the boundary layer around leaves, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient between the leaf interior and the atmosphere, thereby accelerating transpiration.

questions.text:
The application rate for borax is 30g/10m². Calculate the quantity of fertilizer required in a greenhouse measuring 24 m x 50 m.
A 0.25 kg
B 0.36 kg
C 36.0 kg
D 3.6 kg
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – 3.6 kg. Working: Area of greenhouse = 24 × 50 = 1200 m². Application rate = 30 g per 10 m² = 3 g/m². Total borax required = 1200 × 3 = 3600 g = 3.6 kg.

questions.text:
What is the reason for Zimbabwe banning certain pesticides from use?
A low demand
B price fluctuations
C import challenges
D bio accumulations
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – bio accumulations. Certain pesticides are banned because they bioaccumulate in the food chain (biomagnification), posing serious health risks to humans, animals, and the environment.

questions.text:
Why is crop residue destruction important in horticulture?
A breaks pest life cycle
B maintains field hygiene
C promotes nutrient recycling
D rests a field during off season
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – breaks pest life cycle. Crop residue destruction removes the habitat and food source for pests and pathogens that overwinter or complete their life cycles in old plant material, thereby breaking the pest/disease cycle.

questions.text:
Transmission of horticultural plant diseases into the country is enhanced by
A farm visits.
B high exports.
C high imports.
D retaining seeds.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – high imports. High imports of horticultural produce and plant material increase the risk of introducing exotic pests and diseases into the country, as infected material may bypass phytosanitary controls.

questions.text:
Why is couch grass difficult to control?
A It is deep rooted
B It has a trailing growth habit
C It produces many viable seeds
D It propagates by stolons and rhizomes
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – It propagates by stolons and rhizomes. Couch grass (Cynodon dactylon) is notoriously difficult to control because it spreads vegetatively via both stolons (above-ground runners) and rhizomes (underground stems), making mechanical and chemical control challenging.

questions.text:
Select a method commonly used by small holder horticultural farmers in the aeration of lawns.
A pruning
B mowing
C spiking
D shaping
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – spiking. Spiking (using a garden fork or spiking tool to create holes in the lawn) is the most common method used by smallholder farmers to aerate lawns, improving air, water, and nutrient penetration to grass roots.

questions.text:
Ornamental plant maintenance involves the following.
A planting and irrigation
B pruning and irrigation
C shaping and planting
D pruning and harvesting
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – pruning and irrigation. Ornamental plant maintenance primarily involves pruning (to maintain shape, remove dead wood, stimulate growth) and irrigation (to sustain plant health and aesthetics).

questions.text:
Form as an element of landscaping refers to
A lines used in creating beds and walkways.
B outdoor designs that balance size of buildings.
C geometric shapes or combinations of shapes in landscaping.
D varying textures that add to the atmosphere of an outdoor area.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – geometric shapes or combinations of shapes in landscaping. 'Form' as a landscape design element refers to the three-dimensional shape of plants and structures — their geometric shapes or combinations of shapes that define the overall design.

questions.text:
Interpret design principle of focalization.
A distribution of the design material
B stability resulting from equal distribution of weight
C presents an equal visual weight of elements to a viewer
D creates interest and accent for a particular arrangement
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – creates interest and accent for a particular arrangement. Focalization (also called emphasis or focal point) is the design principle that directs the viewer's attention to a specific point of interest, creating accent and visual focus within the landscape.

questions.text:
The male organ of a flower is called
A dioecious.
B gynaecium.
C androecium.
D monoecious.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – androecium. The androecium is the collective term for the male reproductive organs of a flower (stamens), consisting of the anther and filament. The gynaecium is the female organ.

questions.text:
What role do flowers play in offering condolences at funeral occasions?
A they evoke happiness
B offer love and comfort
C offer comfort and support.
D they beautify the occasion.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – offer comfort and support. At funeral occasions, flowers are traditionally used to offer comfort and support to the bereaved, symbolising sympathy and care.

questions.text:
Cut flowers are generally graded according to stem
A size.
B length.
C diameter.
D base cut.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – length. Cut flowers are primarily graded according to stem length, as this is the main determinant of quality grade and market price in the cut flower industry.

questions.text:
How is pot flower growth affected by the following temperature?
                               day temperature 25°C    day temperature above 30°C
A low vegetative growth      low vegetative growth
B high vegetative growth     high vegetative growth
C high vegetative growth     stunted growth
D low vegetative growth      stunted growth
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – high vegetative growth at 25°C; stunted growth above 30°C. At 25°C, conditions are optimal for vegetative growth of most pot flowers. At temperatures above 30°C, heat stress leads to enzyme denaturation, stomatal closure, and stunted growth.

questions.text:
Select a method of adding value to vegetables.
A Drying
B Thinning
C Harvesting
D Advertising
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Drying. Drying is a value-addition process that extends shelf life, reduces weight for transport, and can increase the market value of vegetables. Thinning and harvesting are production/agronomic practices; advertising is marketing.

questions.text:
The following transactions were extracted from a vegetable farmer's diary. Use the information to answer question 30.
15/03/23 Purchased fertilizers for $120-00
         Paid land preparation costs $130-00
20/03/23 Bought cabbage seedlings for $100-00
         Paid labour for transplanting $40-00
         Purchased pesticides for $50-00
5/05/15  Paid management costs $40-00
1/07/23  Paid harvesting labour costs $60-00
         Sold 3000 heads at $0.50 $1500-00
Calculate the total costs for the enterprise.
A 2040
B 1500
C 640
D 540
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – 640. Total costs = Fertilizers ($120) + Land preparation ($130) + Seedlings ($100) + Transplanting labour ($40) + Pesticides ($50) + Management costs ($40) + Harvesting labour ($60) = $540. Note: The revenue of $1500 is not a cost. The closest matching answer for total costs is C ($640) or D ($540). Strictly summing all cost items: 120+130+100+40+50+40+60 = $540, making D the correct answer. Answer: D – $540.

questions.text:
The reason for low vegetable consumption in Zimbabwe is
A consumer preferences.
B unavailability of vegetables.
C low production levels of vegetables.
D high production cost of vegetables.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – consumer preferences. Low vegetable consumption in Zimbabwe is primarily attributed to consumer preferences (cultural dietary habits favouring starchy staples over vegetables), rather than unavailability or production constraints.

questions.text:
Select a method most commonly used by indigenous farmers in the preservation of vegetables.
A boiling
B drying
C spicing
D frying
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – drying. Drying (sun-drying) is the most traditional and commonly used method by indigenous/smallholder farmers in Zimbabwe to preserve vegetables (e.g., dried cowpea leaves, dried pumpkin leaves), as it requires no specialised equipment.

questions.text:
The main factor considered for apple production in the Eastern Highlands of Zimbabwe is
A fertile soils in the region.
B ready market for apples.
C cool and humid conditions.
D favourable soil pH of 5.8 to 6.5.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – cool and humid conditions. Apples require cool temperatures (chilling requirements for dormancy breaking) and the Eastern Highlands' cool, humid climate is the main factor that makes the region suitable for apple production in Zimbabwe.

questions.text:
What is the most important factor that determines mode of transport to the market for horticultural produce?
A fuel cost
B road network
C product value
D product volume
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – product value. The value of the horticultural product is the most important factor in determining the mode of transport; high-value perishables (e.g., cut flowers, exotic fruits) may justify expensive/faster transport modes, while low-value bulk produce uses cheaper options.

questions.text:
The importance of fruit production to the country is
A food.
B educational purposes.
C employment creation.
D foreign currency generation.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – foreign currency generation. At national level, the most significant economic importance of fruit production is foreign currency generation through exports, contributing to the national economy.

questions.text:
A propagation method suitable for commercial mango production is
A suckering.
B budding.
C grafting.
D cutting.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – grafting. Grafting (particularly veneer grafting or epicotyl grafting) is the most widely used commercial propagation method for mango, as it produces true-to-type plants with early bearing and desirable characteristics.

questions.text:
When herbs on the landscape provide pleasing scents in the environment, they are classified as
A culinary.
B ornament.
C fragrance.
D medicinal.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – fragrance. Herbs that are primarily valued for providing pleasing scents/aromas in the landscape environment are classified as fragrance herbs (e.g., lavender, rosemary used for scent).

questions.text:
An appropriate production system for herb and spice in the greenhouse is
A raft water culture.
B the Gerick's system.
C ground culture and container culture.
D soilless culture and ground culture.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – ground culture and container culture. For herbs and spices in greenhouses, ground culture (growing directly in greenhouse beds/soil) and container culture (pots, troughs) are the most appropriate and practical production systems.

questions.text:
Which crop is propagated by cloves?
A onion
B garlic
C ginger
D mustard
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – garlic. Garlic (Allium sativum) is propagated by individual cloves, which are the segments that make up the garlic bulb. Each clove is planted to produce a new plant.

questions.text:
Cat facing disorder in green pepper is caused by
A nutrient deficiency.
B both stamens and pistil.
C exposure of fruits to periods of drought before maturity.
D exposure of the plant to cool temperatures at the time of flower initiation.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – exposure of the plant to cool temperatures at the time of flower initiation. Cat facing in pepper (and tomato) is a physiological disorder caused by exposure to cool/cold temperatures during flower initiation/development, resulting in deformed, scarred, or puckered fruit surfaces.

questions.text:
1 (a)(i) Define the term underflow with respect to binary representation.
(a)(ii) Discuss the impact of underflow on precision.
(b) Compare the efficiency of ASCII and Unicode as data representation schemes for storing a single character.
(c)(i) Convert the decimal number 109 to 8-bit binary.
(c)(ii) Assess the implication of using fixed-width representation for computing and data processing.

subParts.text: Define the term underflow with respect to binary representation.
subParts.label: (a)(i)

subParts.text: Discuss the impact of underflow on precision.
subParts.label: (a)(ii)

subParts.text: Compare the efficiency of ASCII and Unicode as data representation schemes for storing a single character.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Convert the decimal number 109 to 8-bit binary.
subParts.label: (c)(i)

subParts.text: Assess the implication of using fixed-width representation for computing and data processing.
subParts.label: (c)(ii)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Underflow occurs when the result of a calculation is too small (close to zero) to be represented in the available number of bits / falls below the minimum representable value in the given binary format. [2 marks]

(a)(ii) Underflow forces the result to be rounded to zero or the smallest representable value, reducing precision; calculations lose accuracy because tiny differences between values cannot be distinguished, leading to significant errors especially in iterative computations. [2 marks]

(b) ASCII uses 7 or 8 bits per character (1 byte) while Unicode uses 16 or more bits (2–4 bytes). ASCII is more storage-efficient for a single character requiring less memory, but Unicode supports a far larger character set (over 1 million code points) covering multiple languages and symbols, whereas ASCII is limited to 128/256 characters. [2 marks]

(c)(i) 109 ÷ 2 repeatedly: 109 = 64+32+8+4+1 → 01101101₂ [2 marks]
Worked: 109−64=45, 45−32=13, 13−8=5, 5−4=1, 1−1=0 → bits set at positions 6,5,3,2,0 → 01101101

(c)(ii) Fixed-width representation:
• Simplifies hardware design and memory allocation — all values occupy the same storage space, making addressing predictable. [1]
• Limits the range of values that can be stored — numbers outside the fixed range cannot be represented, causing overflow/underflow. [1]
• Can waste memory when storing small values, as unused bits are padded. [1]
• Consistent performance in arithmetic operations since operand size is always known, improving processing speed. [1] [4 marks]

questions.text:
Normalise the following floating point numbers. (NB: the bits for mantissa is 8 and bits for the exponent is 4.)
(i) 0.0001000 0001₂
(ii) 11011.101 1001₂

subParts.text: Normalise the floating point number: 0.0001000 0001₂ (mantissa 8 bits, exponent 4 bits)
subParts.label: (i)

subParts.text: Normalise the floating point number: 11011.101 1001₂ (mantissa 8 bits, exponent 4 bits)
subParts.label: (ii)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
For a normalised positive floating point number the mantissa must start 0.1… and for a negative number 1.0…

(i) 0.0001000 with exponent 0001₂
Shift mantissa left 3 places so that the first significant bit is immediately after the binary point:
Normalised mantissa: 0.1000000 (8 bits)
Exponent must be adjusted: original exponent 0001, subtract 3 → exponent = 0001 − 0011 = 1110 (in 4-bit two's complement = −2) — CHECK: 0.1000000 × 2^(−2) = 0.001000 × 2^0 ✓
Answer: Mantissa = 0.1000000, Exponent = 1110 [2 marks]

(ii) 11011.101 with exponent 1001₂
The number is negative (starts with 1). For normalisation of a negative number, the mantissa should be 1.0…
Shift mantissa right 4 places (add 4 to exponent):
Normalised mantissa: 1.1011101 (8 bits)
New exponent: 1001 + 0100 = 1101 (i.e. original exponent value + 4)
Answer: Mantissa = 1.1011101, Exponent = 1101 [2 marks]

questions.text:
(a) For the IP address 192.100.18.33:
(i) identify the class of the IP address,
(ii) state the subnet mask of the IP address,
(iii) convert the IP address in (ii) to binary format.
(b) For the following URL http://www.zimsec.co.zw/Exams/computer science.pdf identify all the parts of the URL.
(c) Evaluate the role of Domain Name System (DNS) in network addressing.

subParts.text: For the IP address 192.100.18.33, identify the class of the IP address.
subParts.label: (a)(i)

subParts.text: For the IP address 192.100.18.33, state the subnet mask of the IP address.
subParts.label: (a)(ii)

subParts.label: (a)(iii)

subParts.label: (b)

subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) 192 falls in the range 192–223, therefore it is a Class C IP address. [1]

(a)(ii) Default subnet mask for Class C: 255.255.255.0 [1]

(a)(iii) Binary conversion of 255.255.255.0:
255 = 11111111
255 = 11111111
255 = 11111111
0   = 00000000
Answer: 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000 [2]

(b) Parts of the URL http://www.zimsec.co.zw/Exams/computer science.pdf:
• http — Protocol/scheme (the communication protocol used) [1]
• www — World Wide Web subdomain [1]
• zimsec.co.zw — Domain name (second-level: zimsec; top-level country code: co.zw) [1]
• /Exams/ — Directory/path on the server [1]
• computer science.pdf — File name / resource being accessed [1] (any 4 correctly identified parts for 4 marks)

(c) DNS translates human-readable domain names (e.g. www.zimsec.co.zw) into numerical IP addresses that computers use to locate each other on a network. Without DNS, users would have to remember complex IP addresses. DNS therefore enables seamless and user-friendly network addressing, improves efficiency by caching resolved addresses, and is hierarchical allowing distributed management of address space. [2 marks — 1 for the translation function, 1 for evaluative point on importance/impact]

questions.text:
NOCZIM has benefited from cloud computing for data backup.
(a) Describe two cloud service models.
(b) Explain two disadvantages of cloud computing.

subParts.text: Describe two cloud service models.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Explain two disadvantages of cloud computing.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any two of the following (3 marks each = 6 marks):

1. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) — Provides virtualised computing infrastructure (servers, storage, networking) over the internet. Users rent hardware resources and manage their own operating systems and applications. Example: Amazon Web Services EC2. [3]

2. Platform as a Service (PaaS) — Provides a platform and environment for developers to build, test and deploy applications without managing underlying infrastructure. The provider manages the hardware and OS. Example: Google App Engine. [3]

3. Software as a Service (SaaS) — Delivers software applications over the internet on a subscription basis. Users access the software via a browser without installing it locally. The provider manages everything. Example: Google Docs, Microsoft 365. [3]

(b) Any two (2 marks each = 4 marks):
1. Security and privacy risks — Data stored on third-party servers is vulnerable to unauthorised access, hacking or data breaches; the organisation loses direct control over sensitive data. [2]
2. Dependence on internet connectivity — Cloud services require a reliable internet connection; any downtime or slow connectivity disrupts access to data and applications, affecting business operations. [2]
3. Ongoing costs — Subscription/usage fees can accumulate over time, potentially becoming more expensive than owning infrastructure outright. [2]
4. Vendor lock-in — Migrating data and services from one cloud provider to another can be complex and costly. [2]

questions.topic: Computer Architecture — Harvard Architecture, FDE Cycle, Von Neumann Model
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) In Harvard Architecture, separate physical memory and buses exist for instructions and data. This allows the CPU to fetch the next instruction and read/write data simultaneously, eliminating the bottleneck (von Neumann bottleneck) where instruction fetch and data access compete for the same bus. This parallelism increases throughput and processing speed. It also improves security since instruction memory can be made read-only. Overall system performance is enhanced because the processor spends less time waiting for memory access. [4 marks — 1 per valid point up to 4]

(b) Fetch/Decode/Execute cycle using registers:
FETCH:
• The address in the Program Counter (PC) is copied to the Memory Address Register (MAR). [1]
• The PC is incremented to point to the next instruction. [1]
• The instruction stored at that address is fetched from main memory and placed in the Memory Data Register (MDR)/Memory Buffer Register (MBR). [1]
• The instruction is transferred from MDR to the Current Instruction Register (CIR). [1]
DECODE:
• The Control Unit (CU) decodes the instruction in the CIR, identifying the opcode and operand. [1]
EXECUTE:
• The appropriate operation is carried out — e.g. the ALU performs arithmetic/logic, data is read from or written to memory/registers using the MAR and MDR, or data is moved between registers. [2]
[7 marks total]

(c) Three buses in the Von Neumann model (2 marks each = 6 marks):
1. Address Bus (unidirectional, CPU→Memory) — carries the memory address of the instruction or data to be accessed. A wider address bus allows access to more memory locations, increasing addressable memory and system capacity.
2. Data Bus (bidirectional) — transfers actual data/instructions between CPU, memory and I/O devices. A wider data bus increases the amount of data transferred per cycle, improving throughput.
3. Control Bus (bidirectional) — carries control signals (read/write, clock, interrupts) from the CU to coordinate the activities of all components. Without it, components would not know when to send/receive data, making orderly execution impossible.

questions.topic: Data Integrity, Data Protection and Security
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Data integrity refers to the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of data over its entire lifecycle — ensuring that data is not altered, corrupted or lost during storage, processing or transmission. [1]

(b)(i) Any three data protection principles (1 mark each):
1. Data must be collected and processed fairly and lawfully.
2. Data must be kept accurate and up to date.
3. Data must be kept secure and protected against unauthorised access or loss.
4. Data should only be used for the specified, explicit and legitimate purpose for which it was collected.
5. Data should not be kept longer than necessary.
6. Data subjects have the right to access their own data.
[3 marks]

(b)(ii) Two effects of not obeying data protection principles (2 marks each = 4 marks):
1. Legal consequences — The doctor may face prosecution, fines or loss of medical licence for violating data protection laws (e.g., breaching patient confidentiality). [2]
2. Loss of patient trust — Patients may lose confidence in the doctor/healthcare system, reducing willingness to share sensitive health information, which could negatively impact healthcare quality. [2]

(b)(iii) Example: Fingerprint recognition.
How it works: A sensor scans the user's fingerprint and converts the unique ridge patterns into a digital template. This template is compared with a stored template in the database; if they match, access is granted. The technique is difficult to forge since fingerprints are unique to each individual. [2 marks — 1 for naming the technique, 1 for correct explanation]

  id INT PRIMARY KEY

subParts.text: Explain the term data redundancy giving a suitable characteristic which leads to it.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text:
Explain the following SQL command:
CREATE TABLE Students (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY
  name VARCHAR(255));
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Data redundancy is the unnecessary duplication of the same data in multiple places within a database or information system. A characteristic that leads to it is poor database design / lack of normalisation — when data is stored in a single flat table rather than being split into related tables, the same data values (e.g. a student's name) are repeated across many records. [2 marks — 1 for definition, 1 for characteristic]

(b) Explanation of the SQL command (1 mark per valid point, up to 7):
• CREATE TABLE — SQL DDL command used to create a new table in the database. [1]
• Students — the name of the table being created. [1]
• id — the name of the first column/field. [1]
• INT — specifies the data type of 'id' as an integer (whole number). [1]
• PRIMARY KEY — constraint indicating that 'id' is the primary key of the table; it must be unique and not null, used to uniquely identify each record. [1]
• name — the name of the second column/field. [1]
• VARCHAR(255) — specifies the data type of 'name' as a variable-length character string with a maximum length of 255 characters. [1]
[Total: 7 marks]

(c) Five ways Computer Science helps engineers in prototype simulation (1 mark each):

5. Data processing and algorithms allow engineers to optimise designs by analysing large datasets from simulations to find the most efficient parameters.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Award 1 mark each for correct identification of HS3 and HS4. Likely specimen examples: HS3 — a xerophytic/succulent weed e.g. Purslane (Portulaca oleracea) or Khaki weed (Alternanthera pungens); HS4 — a perennial weed that reproduces vegetatively e.g. Couch grass (Cynodon dactylon) or Nutgrass (Cyperus rotundus / Cyperus esculentus). Accept any correct identification that matches the actual specimens provided.

(a)(ii) Differentiation (award 1 mark per valid contrasting point up to 6 marks, i.e. 3 contrasting pairs):
- Leaf shape/structure: HS3 may have succulent/fleshy leaves vs HS4 may have narrow/grass-like leaves.
- Stem type: HS3 may have a fleshy/prostrate stem vs HS4 may have stolons/rhizomes/tubers.
- Root system: HS3 may have a taproot vs HS4 may have fibrous/rhizomatous roots.
- Life cycle: HS3 may be annual vs HS4 may be perennial.
- Reproduction: HS3 may reproduce mainly by seed vs HS4 may reproduce vegetatively.
- Classification: HS3 may be a broadleaf/dicot vs HS4 may be a grass/monocot.

(b)(i) HS3 survives in dry conditions because it has succulent/fleshy stems or leaves that store water / has a thick waxy cuticle to reduce water loss / has CAM photosynthesis / has deep or extensive root system to access soil moisture. (1 mark for any valid reason matching the specimen.)

(b)(ii) Any two dispersal methods: by wind (anemochory) — seeds have hairs/pappus; by animals (zoochory) — seeds stick to fur/feathers or ingested and excreted; by water (hydrochory) — seeds float; by humans — seeds carried on clothing/machinery; by explosive dehiscence — seeds ejected from capsules. (1 mark each × 2 = 2 marks.)

(b)(iii) HS4 reproduces asexually by: stolons (above-ground runners) / rhizomes (below-ground stems) / tubers / bulbs / fragmentation of root/stem pieces. (1 mark for valid method matching specimen.)

(b)(iv) Difficult to control HS4 because: smallholder farmers lack access to herbicides / cannot afford herbicides; tillage/hand-hoeing breaks up rhizomes/stolons into fragments each capable of regenerating new plants; lack of knowledge of effective control methods; perennial nature means it regrows from underground structures even after top growth is removed; any two points × 1 mark = 2 marks.

(c) Effects of weeds on horticultural plants (any 4 × 1 mark = 4 marks):
- Competition for water, nutrients, light and space reducing crop growth and yield.
- Act as alternate hosts for pests and diseases that infect crops.
- Some weeds are allelopathic — release chemicals that inhibit crop germination/growth.
- Weeds increase cost of production (labour/herbicide costs).
- Weeds may physically smother/shade crop plants reducing photosynthesis.
- Reduce quality of harvested produce and increase post-harvest losses.

(d) Importance of IWM (any 2 valid points × 1 mark = 2 marks):
- Combines cultural, biological, mechanical and chemical methods reducing over-reliance on herbicides.
- Reduces development of herbicide resistance in weed populations.
- Environmentally friendly / reduces chemical pollution of soil and water.
- More cost-effective in the long term for the farmer.
- Sustainable weed management that preserves soil health and biodiversity.

subParts.label: (a)(i)

subParts.label: (a)(ii)

subParts.label: (b)(i)

subParts.text: Calculate the bulk density of HS5 and HS6. HS5, HS6.
subParts.label: (b)(ii)

subParts.text: Given that the soil has a particle density of 2.6 g cm⁻³, calculate the porosity of HS5 and HS6. HS5, HS6.

subParts.label: (e)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) & (a)(ii): Candidate records actual mass (in grams) of HS5 and HS6 as weighed. Award 1 mark each for a reading recorded with correct units (g). Expected: HS5 (compacted) will have a higher mass; HS6 (organic matter field) will have a lower mass.

(b)(i) Volume of core:
Formula: V = πr²h, where diameter = 6 cm → radius r = 3 cm, height h = 5 cm.
V = π × 3² × 5 = π × 9 × 5 = 45π ≈ 141.37 cm³.
Award 1 mark for correct formula/substitution and 1 mark for correct answer ≈ 141.4 cm³ (accept 141.3–141.4 cm³).

(b)(ii) Bulk Density:
Formula: Bulk Density (BD) = Mass of oven-dry soil (g) ÷ Volume of core (cm³).
HS5 (compacted): BD = mass of HS5 ÷ 141.4 g cm⁻³. Expected BD ≈ 1.4–1.8 g cm⁻³ (higher, compacted).
HS6 (organic matter): BD = mass of HS6 ÷ 141.4 g cm⁻³. Expected BD ≈ 0.9–1.3 g cm⁻³ (lower, organic).
Award 1 mark for correct formula/substitution and 1 mark for correct calculated value with units for each sample (2 marks per sample, 4 marks total).

(c) Porosity:
Formula: Porosity (%) = (1 − Bulk Density / Particle Density) × 100.
Particle Density = 2.6 g cm⁻³.
HS5: Porosity = (1 − BD_HS5 / 2.6) × 100. Expected ≈ 30–45% (lower porosity, compacted).
HS6: Porosity = (1 − BD_HS6 / 2.6) × 100. Expected ≈ 50–65% (higher porosity, organic).
Award 1 mark for correct formula/substitution and 1 mark for correct answer with % for each sample (2 marks per sample, 4 marks total).

(d) Problems associated with compacted soil (HS5) in horticultural production (any 3 × 1 mark = 3 marks):
- Poor water infiltration and drainage leading to waterlogging / surface runoff.
- Restricted root penetration and growth leading to shallow root systems.
- Reduced aeration/gaseous exchange inhibiting root respiration and microbial activity.
- Reduced water and nutrient holding capacity.
- Increased susceptibility to erosion from surface runoff.
- Difficult/expensive to till — increased fuel/labour costs.
- Reduced germination and seedling emergence.

(e) Management practices to improve soil structure of HS5 (compacted soil): (5 marks — award marks for relevant, well-explained points; expect at least some distinction between communal and commercial practices.)

Communal farmers:
- Addition of organic matter/manure/compost — improves soil structure, adds humus, increases porosity and biological activity.
- Minimum tillage / conservation tillage — reduces further compaction.
- Mulching — protects soil surface, reduces compaction from rain impact, adds organic matter on decomposition.
- Crop rotation with deep-rooted crops — roots break up compacted layers.
- Ripping/subsoiling using ox-drawn rippers — breaks up hardpan/compacted layer.
- Avoiding overgrazing and heavy traffic on wet soils.

Commercial farmers:
- Deep ripping/subsoiling with tractor-mounted subsoilers to break up compacted subsoil/hardpan.
- Application of lime (if acidic) — improves soil structure and flocculation.
- Cover cropping/green manuring — adds organic matter, roots break compaction.
- Controlled traffic farming — restrict heavy machinery to designated lanes to prevent widespread compaction.
- Use of gypsum (calcium sulphate) to improve soil structure in sodic/compacted soils.
- Incorporation of large quantities of organic matter mechanically.

(Award 1 mark per valid, explained point up to 5 marks. Credit answers that specifically distinguish communal vs commercial context.)

questions.text: Your teenage nephew has a birthday party. As part of the entertainment for the event, you decide to do a performance as a clown. Present the performance in which the clown plays the role of an aunt or uncle advising teenagers.
questions.topic: Solo Performance / Physical Theatre / Character Portrayal
questions.aiModelAnswer: Marking focuses on: (1) Convincing clown characterisation — use of costume, physical comedy, exaggerated movement, mime and voice. (2) Relevance of advice given to teenagers — content should be meaningful, age-appropriate and clearly communicated through performance. (3) Audience engagement — use of humour, improvisation and direct address to maintain entertainment value. (4) Structure — clear beginning, middle and end within the 10–15 minute timeframe. (5) Supporting write-up (200–250 words) outlining preparation process, rehearsal decisions, characterisation choices and performance goals. Mark bands typically: Distinction (80–100): Highly polished, confident, creative, fully in character, advice clearly communicated; Good (60–79): Competent characterisation, advice communicated, some lapses; Satisfactory (40–59): Basic clown elements present, advice partially communicated; Poor (below 40): Little characterisation, unclear communication.

(2) Effectiveness in capturing the spirit and cultural diversity of the Intwasa Arts Festival. (3) Quality of lead performer role — confidence, stage presence, ability to transition between genres. Mark bands: Distinction (80–100): All five+ genres expertly integrated, compelling lead performance, highly promotional and engaging; Good (60–79): Five genres present, competent lead, generally engaging; Satisfactory (40–59): Fewer than five genres or weak integration; Poor (below 40): Minimal genre variety, weak characterisation.

questions.text: While visiting a historical monument, you unknowingly violate a traditional custom for which some appeasement has to be performed. Perform the appeasement ceremony. Use elements of music, dance and physical theatre.

questions.aiModelAnswer: Marking focuses on: (1) Convincing depiction of a traditional appeasement ceremony — cultural authenticity, ritual structure (acknowledgement of violation, appeal/prayer, offering, resolution). (2) Integration of all three required elements: music (vocal or instrumental), dance (movement with cultural resonance), and physical theatre (expressive body movement, mime, gesture). (3) Narrative clarity — the audience should understand the context (visiting a monument, violation of custom, need for appeasement). (4) Commitment and believability — performer's engagement with the ritual space and atmosphere. (5) Supporting write-up (200–250 words) explaining preparation process, cultural references used, and how the three elements were incorporated. Mark bands: Distinction (80–100): Highly immersive, all three elements expertly woven in, culturally rich and authentic; Good (60–79): All three elements present, clear ritual narrative; Satisfactory (40–59): One or two elements weak or missing; Poor (below 40): Minimal ritual structure, elements largely absent.

questions.text:
With the help of a colleague, present a performance based on the extract below;

Setting: Semi rural area, at Atete Rutendo's home. On the upper right is the entrance to the kitchen and on the lower right is the exit. There is a window in between. On the left is one door leading to Atete Rutendo's bedroom. There is a coffee table in the middle with three chairs around it. On the coffee table is a container with peanuts to be shelled. It is a Saturday morning. Atete is seated in the middle chair shelling peanuts. She jumps off her seat all of a sudden and peeps through the window.

Atete Rutendo: Oh my muzukuru, I pity you. Marrying for love is old-fashioned but the only way. This is why there are so many unhappy marriages and broken homes nowadays. People now marry for money and not love.
Rudo: I suppose you married for love in your days?
Atete Rutendo: We married out of a social need. (Rudo looks at watch. About to stand up) You must be excited. In fact you look excited.
Rudo: I wonder. (As if she has remembered something) Incidentally, Atete, I had a dream. Well, (Dismissing the matter) we don't need to take dreams too seriously, do we?
Atete Rutendo: You dreamed of him?
Rudo: (Laughing) Leo-James. (More seriously) No, I saw Tambu.
Atete Rutendo: (Shocked) Who?
Rudo: Tambudzayi. My late sister Tambudzayi.
Atete Rutendo: (Stops shelling and shows concern) What was the dream about?
Rudo: (Recalling and making gestures) I was with her family. Her husband, Togara, was seated on my left. Tambudzayi was seated opposite me. Her two children, Nyasha and Ruvimbo, were on my right. We were having a meal. Before we had even finished, she disappeared. She left me with her family. Then I woke up. (Atete has a pensive look) You look worried. What could be the matter? Can the dream be of any significance?
Atete Rutendo: I think Tambu wants you to join her family. You know what she said five years ago before she died?
Rudo: (Flippantly) I'll defy that, I am aware of what she said of course. She left the instruction that Togara should not marry any other woman except me.
Atete Rutendo: Yes, Tambudzayi knew she was going to die. The doctors had indicated to her that her disease was incurable. She was worried about her children. Ruvimbo was seven years old then and Nyasha was only four. She left her husband with the instruction that he should marry you for the sake of the children. Togara has no choice except to marry you.
Rudo: (Emphatically) but I don't love him. I want to get married to Leo.
Atete Rutendo: These are the words of a dead person. They should be considered seriously.
Rudo: I'll simply take care of the children.
Atete Rutendo: Remember, since your sister died, Togara has been responsible for you, your clothing, your education and everything until you become of marriageable age.
Rudo: (Surprised) I don't believe it. I thought my father was. That's incredible. Leo wants to marry me in five years' time when I've completed my degree.
Atete Rutendo: Togara has not indicated when he wishes to take you. You may proceed with your education. When are you expecting your Form Four results?
Rudo: In six weeks' time … (Sound of a bus is heard. Atete and Rudo stand up hurriedly. Atete accidentally drops container onto floor. Rudo rushes left to the bedroom)
Atete Rutendo: (Pacing up and down confused) Hurry! Hurry! That's why I said it's better to be at the bus stop early. (Rudo re-enters carrying handbag and raincoat and still combing her hair. Exits right and Atete Rutendo rushes after her as far as the door. She returns and starts collecting peanuts from the floor. Before she finished, a knock is heard) Come in! (Stands up with container in her left hand to welcome the visitor. Togara enters right) What a lovely surprise to see you, Togara my muzukuru. (The two shake hands)

Adapted from: I will wait by Bertha Msora
questions.topic: Script Interpretation / Dramatic Performance / Character Development

(2) Faithfulness to the script — stage directions followed (shelling peanuts, peeping through window, dropping container, combing hair, entrances/exits). (3) Use of space — correct spatial arrangement as per the stage setting described (kitchen upper right, exit lower right, bedroom left, coffee table centre). (4) Emotional depth — communication of the central tension (forced marriage vs. love marriage; tradition vs. modernity; duty vs. desire). (5) Pacing and dynamics — natural dialogue delivery, effective use of pauses, reactions. (6) Ensemble work — quality of interaction and listening between the two performers. (7) Supporting write-up (200–250 words) explaining rehearsal process, character interpretation, and directorial/staging decisions. Mark bands: Distinction (80–100): Highly naturalistic, emotionally nuanced, excellent use of space and stage directions; Good (60–79): Clear characterisation, stage directions mostly observed, engaging; Satisfactory (40–59): Basic delivery, some stage directions missed; Poor (below 40): Flat delivery, stage directions largely ignored.

questions.text:
Using the extract below, film this short scene from Romeo and Juliet experimenting with different shots, angles and focusing techniques. Present a write up justifying your shots.

LADY CAPULET: Marry, that 'marry' is the very theme I came to talk of. Tell me, daughter Juliet, How stands your disposition to be married?
JULIET: It is an honour that I dream not of.
NURSE: An honour! were not I thine only nurse, I would say thou hadst suck'd wisdom from thy teat.
LADY CAPULET: Well, think of marriage now younger than you, Here in Verona, ladies of esteem, Are made already mothers: by my count. I was your mother much upon these years. That you are now a maid. Thus then in brief. The valiant Paris seeks you for his love.

questions.topic: Film Studies / Cinematography / Shot Types and Angles
