questions.text: Question 1: Applied Theatre, Boal, and Commercial Theatre

subParts.text: Give any four performance techniques suggested by Augusto Boal.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Explain the role of Applied Theatre in addressing social problems in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain any four possible ways of promoting Commercial Theatre in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any four of: Forum Theatre (audience members can replace actors to explore solutions); Image Theatre (use of frozen body images to represent oppression/situations); Invisible Theatre (performed in public spaces without audience awareness it is theatre); Legislative Theatre (theatre used to influence law-making); Rainbow of Desire (therapeutic technique exploring inner conflicts); Newspaper Theatre (dramatising news stories); Cop in the Head (addressing internalised oppression). [1 mark each, up to 4]

(b) Applied Theatre uses theatrical techniques outside conventional theatre spaces to address real community issues. Key points: (1) Theatre for Development (TfD) — used in health campaigns e.g. HIV/AIDS awareness, maternal health education in rural Zimbabwe; (2) Forum Theatre enables communities to rehearse solutions to problems such as domestic violence, corruption, or gender inequality; (3) Applied Theatre gives voice to marginalised communities, allowing them to articulate grievances and advocate for change; (4) Used in schools and prisons for rehabilitation and behavioural change; (5) Facilitates dialogue between community members and policymakers; (6) Encourages critical thinking and civic participation; (7) NGOs and organisations like CHIPAWO use Applied Theatre to address child rights and education. [8 marks — award 2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

(c) Any four of: (1) Sponsorship and partnerships — seeking corporate sponsorship from local businesses and multinationals to fund productions; (2) Marketing and social media promotion — using platforms like Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp to advertise shows and build audiences; (3) Ticketing and pricing strategies — offering affordable ticket prices, group discounts, and online ticket sales to widen accessibility; (4) Establishing dedicated theatre venues — building or maintaining professional theatre spaces to attract audiences; (5) Producing high-quality, relevant content that appeals to local tastes and international markets; (6) Collaborating with schools and universities to build theatre-going culture among the youth; (7) Creating theatre festivals and competitions to raise the profile of commercial theatre; (8) Government policy support — lobbying for grants, tax incentives, and cultural policies that support the arts. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

questions.text: Question 2: Loglines, Scripts, and Characterisation

subParts.text: State four key elements of a logline.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Explain the significance of a script in theatre technical design.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: How does a script form a basis for characterisation.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any four of: (1) Protagonist — the main character whose journey the story follows; (2) Goal/Objective — what the protagonist wants to achieve; (3) Antagonist/Conflict — the opposing force or central problem; (4) Stakes — what is at risk if the protagonist fails; (5) Setting/World — the context or world in which the story takes place; (6) Tone/Genre — the emotional feel or genre of the piece. [1 mark each, up to 4]

(b) The script is the foundational document for all technical design decisions. Key points: (1) Set Design — the script's stage directions, settings, and scene descriptions guide the set designer in creating appropriate environments; (2) Lighting Design — the mood, time of day, and location described in the script inform lighting cues, colour choices, and intensity; (3) Sound Design — the script identifies required sound effects, music cues, and ambient sounds necessary for the production; (4) Costume Design — character descriptions and historical/cultural context in the script guide costume choices; (5) Props — the script specifies objects actors interact with, directing the props master; (6) Technical cues — stage directions provide the basis for the production's technical cue sheet; (7) Communication tool — the script ensures all technical departments work cohesively towards a unified artistic vision. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

(c) Key points: (1) Character descriptions — the playwright's notes and descriptions give actors a starting point for physical and vocal characterisation; (2) Dialogue — the words a character speaks reveal their personality, education, social status, and emotional state; (3) Relationships — the script shows how characters interact, informing status, power dynamics, and emotional connections; (4) Objectives and motivations — the script reveals what each character wants and why, driving actorly choices; (5) Arc and development — the script maps a character's journey and transformation, allowing the actor to track emotional growth; (6) Subtext — what characters do not say directly gives actors material to explore inner life; (7) Stage directions — provide physical actions that reveal character behaviour and psychology. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

questions.text: Question 3: Masks, Cinematography, and Costume Design

subParts.text: Identify any four natural resources which an artist can use to create masks for theatrical performances.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Outline the technical equipment needed by a cinematographer for a film shoot.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: How can a theatre artist express cultural identity through costume design.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.topic: Theatre Design, Cinematography, and Cultural Identity
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any four of: Wood (carved from trees); Clay/mud; Animal hides/skin; Feathers; Grass/reeds; Bark; Gourds/calabash; Papier-mâché (from natural plant-based paper); Stones/pebbles; Bones. [1 mark each, up to 4]

(b) Key technical equipment: (1) Camera body (digital cinema camera e.g. ARRI, RED, or DSLR) — captures images; (2) Lenses (wide-angle, telephoto, prime, zoom) — control field of view and depth of field; (3) Tripod/fluid head — provides stable shots and smooth pan/tilt movements; (4) Camera stabiliser/gimbal or Steadicam — allows smooth handheld movement; (5) Lighting equipment (LED panels, HMI lights, reflectors, diffusers) — controls exposure and mood; (6) Audio equipment (boom microphone, lapel mics, audio recorder) — captures clean sound on location; (7) Memory cards/storage media — records footage; (8) Filters (ND filters, polarising filters) — control light and glare; (9) Monitor/viewfinder — allows the cinematographer to review framing and exposure; (10) Batteries and power supply — ensures uninterrupted operation. [1 mark per valid piece of equipment with brief explanation, up to 8]

(c) Key points: (1) Use of traditional fabrics and materials — e.g. Zimbabwean chitenge/shweshwe fabric immediately communicates African cultural identity; (2) Colour symbolism — certain colours carry cultural meaning (e.g. black for mourning, white for purity in specific traditions); (3) Traditional adornments — incorporation of beadwork, headwear (e.g. doeks, feathered headdresses), and jewellery signify ethnic or social identity; (4) Ceremonial dress — costumes based on traditional ceremonies (e.g. Bira, initiation rites) communicate specific cultural practices; (5) Social status and role — costume communicates a character's rank within a cultural hierarchy (chief, elder, warrior, healer); (6) Historical representation — period-accurate traditional clothing places the narrative in a specific cultural-historical context; (7) Contrast — juxtaposing traditional and Western/modern dress highlights cultural tension or transformation within the narrative. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

questions.text: Question 4: Artistic Director, Culture, and Theatre Criticism

subParts.text: State any four functions of an artistic director in a theatre organisation.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Justify the role of culture in theatre criticism.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: How can theatre critics enhance theatrical productions?
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any four of: (1) Selecting and developing the season's programme/repertoire; (2) Hiring and managing directors, designers, and creative staff; (3) Setting the artistic vision and direction of the organisation; (4) Overseeing the artistic quality of all productions; (5) Building relationships with playwrights and commissioning new works; (6) Representing the organisation publicly and promoting its artistic identity; (7) Collaborating with the executive director on budgeting for artistic needs; (8) Mentoring emerging artists within the organisation. [1 mark each, up to 4]

(b) Key points: (1) Cultural context informs the critic's interpretive framework — understanding the cultural background of a play is essential to evaluate its meaning and intent accurately; (2) Cultural relevance — a critic assesses whether a production authentically represents or misrepresents the culture it portrays; (3) Cultural norms and values — critics judge whether performances uphold, challenge, or subvert cultural expectations, sparking important social conversations; (4) Intercultural theatre — when productions blend or contrast cultures, critics analyse the effectiveness and sensitivity of this blending; (5) Language and symbolism — cultural literacy allows critics to decode culturally specific metaphors, symbols, and references; (6) Audience reception — culture shapes how audiences respond to productions, and critics must account for cultural diversity in their assessments; (7) Preservation of cultural heritage — criticism highlights productions that successfully preserve or evolve traditional art forms. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

(c) Key points: (1) Providing constructive feedback — detailed critiques help directors, designers, and performers identify strengths and weaknesses to improve future work; (2) Raising public awareness — reviews attract audiences and build interest in theatrical productions; (3) Holding productions to artistic standards — criticism encourages high-quality work by creating accountability; (4) Documentation — written criticism creates a historical record of productions for future reference; (5) Stimulating artistic debate — critical discourse pushes theatre-makers to think more deeply about their artistic choices; (6) Advocacy — positive criticism can attract funding, sponsorship, and institutional support for productions; (7) Audience education — critics help audiences understand and appreciate complex or experimental works. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

questions.text: Question 5: Animation Principles, Forms, and Graphic Design Critique

subParts.text: Give any four principles of animation.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text:
Describe the following forms of animation.
(i) stop motion
(ii) flipbook
(iii) claymation
(iv) pixilation
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain the elements used to critique the graphic design of an animation film.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any four of the 12 Disney principles: (1) Squash and stretch; (2) Anticipation; (3) Staging; (4) Straight ahead action and pose to pose; (5) Follow through and overlapping action; (6) Slow in and slow out (ease in/ease out); (7) Arc; (8) Secondary action; (9) Timing; (10) Exaggeration; (11) Solid drawing; (12) Appeal. [1 mark each, up to 4]

(b)
(i) Stop motion: A technique where physical objects (puppets, models, everyday objects) are photographed one frame at a time, with small adjustments made between each shot. When played in sequence the objects appear to move. Examples include Wallace & Gromit and Coraline. [2 marks]
(ii) Flipbook: A small book of sequential drawings or images, each slightly different from the last. When the pages are flipped rapidly, the images create the illusion of movement. It is one of the earliest and simplest forms of animation. [2 marks]
(iii) Claymation: A form of stop-motion animation where characters and objects are sculpted from clay or similar malleable materials (e.g. Plasticine). The clay figures are repositioned slightly between each photographed frame to simulate movement. Example: Morph, Chicken Run. [2 marks]
(iv) Pixilation: A stop-motion technique using live human actors instead of objects or puppets. Actors are photographed in incremental poses between frames, creating surreal, jerky movement effects. Example: Norman McLaren's Neighbours. [2 marks]

(c) Key graphic design elements for critiquing animation: (1) Line and shape — quality and style of drawn lines; use of geometric vs. organic shapes in character and background design; (2) Colour — palette choices, use of colour theory, mood and emotional impact of colour; (3) Composition — how elements are arranged within the frame, use of rule of thirds, balance, and visual hierarchy; (4) Typography — style, readability, and integration of text/titles within the animation; (5) Texture — surface quality of characters and environments, contributing to realism or stylisation; (6) Space and depth — use of foreground, midground, and background to create three-dimensional space; (7) Consistency — visual coherence across the entire film in terms of style and design language; (8) Character design — how effectively the visual design communicates personality, cultural identity, and emotion. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

questions.text: Question 6: Camera Techniques, Photography for Conservation, and Video Camera Safety

subParts.text: Identify any four camera techniques that can be used to capture a wildlife reserve in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: How can photography be used to raise awareness on natural resource conservation in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain any four safe handling procedures for video cameras.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any four of: (1) Wide-angle/establishing shot — captures the vastness of the landscape and habitat; (2) Telephoto/long shot — allows the photographer to capture wildlife from a safe distance without disturbing animals; (3) Macro photography — captures fine detail of plants, insects, and small wildlife; (4) Aerial/drone photography — provides a bird's-eye view of the reserve and its ecosystems; (5) Panning shot — follows a moving animal to convey speed and energy; (6) Slow motion/high frame rate — captures fast animal movement in detail; (7) Time-lapse — shows environmental changes over time (e.g. sunrise, animal migration). [1 mark each, up to 4]

(b) Key points: (1) Documentary photography — compelling images of endangered species and threatened habitats create emotional connections that motivate conservation action; (2) Social media campaigns — viral photography campaigns (e.g. images of poached elephants or deforested areas) can reach global audiences and generate pressure for policy change; (3) Exhibition and gallery shows — photography exhibitions in urban centres raise awareness among communities not directly connected to conservation areas; (4) Educational materials — photographs used in school textbooks and NGO materials educate the next generation about Zimbabwe's natural heritage; (5) Evidence for advocacy — photographic evidence of illegal logging, poaching, or pollution can be used by environmental organisations to lobby government; (6) Celebrating biodiversity — beautiful wildlife photography promotes pride in Zimbabwe's natural resources, encouraging communities to protect them; (7) Photojournalism — news photographs of environmental destruction published in newspapers/online news platforms generate public debate and government response. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

(c) Any four of: (1) Always use a camera strap or harness to prevent accidental dropping; (2) Store the camera in a padded case or bag when not in use to protect it from physical damage; (3) Avoid exposing the camera to extreme heat, moisture, or dust — use a rain cover in wet conditions; (4) Handle the lens carefully — use lens caps when not shooting and avoid touching glass surfaces with fingers; (5) Ensure the battery is fully charged before a shoot and carry spares; (6) Format memory cards properly and back up footage regularly to prevent data loss; (7) Never force connections (cables, batteries, memory cards) to avoid damaging ports; (8) Clean the sensor and lens with appropriate tools (blower, microfibre cloth) to maintain image quality. [2 marks per valid point, up to 4 points]

questions.text: Question 8: Theatre Event Planning, Codes of Conduct, and Production Budgeting

subParts.text: Outline the steps taken when planning a theatre event.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Why are codes of conduct important in theatre practice.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Propose key aspects a producer considers when preparing a budget for a theatre production.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Key steps (any four): (1) Define the concept/purpose of the event — determine the type of production, theme, and target audience; (2) Secure a venue — identify, book, and confirm an appropriate performance space; (3) Assemble the production team — hire/assign director, designers, stage manager, and technical crew; (4) Create a production schedule/timeline — set rehearsal dates, technical rehearsals, dress rehearsals, and performance dates; (5) Plan the budget — estimate all costs and secure funding/sponsorship; (6) Marketing and publicity — design promotional materials, sell tickets, and publicise the event; (7) Conduct rehearsals and technical preparation; (8) Final dress rehearsal and performance. [1 mark each, up to 4]

(b) Key points: (1) Professionalism — codes of conduct set clear expectations for professional behaviour, punctuality, and commitment among cast and crew; (2) Safety — establish safety protocols to protect performers and crew during rehearsals and performances (e.g. safe stage combat, handling of equipment); (3) Respect and inclusion — codes prevent harassment, discrimination, and bullying, fostering a safe and respectful working environment; (4) Conflict resolution — provide a framework for addressing disputes and grievances fairly and constructively; (5) Creative integrity — protect the artistic vision by setting standards for preparation, focus, and collaboration; (6) Legal and contractual compliance — ensure all parties understand their rights and obligations, reducing risk of disputes; (7) Building trust — a clear code of conduct builds mutual trust between all members of a production team; (8) Reputation management — upholding ethical standards protects the reputation of the organisation. [2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points]

(c) Key budget aspects: (1) Venue hire — cost of renting the performance space and any associated facilities; (2) Personnel costs — fees/salaries for director, actors, designers, stage manager, technical crew, and front-of-house staff; (3) Set design and construction — materials and labour for building the set; (4) Costume and wardrobe — purchase, hire, or making of costumes, accessories, and make-up; (5) Lighting — hire or purchase of lighting equipment and consumables (gels, bulbs); (6) Sound — hire or purchase of sound equipment, microphones, and playback systems; (7) Props — purchase or hire of all required props; (8) Marketing and publicity — printing of posters/flyers, social media advertising, programme printing; (9) Contingency fund — a reserve (typically 10–15%) for unexpected expenses; (10) Royalties/rights — payment for rights to perform a copyrighted script. [2 marks per valid point, up to 4 points]

Potani umbisana wakabeshinga kukampani inobhika chinkwa inowhi Lobels. Ikampani yeyi inowanikwa kunaDete. Bashingi bekampani yeyi bakabelipwa imali inji. Potani nabakwayina babe baanoshinga nabo bakabelingila pasi bamwe bashingi banoshinga kuna amwe makampani. Besana yaba bakatatawula mazhimali amadola okuAmerica benwa busukwa nokutenga zwisina nsholo. Sombisana wakabakubukakubuka, Potani wakabatanga kugala ega kuchiloja. Hajakabetenga zwimbalo zwizwe, zwibiya nozwilongo zomungumba. Imali yakabepelela kubusukwa. Potani wakabhatwa nomunchina unonhuwija busukwa kunshingo. Munchina yoyu unoshingiswa kubashingi bose besanu batanga mishingo. Potani wakenda kunshingo ekaguta esinotubula kana kuma zwako. Yelyo izhuba wakabahwa kwaJambanaye nabakwayina babe ebudila bwamabhodela. Wakati efhemela mumunchina ukakwemba kutondejela kuti wakabanwa zwilopindilija. Wakatolwa akalongelwa mumota esengwa kungumba. Zhingwanangwana wakawana lukwalo muhobhodo lunoti unshingo wapela. Wakanwanga munsholo akalinga kudenga ndipo paakabona kuti unshingo wekhuwa busebo bwehobe. Wakayeya kubwilila kunadade babe. Bakontambula somwana bakongajika pasi bondaya. Bakombuja kuti unshingo unolondotwa zwibuyanana kutila kuti ukulondote neebo. Bakondaya akale kuti imali ayitozaniswa. Wakalila Potani akabimbisa kuti hachinopamha kabili.

Figures 1(a) and 1(b) are pictorial sketches of a sofa frame section.

You are required to:

(a) Make the whole section of the sofa frame shown in Figs 1(a) and 1(b), working from sizes given in Figure 2 on the Insert.
(b) Shape part A as shown in Figures 1(a) and 1(b).

All measurements are in millimetres. Any measurements omitted are left to your discretion.

The following pieces of wood, previously prepared to size, are to be used:
- PIECE A: 510 mm × 75 mm × 40 mm
- PIECE B: 450 mm × 100 mm × 45 mm
- PIECE C: 250 mm × 100 mm × 30 mm
- PIECE D: 230 mm × 100 mm × 30 mm
- PIECE E: 300 mm × 50 mm × 40 mm

General Notes:
- A second supply of wood is not allowed. If you make a mistake, do your best to work as near to the dimensions on the drawing as possible.
- All pieces of wood should be finished to the correct length and their ends neatly trimmed with a plane.
- You may use any of the ordinary hand tools, but the use of glue and glasspaper is not allowed.
- A finished piece of work that is carefully done may obtain more marks than one that is completed but is inaccurate and shows poor workmanship.
- Marks are gained if the work is lightly cleaned with a finely set, smoothing plane before being assembled.
- Write your name and candidate number boldly and clearly on each piece of wood in capital letters and numbers which are 6mm high.
- If you do not complete the test, you must however submit all the wood together with all that you will have worked on except waste.
- Assemble your work before handing it to your invigilator.

subParts.text: Make the whole section of the sofa frame shown in Figs 1(a) and 1(b), working from sizes given in Figure 2 on the Insert.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Shape part A as shown in Figures 1(a) and 1(b).
subParts.label: (b)

questions.diagramNote: Figures 1(a) and 1(b) are pictorial/isometric sketches of a sofa frame section showing the arrangement and labelling of Parts A, B, C, D and E. Figure 2 (on the Insert) provides the detailed dimensioned working drawing of the sofa frame section.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Marking Rubric / Key Assessment Points:

PART (a) – Making the sofa frame section:
• Accurate marking out of all five pieces (A–E) to the dimensions specified in Figure 2. [Marks awarded for precision of marking out]
• Correct selection and cutting of joints (typically mortice-and-tenon joints for a sofa frame) joining the members:
  - Piece B (back rail / seat rail, 450 × 100 × 45 mm) joined to uprights/legs.
  - Pieces C and D (side/cross rails, 250 × 100 × 30 mm and 230 × 100 × 30 mm) joined with appropriate joints.
  - Piece E (stretcher/leg, 300 × 50 × 40 mm) joined accordingly.
  - Piece A (shaped top/arm rail, 510 × 75 × 40 mm) joined at each end.
• Mortice and tenon joints cut cleanly, squarely, and to correct depth; shoulders fitting tightly with no gaps. [Marks for quality and accuracy of joints]
• Correct use of tools: mortice chisel, bevel-edged chisels, router (for grooves/rebates if applicable), pillar drill.
• All pieces planed to correct length with ends neatly squared. [Marks for dimensional accuracy]
• Work lightly cleaned with a finely set smoothing plane prior to assembly. [Marks for surface finish/workmanship]
• Correct assembly with all joints fitting squarely; frame is not twisted or racked. [Marks for assembly accuracy]
• Candidate name and number written clearly (6 mm high capitals) on each piece.

PART (b) – Shaping Part A:
• Part A (510 × 75 × 40 mm) shaped as shown in the pictorial sketches – typically a curved or chamfered profile on the arm/top rail.
• Shape is symmetrical, smooth, and matches the profile shown in Figs 1(a) and 1(b).
• Edges/curves cleaned up neatly with a plane, spokeshave, or chisel; no torn grain or rough surfaces.
• Dimensions maintained as close as possible to those indicated in Figure 2.

General Workmanship Marks:
• Overall neatness, care, and quality of finish throughout.
• A carefully finished, slightly inaccurate piece scores higher than a completed but poorly worked piece.
• No glue or glasspaper used (penalty if evidence found).

questions.text:
What is the importance of sharing work?
A makes a family rich
B completion of work is fast
C children become intelligent
D parents become responsible
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – completion of work is fast. Sharing work divides tasks among people, leading to faster and more efficient completion of work.

questions.text:
Self-awareness is
A the ability to complete a given task.
B being punctual all the time.
C assisting those who are in need.
D knowledge about one's body feelings and thoughts.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – knowledge about one's body feelings and thoughts. Self-awareness refers to having conscious knowledge of one's own character, feelings, motives, and desires.

questions.text:
How many main sections are in the Bible?
A two
B nine
C three
D eight
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – two. The Bible has two main sections: the Old Testament and the New Testament.

questions.text:
A family belonging to Indigenous religion has a new born baby. Which religious activity will bring the families together?
A circumcision
B naming the baby
C shaving the baby's hair
D cutting the umbilical cord
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – shaving the baby's hair. In many indigenous African religious traditions, shaving a newborn baby's hair is a communal ceremony that gathers family members together to formally welcome and bless the new child.

questions.text:
The diagram below shows a type of an artefact (an opening permanently closed). What is the function of the artefact?
A to distribute traditional beer
B to be shaken during dances
C to be eaten during ceremonies
D to show the leader when singing
questions.diagramNote: Diagram of an artefact with an opening that is permanently closed (a gourd rattle/hosho).
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – to be shaken during dances. The artefact depicted (a hosho/rattle with a permanently closed opening) is a musical instrument shaken during traditional dances and ceremonies.

questions.text:
The most sacred artefact in Islam religion found only in Mecca is
A the Kaaba.
B the Shabbat.
C a greeting card.
D a prayer mat.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – the Kaaba. The Kaaba is the cube-shaped structure at the centre of the Masjid al-Haram mosque in Mecca and is the most sacred site in Islam.

questions.text:
A girl witnessed a fight. She declined her presence when asked. Which moral is lacking on the part of the girl?
A caring
B kindness
C tolerance
D trustworthy
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – trustworthy. The girl denied what she witnessed, which shows a lack of honesty and trustworthiness.

questions.text:
The diagram shows an officer saluting the Zimbabwean flag. The officer shows
A bravery.
B confidence.
C patriotism.
D intelligence.
questions.diagramNote: Picture of an officer saluting the Zimbabwean flag.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – patriotism. Saluting the national flag is an expression of love and respect for one's country, which is patriotism.

questions.text:
Which one is a way of enterprising in religion?
A selling church uniforms
B visiting sick congregants
C holding prayer and fasting
D conducting holy communion services
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – selling church uniforms. Selling church uniforms is an income-generating (enterprising) activity within a religious context, as opposed to purely spiritual activities.

questions.text:
A community is in need of a school after it was destroyed by floods. Which contribution should families do to help the community?
A create social groups
B share received donations
C fundraising for the school
D transfer children to other schools
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – fundraising for the school. Fundraising is a direct and practical way for families to contribute resources towards rebuilding the community school.

questions.text:
The diagram is an illustration of a family type. What is the type of family shown?
A a nuclear family
B a polygamous family
C a child headed family
D a single parent headed family
questions.diagramNote: Diagram illustrating a specific type of family structure (children living without adults, indicating a child-headed family).
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – a child headed family. Based on context clues in the illustration showing children without adult parents/guardians, the family type is a child-headed family.

questions.text:
A pupil recited the poem below:
I put on colour beads, decorated head gear, animal skin cloth.
I sit on reeds and hide mats.
I treat with herbs.
The poem describes
A a chief.
B an ancestor.
C a spirit medium.
D a traditional healer.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – a traditional healer. The description of wearing colour beads, animal skin cloth, sitting on reeds and hide mats, and treating with herbs is characteristic of a traditional healer (n'anga).

questions.text:
Who was a disciple of Jesus Christ?
A Jacob
B Isaiah
C Andrew
D Joseph
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Andrew. Andrew was one of the twelve disciples (apostles) of Jesus Christ.

questions.text:
The picture shows Christians on a Palm Sunday procession. The procession is held to mark the beginning of
A Easter.
B Christmas.
C Passover.
D Pentecost.
questions.diagramNote: Picture of Christians participating in a Palm Sunday procession.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Easter. Palm Sunday marks the beginning of Holy Week, which leads up to Easter, commemorating Jesus's entry into Jerusalem.

questions.text:
Which one is a good example of conflict management?
A settling a quarrel
B using harsh words
C beating the offender
D exposing the offender's weaknesses
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – settling a quarrel. Settling a quarrel through peaceful dialogue and negotiation is a constructive approach to conflict management.

questions.text:
Gender equality is
A changing from childhood to adulthood.
B the biological difference between boys and girls.
C sharing resources fairly to both boys and girls.
D fighting for the rights of girls.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – sharing resources fairly to both boys and girls. Gender equality means ensuring equal rights, responsibilities and opportunities for all genders, including the fair sharing of resources.

questions.text:
What is monotheism in Judaism?
A belief in eternal life
B creation of man in God's image
C creation of the universe
D belief in one God
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – belief in one God. Monotheism is the belief in the existence of only one God; it is a core tenet of Judaism.

questions.text:
The Islamic pillar that promotes assisting the poor is
A faith.
B prayer.
C pilgrimage.
D almsgiving.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – almsgiving. Almsgiving (Zakat) is the third pillar of Islam and involves giving a portion of one's wealth to assist the poor and needy.

questions.text:
Why should personal cleanliness be maintained during adolescence?
A to manage physical changes
B to manage peer pressure
C to boost self-esteem
D to be able to produce
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – to manage physical changes. During adolescence, the body undergoes significant physical changes (e.g., increased sweating, acne) and personal cleanliness helps manage these changes effectively.

questions.text:
Which one is a myth on HIV and AIDS?
A there is possibility of mother to child transmission
B sleeping with many partners increase chances of infection
C testing positive is like a death penalty
D a healthy diet boosts immunity system
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – testing positive is like a death penalty. This is a myth because HIV-positive individuals can live long, healthy lives with proper antiretroviral treatment. Options A, B, and D are factual statements.

questions.text:
Which one of the Zimbabwean national events is celebrated in the month of August?
A Unity Day
B Heroes' day
C Independence Day
D National Youth Day
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – Heroes' Day. Heroes' Day is celebrated on the second Monday of August in Zimbabwe to honour the country's liberation war heroes.

questions.text:
The picture shows a form of abuse. This form of abuse is
A verbal.
B neglect.
C sexual.
D physical.
questions.diagramNote: Picture depicting a form of abuse being inflicted on a person (physical abuse, such as hitting/beating).
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – physical. The picture depicts physical abuse, which involves the use of bodily force to harm another person.

questions.text:
The picture shows children playing during leisure time. Which leisure facility are the children using?
A a swimming pool
B a stadium
C a park
D a zoo
questions.diagramNote: Picture of children playing in an outdoor leisure facility (a park with playground equipment/open green space).
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – a park. The picture shows children playing in an open recreational green space with playground equipment, which is characteristic of a park.

questions.text:
What is the effect of drought to the environment?
A leads to hunger
B leads to deficiency diseases
C leads to migration of people
D leads to deforestation
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – leads to deforestation. Drought as an environmental effect leads to deforestation because lack of water kills vegetation and also drives people to cut down trees for survival needs. (Note: Options A, B, and C are effects on people/society rather than the environment directly.)

questions.text:
The picture below shows an indigenous processing tool. The tool is a
A knobkerrie.
B fish trap.
C mice trap.
D mortar and pestle.
questions.diagramNote: Picture of an indigenous processing tool (mortar and pestle used for grinding grain).
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – mortar and pestle. The tool depicted is a mortar and pestle, a traditional indigenous processing tool used for grinding grain and other food items.

questions.text:
Medicinal herbs are conserved mostly
A for treatment of ailments.
B to prevent soil erosion.
C as a source of oxygen.
D as a source of fire wood.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – for treatment of ailments. Medicinal herbs are primarily conserved because of their value in treating various illnesses and ailments in both traditional and modern medicine.

questions.text:
Barter trade is
A buying more than enough with intention of selling.
B charging more on the purchased goods.
C the exchange of goods and services.
D production of goods on a large scale.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – the exchange of goods and services. Barter trade is a system of exchange where goods and services are traded directly for other goods and services without using money.

questions.text:
A family, by choice, moves from one area to another within a country. The movement is an example of
A internal migration.
B international migration.
C permanent migration.
D involuntary migration.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – internal migration. Internal migration refers to the movement of people from one region to another within the same country. The movement is also voluntary (by choice), which makes it internal and voluntary migration.

questions.text:
Which one is a role of the village head?
A to monitor the city council
B to preside over the chief's court
C to keep a register of the community
D to lead during rain making ceremonies
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – to keep a register of the community. A village head's role includes keeping records (a register) of community members such as births, deaths, and new arrivals in the village.

questions.text:
The picture below shows a heritage site. In which province is the heritage found?
A Masvingo
B Matabeleland South
C Mashonaland West
D Matabeleland North
questions.diagramNote: Picture of a Zimbabwean heritage site (Great Zimbabwe ruins located in Masvingo Province).
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Masvingo. The picture shows the Great Zimbabwe National Monument, which is located in Masvingo Province, Zimbabwe.

questions.text:
Which productive sector deals with animal production?
A mining
B fishing
C tourism
D agriculture
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – agriculture. The agricultural sector encompasses both crop and animal (livestock) production.

questions.text:
Which one is a cultural way to preserve rock paintings at heritage sites?
A make use of taboos
B use police as security
C put banners with strict measures
D fence the areas to avoid unauthorised entry
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – make use of taboos. Using taboos is a cultural (indigenous) method of preserving heritage sites, as community-held beliefs and prohibitions discourage people from damaging or desecrating the sites.

questions.text:
Which one is a negative impact of information and communication technology (ICT) to people's lives?
A may promote inclusivity
B may increase literature
C may promote academic dishonesty
D may result in better communication
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – may promote academic dishonesty. ICT can be misused to facilitate cheating, plagiarism, and other forms of academic dishonesty. Options A, B, and D are positive impacts of ICT.

questions.text:
Which one is a role of the legislature?
A to enforce laws
B to judge in courts
C to vote for the president
D to make laws of the country
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – to make laws of the country. The legislature (Parliament) is the arm of government responsible for making and passing laws. Enforcing laws is the role of the executive, and judging in courts is the role of the judiciary.

questions.text:
A national strategic service provided by the Zimbabwe National Water Authority (ZINWA) is the provision of
A grain.
B fuel.
C water.
D electricity.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – water. ZINWA (Zimbabwe National Water Authority) is responsible for managing and providing water resources in Zimbabwe.

questions.text:
Which one is a worker's right?
A protect own health
B freedom of association
C treat others with respect
D refrain from harassment
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – freedom of association. Freedom of association is a recognised worker's right, which includes the right to join trade unions. Options A, C, and D are responsibilities/duties rather than rights.

questions.text:
The picture below shows one type of food. The main nutritional value acquired from the food shown is to provide
A proteins.
B vitamins.
C carbohydrates.
D mineral salts.
questions.diagramNote: Picture of a type of food (starchy food such as sadza/bread/rice, indicating carbohydrates as the main nutrient).
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – carbohydrates. The food shown (a starchy staple food) is a primary source of carbohydrates, which provide the body with energy.

questions.text:
What is the importance of the National School Pledge?
A to develop patriotic citizens
B to develop dishonest citizens.
C to impart entrepreneurship skills
D to produce pastors
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – to develop patriotic citizens. The National School Pledge instils a sense of national identity, pride, and love for Zimbabwe, thereby developing patriotic citizens.

questions.text:
Which one is a city by-law?
A murder is not permitted
B selling of drugs is illegal
C loud music is banned at night
D eating fast foods is discouraged
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – loud music is banned at night. A by-law is a regulation made by a local authority (city council). Banning loud music at night is a typical city/local council by-law. Options A and B are national laws, and D is not a law.

questions.text:
Which one is a possible danger of using ICT to the children?
A information provision
B cyberbullying
C less paperwork
D fine motor skills promotion
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – cyberbullying. Cyberbullying is a significant danger of ICT use for children, involving harassment or bullying through digital platforms. Options A, C, and D are benefits of ICT use.

questions.text:
Phalantoa ke ntate oa
A. Maria.
B. Tsoenyeo.
C. Majangoati.
D. Malakia.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. Tsoenyeo. (The passage states Tsoenyeo is the child of Phalantoa Nare.)

questions.text:
Khutsana eona, ene e lula
A. teng e le.
B. ngoana.
C. monyano.
D. notsi.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. notsi. (The passage states 'o lula a le notsi' – he lived alone/by himself.)

questions.text:
Ke mang a mo neileng le ngolo? Ke
A. batho.
B. pitsi.
C. Malakia.
D. Majangoati.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. Majangoati. (The passage states Majangoati gave Tsoenyeo the letter: 'Majangoati a moneha lengolo.')

questions.text:
Tsoenyeo o neiloe lengolo le bolelang ka
A. khaoa.
B. tulo ea hae ale notsi.
C. thuso etsoang ho Malakia.
D. ho sebetsa Gumululo.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. thuso etsoang ho Malakia. (The letter spoke of help/assistance from Morena Malakia who promised to help Tsoenyeo with schooling at Gobatema.)

questions.text:
Univesithing Tsoenyoo o ne a rutela eng? Ho
A. ba lekichara.
B. ba tichere.
C. pasa.
D. thusa.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. ba lekichara. (The passage states: 'a feleletsa a le lekichara univesithing ea Great Zimbabwe' – he ended up as a lecturer at the University of Great Zimbabwe.)

questions.text:
Kataba ea eng Tsoenyeo a feletsoe ke mare? A ne a
A. tsoenyehile.
B. maketse.
C. thothomela.
D. bolela.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. thothomela. (The passage states the letter made him tremble: 'la mo thothomelisa lengolo lena' – the letter made him shiver/tremble.)

questions.text:
Monyana u setse a lutse huntle. Ke lefi le ele le supang polelo enga? Ke le le reng
A. U feletsoe ka mare.
B. U oetsoe ka khaoa.
C. U bohare ha thare le mokokotla.
D. hlapi efe letsoe ke metsi.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. U bohare ha thare le mokokotla. (The passage says 'monyana a ba bohare a thare le mokokotla' – he stood tall/upright with a bag, implying he had done well/settled properly.)

questions.text:
Batho ba boletsoeng mona ke ba
A. supa.
B. tselela.
C. hlano.
D. ne.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. tselela. (Characters mentioned in the passage: Tsoenyeo, Majangoati, Malakia, Tomasi, Maria, and Tsoenyeo's father Phalantoa Nare – six people are named, i.e., bo tselela/six.)

questions.text:
Tomaso p e thutetse hoba
A. lekichara.
B. tichere.
C. moshemane.
D. monyana.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. tichere. (The passage states Tsoenyeo's children, including Tomasi, studied hard and became teachers: 'ba ba matichere'.)

questions.text:
PUO QETISA KA LENTSOE LE NEPEHILENG.
Malakia o na le moea o mobi joale ka
A. noha.
B. phiri.
C. tau.
D. tlou.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. phiri. (The common Sesotho/Sotho simile for a person with an evil/bad spirit is compared to a hyena – 'phiri'.)

questions.text:
Ngoana oa qetellong pholeng ea habo ke
A. lefahla.
B. letsilolo.
C. khunamala.
D. khutsana.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. letsilolo. (The last-born child in the family is referred to as 'letsilolo' in Sesotho.)

questions.text:
Motho a nang le seatla o ea
A. sebetsa.
B. u tsoa.
C. nea.
D. ngola.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. sebetsa. (The expression 'ho na le seatla' means to be hardworking/skilled; such a person goes to work – 'sebetsa'.)

questions.text:
Nea polelo elokileng
A. tsoenyeo ke le tsibolo.
B. "tsoenyeo ke le tsibolo."
C. Tsoenyeo ke le tsibolo.
D. Tsoenyeo ke le tsibolo
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. Tsoenyeo ke le tsibolo. (The correct sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.)

questions.text:
QETISA KA LEBALA LE PELETILOENG SINTLE
Tomasi o aperi hempe e Khoebelu
A. khoebe.
B. tlaka.
C. toa.
D. tlere.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. khoebe. (The correctly spelt word for 'red' in Sesotho is 'khoebe'; the sentence says Tomasi is wearing a red shirt.)

questions.text:
BALA TABANA ENA U ARABE LIPOTSO TSE LATELANG [Tabana: Mamotajo le Khesari]
Ke mang eo a ratang ho ruoa? Ke
A. Khesari.
B. Mamotajo.
C. MaRabeka.
D. MaTharo.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. Mamotajo. (The passage opens: 'Mosali moholo Mamotajo ke mosali oa ho rata holeruoa haholo' – Mamotajo is the woman who loves keeping livestock.)

questions.text:
Lintja li entse eng? Li
A. fumane thuso.
B. khobokane ka bongata.
C. jile libutla.
D. kene.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. jile libutla. (The passage states: 'lintja tsa Khesari tsa kena serubeng sa li butla, tsa ja tsohle' – Khesari's dogs entered Mamotajo's vegetable garden and ate everything.)

questions.text:
Mamotajo o e setse taba ea hae
A. khotleng.
B. serubeng.
C. matoneng.
D. basaling.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. matoneng. (The passage states: 'Matona a ile a molella hore batla fitisetsa taba ea hae ho morena' – she took/referred her matter to the elders/matona.)

questions.text:
Batho ba sebetsang ho thusa morena ba bitsoa eng?
A. Banna
B. Basali
C. Matona
D. Makhoro
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. Matona. (In the passage, 'matona' are the councillors/elders who assist the chief/morena.)

questions.text:
Tabaneng ena hona le batho ba ba kae ba boletsoeng mabitso? Ba ba
A. beli
B. raru
C. hlanu
D. ne
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. ne. (The named characters in the passage are: Mamotajo, Khesari, MaRabeka, and MaThato – four people.)

questions.text:
Ke eng se se etsileng hore Khesari a fumanehe a na le molato?
A. Libutla lijiloe busio.
B. Khoro e mmeile molato.
C. Mamotajo o fumane thuso.
D. Lintja lijile lubutla.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. Lintja lijile lubutla. (Khesari was found guilty because his dogs ate Mamotajo's vegetables: 'Khoro e ile ea fumana Khesari ana le molato ka hobane lintja lijile libutla'.)

questions.text:
Ho isa marapo mangoeng ke ho
A. lebella.
B. robala.
C. mamela.
D. ahlama.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. ahlama. (The idiom 'ho isa marapo mangoeng' means to lie down/relax – to rest, i.e., 'ahlama'.)

questions.text:
Khesari o rele o fumaneha ana le molato batho?
A. Bathaba
B. Bakhubukana
C. Ba otloa bohloko
D. Bahlaisa
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. Bathaba. (The passage states: 'Batho ba ile ba thaba' – the people were happy when Khesari was found guilty and ordered to pay.)

questions.text:
PUO QETISA KA LENTSOE LE NEPEHILENG
Mamotajo __________ Khesari ba ile hongola lengolo.
A. le
B. li
C. lu
D. ebele
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. le. (The correct conjunction connecting two subjects is 'le' – 'Mamotajo le Khesari ba ile ho ngola lengolo'.)

questions.text:
Ngoana a senang batsoali ke
A. sefofo.
B. seretsa.
C. khutsana.
D. tsebototo.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. khutsana. (A child without parents is called 'khutsana' – an orphan – in Sesotho.)

questions.text:
Kahosane ___________ khorong.
A. re tlo
B. re tlaea
C. re ile
D. e re ile
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. re tlo. (Kahosane means tomorrow – a future context – so the future tense form 're tlo' (we will) is correct: 'Kahosane re tlo khorong' – Tomorrow we will go to court.)

questions.text:
HLALOSA LE ELE LELATELANG
"Sebolu se lahloa ka molomo." Ho rea o re
A. oseke oa lahla lijo nea bangoe bali batlang baje.
B. molomo ona le matla a oroala lijo.
C. nama ha e bole.
D. nama e ea jioa.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. molomo ona le matla a oroala lijo. (The proverb 'Sebolu se lahloa ka molomo' means food is wasted through the mouth – i.e., the mouth has the power to reject/waste food, meaning one's words/speech can cause loss.)

questions.text:
KHETHA POLELO E BONG HO BONGATA
A. Mmutla o jiloe ka ntja.
B. Libutla o jiloe ka ntja.
C. Libutla o jiloe ka lintja.
D. Libutla li jiloe ka lintja.
questions.topic: Language / Grammar – Singular and Plural Agreement
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. Libutla li jiloe ka lintja. (The correct plural agreement: 'Libutla' (vegetables – plural) requires the subject concord 'li' and the plural noun 'lintja' (dogs).)

questions.text:

Marks are awarded for content, language accuracy, organisation and appropriate format for the chosen task. Key marking criteria:

- Language (vocabulary, grammar, spelling, punctuation): up to 8 marks
- Organisation (structure, paragraphing, length 80–120 words): up to 4 marks

(a) Lwaano: Should clearly describe the nutritional/health benefits of traditional food (chintu), using appropriate adjectives, giving examples of such foods and explaining why they are beneficial.
(b) Kapeto (poem/essay): Should describe Covid-19 disease — symptoms, spread, prevention — using appropriate Tonga language and structure; rhyme/rhythm expected if a poem.

questions.text:
READ THE FOLLOWING PASSAGE AND ANSWER THE QUESTIONS THAT FOLLOW.

[Passage: The two o'clock bell rang to signal the end of lunch and all the learners at Forogo Primary School ran to the assembly point. The teacher on duty, Mr Gwekwerere, was a no nonsense man. No learner wanted to be caught offside and endure the hard punishments he often gave to those who broke school rules. The learners watched him as he strolled to the assembly point. Mr Gwekwerere stood quietly in front of the learners and smiled. We had had lessons from eight o'clock in the morning till one o'clock in the afternoon. Mrs Maroro, the school Head, had tasked Mr Gwekwerere to supervise the making of a fire-guard around the school premises. Learners had brought different tools, such as hoes, slashers and axes for use during the activity. More often, people in Jasi area start veld fires for no reason at all. Every year, veld fires destroy vegetation in the area. Both wild and domestic animals suffer too, owing to the scarcity of food. What further worsens the situation is that farmers in the area cannot afford to buy fodder for their animals. The teacher on duty divided us into four groups which operated in the eastern, western, southern and northern sides of the school. Our group worked in the southern part. The girls did the weeding while the boys were slashing grass, cutting the trees and bushes. By four o'clock, we had finished making the fire-guard. Mrs Maroro came to inspect the work and was delighted. She expressed her gratitude and asked the teacher on duty to dismiss the learners.]

What signal was used to gather the learners at the assembly point?
A ringing of the bell
B strolling of the teacher
C the running of the learners
D fear for punishment
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – ringing of the bell. The passage states 'The two o'clock bell rang to signal the end of lunch and all the learners…ran to the assembly point.'

questions.text:

A He strolled to the assembly point.
B He smiled at the learners.
C He gave learners hard punishments.
D The learners watched him while he was walking.

questions.text:

B they feared him
C he was friendly
D he was the teacher on duty

questions.text:

A plant trees in the area
B educate the villagers on the dangers of veld fires
C report to the police all cases of veld fires
D try all those who would have caused veld fires
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – educate the villagers on the dangers of veld fires. Education is the most preventive and sustainable measure to stop veld fires from occurring in the first place.

questions.aiModelAnswer: D – The fire-guard. The passage is predominantly about the learners making a fire-guard around the school premises.

questions.text:
READ THE FOLLOWING PASSAGE AND ANSWER THE QUESTIONS THAT FOLLOW.

[Passage: Bishop Bhunu was late for a church service. He drove past buses, taxis and lorries along the way to the capital city where the church service was to be held. As he approached the flyover, near the capital city, he noticed a dark object lying lifelessly in the middle of his lane. 'Could this be a human being?' he wondered. Ttoo! Ttoo! sounded the deafening sound of his car's hooter. A heavy change down of gears was followed by a screeching of brakes. Bishop Bhunu failed to stop the car and ran over the object. A boom sound was finally heard. The car skidded and veered off the road. It crashed onto a huge rock by the road side and it was badly damaged. People around the accident scene heard the boom sound. Out of curiosity, some vendors, motorists, customers from shops and workers from offices rushed to the scene of the accident. They wanted to know what exactly had happened. 'Who has been hit by this car?' someone from the crowd asked. A woman in the crowd, burst into tears when she discovered that the victim lying on the ground was her only son. He was seriously injured. The woman cried pitifully as she explained how she had always warned her son, Sham, not to play on such busy roads. With a courageous voice, the poor woman warned the crowd to be careful when using busy roads. Sham was taken to a nearby clinic by Bishop Bhunu.]

From where did the hooting sound come from? It came from the
A taxis.
B buses.
C lorries.
D Bishop's car.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – Bishop's car. The passage states 'Ttoo! Ttoo! sounded the deafening sound of his car's hooter,' referring to Bishop Bhunu's car.

questions.text:
The hooter was sounded to warn the ____________ of the approaching danger.
A dark object lying on the ground
B customers from the shops
C workers from the offices
D motorists around
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – dark object lying on the ground. Bishop Bhunu hooted to warn the object (which turned out to be a person, Sham) lying in his lane of the approaching car.

questions.text:
Why did Bishop Bhunu apply the car breaks?
A to avoid crashing onto a huge rock
B to avoid hitting the object
C to change the car gears
D to skid the car
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – to avoid hitting the object. Bishop Bhunu applied the brakes after noticing the dark object lying in his lane, in an attempt to stop before hitting it.

questions.text:

B She was explaining how she had always warned her son.
C She blamed her son for not taking her advice.
D The accident victim was her son.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – The accident victim was her son. The passage states 'A woman in the crowd burst into tears when she discovered that the victim lying on the ground was her only son.'

questions.text:

B He did not quickly apply the car breaks.
C He was speeding.

questions.aiModelAnswer: C – He was speeding. Bishop Bhunu was late and driving fast past other vehicles; the passage implies speed as the reason he could not stop in time.

questions.text:
How could Bishop Bhunu have avoided this accident?

B Driving at a safe speed
C Keeping the steering wheel straight
D Not sounding the hooter
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – Driving at a safe speed. Had he been driving at a safe/lower speed, he would have had sufficient time and distance to stop the car before hitting Sham.

questions.text:
READ THE FOLLOWING PASSAGE AND ANSWER THE QUESTIONS THAT FOLLOW.

[Passage: The Lucky Girl – Revai did not enjoy the benefits of parental care. Some children in Zimbabwe face the same problem. Revai's parents abandoned her soon after she was weaned. Promising to return a couple of months later, they left her in the care of her paternal grandmother. The parents went to seek for employment beyond our country's borders. Revai's grandmother took care of all her basic needs, except school fees. She is now in the Seventh Grade and has never heard from her parents. Her grandmother taught her many survival skills. She knows how to cook, wash clothes and kitchen utensils. Revai is a role model at her school. She is hardworking, polite and adheres to school rules. She often encourages her classmates to take after her. Everyone admires her. Some girls of her age complain when they are given work but she does not. Although she comes from a poor background, her academic performance is excellent. It was for that reason that her class teacher recommended her to get a school fees grant. A church organisation called Carpenaum Trust provided the scholarship. The organisation promised to pay her school fees from primary to university level. The beneficiaries of the fees grant sometimes get donations of school uniforms and food humpers. That donation has given Revai great hope to advance with her education.]

According to the passage, what problem do some children face?
A Being weaned at an early age.
B Being cared for by grandmothers.
C Not enjoying the benefits of parental care.
D Being abused by being overworked.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Not enjoying the benefits of parental care. The passage opens with 'Revai did not enjoy the benefits of parental care. Some children in Zimbabwe face the same problem.'

B at home
C at the university
D beyond our country's borders

B She knew how to cook and wash clothes.

questions.text:

B grant

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:

B Yes, she doesn't.
C Yes, she didn't.

questions.aiModelAnswer: A – No, she doesn't. Based on the passage, Revai does enjoy going to school, so the correct short answer to a negative tag question ('does she?') where the statement is false would be 'Yes, she does.' However, as a grammar exercise testing the correct short-answer form for the negative statement given, the grammatically consistent answer matching the negative question is 'No, she doesn't.' (Answer A as printed).

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:
Tabana ea kotloisiso. Bangoli ba lemosoa hore ba qete metsotso emashome amane le metso emihlano (45) ba araba lipotso li leng khaolong ena. Bala tabana elatelang u arabe lipotso tse latelang usebelisa lipolelo tse tletseng.

Lefatse kabophara le tletse lifate tse sianeng tse batho baka lisebelisang katsela tse sianeng. Sefate sa muu ke sengoe sa lifate tsa bohlokoa sechabeng sa baSotho. Sefate sena sa muu sefumaneha haholo polekeng tse omileng. Sefate sa muu se etsa lithoaloana tse liratoang kabatho ba bangata. Ekaba batho ba baholo kapa ba ba nyenyane bohle ba ea ja litholoana tse. Bashemane banka litholoana tse balikopantsa lebese, ba etsa se bareng ke "eogathi" e monate haholo. Eogathi ena e jioa ke motho ohle. Bafumahali bona bakopantsa litholoana tse le metsi ba pheha motoho oa motho ohle lapeng oa jioa phakela. Baholoane bare, "Tsie efufa ka mosoange," tse lipaka hore motho ohle oqala tsatsi la hae a na le matla. Banyana bona ba kopantsa litholoana tse le metsi ba etsa malekere a barena ke "malolo". Malolo ana a ea kentsoa ferijing hore atsilihale. Batho ba bangata baea athabela kahore amonate hape a ba nea matla. Bo ntatemoholo le bona a basale kantle. Banka lithaka tsa litholoana tse tsa muu ba li sila ba nea li ruo tsa bona tsa ja. Batho lebona baka ja lijo tsena, li aha mmele haholo. Sengoe sabohlokoa ka sefate se, ke hore batho ba ka khona ho rekisa litholoana tse hape, barekise le malekere a malolo. Ke sefate sehlokehang sechabeng ka hore sea thusa haholo.

Lipotso:
(a) Tabana ena e bolela ka eng?
(b) Ke eng se ratoang ke batho ho sefate sa muu?
(c) Kabaka la eng bana barata oja malolo?
(d) Lithaka tsa litholoana li etsoang ka bo ntatemoholo?
(e) Mantsoe a a supung hore batho ha ba ja litholoane tsa muu bae a khura, le ea a reng.
(f) Nyenyefatsa tabana ena ka mantsoe a mashome amane le metso emihlano (45) u bontsa mesebetsi ea litholoana tsa muu.

questions.text:
Read the following passage very carefully before you attempt any question. Answer all the questions in full sentences.

The Baobab: A Wonder Tree

The baobab is Zimbabwe's wonder tree. It looks like a giant carrot planted upside down. In Zimbabwe, baobab trees are protected under the law, reflecting their importance. The tree is a symbol of hope and strength. The tree is our national heritage and once it is destroyed, it is hard to replace. People are putting the baobab tree under threat by removing its bark to make mats and brooms. As one passes through the Southern Eastern Lowveld, one will not miss the quick business the community is engaged in through the skinning of the baobab tree of its bark. However, the tree can easily get diseases when skinned. Man and elephants love to eat its fruit. The seeds can be soaked to dissolve the pulp that coats the seed. The liquid is then frozen to produce a refreshing drink commonly known as 'ice lolo'. The pulp powder can also be used as a supplement for energy and digestion. Some people also take its leaves and use them as relish. These also treat fever and diarrhoea. Mature baobab trees have hollow trunks towards the base which can be used as shops or bus stop shelters. These trees can withstand drought because they store lots of water. Their massive root systems also help to slow down soil erosion.

Adapted from: 'The Manica Post', March 11-17, 2011, by Abraham Mudefi, Zimpapers.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
Munyori anofanirwa kusarudza musoro umwe chete (a–e) uye kunyora zvirevo zvakakwana zana nemakumi maviri (120). Mhinduro inopiwa mapoindi nezvikamu izvi:

1. ZVIREVO (Content/Ideas) [8 marks]: Zvinofanira kuva nezvimbo zvakawanda, zvine musoro uye zvinobatana namusoro wasarudzwa. Mambo/mhedzisiro inofanira kugumisa zvakanaka.

2. MUTAURO (Language Use) [6 marks]: Kushandisa Chishona chakanaka — mazwi akanaka, mafigu, mitsara, matipi akanaka, kudzokorora mazwi kunobatsira. Kushandisa tsumo, madimikira uye zvimiro zvechiShona kunobatsira.

3. KURONGEKA (Organisation/Structure) [4 marks]: Ndima dzine musoro, mazwi anobatana, kushandisa mavara makuru nekuspringa ndima zvakanaka.

4. ZVINYORWA (Mechanics) [2 marks]: Kunyora zvakanaka — kuchinja mavara, ndobvi, mavara makuru panofanirwa, njodzi dzezvinyorwa dzishoma.

Muenzaniso wemhinduro yenMusoro (a) — Tsumo 'Rina manyanga hariputirwi mumushunje':
Tsumo iyi inoreva kuti munhu ane simba kana mukurumbira haakwanisiki kuvanzwa. Rondedzero inofanirwa kuburitsa pfungwa iyi kuburikidza nengano kana zviitiko. Muenzaniso: Rondedzero inogona kutaura nezvemurume ane pfuma huru aigara mumusha wake... inofanirwa kuguma ichisimbisa pfungwa yetsumo.

Muenzaniso wemhinduro yenMusoro (b) — Hurukuro:
Hurukuro inofanirwa kuva nemagwaro ekutaura (dialogue) pakati pevarimi vaviri. Matambudziko ekushanduka kwemamiriro ekunze anofanira kujumuiswa: mvura isiri kunaya, zuva rinopisa, nzara, kurasa zvirimwa, nemimwe matambudziko. Kushandisa mazwi anobatana hurukuro: 'Ndiri kufunga kuti...' 'Zvirokwazvo...' 'Ndinobvumirana newe...'

Muenzaniso wemhinduro yenMusoro (c) — Tsamba:
Tsamba inofanira kuva nechimiro chakanaka: kero yemunyori, kero yemunogamuchira, zuva, mutumbi, mhedzisiro. Mhinduro inofanira kutsanangura: mbavha yakabiwa sei, zvakaitika, kuda rubatsiro rwemubereki. Kutaura nemutauro wechitendero neerudo pakutumira tsamba kumubereki.

Muenzaniso wemhinduro yenMusoro (d) — Mhan'arwa:
Mhan'arwa inofanira kuva yakanyorwa zvakanaka, ichitaura matambudziko: kushayiwa rukudzo, kubiwa mari, kusanyatsobatsirwa, unyanzvi hwashandi. Kutaura kuti muridzi wephazi afunge nzira dzekugadziridza zvinhu.

Muenzaniso wemhinduro yenMusoro (e) — Rondedzero yenzvimbo:
Rondedzero inofanira kutsanangura nzvimbo seVictoria Falls, Nyanga, Great Zimbabwe. Kutsanangura: mufananidzo wenzvimbo, zvakaita nzvimbo, kukurudzira vanhu kuenda kuma. Kushandisa mazwi anoyevedza (descriptive language).

questions.text:
Verenga ndima inotevera ugopindura mibvunzo yakapiwa nezvirevo zvizere.

VaGondo vaigara muguta guru reHarare. Murume uyu aiva nemudzimai nevana vatatu. Nhamo yakavatamba tsvina pakavhara kambani yavaishandira. Vakaedza kutsvaga basa asi zvakakona n'anga murapwa achida. Mari yakaramba kutamba kusvika VaGondo nemhuri yavo vabudiswa mumba mavaigara. Vakafunga zano rekuvaka kamba kemapepa pachisango chaive pedyo neguta. Vana vavo vakanga vasisaende kuchikoro. Mangwanani ega ega raiva besanwa kunopemha nekunhonga zvekudya mumabhini. Zvipfeko zvavo zvaiva zvava nezvigamba uye tsvina nekuti zvaisagezwa. Miviri yavo yaiva yasviba kuti ndoo nekuti mvura yekugeza vaisaiwana. Murume akakwenya mhanza kufunga zano rekuita. Hope dzaisauya. VaGondo vakazobuda nezano rekuti vabude mupfumvu iyi. Vakatanga kunhonga zvigubhu nemagaba ezvinwiwa zvairaswa nevanhu mudhorobha. Vakaunganidza zvinhongwa izvi zvikaita matutu pakamba kavaigara. Izvi vaizviita nemhuri yavo zuva rega rega rakasikwa naMwari. VaGondo vakanotsvaga kwekuzvitengesera vakakuwana, kukambani yaiita basa rekutenga zvigubhu namagaba ezvinwiwa mudhorobha reHarare. Pakauya motokari hombe ikatakura zvinhu zviya zvikanotengwa zvose. Murume akafara seachabata denga apo akapiwa mari yaaisafungira. Vakashandisa mari iya kutenga zvinwiwa izvo zvakatanga kutengeswa nemudzimai wavo pamusika weMbare. Vakatsvaga imba yekuroja yekuti vagare nemhuri yavo zvakanaka. Vakashandisa mari yaivaive vasara nayo kubhadhara muripo wekugara muimba umu. Murume uyu akasvika pakutsvaga vamwe vashandi vatatu vaimubetsera kuunganidza zvigubhu nemagaba ezvinwiwa. Vanhu vachiona shanduko mukurarama kwaVaGondo, vakatanga kunhongawo zvigubhu namagaba ezvinwiwa vachiunganidza. Vazhinji vaitengesera VaGondo nemari yakaderera ivo vozoendesa kukambani yavaitengesera zvinongwa izvi zvawanda chaizvo. Vana vavo vakanopinda chikoro chaiva pedyo nerokishini rwavaigara. Vaibetserawo vabereki vavo nekutengesa mazai musi weMugovera neSvondo. Hutano hwemhuri yaVaGondo hwaiva hwoyevedza nekuti zvekudya zvaiva zvava sharaude. Ivo VaGondo vakapedzisira vave hofori yerume. Vaive vogara vakatsvinda uye vakazvishongedza nezvipfeko zvakanaka chose. Mhuri iyi yakaramba ichishanda nesimba zvekuti waisafunga kuti ndiyo yaimbonhonga svosve nemuromo.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any two disadvantages of CAD: 1. High initial cost of software and hardware. 2. Requires trained/skilled operators. 3. Risk of data loss due to system failure. 4. High maintenance costs. (1 mark each, any 2)

(b) Any two types of 3D printers: 1. Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) printer. 2. Stereolithography (SLA) printer. 3. Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) printer. 4. Digital Light Processing (DLP) printer. (1 mark each, any 2)

(c) A line is a single straight segment drawn between two points and each segment is a separate object; a polyline is a connected sequence of line and/or arc segments treated as a single object. (1 mark for line description, 1 mark for polyline description)

(d) Any two disadvantages of CAM: 1. High initial capital investment in machinery/equipment. 2. Requires skilled/trained personnel for programming and operation. 3. High maintenance costs. 4. Job losses/redundancy for manual workers. (1 mark each, any 2)

(e) Object Snap (OSNAP) is used to precisely locate and snap the cursor to specific geometric points on existing objects (e.g., endpoints, midpoints, centres, intersections), ensuring accurate and exact drawing construction. (2 marks for a complete explanation)

(f) Marking criteria for stool reproduction in 3D: Correct 3D representation of stool shape (2); Appropriate and consistent dimensions applied (2); Correct use of CAD commands/tools (2); Proper proportions maintained (2); Neatness and presentation of the final drawing (2). Total: 10 marks.

questions.text: Figure 2 shows a multi-purpose Hall with a retractable flat roof. Answer all parts below.

subParts.text: Design in 3D, two methods of opening and closing the roof when necessary.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Show the type of truss or roof support structure to be used on the roof design.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Show a method of ensuring that the retractable roof is storm proof.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Name any two materials that can be used in the construction of the retractable roof.
subParts.label: (d)(i)

subParts.text: State any three mechanical properties of the materials named in (d)(i) above.
subParts.label: (d)(ii)

questions.diagramNote: Figure 2 shows a multi-purpose Hall with a retractable flat roof, including roof, walls (left and right) labelled.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Two methods of opening and closing the retractable roof (3D design, 25 marks each method):
Method 1 – Sliding/Rolling Roof Panels: Roof panels mounted on rails/tracks along the top of the walls; motorised or manual mechanism slides panels to one or both sides to open; award marks for: 3D accuracy and clarity (10), functional mechanism shown (8), correct proportions (4), presentation/neatness (3).
Method 2 – Folding/Bi-fold Roof: Roof divided into hinged sections that fold accordion-style; actuated by hydraulic, pneumatic, or manual linkage; award marks as above.
Marking: Originality/creativity of design (up to 5 marks each method); correct 3D representation; mechanism clearly labelled and functional.

(b) Truss/roof support structure: Acceptable types include Pratt truss, Warren truss, Howe truss, flat/parallel chord truss. Award marks for: correct 3D/2D representation of truss type (8), appropriate spacing and sizing (4), labelling of members (3). Total 15 marks.

(c) Storm-proofing method: Examples include – overlapping sealed joints between roof panels; rubber/neoprene weather seals/gaskets along panel edges; raised lips/flanges that interlock when closed; drainage channels to prevent water pooling; locking mechanisms to prevent wind uplift. Award marks for: a clearly shown and labelled method (7), practicality and effectiveness (3). Total 10 marks.

(d)(i) Any two materials: Polycarbonate sheeting; Steel/aluminium sheeting; Tempered glass; UPVC/fibreglass panels; Timber with waterproof membrane. (1 mark each, any 2)

(d)(ii) Any three mechanical properties: Tensile strength; Compressive strength; Elasticity/stiffness (Young's modulus); Hardness; Toughness; Ductility; Malleability. (1 mark each, any 3)

questions.text: At a local college, there is a bathroom for both able-bodied learners and wheelchair bound ones. A cabinet has to be fitted and has to be mounted in such a way that it can be raised or lowered to the required height. Answer all parts below.

subParts.text: Design in 3D, a mounted bathroom cabinet that can be used by the learners in the college mentioned above.
subParts.label: (a)(i)

subParts.text: Show in 3D, any two mechanisms/methods that can be used to raise or lower the cabinet.
subParts.label: (a)(ii)

subParts.text: Show in 3D, the method of securing or locking the mounted cabinet in a particular position.
subParts.label: (a)(iii)

subParts.text: State any three possible materials that can be used to make the cabinet.
subParts.label: (b)(i)

subParts.text: Explain how the cabinet will be finished in relation to the different possible materials you have stated in (b)(i).
subParts.label: (b)(ii)

subParts.text: Apply a chamfer on the outside edges of the cabinet you have designed.
subParts.label: (b)(iii)

subParts.text: Show a method of fixing a mirror on the bathroom cabinet.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) 3D Mounted Bathroom Cabinet Design (25 marks):
The cabinet should be wall-mounted on a vertical rail/channel system allowing height adjustment. Mark scheme: Overall 3D shape and form of cabinet (6); Correct proportions suitable for both able-bodied and wheelchair users (5); Wall-mounting system clearly shown (5); Interior shelving/storage features (5); Neatness and presentation (4).

(a)(ii) Two mechanisms/methods to raise or lower the cabinet (25 marks, ~12–13 marks each):
Method 1 – Motorised linear actuator/electric motor driven rack-and-pinion or lead screw: cabinet attached to carriage that travels up/down a vertical rail driven by motor.
Method 2 – Manual counterbalance/pulley system: cabinet attached to cables routed over pulleys with a counterweight, allowing easy manual height adjustment.
Other acceptable methods: hydraulic/pneumatic cylinder; scissor-lift mechanism; spring-assisted slide mechanism.
Mark scheme per method: 3D accuracy (5); mechanism clearly shown and labelled (5); practicality/functionality (3).

(a)(iii) Securing/locking method (16 marks):
Examples: spring-loaded pin/detent locking into holes drilled at intervals on the rail; cam-lock lever that clamps onto the rail; ratchet and pawl system; screw clamp/tightening collar. Mark scheme: Method clearly shown in 3D (8); effectiveness/reliability of lock (5); labelling and presentation (3).

(b)(i) Any three materials for the cabinet: Solid hardwood (e.g., teak, mahogany); MDF (Medium Density Fibreboard); Plywood; Chipboard/particleboard; Stainless steel; PVC/plastic. (1 mark each, any 3)

(b)(ii) Finishing per material:
– Solid hardwood: sanded smooth, sealed with waterproof varnish/lacquer or oil finish suitable for humid bathroom environment.
– MDF: sealed with primer, painted with moisture-resistant paint or covered with melamine/veneer.
– Plywood: sanded, sealed with polyurethane varnish or painted with moisture-resistant enamel paint.
– Stainless steel: polished/brushed finish, no additional coating required but may be powder-coated.
– PVC: factory-finished; may be wiped clean; no further finishing usually needed.
(1 mark per material matched to appropriate finish, any 3)

(b)(iii) Chamfer: A chamfer (angled cut, typically 45°) applied to all outer edges of the cabinet using the AutoCAD CHAMFER command. Award 1 mark for correctly applying the chamfer in the 3D model and 1 mark for appropriate chamfer dimensions/consistency.

(c) Method of fixing a mirror (6 marks):
Acceptable methods: Mirror adhesive/mastic applied to back of mirror and cabinet face (2); Mirror clips/brackets screwed to cabinet top and bottom edges retaining mirror (2); Recessed rebate/groove routed into cabinet door/front panel into which mirror is set and secured with beading (2).
Mark scheme: Method clearly shown (3); practicality and security of fixing (2); labelling/presentation (1). Total 6 marks.

questions.text:
Ndebwana Yewhisisa
Bala mbiko unotebela uhandule mibhuzo uhingisa mitshara yakapelela.

Wabva kuna : Lozibo Dube
Unda ku : Rediyo BuKalanga
Hhuba : 17 Tjabewombe 2024

Kwakatikala gabadzo mukwele tjeSibomvu nsi wa10 Tjabewombe muviki yakapela. Bana bekwele bezwizanila zwabo nelubaka gwenyaluluka. Kwakawhakala kutitima hangwana yose, kati idutu lakalibva kuBurwa. Lakalinda lidzipula matenjana liwaposela pehhugwi kwemiti mikulu. Yakahha mhepo isingamilike yakalinga kukwele tjabo. Kwakabonakala bhulubusi lisingamilike lipfungayila nemasimba linda pehhugwi. Kwakakutitima sevula yetjilimo. Bana bekwele bakatihha behhala hangwanyana yose. Dutu lakati labepedlo nekwele kukabonakala badiyi babo belabuka bo nemasimba benda kubali. Bejalo bedana newhi lipehhugwi kuti wose mwana alale pasi nentumbu ipapo kwayako. Bana bakati vutjalala pasi, bakabubatilana sezwikukwana zwakhuthiwa nelumhangu. Tjinyolotjo kwakabe hhalima ndawana dzose, mavu emilika enga atjoba vukidza. Mazenge en'umba dzekwele dzose akawuluka enda pehhugwi semaphepha. Ndzimu wakagwa nekuti bunji gwemazenge iwawa akanowila kule nebana.

Nelubakanyana mhepo yakayatjipinda koga bana kusina unomuka. Badiyi baka loba tshipi yekwele yakayilila nezila isakawolobegwa nebunji. Bana bakamuka sehulo belabuka benda pabano hanganila. Bakahogwa kuka wanika kuti bose bayapo kakale akuna wakubala. Kwele tjakasala tjili dongo.

Watugwa na : Lozibo Dube

BALA LWAANO USANDULE MIBUZYO IITOBELA

Nsiku bantu bakalikujana mulilo kwiindilila mukupikisa musikkabakandu muchisamu chamukompedo kwawunta busi. Mulilo wankuni nguwo wakalikubelesegwa kapati mukumwinisya akujisya. Mukuvula kwabusongo kwakatalikwa kulungisigwa magesi. Magesi alungisigwa kakubelesegwa malasa, meenda, zuka, nyukkiliya aluuwo. MuZimbabwe magesi alungisigwa aamalasa kuMunyati, kuMunyati, kuBulawayo akuHwange. Nzila yakulungisya magesi kakubelesegwa malasa isofwaazya muuya mumulengalenga. Kusofwaala kwamuuya wamumulengalenga kweetelezya bbalangwe anzala muZimbabwe kuMozambique akuMadagasca mazambangulwe luzutu. Maanda, madani migwagwa azikolo zyakamwayuuka. Nkaako akulungisigwe magesi kakubelesegwa nzila zikwabilila muuya wamumulengalenga. Kulungisya magesi kakubelesegwa maanzi, zuba aluuwo kukwabilila mulengalenga. MuZimbabwe magesi alungisigwa aamaanzi kuKariba. Masola alokuyanzalwa aajulu aamaanda kuti kubelesegwe magesi aazwa kuzuba. Matechi ngitumunisya mumaanda abelesya masola. Bantu balungisya magesi bachenjezegwa kuti banike mumfunkununo yanzila zyakalungisya magesi zikwabilila mulengalenga abuumi bwabantu.

questions.text:
BALA NJOOMO USANDULE MIBUZYO IITOBELA.

Choolwe: Mulimu ngutwapegwa aamuyiisi mwiingi alimwi muyumu loko.
Lubbe: Nchobeni mwiingi pesi tuyoobelesya njobolamakani kukusandula mibuzyo. Nkinkaako tuyofwambaana kumanisya.
Choolwe: Masimpe njobolamakani zilatugwasya pesi bayiiyi biingi tabazibelesyi munzila iiluleme pe, nga basika nkubasweeka kumaboneno aabo.
Lubbe: Njobolamakani zilaalugwasyo lwiingi. Zilatugwasya mulizyachikolo alimwi tulakonzya kumwaya milumbe kumasena aasiyene siyene muchiindi chifwiifwi.
Choolwe: Wayasa nondo muliso kusisya milumbe kwiinda mukulemba magwalo kulanonoka. Chiindi bakalikubelesya ngoma, mulilo naa kulayizya bantu kuti bakatusisizye milunde. Zyoonse eezi zyakali nzila zinonoka.
Lubbe: Milumbe iisisigwa aabantu ilakonzya kusandulwa, yaakusika munzila iitalinjiyo pe, nkinkaako nzila eeyi iilaabulewusi.
Choolwe: Njobalamakani zigwasizya ndiswe nitukonzya kuzyuula peepe balaabuyumuyumu mukuzyuula.
Lubbe: Bwaami aLuzibo zyakabagwasya loko nkaambo choonse chindi bakali kuzibelesya chiindi nibakali kubalila misunko. Zyakapa kuti bazwidilile muzyiiyo zyabo.
Choolwe: Yii nikuliboobo njobolamakani zilokunyongania chisi. Myuunzi myiingi ilookufwa nkaambo kanzizyo. Bazyali tabachisyomeki pe. Zyanzaania bantu mumaanda. Nikuba uwambuule aamuzyali tafwambaani kukavwiila nkaambo meso amiyeeyo yoonse unoyibikkide aalinjiyo.

Markers award up to 20 marks for ONE chosen piece of writing. General marking rubric:

**Content & Ideas (8 marks):** Relevant, well-developed ideas; clear focus on the chosen topic; sufficient detail and creativity; appropriate length (80–120 words — letters/dialogues: excluding address/greeting/farewell/character names).

**Language & Expression (8 marks):** Correct and natural isiNdebele; varied vocabulary; appropriate register for the task (formal for letter, narrative for story, dialogue format for ingxoxo, poetic devices for inkondlo); good sentence construction.

**Organisation & Structure (4 marks):** Logical sequencing; correct format for the chosen task (e.g., letter format with address, date, salutation, body, closing; dialogue with speaker labels; poem with stanzas/rhythm).

**Task-specific notes:**
- (a) Dialogue between two people about handcraft/manual work and its importance — must show turns of conversation.
- (b) Personal narrative about a favourite town — descriptive, first-person or third-person.
- (c) Story incorporating the phrase 'Ngatshaywa luvalo ngaphosa ngafa' — must use the phrase naturally within the narrative.
- (d) Formal letter to a neighbouring school's headmaster requesting a friendly sports/games tournament — must include all letter conventions.
- (e) Poem about one of Zimbabwe's valuable minerals — must employ at least some poetic features (rhythm, imagery, repetition, etc.).
