questions.text:
The study of living organisms and their environment
A microbiology.
B zoology.
C cytology.
D ecology.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – ecology. Ecology is the study of living organisms and their relationships with their environment.

questions.text:
The diagram shows a safety symbol. The symbol indicates
A the possibility of electric shock.
B exposure to a bio-hazard.
C allow cooling before handling.
D limit time of exposure to equipment.
questions.diagramNote: A safety/hazard symbol is shown; students must identify what it represents.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – exposure to a bio-hazard. The biohazard symbol (three interlocking circles forming a trefoil on a central ring) indicates a biological hazard.

questions.text:
Which one is a test for starch?
A Benedict's test
B Buret test
C Emulsian test
D Iodine test
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – Iodine test. Iodine solution turns blue-black in the presence of starch.

questions.text:
Which pair of atoms are part of a water molecule?
A hydrogen and nitrogen
B hydrogen and oxygen
C carbon and oxygen
D oxygen and nitrogen
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – hydrogen and oxygen. A water molecule (H₂O) is composed of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.text:
The movement of solute molecules down a concentration gradient is
A active uptake.
B osmosis.
C plasmolysis.
D diffusion.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – diffusion. Diffusion is the net movement of solute molecules from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration (down the concentration gradient), requiring no energy.

questions.text:
Transmission of impulses is an adaptation of
A white blood cells.
B muscle cells.
C egg cells.
D nerve cells.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – nerve cells. Nerve cells (neurons) are specialised for the transmission of electrical impulses, having long axons and myelin sheaths for this purpose.

questions.text:
Which part is found in plant cells only?
A cell wall
B cell membrane
C cytoplasm
D nucleus
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – cell wall. The cell wall (made of cellulose) is found in plant cells only; cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus are present in both plant and animal cells.

questions.text:
Which enzyme, in washing powders, removes fat stains from fabric?
A catalase
B protease
C lipase
D amylase
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – lipase. Lipase breaks down fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol, making it effective at removing fat-based stains from fabric.

questions.text:
Which one contributes to enzyme specificity?
A temperature
B concentration
C shape
D nature
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – shape. Enzyme specificity is determined by the shape of the active site (lock-and-key / induced-fit model), which only accommodates a complementary-shaped substrate.

questions.text: The graph shows the effects of temperature on the souring of milk as an enzyme controlled reaction. At which point, A, B, C or D, is the temperature optimum?
questions.topic: Effect of Temperature on Enzyme Activity
questions.diagramNote: A graph of 'time taken for reaction to end (min)' vs temperature with points A, B, C, D marked; the curve shows a minimum time (fastest reaction) at one point.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – the optimum temperature is where the time taken for the reaction to end is shortest (lowest point on the curve), indicating the fastest reaction rate. Students should identify the point corresponding to the minimum value on the y-axis.

questions.text:
Destarching involves placing a potted plant in
A water for 24 hours.
B transparent glass for 24 hours.
C dark cupboard for 24 hours.
D direct sunlight for 24 hours.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – dark cupboard for 24 hours. Placing a plant in darkness for 24 hours allows it to use up all stored starch through respiration, ensuring leaves are starch-free before photosynthesis experiments.

questions.text:
Phosphorus deficiency results in
A stunted shoot growth.
B stunted root growth.
C brown leaf margins.
D premature death.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – stunted root growth. Phosphorus is essential for root development and ATP/DNA synthesis; its deficiency typically causes poor root growth, and may also result in purple discolouration of leaves.

questions.text:
Pests affect productivity by
A increasing pollination.
B disrupting soil structure.
C improving soil texture.
D reducing photosynthesis.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – reducing photosynthesis. Pests (e.g. leaf-eating insects) damage or destroy leaves, reducing the photosynthetic area and thus lowering the plant's productivity.

questions.text:
Cultural pest control involves the use of
A nematodes to control numbers.
B wasp parasites for suppression.
C crop rotation to break life cycles.
D lace wing larvae as predators.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – crop rotation to break life cycles. Cultural control uses farming practices such as crop rotation, which prevents pests from completing their life cycles by changing the host plant each season.

questions.text:
Which one does not affect the rate of photosynthesis?
A oxygen concentration
B temperature
C light intensity
D carbon dioxide concentration
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – oxygen concentration. The rate of photosynthesis is affected by light intensity, temperature and carbon dioxide concentration (limiting factors). Oxygen concentration does not limit the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.text:
A toddler is fed mainly sadza and vegetables in large amounts everyday. The toddler has been feeling tired and losing weight. This is because the diet taken lacks
A proteins in correct proportions.
B fats in correct proportions.
C vitamins in correct proportions.
D mineral ions in correct proportions.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – proteins in correct proportions. Sadza (maize porridge) and vegetables are low in protein. Tiredness and weight loss indicate protein deficiency (kwashiorkor-like symptoms), as proteins are needed for growth, repair and energy.

questions.text:
Which one is not a nutrient in animal nutrition?
A carbohydrate
B fibre
C proteins
D vitamins
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – fibre. Fibre (dietary roughage) is not a nutrient in the strict sense; it is not digested or absorbed to provide energy or building materials. Carbohydrates, proteins and vitamins are all classified as nutrients.

questions.text:
The information shows the composition of four diets. Which diet, A, B, C or D, is suitable for a farm labourer?
A potatoes, protein, fruits
B milk, fluids, lean protein
C whole grain, vegetables, low fat milk
D nuts, lean proteins, low fat milk
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – whole grain, vegetables, low fat milk. A farm labourer performs heavy physical work and needs a high-energy, balanced diet. Whole grains provide sustained carbohydrate energy; vegetables provide vitamins and minerals; low fat milk provides protein and calcium — making this the most balanced and energy-sufficient diet.

questions.text:
The table shows the results of food tests on four food samples. Which food sample, A, B, C or D, contained reducing sugars?
food sample | results
A | blue-black
B | violet/purple
C | orange/brick red
D | cloudy/chalky
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – orange/brick red. Benedict's test for reducing sugars gives an orange/brick-red precipitate when reducing sugars are present. Blue-black indicates starch (iodine test); violet/purple indicates protein (Biuret test); cloudy/chalky indicates fats (emulsion test).

questions.text: The diagram shows a mammalian heart. Which one, A, B, C or D, is the vena cava?
questions.diagramNote: A labelled diagram of a mammalian heart with four parts (A, B, C, D) indicated; students must identify the vena cava.
questions.aiModelAnswer: The vena cava is the large vein returning deoxygenated blood to the right atrium. In standard heart diagrams it enters the top-right of the heart. Students should identify the label pointing to the large vessel entering the right atrium (typically label A or B depending on diagram orientation). Key feature: it carries deoxygenated blood into the right atrium.

questions.text:
The diagram shows the menstrual cycle. Which stage, A, B, C or D, is ovulation?
(Diagram shows oestrogen and progesterone levels over 0–28 days with points A, B, C, D marked.)
questions.diagramNote: A graph of the menstrual cycle showing oestrogen and progesterone hormone levels over 28 days, with four labelled points (A, B, C, D).
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – ovulation occurs at approximately day 14 of the menstrual cycle, corresponding to the peak/surge of oestrogen followed by a sharp drop. Students should identify the point at approximately day 14 where oestrogen peaks before progesterone rises.

questions.text:
Which part of the respiratory system separates the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity?
A bronchus
B bronchioles
C diaphragm
D larynx
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – diaphragm. The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscular sheet that separates the thoracic (chest) cavity from the abdominal cavity and plays a key role in breathing movements.

questions.text:
What separates the left side from the right side of the heart?
A valves
B septum
C atrium
D ventricle
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – septum. The septum is the muscular wall that divides the heart into left and right sides, preventing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

questions.text:
The equation shows anaerobic respiration in plants.
glucose → carbon dioxide + X + energy.
What is X?
A water
B carbon dioxide
C alcohol
D lactic acid
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – alcohol (ethanol). In anaerobic respiration in plants (and yeast), glucose is converted to ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide. The equation is: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + (small amount of) energy.

questions.text:
Which is not a use of energy in living organisms?
A uptake of mineral ions
B absorption of water
C conduction of impulses
D division of cells
questions.topic: Uses of Energy in Living Organisms
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – absorption of water. Water is absorbed by osmosis, which is a passive process requiring no energy (ATP). Uptake of mineral ions (active transport), conduction of impulses and cell division all require energy.

questions.text:
Genetic material formed from more than one species is called
A vector DNA.
B recombinant DNA.
C chromosomal DNA.
D plasmid DNA.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – recombinant DNA. Recombinant DNA is DNA that has been formed by combining genetic material from two or more different species (e.g. inserting a human gene into a bacterial plasmid).

questions.text: The diagram shows the structure of a bacterium. Which part, A, B, C or D, is responsible for locomotion?
questions.diagramNote: A diagram of a bacterium with four parts (A, B, C, D) labelled; students must identify the structure responsible for locomotion.
questions.aiModelAnswer: The flagellum is the structure responsible for locomotion in bacteria. Students should identify the label pointing to the whip-like tail/appendage (flagellum) extending from the bacterial cell body.

questions.text:
The basic unit of inheritance is the
A chromosome.
B nucleus.
C gene.
D allele.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – gene. A gene is the basic unit of inheritance; it is a specific sequence of DNA that codes for a particular protein/characteristic and is passed from parent to offspring.

questions.text:
The genotype for a particular characteristic is represented by alleles T and t. T is dominant to t. Which is correct about Tt and TT?
        Tt          TT
A recessive phenotype | recessive phenotype
B dominant phenotype | dominant phenotype
C recessive phenotype | dominant phenotype
D dominant phenotype | recessive phenotype
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – dominant phenotype / dominant phenotype. Since T is dominant over t: TT (homozygous dominant) expresses the dominant phenotype, and Tt (heterozygous) also expresses the dominant phenotype because T masks the effect of t.

questions.text:
Which one is a factor of discontinuous variation?
A temperature
B environment
C genes
D nutrition
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – genes. Discontinuous variation (e.g. blood groups, tongue rolling) is controlled solely by genes and is not influenced by environmental factors like temperature, nutrition or other environmental conditions.

questions.text:
A Zimbabwean dairy farmer can improve milk production by
A artificial selection.
B natural selection.
C sterilising cows.
D penning cows.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – artificial selection. Artificial (selective) breeding involves choosing cows with the highest milk yield and breeding them together over successive generations to improve milk production in the herd.

questions.text:
In natural selection, organisms
A best adapted to the environment survive.
B that are the strongest survive and reproduce.
C desired by humans are allowed to reproduce.
D randomly mate leading to variation.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – best adapted to the environment survive. Natural selection (survival of the fittest) means that organisms with characteristics best suited to their environment are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their genes.

questions.text:
Which one is not a threat to biodiversity?
A invasive species
B climate change
C subdividing land into farms
D creation of nature reserves
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – creation of nature reserves. Nature reserves protect habitats and species, thereby enhancing biodiversity rather than threatening it. Invasive species, climate change and subdividing land into farms all reduce biodiversity.

questions.text:
Which is a diagnostic feature of the kingdom Protista?
A unicellular prokaryote
B multicellular eukaryote
C unicellular eukaryote
D multicellular prokaryotes
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – unicellular eukaryote. Protists are defined as unicellular (single-celled) eukaryotic organisms (they have a membrane-bound nucleus), distinguishing them from prokaryotes (bacteria) and multicellular eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi).

questions.text:
What is the source of energy in a food chain?
A the sun
B carbon dioxide
C the water
D soil nutrients
questions.topic: Food Chains / Energy Flow in Ecosystems
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – the sun. The sun is the ultimate source of energy in almost all food chains. Producers (plants) capture solar energy through photosynthesis and convert it to chemical energy, which is then passed along the food chain.

questions.text:
Which one is a physical component of an ecosystem?
A litter
B humus
C bacteria
D soil
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – soil. Soil is a physical (abiotic) component of an ecosystem. Litter (dead leaves) and humus (decomposed organic matter) are organic/biological materials, and bacteria are living (biotic) organisms.

questions.text:
The table shows results obtained from an experiment to determine air content of a soil sample. The volume of water used was 20 cm³.
Volume of soil only: 20 cm³
Volume of soil + water: 34 cm³
What is the percentage of air in the soil?
A 15%
B 30%
C 59%
D 85%
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – 30%. Working: Volume of air = Volume of soil + Volume of water − Volume of soil + water mixture = 20 + 20 − 34 = 6 cm³. Percentage air = (6 ÷ 20) × 100 = 30%.

questions.text:
A young adult develops chills, fever and sweating accompanied by shivering. The doctor suspects malaria. Which organism is likely causing the symptoms?
A bacteria
B virus
C fungi
D protozoa
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – protozoa. Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan (unicellular eukaryotic) parasite transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito.

questions.text:
Which drug may cause hallucination?
A cannabis
B nicotine
C alcohol
D paracetamol
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – cannabis. Cannabis (marijuana) is a hallucinogenic drug that can cause hallucinations, altered perception and distorted sense of time. Nicotine is a stimulant, alcohol is a depressant, and paracetamol is an analgesic/painkiller.

questions.text:
Fungi are used in the production of
A paracetamol.
B penicillin.
C chloroquine.
D aspirin.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – penicillin. Penicillin is an antibiotic produced by the fungus Penicillium notatum (Penicillium chrysogenum). Paracetamol and aspirin are synthetically produced analgesics; chloroquine is a synthetic antimalarial drug.

questions.topic: Ku tsala xitsalwana / n'wangulano (Composition / Letter / Dialogue Writing)
questions.aiModelAnswer: Student must choose ONE topic only and write a composition or dialogue of 100–120 words in correct Xichangana. Marks are awarded for: (1) Correct format appropriate to the chosen task (letter format for (a), proverb explanation essay for (b), expository essay for (c), descriptive essay for (d), dialogue format for (e)); (2) Relevance and development of the chosen topic/nhlokomhaka; (3) Correct Xichangana grammar, spelling, and punctuation; (4) Vocabulary range and sentence variety; (5) Word count within 100–120 words. questions.text:
Hlaya ndzima leyi u ta hlamula swivutiso leswi landzelaka hi swivulwa swi nga helela.

I nhlikanhi! Ndza mi xeweta hinkwenu, n'wina mi nga ta eka nkhuvo lowu. Ndzi xixima Muhlonipheki, Muyimeri wa Palamente Tatana Masokisi, Muyimeri wa Masipala Tatana Mahlo, tinhloko ta swikolo, van'wabuku lava koteke ku fika laha, maxaka na vanghana. Swa ku ti tivisa ndzo endlela nawu, ane hinkwerhu ma ndzi tiva? Loyi a yimeke mahlweni ka n'wina i Xalati, rikotswe ra N'wa-Yingwani. Ndzi yime hi ku titshongahata na ku twa nyanyuko lowu khapaka hikokwalaho ka ku nyikiwa xindzhuti hi n'wina. Hambileswi mi ndzi hluvulelaka swihuku hikuva se ndzi xidyondzeki, a hi tiveni leswaku i ndlopfu ya hina hinkwerhu. N'wana loyi a nga na vumunhu loko a dyondzekile swi vula leswaku ku dyondzikile ndyangu na muganga wa ka vona. Hinkwenu a hi tibeni swifuva. A ndzi nge swi koti ku longoloxa hinkwaswo leswi swi sasekeleke dyondzo. Manguva lawa ku hava loyi a nga tiviki nkoka wa dyondzo lowu nga lo tlangandla, erivaleni. Xana kwalaha hi hlengeletelane yini? Kasi a hi yona mitirho ya dyondzo leyi yi hi hlanganisaka hi nkarhi hi tlangela ku heta ka mina khoso ya vudokodela? N'wina vatswari va mina a ndzi tivi leswaku ndzi ta mi khensa hi yini lexi ringanelaka ku tikharhata ka n'wina ku endlela leswaku ndzi kuma vutomi bya kahle? Mi ndzi lehisele mbilu hambi laha a ndzi rheta kona ndzi karhi ndzi mi dyisa mbitsi. Ku sukela laha ndzi nga sungula ntangha yo sungula hi lembe ra 2000 ku kondza ndzi heta tidyondzo ta sekondari, vatswari va mina a mi kokangi moya. A ku hakeriwa timali to tlhuma. Loko se ndzi ya endla khoso ya vudokodela eYunivhesiti ya Zimbabwe timali a ti gayiwa kunene bya mavele exigayeni. Ndzi khensa Xikwembu hi ku ndzi tiyisa enkarhini lowu a swi tika. Mina xikolo ndzi vona yi ri nyimpi. Hi vahluri hinkwerhu na n'wina varhandziwa. Ndzi khensile.

SWIVUTISO
(a) Nkhuvo wu sungurile nkarhi muni?
(b) Boxa vito ra muvulavuri.
(c) Xana i mani loyi a nga khensiwa hi muvulavuri?
(d) Vanhu a va hlengeletelana yini siku leri?
(e) Hlamusela leswi vulaka marito ya ku 'vatswari va mina a mi kokangi moya.'
(f) Katsakanya ndzima leyi u hlayeke hi marito lama nga hundziki makumenkombo (70).

questions.text:
1 (a) State any two stages of production.
(b) Explain batch production as used by bread manufacturers in Zimbabwe.
(c) Identify any two principles of insurance adopted by insurance companies.

subParts.text: State any two stages of production.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Explain batch production as used by bread manufacturers in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Identify any two principles of insurance adopted by insurance companies.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any two of: Primary production (extractive), Secondary production (manufacturing/construction), Tertiary production (services). [1 mark each, max 2]
(b) Batch production is a method where a specific quantity (batch) of a product is made at one time before switching to another product. For bread manufacturers, a set number of loaves are baked together in one batch, then a different variety or quantity is produced in the next batch. This allows flexibility and variety in output. [2 marks for clear explanation with relevant example]
(c) Any two of: Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) – both parties must disclose all relevant information honestly; Insurable interest – the insured must have a financial interest in the subject matter; Indemnity – the insured is restored to the same financial position as before the loss (not better off); Subrogation – after paying a claim, the insurer takes over the insured's rights to recover losses from a third party; Contribution – if insured with multiple insurers, each pays a proportionate share; Proximate cause – the loss must be directly caused by an insured peril. [1 mark each, max 2]

questions.text:
2 (a) Distinguish between home trade and foreign trade.
(b) Explain any two advantages of operating as a sole trader business in your community.

subParts.text: Distinguish between home trade and foreign trade.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Explain any two advantages of operating as a sole trader business in your community.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Home trade refers to the buying and selling of goods and services within the borders of a country (Zimbabwe), e.g. a retailer selling goods to local customers. Foreign trade (international trade) refers to the exchange of goods and services between two or more countries, e.g. Zimbabwe exporting tobacco to China or importing machinery from South Africa. Key distinctions: home trade uses local currency; foreign trade involves foreign currency, customs duties, and exchange rates. [2 marks for home trade, 2 marks for foreign trade, award marks for clear distinction]
(b) Any two of: Easy/cheap to set up – minimal legal formalities and low start-up costs; Full control – the owner makes all decisions quickly without consulting others; Owner keeps all profits – no profit-sharing with partners or shareholders; Privacy/confidentiality – no obligation to publish accounts; Personal customer relationships – owner knows customers personally, building loyalty; Flexibility – can easily change products/services to meet customer needs; Motivation – owner works hard as they directly benefit from success. [2 marks each: 1 mark for identifying the advantage + 1 mark for explanation, max 4]

(b) Identify any two stakeholders of any retail shop in your local area.
(c) Explain the importance of communication in a business.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) The business environment refers to all the internal and external factors/forces that affect a business's operations, decision-making, and performance. It includes economic, political, social, technological, legal, and competitive factors surrounding the business. [2 marks for a complete, accurate definition]
(b) Any two of: Owner/shareholders, employees/workers, customers, suppliers, government, local community, creditors/banks, competitors. [1 mark each, max 2]
(c) Communication is important in a business because: it ensures instructions and information are passed clearly between management and employees, reducing errors and misunderstandings; it enables effective coordination of activities and departments; it helps in customer relations and marketing; it aids decision-making by providing relevant information; it motivates employees when feedback is communicated. [2 marks for a well-explained point; 1 mark for a basic correct point]

questions.text:
The following information was extracted from the financial statement of a local manufacturer of traditional musical instruments in your local community.

ZWG
Sales         60 000
Gross profit  30 000
Expenses      18 000
Net profit    12 000

Calculate:
(a) Gross profit margin.
(b) Net profit margin.

subParts.text: Calculate the Gross profit margin.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Calculate the Net profit margin.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Gross Profit Margin = (Gross Profit ÷ Sales) × 100
= (30 000 ÷ 60 000) × 100
= 50%
[1 mark for correct formula, 1 mark for correct substitution, 1 mark for correct answer of 50%]

(b) Net Profit Margin = (Net Profit ÷ Sales) × 100
= (12 000 ÷ 60 000) × 100
= 20%
[1 mark for correct formula, 1 mark for correct substitution, 1 mark for correct answer of 20%]

questions.text:
5 (a) Explain why farmers in Zimbabwe need warehouses.
(b) Assess the importance of becoming an entrepreneur in Zimbabwe.

subParts.text: Explain why farmers in Zimbabwe need warehouses.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Assess the importance of becoming an entrepreneur in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Farmers need warehouses to: store surplus/excess produce after harvest to sell later when prices are higher (price stabilisation); protect goods from weather, pests, and deterioration; bridge the time gap between production and consumption (time utility); act as a central distribution point; provide collateral/security for loans (warehouse receipts); allow goods to be graded and sorted before sale. [1 mark per valid explained point, max 4]

(b) Importance of becoming an entrepreneur in Zimbabwe: Creates employment for others, reducing unemployment; Generates income and improves personal/family living standards; Contributes to national economic growth and GDP; Encourages innovation and introduction of new products/services; Reduces dependence on formal employment/government jobs; Utilises local resources effectively; Contributes to government revenue through taxes; Promotes self-reliance and economic independence. [1 mark per valid assessed point, max 4; award higher marks for points that show assessment/evaluation rather than mere identification]

questions.text:
6 (a) Identify any two stages of the purchasing cycle.
(b) Explain two advantages of virtual markets to local entrepreneurs.

subParts.text: Identify any two stages of the purchasing cycle.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Explain two advantages of virtual markets to local entrepreneurs.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any two of the stages of the purchasing cycle: Recognition of need; Preparation of purchase requisition; Selection of supplier/sourcing; Issue of purchase order; Receipt of goods/delivery; Inspection/quality check; Invoice verification/payment; Recording the transaction. [1 mark each, max 2]

(b) Any two of: Wider market reach – entrepreneurs can sell to customers across Zimbabwe and internationally without physical boundaries; Lower operating costs – no need to pay rent for physical shop premises, reducing overheads; 24/7 trading – the virtual market operates around the clock, increasing sales opportunities; Easier marketing – entrepreneurs can advertise products online at a low cost to a large audience; Convenience for customers – customers can browse and order from anywhere, attracting more buyers; Access to customer data – entrepreneurs can track buying patterns and preferences to improve their business. [2 marks each: 1 mark for identifying the advantage + 1 mark for explanation, max 4]

questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of specialisation to a Zimbabwean clothes manufacturer.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Advantages of specialisation to a Zimbabwean clothes manufacturer:
• Increased productivity – workers focus on one task, becoming faster and more skilled, producing more output in less time.
• Higher quality output – repetition of tasks improves skill and consistency, leading to better quality garments.
• Cost efficiency – higher output per worker reduces cost per unit (economies of scale).
• Better use of machinery – specific machines can be dedicated to specific tasks, maximising their efficiency.
• Time saving – no time wasted switching between different tasks.
• Encourages innovation – workers become experts in their area and can suggest improvements.

Disadvantages of specialisation:
• Boredom/monotony – workers performing the same task repeatedly may become demotivated and less productive.
• Structural unemployment – if demand for a specific type of clothing falls, highly specialised workers may struggle to find alternative employment.
• Interdependence – if one specialised worker or machine breaks down, the entire production line may halt.
• Lack of flexibility – the manufacturer may find it difficult to diversify or switch to producing different products.
• Over-reliance on a narrow product range – vulnerable to changes in fashion trends.

[Award up to 10 marks for advantages and 10 marks for disadvantages; 2 marks per well-explained point (1 mark for identification + 1 mark for development/discussion); expect at least 5 points per side for full marks]

questions.text:
8 (a) Explain the management functions that can be used by Zimbabwean secondary schools administration.
(b) Discuss how small scale retailers in Zimbabwe survive in a market with big firms.

subParts.text: Explain the management functions that can be used by Zimbabwean secondary schools administration.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Discuss how small scale retailers in Zimbabwe survive in a market with big firms.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Management functions (POLCA/POSDCORB framework) applicable to secondary schools:
• Planning – the school administration sets goals/objectives, e.g. academic targets, timetables, and budgets for the school year.
• Organising – arranging resources (teachers, classrooms, materials) and assigning duties to ensure smooth running of the school.
• Leading/Directing – the head and deputies motivate and guide teachers and students toward achieving school goals.
• Controlling – monitoring performance against set standards, e.g. checking exam results, attendance records, and staff punctuality, then taking corrective action.
• Staffing/HR – recruiting, training, and appraising teachers and non-teaching staff.
• Coordinating – ensuring all departments (academic, administration, finance) work together harmoniously.
[2 marks per well-explained function, max 8]

(b) How small scale retailers survive against big firms:
• Personal/close customer relationships – they know customers by name, offer personalised service that large supermarkets cannot match.
• Convenient location – small retailers are often closer to residential areas, saving customers travel time and costs.
• Extended/flexible trading hours – willing to open early or late and on public holidays.
• Credit facilities – offer informal credit to trusted community members.
• Small/flexible quantities – sell goods in smaller quantities (e.g. by the cup or piece) suited to low-income customers.
• Niche/specialised products – stock locally demanded or specialised products not found in big stores.
• Lower overheads – lower operating costs mean they can remain competitive on certain items.
• Adaptability – quickly adjust stock and services to local demand changes.
• Community trust and loyalty – deeply embedded in the community, customers prefer to support local businesses.
[2 marks per well-explained point, max 12]

questions.text:
9 (a) Explain the different types of intellectual property owned by Zimbabwean businesses.
(b) Discuss the importance of public sector corporations to society.

subParts.text: Explain the different types of intellectual property owned by Zimbabwean businesses.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Discuss the importance of public sector corporations to society.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Types of intellectual property:
• Patents – exclusive rights granted to an inventor for a new invention/product for a set period (e.g. a new agricultural tool), preventing others from copying it without permission.
• Trademarks – distinctive signs, logos, or names that identify a business's products/services (e.g. a company logo), protecting the brand identity.
• Copyright – legal protection for original creative works such as books, music, software, and artistic works produced by Zimbabwean creators.
• Trade secrets – confidential business information such as recipes, formulas, or processes that give a business a competitive advantage (e.g. a food manufacturer's secret recipe).
• Industrial designs – protection of the visual/aesthetic aspects of a product (shape, pattern, colour) that make it unique.
• Geographical indications – identification of goods as originating from a specific region known for particular qualities (e.g. Zimbabwean tobacco).
[2 marks per well-explained type, max 10]

(b) Importance of public sector corporations:
• Provision of essential services – supply water, electricity, transport, and healthcare to all citizens, including those in remote/unprofitable areas.
• Employment creation – public corporations are major employers, reducing unemployment.
• Infrastructure development – build and maintain roads, railways, and public facilities for national development.
• Price stabilisation – government can control prices of essential goods/services to prevent exploitation of consumers.
• National security – some industries (e.g. defence, broadcasting) must remain under government control for security reasons.
• Revenue generation – profitable public corporations contribute to government revenue through surpluses/dividends.
• Social equity – ensure that even low-income communities have access to basic services.
• Stimulate economic growth – public investments in infrastructure attract private investment.
[2 marks per well-explained point, max 10]

questions.text:
10 (a) Explain marketing mix variables which can be used in the marketing of grain products in your area.
(b) Differentiate free market economy from planned economy.

subParts.text: Explain marketing mix variables which can be used in the marketing of grain products in your area.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Differentiate free market economy from planned economy.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Marketing mix variables (4Ps) for grain products:
• Product – the grain product (e.g. maize, sorghum, wheat) must meet customer needs; consider variety, quality, packaging, and branding to differentiate from competitors.
• Price – set competitive prices that farmers/consumers can afford; consider cost-plus pricing, market pricing, or discounts for bulk buyers.
• Place – ensure grain is available where and when needed; use local markets, grain depots, GMB collection points, or direct farm sales to maximise accessibility.
• Promotion – use advertising (radio, community notice boards), word-of-mouth, or promotional offers (e.g. discounts for early buyers) to create awareness and drive sales.
[2 marks per well-explained P, max 8]

(b) Differences between free market economy and planned economy:
• Ownership: In a free market, resources/businesses are privately owned; in a planned economy, the government/state owns the means of production.
• Decision-making: In a free market, decisions on what, how, and for whom to produce are made by individuals and businesses through price signals; in a planned economy, the central government makes these decisions.
• Price mechanism: Free market prices are determined by supply and demand; in a planned economy, prices are set by the government.
• Competition: Free markets encourage competition among businesses; planned economies have little or no competition as the state controls production.
• Consumer choice: Free markets offer wide consumer choice; planned economies offer limited choice as the state determines what is produced.
• Profit motive: Businesses in a free market are driven by profit; in a planned economy, production targets rather than profit guide decisions.
• Efficiency: Free markets tend to be more efficient due to competition; planned economies may be less efficient due to lack of incentives.
• Examples: Free market – USA; Planned economy – Cuba, North Korea.
[2 marks per well-explained difference, max 12]

questions.text:
11 (a) Explain the factors to consider when choosing the most appropriate mode of transport to carry different goods in your local area.
(b) Discuss how stakeholders affect business activities in a business which sells traditional foodstuffs in a local restaurant.

subParts.text: Explain the factors to consider when choosing the most appropriate mode of transport to carry different goods in your local area.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Discuss how stakeholders affect business activities in a business which sells traditional foodstuffs in a local restaurant.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Factors when choosing mode of transport:
• Nature/type of goods – perishable goods (e.g. vegetables) require fast transport; bulky goods may need trucks or rail; fragile goods need careful handling.
• Distance – short distances favour road transport; long distances may favour rail or air.
• Cost – choose the most affordable option relative to the value of goods; road is usually cheaper for local deliveries.
• Speed – urgency of delivery; air is fastest but most expensive; road is suitable for moderate speed locally.
• Availability of infrastructure – consider road quality, rail lines, or proximity to airports in the local area.
• Value of goods – high-value goods may justify the cost of air transport for security and speed.
• Safety/security – some modes offer better protection against theft and damage.
• Reliability – consistency and punctuality of the transport mode.
[2 marks per well-explained factor, max 8]

(b) How stakeholders affect a traditional foodstuffs restaurant:
• Owners/shareholders – provide capital and set the business objectives; their profit expectations drive pricing and cost-cutting decisions.
• Employees – their skills, attitude, and service quality directly affect customer satisfaction and the restaurant's reputation.
• Customers – their tastes, preferences, and feedback determine the menu, quality, and pricing of traditional dishes; loss of customers reduces revenue.
• Suppliers – reliability and pricing of food ingredient suppliers affect menu availability and food costs; unreliable suppliers disrupt operations.
• Government – health and safety regulations, food handling licences, and tax policies affect operating costs and compliance requirements.
• Local community – community acceptance and support (or opposition) affect the restaurant's reputation and customer base.
• Competitors – competing restaurants force the business to maintain quality, competitive pricing, and innovation.
• Creditors/banks – loan terms and interest rates affect the restaurant's financial decisions and expansion plans.
[2 marks per well-explained stakeholder impact, max 12]

questions.text:
12 (a) Outline the procedure in obtaining an insurance policy by a local business.
(b) Evaluate the short term sources of finance available to a manufacturer of mahewu product.

subParts.text: Outline the procedure in obtaining an insurance policy by a local business.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Evaluate the short term sources of finance available to a manufacturer of mahewu product.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Procedure for obtaining an insurance policy:
1. Identify the need – the business identifies the risk to be insured (e.g. fire, theft, stock loss).
2. Contact an insurer/broker – the business approaches an insurance company or broker for information on available policies.
3. Complete a proposal form – the business fills in a proposal form disclosing all relevant information about the subject matter to be insured (utmost good faith).
4. Risk assessment – the insurer assesses and evaluates the risk involved (may send a surveyor to inspect premises).
5. Quotation/premium calculation – the insurer calculates and quotes the premium based on the level of risk.
6. Acceptance and payment of premium – the business accepts the terms and pays the first premium.
7. Issuance of cover note/policy document – the insurer issues a cover note (immediate temporary cover) followed by the official policy document, which is the legal contract.
[1-2 marks per clearly outlined step, max 8]

(b) Short-term sources of finance for a mahewu manufacturer:
• Bank overdraft – allows the business to withdraw more than its account balance up to an agreed limit; useful for day-to-day cash flow shortfalls; however, interest is charged and the bank can demand repayment at any time.
• Trade credit – suppliers allow the business to receive raw materials (e.g. maize meal, sugar) now and pay later (30–90 days); improves cash flow at no immediate cost; risk of losing supplier goodwill if payment is delayed.
• Short-term bank loan – a fixed amount borrowed for a short period (up to 1 year) with agreed repayments; provides a lump sum for working capital; interest cost is a disadvantage.
• Factoring/invoice discounting – selling debtors' invoices to a factoring company for immediate cash (less a fee); improves liquidity quickly but reduces the amount received.
• Retained profits – using profits already earned and kept in the business; no interest cost and no dilution of ownership; but may limit business reinvestment.
• Owner's personal savings – quick and interest-free; but limited in amount and puts personal finances at risk.
[2 marks per well-evaluated source (benefit + limitation), max 12]

questions.text:
The smell of perfume in a room spreads quicker on a hot day than on a cold day because the particles
A become lighter.
B become heavier.
C have more kinetic energy.
D have less kinetic energy.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — On a hot day, particles have more kinetic energy, so they move faster and diffuse more quickly, spreading the smell more rapidly.

A measuring cylinder
B burette

substance | pH range

questions.text:
Which method is used to separate a mixture of hydrocarbons of different boiling points?
A evaporation.
B simple distillation.
C fractional distillation
D decanting.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — Fractional distillation is used to separate mixtures of liquids (hydrocarbons) with different but close boiling points, as in the refining of crude oil.

questions.text:
The table shows information about ethanol and sulphur.

           | melting point / °C | boiling point / °C
ethanol    | −15                | 78
sulphur    | 119                | 445

Which statement is true about the two substances?
A ethanol is a solid at room temperature
B sulphur is a solid at room temperature
C ethanol is a gas at room temperature
D sulphur is a gas at room temperature
questions.topic: States of Matter / Melting and Boiling Points
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Room temperature is approximately 25 °C. Sulphur's melting point is 119 °C, so it is a solid at 25 °C. Ethanol's melting point is −15 °C and boiling point is 78 °C, so ethanol is a liquid at room temperature.

questions.text:
The active ingredient, Mg(OH)₂, in indigestion tablets reacts with excess acids in the stomach according to the equation:
Mg(OH)₂(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O
What is the effect, on the rate of reaction, of using the tablets in powder form?
A increases
B decreases
C no effect
D decreases then increases
questions.aiModelAnswer: A — Using the tablets in powder form increases the surface area of Mg(OH)₂ exposed to the acid, which increases the rate of reaction.

questions.text:
Which statement is true about the electronic structure of atoms?
A outer shells of different atoms have the same number of electrons
B inner shells of different atoms have the same number of electrons
C electrons enter into different shells across a period.
D electrons enter into the same shell across a period.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D — Across a period, electrons are added to the same (outermost) shell. The number of protons increases but electrons fill the same principal energy level across a period.

questions.text:
Which substance conducts electricity when in solid state?
A diamond
B graphite
C sodium chloride
D magnesium oxide
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Graphite conducts electricity in the solid state because it has delocalised electrons free to move along its layers. Diamond, sodium chloride and magnesium oxide do not conduct electricity in the solid state.

questions.text:
Which chemical equation represents the final stage in the production of nitric acid?
A
B
C
D
questions.topic: Industrial Chemistry / Manufacture of Nitric Acid
questions.diagramNote: Four chemical equations (A, B, C, D) representing stages in nitric acid production; the correct one shows NO₂ reacting with water and oxygen to form HNO₃.
questions.aiModelAnswer: The final stage in the manufacture of nitric acid is: 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃. The correct answer is the option showing this equation.

questions.text:
Alcohols are formed when alkenes react with
A water.
B steam.
C hydrogen.
D sodium hydroxide.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Alcohols are formed when alkenes undergo hydration by reacting with steam (H₂O in the vapour/steam form) in the presence of an acid catalyst, e.g. C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH.

questions.text:
What is the role of aluminium sulphate in the water purification process?
A chlorination
B coagulation
C softening
D flocculation
questions.aiModelAnswer: D — Aluminium sulphate acts as a flocculant (flocculation agent) in water treatment. It causes fine suspended particles to clump together into larger masses (flocs) that settle out. (Note: some mark schemes accept either 'coagulation' or 'flocculation'; the primary ZIMSEC answer is D — flocculation.)

questions.text:
Catalytic converters reduce the emission of the following except
A carbon monoxide.
B carbon dioxide.
C nitrogen oxides.
D unburnt hydrocarbons.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Catalytic converters convert CO, NOₓ and unburnt hydrocarbons into less harmful substances. However, they actually produce CO₂ as a product of these reactions, so they do NOT reduce carbon dioxide emissions.

questions.text:
Nitric acid was added to solution X, followed by aqueous silver nitrate. A white precipitate was obtained. Which anion could be present in solution X?
A
B
C
D
questions.diagramNote: Four anion formulae (A, B, C, D) as answer options; a white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate indicates the chloride ion (Cl⁻).
questions.aiModelAnswer: The white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate solution indicates the presence of the chloride ion (Cl⁻). AgCl is a white precipitate insoluble in dilute nitric acid. The correct answer is the option showing Cl⁻.

questions.text:
Atoms represented by [two atomic symbols with same atomic number but different mass numbers] are examples of
A isomers.
B isotopes.
C alloys.
D allotropes.
questions.diagramNote: Two atomic symbols showing same atomic/proton number but different mass numbers (isotopes of the same element).
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons) are called isotopes.

questions.text:
When calcium carbonate is heated, it decomposes according to the equation:
CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
What is the volume of carbon dioxide produced when 5 g of calcium carbonate were heated?
[molar gas volume at r.t.p = 24 dm³]
A 2.73 dm³
B 1.76 dm³
C 1.20 dm³
D 0.81 dm³
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100 g/mol. Moles of CaCO₃ = 5/100 = 0.05 mol. From the equation, 1 mol CaCO₃ produces 1 mol CO₂, so moles of CO₂ = 0.05 mol. Volume = 0.05 × 24 = 1.20 dm³. Answer: C.

questions.text:
A volume of 50 cm³ of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide were completely neutralised by 25 cm³ of 0.1 mol dm⁻³ sulphuric acid. The heat change for the reaction was 1575 J. The enthalpy of neutralisation is
A 630.000 kJ mol⁻¹
B 315.000 kJ mol⁻¹
C 105.000 kJ mol⁻¹
D 1.575 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Moles of NaOH = 0.050 × 0.1 = 0.005 mol. The neutralisation reaction: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Moles of water formed = 0.005 mol. Enthalpy of neutralisation = heat change / moles of water = 1575 J / 0.005 mol = 315,000 J mol⁻¹ = 315.000 kJ mol⁻¹. Answer: B.

questions.text:
Which statement(s) 1, 2 or 3 refer to elements in the same group?
(i) same number of valence electrons
(ii) similar chemical properties
(iii) same colour and reactivity
A 3 only
B 2 and 3
C 1, 2 and 3
D 1 and 2
questions.aiModelAnswer: D — Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons (i) and therefore similar chemical properties (ii). They do NOT necessarily have the same colour and reactivity (iii) — reactivity varies down a group. Answer: D (1 and 2).

questions.text:
The effect of global warming on the environment is that it causes an increase in
A ozone depletion.
B eutrophication.
C atmospheric temperature.
D oxygen in the atmosphere.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — Global warming refers to the rise in the Earth's average atmospheric temperature due to the greenhouse effect caused by increased concentrations of greenhouse gases such as CO₂ and CH₄.

questions.text:
The molecular formula of an organic alcohol that contains 60% carbon by mass is
A CH₃OH
B C₂H₅OH
C C₃H₇OH
D C₄H₉OH
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry / Empirical and Molecular Formulae
questions.aiModelAnswer:
C — Check each alcohol for % carbon by mass:
• CH₃OH (Mr=32): %C = 12/32 × 100 = 37.5%
• C₂H₅OH (Mr=46): %C = 24/46 × 100 = 52.2%
• C₃H₇OH (Mr=60): %C = 36/60 × 100 = 60%
• C₄H₉OH (Mr=74): %C = 48/74 × 100 = 64.9%
Answer: C (C₃H₇OH).

questions.text:
Which pair of reactants are used to form potassium nitrate?
       acid                  base
A  nitric acid         sodium hydroxide
B  hydrochloric acid   potassium hydroxide
C  nitric acid         potassium hydroxide
D  hydrochloric acid   sodium hydroxide
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — Potassium nitrate (KNO₃) is made by reacting nitric acid (HNO₃) with potassium hydroxide (KOH): HNO₃ + KOH → KNO₃ + H₂O.

questions.text:
The equation shows the formation of ethanol from ethene using steam.
C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH
What temperature is used in the reaction?
A 300 °C
B 450 °C
C 700 °C
D 900 °C
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry / Industrial Production of Ethanol
questions.aiModelAnswer: A — The industrial hydration of ethene to produce ethanol uses a temperature of approximately 300 °C (with a phosphoric acid catalyst and high pressure of about 60–70 atm).

questions.text:
The table shows the changes that occur when halogens react with different potassium halides.

[Table showing: some combinations result in no change, turns orange, or turns brown]

Which statement explains the changes in colour?
A chlorine and bromine displace iodine
B bromine displaces iodine and chlorine
C iodine and chlorine displace bromine
D iodine displaces chlorine and bromine
questions.diagramNote: Table showing colour changes when halogens (Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) are added to solutions of potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide — some turn orange or brown, others show no change.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A — Chlorine (more reactive) displaces iodide ions to produce iodine (brown colour), and bromine (more reactive than iodine) also displaces iodine (turns orange/brown). The reactivity order is Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. Answer: A.

questions.text:
During the liquefaction and fractional distillation of air, air is first cooled to −196 °C because
A carbon dioxide solidifies.
B rare gases solidify.
C oxygen liquefies
D nitrogen liquefies.
questions.topic: Industrial Chemistry / Fractional Distillation of Air
questions.aiModelAnswer: D — Air is cooled to approximately −196 °C (the boiling point of nitrogen) so that nitrogen liquefies. Nitrogen has the lowest boiling point of the main components of air and liquefies at this temperature, allowing fractional distillation to separate nitrogen, oxygen, and argon.

questions.text:
A floatation cell is used to concentrate the ore in the extraction of
A nickel.
B copper.
C diamonds.
D iron.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Froth flotation cells are used to concentrate copper ore (e.g. copper pyrites/chalcopyrite) before further processing. The ore particles attach to air bubbles and float to the surface while waste rock sinks.

questions.text:
An object is electroplated with copper. Which statement about the process is correct?
A oxygen is evolved at the anode
B copper ions gain electrons at the object being electroplated
C copper is used as the cathode
D the concentration of copper ions in the electrolyte decreases
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — In electroplating with copper, the object to be plated is the cathode. At the cathode (object), Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons (are reduced) to form copper metal: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. The copper anode dissolves to replenish Cu²⁺ ions, keeping concentration constant.

questions.text:
Which pair of metals gives the highest voltage reading when used in a simple cell?
A Mg and Fe
B Mg and Cu
C Zn and Pb
D Fe and Cu
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — The voltage produced by a simple cell depends on how far apart the two metals are in the electrochemical (reactivity) series. Mg and Cu are the furthest apart (Mg is very reactive, Cu is low in the series), producing the highest voltage.

questions.text:
Which reagents are used in the production of ammonium nitrate fertiliser?
A HNO₃, NH₃
B NO, NH₃
C HNO₂, N₂H₄
D NO₂, NH₄OH
questions.aiModelAnswer: A — Ammonium nitrate is produced by reacting nitric acid (HNO₃) with ammonia (NH₃): HNO₃ + NH₃ → NH₄NO₃.

questions.text:
Which one is a correct physical property of solid ionic compounds?
A low boiling point and melting point
B high boiling point and melting point
C good electrical conductors
D highly soluble in organic solvents
questions.topic: Ionic Bonding / Properties of Ionic Compounds
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Solid ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points due to the strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions in the giant ionic lattice. They are poor electrical conductors in solid state, generally insoluble in organic solvents, and soluble in polar solvents like water.

questions.text:
Iron can be extracted from its ore by direct reduction using carbon monoxide whereas aluminium can only be extracted by electrolysis because
A iron is more reactive than aluminium and more difficult to extract.
B aluminium is more reactive than iron and more difficult to extract.
C aluminium is common and its extraction must be simple.
D iron is common and its extraction must be simple.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Aluminium is more reactive than iron (higher in the reactivity series). More reactive metals form stronger bonds with oxygen and require more energy (electrolysis) to extract. Carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide at economically viable temperatures.

questions.text:
Which oxide reacts with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide?
A CaO
B NaO
C Al₂O₃
D NO₂
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — Al₂O₃ (aluminium oxide) is amphoteric — it reacts with both acids (e.g. HCl) and bases (e.g. NaOH): Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O.

questions.text:
A mass of 8 grams of calcium chloride reacted with silver nitrate to produce a white precipitate of silver chloride. The chemical equation for the reaction is:
CaCl₂ + 2AgNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + 2AgCl
The mass of silver chloride produced is
A 6.80 g
B 10.40 g
C 13.60 g
D 20.70 g
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — Mr of CaCl₂ = 40 + 71 = 111 g/mol. Moles of CaCl₂ = 8/111 = 0.07207 mol. From equation, 1 mol CaCl₂ produces 2 mol AgCl, so moles of AgCl = 0.1441 mol. Mr of AgCl = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5 g/mol. Mass of AgCl = 0.1441 × 143.5 = 20.68 g ≈ 20.70 g. Wait — let me recheck: 0.07207 × 2 × 143.5 = 0.07207 × 287 = 20.68 g ≈ 20.70 g. Answer: D (20.70 g). [Note: the correct answer is D.]

questions.text:
Which chemical equation shows how barium reacts with water?
A Ba + 2H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ + H₂
B Ba + H₂O → 2BaO + H₂
C Ba + H₂O → BaO + H₂
D Ba + H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ + H₂
questions.aiModelAnswer: A — Barium reacts with water to form barium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. The correctly balanced equation is: Ba + 2H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ + H₂. Answer: A.

questions.text:
Ammonia can be produced industrially from nitrogen and hydrogen. The equation for the reaction is:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat
Which change would increase the yield of ammonia during the reaction?
A adding a catalyst.
B decreasing the pressure.
C increasing the temperature.
D increasing the pressure.
questions.topic: Industrial Chemistry / Haber Process / Le Chatelier's Principle
questions.aiModelAnswer: D — Increasing the pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. The left side has 4 moles of gas (1 + 3) and the right has 2 moles of gas, so increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to the right, increasing yield of NH₃. (A catalyst increases rate but not yield; increasing temperature decreases yield; decreasing pressure decreases yield.)

questions.text:
Ammonium dichromate, (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇(s) decomposes on heating to form chromium (III) oxide, Cr₂O₃, nitrogen gas and water according to the equation:
(NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇(s) → Cr₂O₃(s) + N₂(g) + 4H₂O(l)
When a sample containing 50.40 g of (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇ was heated, 4.32 g of water were produced. What was the percentage purity of the ammonium dichromate?
A 30.00%
B 9.00%
C 0.30%
D 0.09%
questions.aiModelAnswer: A — Mr of (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇ = (2×14 + 8×1 + 2×52 + 7×16) = (28+8+104+112) = 252 g/mol. Mr of H₂O = 18 g/mol. From equation, 1 mol (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇ produces 4 mol H₂O. Moles of H₂O produced = 4.32/18 = 0.24 mol. Moles of (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇ that reacted = 0.24/4 = 0.06 mol. Mass of pure (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇ = 0.06 × 252 = 15.12 g. % purity = (15.12/50.40) × 100 = 30.00%. Answer: A.

questions.text:
Which reagent can be used to distinguish between propene and propane?
A ethanol
B aqueous bromine
C aqueous ammonia
D dilute sulphuric acid
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry / Alkenes vs Alkanes / Tests
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Aqueous bromine (bromine water) is decolourised by propene (an alkene) through an addition reaction (C₃H₆ + Br₂ → C₃H₆Br₂), but propane (an alkane) does not decolourise bromine water under normal conditions. This distinguishes the two.

questions.text:
Ethane reacts with chlorine to form chloro-ethane in the presence of
A an aluminium oxide.
B concentrated sulphuric acid.
C ultraviolet light.
D bromine solution.
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry / Substitution Reactions of Alkanes
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — Alkanes such as ethane react with halogens (e.g. Cl₂) via a free radical substitution reaction, which is initiated by ultraviolet (UV) light: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl (in the presence of UV light).

questions.text:
Which compound is formed when an organic acid reacts with an alcohol?
A CH₃CH₂OH
B CH₃COOH
C CH₃COOCH₃
D CH₃COCH₃
questions.aiModelAnswer: C — When an organic (carboxylic) acid reacts with an alcohol, an ester and water are formed. CH₃COOCH₃ is methyl ethanoate, an ester. (CH₃CH₂OH is an alcohol; CH₃COOH is a carboxylic acid; CH₃COCH₃ is a ketone.)

questions.text:
Magnesium metal reacts with hydrochloric acid as follows:
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
What mass of magnesium will produce 36 dm³ of hydrogen at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p)?
A 24 g
B 36 g
C 48 g
D 72 g
questions.aiModelAnswer: B — Molar gas volume at r.t.p = 24 dm³/mol. Moles of H₂ = 36/24 = 1.5 mol. From equation, 1 mol Mg produces 1 mol H₂, so moles of Mg needed = 1.5 mol. Mass of Mg = 1.5 × 24 = 36 g. Answer: B.

questions.text:
Which equation shows a balanced chemical equation for the reaction of barium and sulphuric acid?
A
B
C
D
questions.topic: Stoichiometry / Balancing Equations / Reactions of Metals with Acids
questions.diagramNote: Four chemical equations (A, B, C, D) for the reaction of barium (Ba) with sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄); the correct balanced equation is Ba + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + H₂.
questions.aiModelAnswer: The balanced equation for barium reacting with sulphuric acid is: Ba + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + H₂. The correct answer is the option showing this balanced equation (1 Ba, 1 H₂SO₄, 1 BaSO₄, 1 H₂).

questions.text: Wildlife and Ecology

subParts.text: Explain any two socio-economic importance of wildlife.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Describe sustainable ways of dealing with problem animals in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Describe the following term used in Agriculture: biodiversity.
subParts.label: (c)(i)

subParts.text: Describe the following term used in Agriculture: poaching.
subParts.label: (c)(ii)

subParts.text: Describe the following term used in Agriculture: ecology.
subParts.label: (c)(iii)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any TWO of: 1. Tourism revenue / foreign currency earnings from wildlife-based tourism. 2. Wildlife provides food (game meat) for communities. 3. Source of employment for local communities (game rangers, guides, lodge workers). 4. Wildlife products (skins, ivory — legally) provide income. 5. Cultural and aesthetic value to communities. (1 mark each, max 2)

(b) Any THREE of: 1. Translocation — moving problem animals to game parks/conservancies. 2. Establishing CAMPFIRE (Communal Areas Management Programme for Indigenous Resources) — communities benefit from and manage wildlife sustainably. 3. Erecting electric fences/game fences to separate wildlife from farmland. 4. Compensation schemes for farmers affected by wildlife. 5. Use of non-lethal deterrents (chilli fences, beehive fences, lights). 6. Community education on coexistence with wildlife. (1 mark each, max 3)

(c)(i) Biodiversity: The variety of all living organisms (plants, animals, micro-organisms) and their ecosystems found in a given area.

(c)(ii) Poaching: The illegal hunting, capturing or killing of wild animals, or illegal harvesting of wild plants, without authorisation from the relevant authorities. (1 mark definition + 1 mark elaboration)

(c)(iii) Ecology: The scientific study of the relationships/interactions between living organisms and their environment (both biotic and abiotic factors). (1 mark definition + 1 mark elaboration)

questions.text: Soil Science and Seedbed Preparation

After 30 minutes the reading in the cylinder with a mixture of water and soil was 80 ml. Calculate the percentage of air in the soil sample.

questions.topic: Soil Science, Seedbed Preparation and Erosion Control
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Application of lime in seedbed preparation: 1. Lime is applied to correct/raise soil pH (reduce acidity). 2. Applied before ploughing/at least 2–3 months before planting so it can be incorporated. 3. Spread evenly/broadcast on the surface of the land. 4. Incorporated into the soil by ploughing/discing. 5. Rate of application depends on soil pH test results. 6. Dolomitic or agricultural lime is commonly used. (Any 4 points, 1 mark each)

(b) Volume of air = (Volume of water added + Volume of soil) − Volume of mixture reading
= (50 + 50) − 80 = 100 − 80 = 20 ml
Percentage air = (Volume of air / Volume of soil) × 100
= (20/50) × 100 = 40%
(Award marks: correct formula 1, correct substitution 1, correct volume of air 1, correct final answer 1)

(c) Any ONE of: 1. Contour ploughing/ploughing across the slope — furrows act as barriers to water flow, reducing runoff and erosion. 2. Strip cropping — alternating strips of crops and grass/legumes reduce velocity of runoff. 3. Mulching — covering soil surface with crop residues reduces impact of raindrops and runoff. 4. Minimum tillage/conservation tillage — reduces disturbance of soil structure. 5. Cover cropping — growing cover crops protects soil surface. (2 marks: 1 for naming, 1 for explanation)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Importance of crop breeding to the farmer (any 4): 1. Development of high-yielding varieties — increased production and profits. 2. Development of disease/pest-resistant varieties — reduces cost of chemicals. 3. Development of drought-tolerant varieties — crops survive dry spells. 4. Development of early-maturing varieties — allows more crops per season. 5. Improved quality of produce (nutritional content, taste, marketability). 6. Development of varieties suited to local conditions. (1 mark each, max 4)

(b) Open pollinated varieties (OPVs): Pollinated naturally (by wind/insects); seeds can be saved and replanted in subsequent seasons; relatively stable genetically; lower yielding than hybrids.
Hybrids: Result of crossing two or more pure/inbred lines; exhibit hybrid vigour (heterosis); higher yielding; seeds cannot be saved and replanted (performance declines in subsequent generations). (1 mark for OPV characteristics, 1 mark for hybrid characteristics)

(c) Heterosis (hybrid vigour): The phenomenon where the offspring (F1 hybrid) resulting from crossing two genetically different parent lines shows superior performance/traits (e.g., higher yield, greater vigour, better disease resistance) compared to either parent. (2 marks)

(d)(i) Emergency (emergence): The process by which a seedling/shoot breaks through the soil surface after germination. (1 mark)

(d)(ii) Germination: The process by which a seed begins to sprout/grow into a new plant when provided with the necessary conditions (water, warmth, oxygen). (1 mark)

questions.topic: Farm Machinery, Grain Storage and Farm Structures
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Roller: Rotates/revolves to shell/remove maize grain from the cob by friction/rubbing action.
(a)(ii) Base plate: Provides a surface against which the cob is pressed/held during shelling; supports the shelling mechanism.
(a)(iii) Pressing fan: Blows/separates chaff and light material from the grain after shelling (winnowing action).
(a)(iv) Threshing cylinder: Rotates at high speed to beat/thresh the cobs and remove/separate grain from the cob.
(a)(v) Feed tray: Receives/holds the maize cobs and feeds them into the shelling mechanism in a controlled manner.

(b) Traditional grain storage (e.g., mukatapiko/rukuvhute/crib): Grain is stored on a raised platform to keep it off the ground (preventing moisture absorption and pest entry). The structure is built with gaps/open sides to allow air circulation, keeping grain dry. Ash/sand/traditional repellents may be mixed with grain to deter insects. The dry, aerated conditions reduce moisture content and inhibit mould and pest activity. (2 marks for correct explanation of principles)

(c) Perimeter of plot = 2(200 + 80) = 2 × 280 = 560 m
Total wire needed = 560 m × 4 strands = 2240 m
Number of rolls = 2240 ÷ 700 = 3.2 rolls ≈ 4 rolls (round up to nearest whole roll)
(Award: 1 mark perimeter, 1 mark total wire, 1 mark number of rolls)

(a) Any THREE importances of financial records (1 mark each): 1. Help the farmer to monitor income and expenditure (profit/loss). 2. Assist in planning and budgeting for future seasons. 3. Provide evidence for loan applications from banks/financial institutions. 4. Help in calculating tax obligations. 5. Useful for evaluating the profitability of different enterprises. 6. Gross Margin = Gross Revenue − Variable Costs = $1 800 − $400 = $1 400

Government policies (price controls, subsidies). 4. Inflation/economic conditions. 5. Competition from imports. 6. Quality/grading of produce.

(d)(i) Theft: Install security fencing/locks; employ security guards; install CCTV; take out insurance against theft.
(d)(ii) Fire: Install fire extinguishers; create firebreaks; store flammable materials safely; take out fire insurance; have a fire management plan.

questions.topic: Forestry, Gumtree Establishment and Indigenous Tree Plantation Management
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Socio-ecological importance of forestry (any 8 points, 1 mark each): Social: 1. Source of timber for construction. 2. Source of fuelwood/charcoal for energy. 3. Source of non-timber forest products (fruits, mushrooms, medicinal plants). 4. Employment creation (logging, sawmilling, tourism). 5. Source of income/revenue for communities and government. 6. Cultural/spiritual significance of forests to communities. Ecological: 7. Carbon sequestration — trees absorb CO₂, mitigating climate change. 8. Watershed protection — forests regulate water cycles and protect catchment areas. 9. Prevention of soil erosion — tree roots bind soil. 10. Habitat for wildlife/biodiversity conservation. 11. Windbreaks — reduce wind erosion and protect crops. 12. Improvement of soil fertility through leaf litter/organic matter.

(b) Pricking out in gumtree establishment: 1. Pricking out is the transplanting of young seedlings from the seedbed/germination tray to individual containers/tubes/poly bags. 2. Carried out when seedlings have developed 2–4 true leaves (large enough to handle). 3. A dibber/stick is used to make a hole in the potting medium in the container. 4. Seedlings are carefully lifted from the seedbed with minimal root disturbance. 5. Each seedling is placed individually into a prepared container at the correct depth. 6. Soil is firmed around the roots. 7. Seedlings are watered immediately after pricking out. 8. Purpose: gives each seedling enough space and nutrients to develop a strong root system before field planting. (Any 4 points, 1 mark each)

(c) Management practices in an indigenous tree plantation (any 8 points, 1 mark each): 1. Weeding — removing competing weeds around young trees. 2. Mulching — applying organic matter around trees to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. 3. Watering/irrigation — especially during dry spells for young trees. 4. Pruning — removing dead/diseased/unwanted branches to improve form and health. 5. Thinning — removing excess trees to reduce competition and allow remaining trees to grow better. 6. Pest and disease control — monitoring and treating pest/disease outbreaks. 7. Firebreak maintenance — clearing firebreaks to protect plantation from veld fires. 8. Fencing — protecting trees from livestock and wildlife damage. 9. Fertiliser application — applying fertiliser to boost growth where soils are poor. 10. Monitoring/record keeping — keeping records of growth, survival rates and interventions.

questions.topic: Agro-chemicals, Tillage Practices and Crop Rotation
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Toxicity levels of agro-chemicals (typically classified by WHO/colour-coded labels): 1. Class Ia — Extremely hazardous (RED label): Very small dose can be lethal, e.g., some organophosphates. 2. Class Ib — Highly hazardous (RED label): Highly toxic; requires strict protective clothing. 3. Class II — Moderately hazardous (YELLOW label): Moderate risk; requires protective equipment. 4. Class III — Slightly hazardous (BLUE label): Low risk under normal use. 5. Class U — Unlikely to present acute hazard (GREEN label): Relatively safe under normal conditions. Key points: Toxicity measured by LD50 (lethal dose for 50% of test population); lower LD50 = higher toxicity. Labels indicate active ingredient, dosage, safety precautions and first aid. (Award marks for identifying and explaining at least 4 levels/aspects)

(b) Advantages of traditional tillage practices (e.g., hand hoeing, ox-drawn ploughing) — any 7 points: 1. Low cost — does not require expensive machinery or fuel. 2. Accessible to small-scale/subsistence farmers with limited resources. 3. Reduces soil compaction compared to heavy mechanised tillage. 4. Allows precision tillage — farmers can work around obstacles (trees, stumps). 5. Creates employment for farm labourers. 6. Timely operations — can be carried out flexibly when conditions are right. 7. Less risk of soil structure damage. 8. Maintenance is simple and affordable. 9. Incorporates organic matter adequately. 10. Culturally familiar to smallholder farmers. (1 mark each, max 7)

(c) Sample four-year rotation (5 marks): Year 1 — Maize (cereal/heavy feeder); Year 2 — Soyabean/groundnuts (legume — fixes nitrogen); Year 3 — Sorghum/millet (cereal — different root depth); Year 4 — Sunflower/cotton (cash crop/different family). Justification: Rotation breaks pest and disease cycles, improves soil fertility (legumes fix nitrogen), reduces weed pressure, improves soil structure. (2 marks for correct sequence, 3 marks for justification/reasoning)

questions.topic: Organic Fertilisers, Grain Storage and Environmental Factors in Crop Production
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Advantages of organic fertiliser (any 5, 1 mark each): 1. Improves soil structure/texture. 2. Improves water retention capacity of sandy soils. 3. Slow-release nutrients — sustained feeding of crops. 4. Improves soil microbial activity. 5. Cheaper/locally available (farm-produced). 6. Reduces reliance on expensive inorganic fertilisers. 7. Improves soil pH gradually. 8. Reduces risk of over-fertilisation/scorching. Disadvantages (any 4, 1 mark each): 1. Nutrient content is variable and low compared to inorganic fertilisers. 2. Bulky — difficult to transport and apply in large quantities. 3. Slow to release nutrients — not suitable for immediate crop needs. 4. May introduce weed seeds if not well composted. 5. May harbour disease pathogens/pests if poorly managed. 6. Labour-intensive to collect, compost and apply.

(b) Evaluation of traditional grain storage facilities: Advantages: 1. Low cost — made from locally available materials. 2. Accessible to rural/smallholder farmers. 3. Raised design reduces moisture and pest entry. 4. Allow air circulation, keeping grain dry. Disadvantages: 1. Susceptible to rodent and insect pest damage. 2. Limited storage capacity. 3. Not weatherproof — vulnerable to rain and humidity. 4. No temperature or humidity control. 5. Grain quality may deteriorate over time. (Balance of advantages and disadvantages for full marks)

(c) Ways of reducing effects of environmental factors (any 6): 1. Drought: Irrigation; drought-tolerant varieties; mulching to conserve moisture. 2. Temperature extremes: Greenhouses; windbreaks; choosing appropriate planting dates. 3. Wind: Erecting windbreaks/shelterbelts; staking tall crops. 4. Flooding/waterlogging: Constructing drainage channels; raised beds; selecting flood-tolerant varieties. 5. Low soil fertility (soil factor): Applying fertilisers; liming; crop rotation. 6. Pests and diseases (biotic): Crop rotation; resistant varieties; integrated pest management. (1 mark each correct way with brief explanation, max 6)

questions.topic: Poultry Housing, Digestive System and Breeding in Non-ruminants
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Characteristics of an acceptable fowl run (any 5, 1 mark each): 1. Adequate space — sufficient floor area per bird to prevent overcrowding. 2. Good ventilation — windows/openings to allow fresh air circulation and reduce ammonia build-up. 3. Protection from predators — strong fencing/netting, secure door. 4. Easy to clean — smooth floors (concrete) for easy cleaning and disinfection. 5. Provision of perches for roosting. 6. Nesting boxes for egg laying. 7. Access to clean water and feed troughs. 8. Well-drained site — prevents waterlogging and dampness. 9. Orientation — positioned to maximise natural light and warmth (east–west axis). 10. Biosecurity features — footbaths, restricted entry.

(b) Named animal: Pig. Four parts and functions (2 marks each — 1 name + 1 function): 1. Mouth — mechanical breakdown of food by chewing/mastication; saliva begins starch digestion. 2. Stomach — secretes HCl and pepsin; begins protein digestion; churns food into chyme. 3. Small intestine — main site of digestion and absorption of nutrients into the bloodstream. 4. Large intestine/caecum — absorption of water; some microbial fermentation of fibre. 5. Liver — produces bile for fat emulsification; detoxifies blood. 6. Pancreas — secretes digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, protease) into small intestine. (Any 4 correct parts with correct functions)

(c) Named breeding female: Sow (pig). Desirable characteristics (any 7, 1 mark each): 1. Large litter size — ability to produce many piglets per litter (high prolificacy). 2. Good mothering ability — does not overlay/crush piglets; attentive mother. 3. Well-developed udder with sufficient functional teats (at least 12). 4. High milk production — able to nurse all piglets adequately. 5. Good body conformation — well-muscled, deep body, strong legs. 6. Good health record — free from hereditary diseases and parasites. 7. High feed conversion efficiency — converts feed to body mass economically. 8. Good temperament — docile and easy to handle. 9. Proven reproductive record — regular oestrus cycles, high conception rate. 10. Adaptability to local environmental conditions.

subParts.text: State and explain two types of livestock immunity.

questions.topic: Livestock Immunity, Animal Health Legislation and Calf Management
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Two types of livestock immunity (2 marks each): 1. Active immunity: The animal's own immune system produces antibodies in response to exposure to a pathogen or vaccine. Can be natural (recovery from disease) or artificial (vaccination). Long-lasting. 2. Passive immunity: Antibodies are transferred to the animal from an external source — naturally through colostrum (mother's first milk) to newborns, or artificially through injection of antiserum. Provides immediate but temporary protection.

(b) The Animal Health Act of Zimbabwe: 1. Provides the legal framework for the control and prevention of animal diseases in Zimbabwe. 2. Empowers the Director of Veterinary Services/government to declare disease control areas and quarantine zones. 3. Provides for compulsory dipping, vaccination and treatment of livestock. 4. Controls the movement of animals to prevent spread of disease (movement permits required). 5. Provides for the slaughter/destruction of diseased animals to prevent disease spread. 6. Controls importation and exportation of animals and animal products. 7. Establishes penalties/fines for non-compliance. 8. Provides for appointment of veterinary inspectors and their powers. (Any 7 relevant points, 1 mark each)

(c) Management operations on a calf from birth to weaning (any 9, 1 mark each): 1. Ensure calf receives colostrum within the first 6 hours of birth (passive immunity). 2. Dry the calf/ensure it is breathing properly at birth. 3. Disinfect the navel cord with iodine to prevent navel ill. 4. Ear tagging/identification of the calf. 5. Recording birth weight and date of birth. 6. Dehorning — at 1–2 weeks using caustic paste or hot iron. 7. Castration of male calves not required for breeding. 8. Vaccination against common diseases (e.g., blackleg, anthrax). 9. Regular drenching/treatment for internal parasites (worms). 10. Dipping/spraying for external parasites (ticks, lice). 11. Gradual introduction of solid feed (creep feeding) from 2–3 weeks. 12. Provide clean fresh water from early age. 13. Regular weighing to monitor growth. 14. Weaning at approximately 6–8 months or at target weight.
