subParts.text: Describe the management of indigenous chicks from day old to two weeks of age.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Describe the life cycle of a named internal parasite of a farm animal.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Evaluate the importance of roughage in the diet of ruminant farm animals.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.topic: Indigenous Chick Management, Internal Parasites and Ruminant Roughage
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Management of indigenous chicks from day old to two weeks (any 8 points, 1 mark each): 1. Provide a brooding area with adequate warmth — temperature 35°C at day old, reducing by ~3°C per week. 2. Use heat source: infrared lamp, charcoal stove/jiko. 3. Provide clean fresh water from day one (shallow drinkers to prevent drowning). 4. Feed chick starter mash/finely ground feed from day one. 5. Ensure clean, dry litter (wood shavings/sawdust) on brooder floor. 6. Adequate ventilation in brooder house to prevent respiratory disease. 7. Prevent overcrowding — provide adequate floor space per chick. 8. Keep brooder area dry and hygienic — clean and disinfect regularly. 9. Vaccination against Newcastle disease (at 3–7 days via eye drop or drinking water). 10. Monitor chick behaviour — huddling indicates cold; spreading away from heat indicates overheating. 11. Provide adequate feeder space to ensure all chicks feed. 12. Protect from predators and draughts.

(b) Named internal parasite: Roundworm (Ascaris suum in pigs / Ascaridia galli in poultry). Life cycle: 1. Adult female worm in the intestine lays thousands of eggs. 2. Eggs passed out in faeces onto the pasture/ground. 3. Eggs develop into infective larvae (L2) in the soil (this takes days to weeks depending on conditions). 4. Host animal ingests infective eggs while grazing or foraging. 5. Eggs hatch in the small intestine; larvae migrate through the gut wall into the bloodstream. 6. Larvae travel to the liver, then the lungs (causing pneumonia/'milk spot' liver). 7. Larvae coughed up, swallowed and return to the small intestine. 8. Larvae mature into adult worms in the intestine; cycle repeats. (Award marks for correct sequential stages, 1 mark each up to 7)

(c) Importance of roughage in ruminant diet (any 5, 1 mark each): 1. Stimulates rumen motility/movement — keeps the rumen functioning properly. 2. Provides energy through microbial fermentation producing volatile fatty acids (VFAs). 3. Maintains correct rumen pH — prevents acidosis. 4. Provides dietary fibre necessary for healthy digestion. 5. Cheap and readily available source of nutrition for ruminants. 6. Supports rumen microbial population — microbes break down cellulose. 7. Provides bulk/fill — satisfies the animal's appetite. 8. Excess roughage can limit production if energy density is too low (limitation/disadvantage).

title: Business And Enterprise Skills O-Level 2025 Paper 2
subject: Business And Enterprise Skills

questions.text:
Read the case study below and answer all the questions that follow.

Tamarind Soft Drinks
Tamari and Linda are childhood friends. They formed a partnership business together. Linda studied entrepreneurship at the University of Zimbabwe, where she acquired enterprising skills needed by an entrepreneur and also the roles of an entrepreneur in society. After graduating Linda brought forward her knowledge of entrepreneurship to be implemented in running their partnership business. Due to availability of tamarind fruits in their community, they decided to start the manufacturing of tamarind soft drinks. The partnership managed to borrow money from the bank so that they can buy other resources needed to produce tamarind non-carbonated soft drinks. Due to economic constraints in the country they did not operate profitably in the first year. They managed to get an overdraft and borrowed from friends so as to enter into foreign markets. Borrowing from friends was cheap because of no interest on the borrowed amount. Due to nutritional value of tamarind soft drinks, many countries are now interested in the drink and the two friends have decided to grow their enterprise into a private limited company.

questions.topic: Business Enterprise Skills – Mixed Topics (Case Study)
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Any FOUR of: communication skills; financial/numeracy skills; marketing skills; problem-solving/decision-making skills; leadership/management skills; negotiation skills; ICT/digital skills; time management skills. (1 mark each, max 4)

(a)(ii) Enterprising refers to the ability and willingness to take initiative, be creative, identify opportunities and take calculated risks in order to start or grow a business venture. (2 marks for a clear definition referencing initiative/creativity and opportunity-taking)

(b)(i) Any TWO of: Tamari and Linda (owners/partners); bank (lender/creditor); friends (lenders); customers/consumers; employees; government; suppliers. (1 mark each, max 2)

(b)(ii) Roles of entrepreneurs/partners: organising and managing resources; providing capital/finance; taking risks; making decisions; innovating and identifying opportunities; managing day-to-day operations; sharing profits and losses equally (as partners). (Award 1 mark per well-explained role, max 4)

(c)(i) Any TWO of: economic constraints (e.g., inflation, recession); political/legal constraints; competition; technological change; social/cultural factors; environmental/natural factors. (1 mark each, max 2)

(c)(ii) Advantages of converting to a private limited company: limited liability – shareholders' personal assets are protected; ability to raise more capital by selling shares; separate legal entity – the company can own property/sue independently; greater continuity/perpetual succession; more credibility/trust with lenders and customers; easier to attract investment. (Award 1 mark per advantage + brief explanation, max 4)

(d)(i) Any TWO of: bank loan; overdraft; retained profits; sale of shares; borrowing from friends/family; trade credit; grants. (1 mark each, max 2)

(d)(ii) Internal sources of finance are funds generated from within the business itself (e.g., retained profits, sale of assets, owner's savings), whereas external sources of finance are funds obtained from outside the business (e.g., bank loans, overdrafts, issuing shares, borrowing from friends). Key distinction: internal = no repayment obligation/no interest; external = usually involves repayment and/or interest. (2 marks for internal definition, 2 marks for external definition with clear distinction)

(e)(i) Any TWO of: cost/interest rate; amount required; purpose/how funds will be used; repayment period/time; risk involved; availability of collateral/security; business size and type; credit rating of the business. (1 mark each, max 2)

(e)(ii) Any TWO of: language/communication barriers – different languages make it difficult to negotiate and market products; cultural differences – different tastes, preferences and customs may reduce demand; trade barriers/tariffs – import duties increase costs and reduce competitiveness; foreign exchange/currency risk – fluctuating exchange rates affect profitability; legal/regulatory differences – compliance with foreign laws is complex and costly; strong competition from established foreign brands. (1 mark for identifying challenge + 1 mark for explanation, max 4)

(f) Evaluation of the impact of ICT in operations management:
Positive impacts: automation of production processes increases efficiency and reduces labour costs; real-time inventory management reduces wastage and stockouts; improved communication (email, video conferencing) speeds up decision-making; data analytics helps forecast demand and plan production; ICT enables online marketing and e-commerce reaching wider markets; quality control systems improve product consistency; record-keeping becomes faster and more accurate.
Negative impacts/limitations: high initial cost of ICT infrastructure; risk of cyber-attacks and data loss; requires staff training which adds cost; over-reliance on technology can cause major disruptions if systems fail; may lead to job losses causing social problems.
Overall judgement: On balance, ICT has a net positive impact on operations management as it significantly boosts productivity, reduces costs and improves competitiveness, provided businesses invest adequately in security and staff training. (Award marks for: identifying positive impacts 4 marks; identifying negative impacts/challenges 3 marks; balanced evaluative judgement/conclusion 3 marks)

questions.text:
(a) Describe the importance of business planning to a local mushroom farmer.
(b) Assess the effects of business growth.

subParts.text: Describe the importance of business planning to a local mushroom farmer.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Assess the effects of business growth.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Importance of business planning to a local mushroom farmer (any well-explained points up to 10 marks):
• Sets clear goals and objectives – gives the farmer direction on what to achieve, e.g., target output per season.
• Helps secure finance – a business plan is required by banks/lenders before granting loans to buy equipment or spores.
• Resource planning – ensures the farmer acquires the right inputs (substrate, humidity control, packaging) at the right time.
• Risk identification and management – anticipates challenges such as crop failure, price fluctuations, and prepares contingency measures.
• Guides marketing strategy – identifies target customers (hotels, supermarkets, individuals) and pricing.
• Enables performance monitoring – actual results can be compared against planned targets to identify variances.
• Attracts investors/partners – demonstrates seriousness and viability of the farming venture.
• Cash flow management – helps the farmer plan income and expenditure to avoid cash shortages.
• Legal and operational compliance – reminds the farmer of licences, health regulations, etc.
(Award 2 marks per well-described point: 1 mark for identification + 1 mark for explanation/application to mushroom farming, max 10)

(b) Assessment of the effects of business growth (balanced — positive and negative):
Positive effects:
• Economies of scale – larger output reduces average costs, improving profitability.
• Increased market share and competitive advantage.
• Greater ability to raise finance – larger businesses are seen as lower risk by lenders.
• More diversification opportunities – can expand product range reducing risk.
• Enhanced reputation and brand recognition.
• Better bargaining power with suppliers.
Negative effects:
• Diseconomies of scale – management becomes complex, communication breaks down, costs may rise.
• Loss of personal touch/customer relationships – business may become impersonal.
• Increased financial risk – growth often requires borrowing, raising debt levels.
• Difficulty maintaining quality control across larger operations.
• Staff management challenges – more employees require formal HR systems.
• Possible loss of original entrepreneurial culture.
Overall assessment: Business growth is generally beneficial if managed carefully, but requires strong management systems to avoid diseconomies of scale and overextension. (Award up to 4 marks positive effects, up to 4 marks negative effects, 2 marks for evaluative judgement/conclusion)

questions.text:
(a) Explain the factors that influence the choice of mode of transport used by an enterprise.
(b) Evaluate benefits and challenges encountered in foreign markets to a banana grower.

subParts.text: Explain the factors that influence the choice of mode of transport used by an enterprise.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Evaluate benefits and challenges encountered in foreign markets to a banana grower.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Factors influencing choice of mode of transport (any well-explained points, max 8 marks):
• Nature of goods – perishable goods like tamarind/soft drinks require fast, refrigerated transport; heavy/bulky goods suit rail or road.
• Cost – the enterprise must choose an affordable mode; road may be cheaper for short distances, air is expensive but fast.
• Distance/destination – long distances or overseas markets may require air or sea transport.
• Speed required – urgent deliveries favour air or express road transport.
• Reliability and availability – the chosen mode must be dependable and accessible in Zimbabwe.
• Infrastructure – quality of roads, rail network, airports available in the area.
• Safety and security of goods – fragile or high-value goods need secure, careful transport.
• Size/volume of consignment – large volumes suit rail or sea; small parcels may use road.
(Award 1 mark identification + 1 mark explanation per factor, max 8)

(b) Benefits and challenges in foreign markets for a banana grower:
Benefits:
• Access to larger markets – more customers means higher sales revenue and profits.
• Higher prices – foreign markets, especially developed countries, may pay premium prices for quality bananas.
• Reduced dependence on local market – diversification reduces risk of local demand fluctuations.
• Foreign currency earnings – helps the grower access hard currency for importing inputs.
• Business growth opportunities – exporting can lead to expansion of farm and operations.
• Brand recognition and reputation – being an exporter enhances credibility.
Challenges:
• Strict quality and phytosanitary standards – foreign markets require compliance with health and safety regulations, which is costly.
• Currency/exchange rate fluctuations – may reduce the value of earnings.
• High transport costs – shipping perishable bananas internationally is expensive and requires refrigeration.
• Competition from established producers – e.g., Ecuador, Philippines produce bananas at much lower cost.
• Language and cultural barriers – different consumer preferences and communication difficulties.
• Trade barriers and tariffs – import duties in foreign countries reduce competitiveness.
• Documentation and bureaucracy – export permits, certificates of origin, etc., are time-consuming.
Evaluation: Foreign markets offer significant growth potential for a banana grower, but success requires investment in meeting quality standards and managing logistical challenges. The benefits outweigh challenges if the grower is well-organised and supported by government export promotion schemes. (Award 5 marks benefits, 5 marks challenges, 2 marks evaluative conclusion)

questions.text:
(a) Explain the advantages of economic integration.
(b) Evaluate the methods of measuring business size.

subParts.text: Explain the advantages of economic integration.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Evaluate the methods of measuring business size.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Advantages of economic integration (e.g., SADC, COMESA, AfCFTA):
• Free trade/reduced tariffs – member countries trade with fewer or no tariffs, lowering costs for businesses and consumers.
• Larger market access – businesses can sell to a bigger combined market, increasing revenue potential.
• Economies of scale – larger production for bigger markets reduces average costs.
• Increased foreign direct investment – integrated regions attract more investment due to larger, stable markets.
• Improved infrastructure – joint projects (roads, rail, energy) benefit all member states.
• Political stability and cooperation – economic ties encourage peaceful relations among member states.
• Sharing of technology and knowledge – member countries exchange expertise and innovations.
• Specialisation – countries produce goods they have a comparative advantage in, improving efficiency.
• Greater bargaining power – the bloc negotiates better trade deals with non-members.
• Employment creation – expanded trade and investment create more jobs.
(Award 1 mark identification + 1 mark explanation per advantage, max 10)

(b) Evaluation of methods of measuring business size:
Methods:
• Number of employees – simple and easy to measure; however, capital-intensive businesses may be large but employ few people, making this measure misleading.
• Turnover/Sales revenue – reflects market activity; but businesses with high sales may have low profits due to high costs.
• Capital employed/Net assets – measures investment in the business; but asset values can be distorted by depreciation or valuation methods.
• Market share – shows dominance in an industry; however, difficult to calculate in informal/unregulated markets.
• Profit levels – indicates financial success; but can be manipulated through accounting practices.
• Output/Production volume – useful for manufacturing; but services businesses are hard to measure by output.
Evaluation: No single method is universally perfect; the most appropriate measure depends on the industry and purpose of measurement. A combination of methods gives a more accurate picture of business size. (Award 2 marks per method with evaluation point, max 8; 2 marks for overall evaluative conclusion)

questions.text:
(a) Explain business constraints affecting local manufacturing businesses.
(b) Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of small enterprises.

subParts.text: Explain business constraints affecting local manufacturing businesses.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of small enterprises.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Business constraints affecting local manufacturing businesses:
• Economic constraints – inflation, high interest rates, and foreign currency shortages increase production costs and reduce purchasing power.
• Power/energy shortages (load shedding) – frequent electricity outages disrupt production schedules and increase costs (reliance on generators).
• High cost of raw materials – imported inputs are expensive due to exchange rate depreciation.
• Limited access to finance – banks demand collateral that small manufacturers may not have; high borrowing costs.
• Competition from cheap imports – locally manufactured goods compete with cheaper foreign products, especially from China.
• Outdated technology/machinery – lack of capital to invest in modern equipment reduces efficiency and quality.
• Political and regulatory constraints – policy inconsistency, excessive taxation, licensing requirements add to the cost of doing business.
• Limited market size – low consumer purchasing power in Zimbabwe restricts demand for locally manufactured goods.
• Skills shortage – emigration of skilled workers reduces the quality of the local labour force.
• Infrastructure constraints – poor road networks and logistics increase distribution costs.
(Award 1 mark identification + 1 mark explanation per constraint, max 10)

(b) Advantages and disadvantages of small enterprises:
Advantages:
• Personal/close customer relationships – owners know customers personally, improving service quality and loyalty.
• Flexibility and adaptability – can quickly respond to changes in customer needs and market conditions.
• Low overheads – fewer employees and smaller premises mean lower fixed costs.
• Strong owner motivation – owners work hard as they directly benefit from profits.
• Niche market expertise – can specialise in specific products/services that larger businesses ignore.
• Easy decision-making – fewer layers of management allow quick decisions.
• Contribution to local employment – employ community members, supporting local economy.
Disadvantages:
• Limited access to finance – perceived as high risk by banks; lack of collateral.
• Limited economies of scale – cannot buy in bulk or spread fixed costs over large output.
• Heavy workload on owner – owner may be overworked leading to burnout.
• Vulnerability to competition – large businesses can undercut prices.
• Limited growth potential – restricted by lack of resources and capital.
• Lack of specialisation – owner may lack expertise in all business functions (finance, marketing, HR).
• High failure rate – many small businesses fail within the first few years.
(Award 1 mark per advantage + 1 mark per disadvantage with brief explanation, balanced discussion, max 10)

questions.text:
(a) Explain the importance of budgeting to a potato grower.
(b) Evaluate the importance of being ethical in businesses.

subParts.text: Explain the importance of budgeting to a potato grower.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Evaluate the importance of being ethical in businesses.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Importance of budgeting to a potato grower:
• Financial planning – helps the grower plan how much money is needed for seeds, fertiliser, labour, and irrigation before the season begins.
• Cost control – by setting spending limits, the grower avoids overspending and ensures resources are used efficiently.
• Guides decision-making – helps the grower decide whether to expand acreage, buy new equipment, or hire more workers.
• Cash flow management – ensures the grower has enough cash at each stage of production and harvest.
• Performance monitoring – actual income and expenditure can be compared with budgeted figures to identify variances and take corrective action.
• Securing finance – a budget demonstrates financial planning capability, which is required by lenders/microfinance institutions.
• Goal setting – formalises output targets (tonnes per hectare) and revenue targets for the season.
• Reduces financial risk – anticipates periods of cash shortage so the grower can arrange overdrafts or credit in advance.
(Award 1 mark identification + 1 mark explanation/application to potato growing per point, max 8)

(b) Evaluation of the importance of being ethical in business:
Importance/Benefits of ethical behaviour:
• Builds trust and reputation – customers, suppliers and investors prefer to deal with ethical businesses, leading to long-term loyalty.
• Legal compliance – ethical businesses are less likely to face fines, lawsuits, or prosecution.
• Employee morale and retention – staff are more motivated and productive in organisations with strong ethical values.
• Sustainable business relationships – ethical dealings with suppliers and partners create stable supply chains.
• Competitive advantage – ethical branding (e.g., fair trade, organic) can differentiate a business and attract premium-paying customers.
• Social responsibility – ethical businesses contribute positively to the community, earning goodwill.
• Attracts investors – ethical, transparent businesses are preferred by socially responsible investors.
Limitations/Challenges of being ethical:
• Short-term cost – ethical sourcing, fair wages, and environmental compliance increase costs and may reduce short-term profits.
• Competitive pressure – unethical competitors may undercut prices by cutting corners, making it hard for ethical businesses to compete.
• Subjectivity – what is considered ethical varies across cultures and contexts, making it hard to define universally.
• Greenwashing risk – some businesses claim to be ethical purely for marketing without genuine commitment.
Overall evaluation: Being ethical is fundamentally important for long-term business success, stakeholder trust, and sustainability, even though it may involve higher short-term costs. Businesses that compromise ethics for short-term gains risk reputational damage, legal penalties, and ultimate failure. (Award 5 marks for importance, 4 marks for limitations/challenges, 3 marks for balanced evaluative conclusion)

questions.text: Discuss the drivers towards enterprising in the Zimbabwean economy.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Drivers towards enterprising in the Zimbabwean economy (any well-discussed points, balanced discussion expected for full marks):

• Unemployment – high unemployment rates push individuals to create their own income-generating activities through self-employment and enterprise.
• Availability of natural resources – Zimbabwe is endowed with minerals, fertile land, forests, and water, providing raw materials for entrepreneurial ventures.
• Technological advancement/ICT – the growth of mobile money (EcoCash), internet access, and e-commerce platforms enable new business models and lower start-up costs.
• Government support and policy – initiatives such as the National Entrepreneurship Policy, SMEDCO, and ZIMTRADE provide funding, training, and market access for entrepreneurs.
• Education and training – universities, polytechnics, and vocational training centres produce graduates with business and technical skills.
• Role models and success stories – successful Zimbabwean entrepreneurs inspire others to start businesses.
• Market opportunities – gaps in the market for locally produced goods and services, especially import substitution, encourage enterprise.
• Remittances and diaspora investment – money sent home by Zimbabweans abroad provides start-up capital for enterprises.
• Micro-finance institutions – organisations like POSB, CABS, and MFIs provide accessible credit to small entrepreneurs.
• Cultural and social factors – communal values (Ubuntu), family support networks, and informal savings clubs (ROSCAs/mikando) support enterprise start-up.
• Economic hardship/necessity – economic downturns force people to be creative and start enterprises to survive.
• Demand for local products – growing consumer preference for locally made goods (Buy Zimbabwe campaigns) encourages production.
• Regional integration (SADC/COMESA) – access to regional markets motivates entrepreneurs to expand and export.

(Award 2 marks per well-discussed driver: 1 mark for identifying the driver + 1 mark for explaining how it drives enterprise in Zimbabwe, max 18 marks; 2 marks for overall conclusion/synthesis)

questions.text:
You are required to determine the concentration of dilute sulphuric acid, H2SO4 through titration with sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH). You are provided with dilute sulphuric acid, 1.0 mol/dm3 sodium hydroxide solution, phenolphthalein indicator, a conical flask, a 25 cm3 pipette, a pipette filler, a burette, a filter funnel, a dropper, a retort stand and clamp and a white tile.

Measure 25.00 cm3 of the sodium hydroxide solution using the pipette. Put the 25.00 cm3 of the sodium hydroxide solution, NaOH, into the conical flask. Using a dropper, add two or three drops of phenolphthalein indicator into the conical flask and shake gently. Pour the dilute sulphuric acid into the burette (already mounted). Read the initial volume of the dilute sulphuric acid. Record the initial volume of the dilute sulphuric acid in Table 1.1. Titrate the sodium hydroxide solution against the dilute sulphuric acid until the indicator just changes. NB: Shake the conical flask continuously during the titration. Record the final volume of the dilute sulphuric acid in the burette in Table 1.1. Complete Table 1.1 by calculating the volume of the dilute sulphuric acid, H2SO4, used.

subParts.text:
Record titration results in Table 1.1:

Table 1.1
| | Rough | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| final burette reading/cm3 | | | |
| initial burette reading/cm3 | | | |
| volume of H2SO4 used/cm3 | | | |
subParts.label: (a)(i)

subParts.text: Calculate the average volume of the dilute sulphuric acid needed to react with 25.00 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution, NaOH.
subParts.label: (a)(ii)

subParts.text: Explain why an indicator is used in the experiment.
subParts.label: (a)(iii)

subParts.text: State the type of reaction that occurs in the conical flask.
subParts.label: (a)(iv)

subParts.text: Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide in the 25.00 cm3 of solution.
subParts.label: (a)(v)

subParts.text:
Sodium hydroxide solution, NaOH, and dilute sulphuric acid, H2SO4 react according to the equation:
2NaOH(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l)
Determine the number of moles of the dilute sulphuric acid, H2SO4 which reacted with the 25.00 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution, NaOH.
subParts.label: (a)(vi)

subParts.text: Calculate the concentration of the dilute sulphuric acid, H2SO4.
subParts.label: (a)(vii)

subParts.text: Suggest one application of the titration procedure.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.diagramNote: Table 1.1 — a results table with columns for Experiment (Rough, 1, 2), final burette reading/cm3, initial burette reading/cm3, and volume of H2SO4 used/cm3.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Award marks for correct and consistent recording of burette readings (final and initial) for Rough, 1, and 2 titrations, and correct calculation of volume used (final − initial) for each. Correct readings to 2 decimal places (e.g. 0.00, 0.05). Award up to 9 marks: 1 mark each for each correct final reading (×3), each correct initial reading (×3), and each correct titre volume (×3).

(a)(ii) Average volume = sum of titres from experiments 1 and 2 (concordant results, i.e. within 0.10 cm3 of each other) ÷ 2. Rough titre is excluded from the average. e.g. if titre 1 = 12.50 cm3 and titre 2 = 12.60 cm3, average = (12.50 + 12.60)/2 = 12.55 cm3. [1 mark for correct average using concordant results]

(a)(iii) An indicator is used to show the end point / equivalence point of the titration [1 mark]; it changes colour (phenolphthalein turns from pink/purple to colourless) when the reaction is complete / all the NaOH has been neutralised [1 mark].

(a)(iv) Neutralisation reaction. [1 mark]

(a)(v) Moles of NaOH = concentration × volume = 1.0 mol/dm3 × (25.00/1000) dm3 = 0.025 mol. [1 mark for correct formula; 1 mark for correct substitution; 1 mark for correct answer = 0.025 mol]

(a)(vi) From the equation, molar ratio NaOH : H2SO4 = 2 : 1. Therefore moles of H2SO4 = 0.025/2 = 0.0125 mol. [1 mark]

(a)(vii) Concentration of H2SO4 = moles / volume (in dm3) = 0.0125 / (average titre / 1000). e.g. using average titre of 12.55 cm3: concentration = 0.0125 / 0.01255 ≈ 0.996 mol/dm3 ≈ 1.0 mol/dm3. [1 mark for correct method; 1 mark for correct final answer with appropriate units]

(b) Any ONE valid application, e.g.: determining the concentration of an unknown acid or base in industry / water treatment / food industry / pharmaceutical manufacturing / determining acidity of vinegar or lemon juice / quality control in manufacturing. [1 mark]

questions.text:
You are required to determine the effect of diameter on the resistance of a wire. You are provided with four wires of different diameters labelled E, F, G and H. NB: The wires are of the same material and same length. The circuit shown in Fig 2.1 has been set up for you.

Fig 2.1 shows a circuit with a voltmeter (V) connected in parallel and an ammeter (A) in series, with points X and Y where the test wire is connected.

Connect wire E between point X and point Y using crocodile clips. Close the switch and record the ammeter and voltmeter readings in Table 2.1. Open the switch and remove wire E. Repeat the procedure using wires F, G and H.

Complete Table 2.1 by recording the voltmeter and ammeter readings for wires E, F, G and H, and calculating the resistance for each wire.

Table 2.1
| wire | diameter/mm | voltage/V | current/A | resistance/Ω |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E | 0.56 | | | |
| F | 0.46 | | | |

subParts.label: (a)

subParts.label: (b)(i)

subParts.label: (b)(ii)

subParts.label: (b)(iii)

questions.topic: Resistance and Wire Diameter / Ohm's Law
questions.diagramNote: Fig 2.1 — a circuit diagram showing a battery/power source, a switch, an ammeter (A) in series, a voltmeter (V) in parallel, and two terminals X and Y where the test wire is connected using crocodile clips. Also Table 2.1 with columns: wire, diameter/mm, voltage/V, current/A, resistance/Ω for wires E (0.56 mm), F (0.46 mm), G (0.38 mm), H (0.25 mm). Graph grid for resistance vs diameter.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) For each wire: record voltage (V) and current (A) readings from the meters; calculate resistance using R = V/I (Ohm's Law). Award marks: 1 mark per wire for correct voltage reading (×4) and 1 mark per wire for correct current reading (×4) = 8 marks; 1 mark per correct resistance calculation for any 2 wires = 2 marks. (Total 10 marks.) Expected trend: as diameter decreases (E→H), resistance increases (thinner wire = higher resistance).

(b)(i) Graph of resistance (y-axis) vs diameter (mm) (x-axis). Award marks for: correct labelled axes with units [1]; suitable scale [1]; correctly plotted points [1]; smooth curve or best-fit line [1]. Expected shape: as diameter increases, resistance decreases (inverse/non-linear relationship).

(b)(ii) Draw a vertical line from diameter = 0.32 mm to the curve, then a horizontal line to the resistance axis; read off the resistance value at that point. Mark clearly on the graph. Award 1 mark for correct construction lines shown on graph; 1 mark for correct reading of resistance value consistent with the graph (answer depends on experimental data).

(b)(iii) As the diameter of the wire increases, the resistance decreases / the resistance of a wire is inversely related to its diameter (for wires of the same material and length). [1 mark]

(c) Power P = V × I (or P = V²/R or P = I²R) using wire G's voltage and current values from Table 2.1. e.g. if V = 2.0 V and I = 0.5 A, then P = 2.0 × 0.5 = 1.0 W. [1 mark for correct formula; 1 mark for correct substitution of wire G values; 1 mark for correct final answer with unit (W)].

questions.text:
An example of primary production in Zimbabwe is
A accounting.
B baking.
C farming.
D teaching.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – farming. Primary production involves the extraction of natural resources directly from the earth (agriculture, mining, fishing, forestry). Farming is a classic example of primary production in Zimbabwe.

questions.text:
Which consumer right is observed when workers are mining in an accident free environment?
A right to a healthy environment
B right to be heard
C right to be informed
D right to safety
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – right to safety. The right to safety protects consumers (and workers) from hazardous conditions, products, and processes. An accident-free mining environment directly reflects the right to safety.

questions.text:
Which one is the best channel for distributing fresh vegetables?
A producer ⎯⎯⎯→ consumer
B producer ⎯⎯⎯→ retailer ⎯⎯⎯→ consumer
C producer ⎯⎯⎯→ wholesaler ⎯⎯⎯→ consumer
D producer ⎯⎯⎯→ wholesaler ⎯⎯⎯→ retailer ⎯⎯⎯→ consumer
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – producer → consumer. Fresh vegetables are perishable and need to reach the consumer as quickly as possible. The shortest channel (direct from producer to consumer) minimises handling, time, and deterioration.

questions.text:
Under the Sale of Goods Act, goods sold should
A be sold in hygienic conditions.
B have correct weight.
C have correct price.
D be of merchantable quality.
questions.topic: Consumer Protection / Sale of Goods Act
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – be of merchantable quality. The Sale of Goods Act requires that goods sold must be of merchantable (satisfactory/acceptable) quality — fit for purpose and free from defects.

questions.text:
In Zimbabwe, vendors survive competition from supermarkets because they
A are situated near homes.
B employ qualified personnel.
C have large amount of capital.
D offer self-service.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – are situated near homes. Vendors operate in residential areas and informal settings, giving them a locational advantage over supermarkets, making it convenient for customers to access goods quickly without travelling far.

questions.text:
Which statement is correct for hire purchase?
A A written agreement is not necessary.
B The buyer owns the goods immediately.
C The seller repossesses the goods if buyer defaults in payment.
D There is low rate of interest.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – The seller repossesses the goods if the buyer defaults in payment. Under hire purchase, ownership does not pass to the buyer until the final instalment is paid; therefore the seller retains the right to repossess goods if the buyer fails to meet payments.

questions.text:
On 1 July 2024 a farmer bought goods worth $40 000 ZWL on credit and was allowed a trade discount of 40%. How much did he pay?
A $16 000 ZWL
B $24 000 ZWL
C $40 000 ZWL
D $56 000 ZWL
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – $24 000 ZWL. Trade discount = 40% × $40 000 = $16 000. Amount payable = $40 000 − $16 000 = $24 000 ZWL.

questions.text:
A document used when goods are bought on credit in Zimbabwe is
A a catalogue.
B an invoice.
C a quotation.
D a receipt.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – an invoice. An invoice is the document sent by the seller to the buyer listing goods supplied, quantities, prices, and terms of payment. It is the key document used in credit transactions.

questions.text:
Which one is the difference between home and foreign trade?
                Home trade                    Foreign trade
A  Different currencies are used     Same currency is used
B  Different laws are used            Same laws are used
C  Shorter distances are involved    Longer distances are involved
D  Trade within the country           Trade within China
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Home trade involves shorter distances; foreign trade involves longer distances. Home trade takes place within a country's borders (shorter distances), while foreign/international trade crosses national boundaries (longer distances). Options A and B are reversed, and D is incorrect as foreign trade is not limited to China.

questions.text:
Which one is a service provided by a wholesaler to a retailer?
A bearing risks of storage
B buying in bulk
C clearing production lines
D providing a ready market
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – bearing risks of storage. The wholesaler buys in bulk from producers and stores goods, thereby bearing the risks of storage (deterioration, price changes, theft) on behalf of the retailer. Note: buying in bulk is a service to the producer, not the retailer.

questions.text:
A Zimbabwean trader who converts $28 000 ZWL to American dollars at the rate of US$1 = $28 ZWL receives
A US$1 000.
B US$27 972.
C US$28 028.
D US$784 000.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – US$1 000. Calculation: $28 000 ZWL ÷ 28 ZWL per US$ = US$1 000.

questions.text:
Land reform helped Zimbabweans to transfer ownership and control of
A foreign farms to indigenous people.
B foreign owned farms to indigenous people.
C indigenous owned farms to foreign farmers.
D indigenous owned land to few white farmers.
questions.topic: Land Reform / Economic History of Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – foreign owned farms to indigenous people. Zimbabwe's land reform programme transferred ownership and control of foreign (predominantly white-owned) farms to indigenous Zimbabweans.

questions.text:
Consumers can protect themselves by avoiding
A shopping around.
B listening to advertisements.
C keeping records of transactions.
D impulse buying.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – impulse buying. Impulse buying (unplanned, spontaneous purchases) can lead consumers to buy unnecessary or overpriced goods. Avoiding it protects consumers financially. Shopping around, keeping records, and being aware of advertisements are protective measures, not things to avoid.

questions.text:
A business environment which promotes customs and traditions in Zimbabwe is
A economic.
B political.
C social.
D technological.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – social. The social (or socio-cultural) environment encompasses customs, traditions, culture, values, and societal norms that influence business operations.

questions.text:
Which one is a type of incorporated business unit?
A independent store
B partnership
C public corporation
D public limited company
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – public limited company. An incorporated business has a separate legal identity from its owners (limited liability). A public limited company (PLC) is incorporated. Independent stores and partnerships are unincorporated; public corporations can be incorporated but the most precise answer here is public limited company.

questions.text:
The Articles of Association is a document which contains the
A extent of the powers of the company.
B name of the company.
C objectives of the company.
D rules governing internal affairs of the company.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – rules governing internal affairs of the company. The Articles of Association sets out the internal rules and regulations of a company (e.g., conduct of meetings, directors' powers, share transfer procedures). The Memorandum of Association contains the company name, objectives, and extent of powers.

questions.text:
Which one is a feature of multi-national corporations?
A All profits benefit the host country.
B They are controlled by the Registrar of companies.
C They have production and marketing operations in several countries.
D They use cheap labour from the parent country.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – They have production and marketing operations in several countries. A defining feature of a multinational corporation (MNC) is that it operates (produces and sells) in more than one country.

questions.text:
The importance of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Zimbabwe is that they
A allow workers to use their collective strength to negotiate for better wages.
B employ a large number of local people.
C have unlimited liability.
D take part in bilateral and multilateral trade negotiations.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – employ a large number of local people. SMEs are significant contributors to employment in Zimbabwe, providing jobs for a large portion of the local population. The other options describe trade unions (A), a disadvantage (C), or activities of governments (D).

questions.text:
In business ethics, integrity is
A ability to see a need that has not been addressed.
B consistency in operation of a business.
C investing own money to start a business.
D passion for creation and ability to follow own ideas.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – consistency in operation of a business. Integrity in business ethics refers to being honest, consistent, and adhering to moral and ethical principles in all business operations.

questions.text:
Photocopying text books by students is an infringement of
A copyright law.
B patent rights.
C piracy.
D trade mark.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – copyright law. Copyright protects original literary, artistic, and educational works (such as textbooks). Reproducing them without permission (e.g., photocopying) is a direct infringement of copyright law.

questions.text:
Which one is a function of Zimbabwe Patents office?
A To enable investors to earn a living from their work.
B To protect intellectual property.
C To sue businesses who violate intellectual property.
D To turn ideas into profit making.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – To protect intellectual property. The Zimbabwe Patents Office (part of ZIPO) is responsible for protecting intellectual property rights, including patents, trademarks, and copyrights.

questions.text:
Individuals borrow money in order to
A earn interest.
B pay with interest.
C save money.
D start projects.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – start projects. Individuals typically borrow money to fund activities or projects they cannot immediately afford, such as starting a business, buying property, or financing education. Earning interest is a reason to lend, not borrow.

questions.text:
Financial advice can be obtained from
A banks, customers and friends.
B financial institutions, customers and friends.
C media, banks and relatives.
D suppliers, customers and financial institutions.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – media, banks and relatives. Credible sources of financial advice include banks (professional institutions), the media (financial news, programmes), and relatives (personal guidance). While not exhaustive, this is the best combination among the options given.

questions.text:
Which one is a role of commercial banks in Zimbabwe?
A lender of last resort
B regulates other financial institutions
C send and receive payments
D supervises the financial institutions
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – send and receive payments. Commercial banks facilitate payment transactions on behalf of customers (e.g., electronic transfers, cheques). The lender of last resort, regulation, and supervision roles belong to the central bank (Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe).

questions.text:
An internal source of capital is
A hire purchase.
B leasing.
C retained profits.
D trade credit.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – retained profits. Retained profits are earnings kept within the business after dividends are paid — a classic internal source of finance. Hire purchase, leasing, and trade credit are all external sources.

questions.text:
An example of a long term capital is
A bank overdraft.
B debenture.
C factoring.
D bank draft.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – debenture. A debenture is a long-term loan instrument (typically over 5–25 years) issued by a company. Bank overdrafts and factoring are short-term; a bank draft is a payment instrument, not a capital source.

questions.text:
A Zimbabwean cross border trader's sales for the month of December 2024 were $30 000 USD. She made a gross profit of $21 000 USD and incurred expenses of $8 000 USD. What was the cross border's net profit?
A $13 000 USD
B $22 000 USD
C $29 000 USD
D $59 000 USD
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – $13 000 USD. Net profit = Gross profit − Expenses = $21 000 − $8 000 = $13 000 USD.

questions.text:
An example of a non-insurable risk is
A damage to a car.
B loss by gambling.
C loss by fire.
D stolen scotch cart.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – loss by gambling. Non-insurable risks are speculative risks where there is a chance of gain or loss (e.g., gambling, business investment). Insurance covers pure risks (only loss possible) such as fire, theft, or accident damage.

questions.text:
Which one is a communal system of insurance and assurance?
A The availability of chief's program of gathering grain together.
B The availability of land provided by the chief in the village.
C The availability of funeral policies to bury the loved one in the community.
D The availability of statistics of deaths taking place in the village.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – The availability of funeral policies to bury the loved one in the community. A communal insurance/assurance system involves community members pooling resources to cover shared risks such as death/funeral expenses, which is an example of community-based assurance.

questions.text:
Which principle focuses on identifying the causes of damage in an insurance claim which is the most immediate of all possible causes?
A average clause
B insurable interest
C proximate clause
D utmost good faith
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – proximate clause (proximate cause). The principle of proximate cause requires that the insurer pays only if the nearest/most direct cause of loss is an insured peril. It identifies the most immediate and dominant cause of the damage or loss.

questions.text:
National Social Security Authority (NSSA) was formed to
A fund all the people in Zimbabwe when injured.
B promote safety and health everywhere.
C provide financial help to the elderly and children.
D provide rehabilitation service to disabled employees.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – provide rehabilitation service to disabled employees. NSSA was established to provide social security benefits including compensation and rehabilitation to workers who are injured or disabled in the course of their employment. It also covers pensions and accident prevention.

questions.text:
Which one is an advantage of internet to Zimbabweans?
A It contains some obscene scenes.
B It is used to advertise.
C It is used to bully others.
D It leads to cultural erosion.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – It is used to advertise. The internet provides a cost-effective and wide-reaching platform for advertising products and services — a clear advantage to Zimbabwean businesses. Options A, C, and D are disadvantages.

questions.text:
Which factor is considered when requesting for an ambulance?
A cost of mode
B distance involved
C security of mode
D speed of delivery
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – speed of delivery. When requesting an ambulance, the most critical factor is speed — how quickly the emergency vehicle can reach the patient. Time is of the essence in medical emergencies.

questions.text:
Which postal service is hired from the post office by a business?
A data post
B franking machine
C free post
D poste restante
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – franking machine. A franking machine is a device hired or leased from the post office by businesses to print postage directly onto envelopes/parcels, replacing traditional stamps. Poste restante is a collection service; data post and free post are mail services, not hired equipment.

questions.text:
A business can overcome barriers to effective communication by using
A indirect lines of communication.
B long messages.
C technical terms.
D simple language.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – simple language. Using simple, clear language removes barriers such as jargon, complex terminology, and misunderstanding. Indirect communication, long messages, and technical terms all create or worsen communication barriers.

questions.text:
Which factor is considered when choosing a mode of transport for goods?
A distribution of goods
B nature of goods
C packaging of goods
D price of goods
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – nature of goods. The nature of the goods (e.g., perishability, fragility, bulk, weight, hazardous properties) is a primary factor in selecting an appropriate mode of transport. For example, perishable goods require fast/refrigerated transport.

questions.text:
Which one is a benefit of Information Communication Technology (ICT) in transport?
A It facilitates cargo-tracking.
B It leads to high demand of transport.
C It leads to retraining of workers.
D It requires high investment in hardware systems.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – It facilitates cargo-tracking. ICT enables real-time tracking of goods in transit, improving efficiency, security, and customer service. Options B, C, and D are either neutral or disadvantages of ICT in transport.

questions.text:
An indigenous storage system for sweet potatoes in Zimbabwe is a
A calabash.
B crib.
C granary.
D pit.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – pit. Sweet potatoes in Zimbabwe are traditionally stored in underground pits, which maintain cool, stable temperatures and humidity to preserve the tubers. A granary stores grain; a crib stores maize; a calabash stores liquids.

questions.text:
Which marketing concept considers customer needs before developing a product?
A market
B product
C production
D selling
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – market (marketing concept). The market/marketing concept starts with identifying and understanding customer needs and wants, then develops products to satisfy those needs. The product and production concepts focus on the product/production first, and the selling concept focuses on aggressive selling after production.

questions.text:
A reason for market segmentation in Zimbabwe is to
A advertise products.
B attract competition.
C retain customers.
D use more money.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – retain customers. Market segmentation divides a market into distinct groups with similar needs, allowing businesses to tailor their products/services specifically to each segment, thereby satisfying customers better and retaining them. It does not aim to attract competition or use more money.

questions.text: Originate a menu card for a food outlet of your choice. Maximum size for the design should be A4.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original, fully resolved menu card design for a chosen food outlet. Key marking points: (1) Originality and creativity of concept; (2) Effective layout and composition within A4 size; (3) Appropriate use of typography (font choice, hierarchy, legibility); (4) Colour scheme that suits the food outlet theme; (5) Inclusion of relevant menu items/sections, outlet name/logo; (6) Quality of craftsmanship and neatness of execution; (7) Appropriate use of chosen media or combined media (excluding oil paint). Preparatory/developmental work should be submitted alongside the final piece.

questions.text: Design a cover for a book entitled, "Zimbabwean Heritage."
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original book cover design for a book entitled 'Zimbabwean Heritage'. Key marking points: (1) Strong, original concept that clearly reflects Zimbabwean heritage themes (e.g. cultural symbols, Great Zimbabwe, traditional motifs, wildlife, etc.); (2) Effective integration of title typography with imagery; (3) Balanced and visually appealing composition; (4) Appropriate and harmonious use of colour; (5) Inclusion of essential book cover elements (title, author name, imagery); (6) Quality of craftsmanship and use of media; (7) Evidence of design development in preparatory work.

questions.text: Develop a label for, "Sunshine Cleaners Company." Label should be 12 cm x 7 cm.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original product label for 'Sunshine Cleaners Company' at the specified size of 12 cm x 7 cm. Key marking points: (1) Adherence to specified dimensions (12 cm × 7 cm); (2) Originality and appropriateness of design concept for a cleaning product brand; (3) Clear and legible use of typography for company name and any additional text; (4) Use of colour and imagery that conveys cleanliness, freshness, or sunshine theme; (5) Effective composition within the given format; (6) Inclusion of relevant label elements (brand name, possible logo/motif, product details); (7) Quality of craftsmanship and media use; (8) Preparatory work submitted.

questions.text: Develop an invitation card for the inauguration of your local chief.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original invitation card design for the inauguration of a local chief. Key marking points: (1) Originality and cultural appropriateness of the design concept; (2) Incorporation of traditional/cultural motifs or symbolism relevant to chieftainship and Zimbabwean heritage; (3) Clear and legible typography conveying event details (event name, date, venue, etc.); (4) Appropriate colour scheme reflecting the dignity and importance of the occasion; (5) Well-balanced and visually appealing composition; (6) Quality of craftsmanship and use of media; (7) Preparatory work submitted.

questions.text: Using geometric shapes design a pattern for a carpet.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original carpet pattern design using geometric shapes. Key marking points: (1) Effective and creative use of geometric shapes (circles, squares, triangles, hexagons, etc.); (2) Clear repetition, symmetry, or other organisational principle creating a coherent pattern; (3) Harmonious and appropriate colour scheme suitable for a carpet; (4) Originality and aesthetic appeal of the overall pattern; (5) Evidence of rhythm, balance, and visual unity; (6) Quality of execution and craftsmanship; (7) Preparatory/developmental work submitted.

questions.text: Ubuntu/Hunhu/Bumunhu/Botho.
questions.section: Option B - Imaginative Composition in Colour
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original composition in colour inspired by the theme of Ubuntu/Hunhu/Bumunhu/Botho (the philosophy of communal humanity, compassion, and togetherness). Key marking points: (1) Clear and imaginative interpretation of the theme (e.g. community helping, sharing, unity, togetherness); (2) Strong compositional arrangement with a clear focal point; (3) Effective and expressive use of colour to convey mood and meaning; (4) Originality and personal expression; (5) Evidence of understanding of art elements (line, shape, form, texture, tone) and principles (balance, rhythm, contrast); (6) Quality of craftsmanship and appropriate use of media; (7) Preparatory work submitted.

questions.text: Folktale.
questions.section: Option B - Imaginative Composition in Colour
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original composition in colour based on a folktale of their choice. Key marking points: (1) Clear narrative content drawn from a recognisable or imagined folktale; (2) Strong imaginative interpretation and storytelling through visual elements; (3) Effective compositional arrangement that guides the viewer through or into the story; (4) Expressive and appropriate use of colour to convey atmosphere and narrative; (5) Originality and creativity in depicting characters, setting, and action; (6) Quality of craftsmanship and use of media; (7) Preparatory work submitted.

questions.text: Tragedy.
questions.section: Option B - Imaginative Composition in Colour
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original composition in colour based on the theme of Tragedy. Key marking points: (1) Effective and imaginative interpretation of the concept of tragedy (loss, disaster, grief, conflict, etc.); (2) Strong emotional impact conveyed through composition and colour choices (e.g. sombre tones, dramatic contrasts); (3) Clear focal point and well-organised compositional arrangement; (4) Originality and personal expression in depicting the theme; (5) Skillful use of art elements and principles to evoke the mood of tragedy; (6) Quality of craftsmanship and use of media; (7) Preparatory work submitted.

questions.text: Landscape.
questions.section: Option B - Imaginative Composition in Colour
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original imaginative composition in colour depicting a landscape. questions.text: Clean up.
questions.section: Option B - Imaginative Composition in Colour
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should produce an original composition in colour based on the theme of 'Clean up'. questions.text:
Intsomi ithetha ngabantwana bakabani?

B. bakaDyakalashe

D. bakaNgwenya
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. bakaHobe

questions.text:
Ngokwasentsomini yintoni eyayikhalisa uHobe?
A. liqhinga
B. yindlala
C. ngumsebenzi
D. zinyosi
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. yindlala

questions.text:
Babebangaphi abantwana bakaHobe?
A. babebahlanu
B. babebathathu
C. babebabini
D. babebane
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. babebathathu — uDyakalashe wachola usane (1st), wabuyisa omnye emphinda kabini (2nd), wabuyisa elesibini emphinda kathathu (3rd), implying three children were eventually eaten.

questions.text:
Wawufumana phi umsebenzi uHobe?
A. kwaDyakalashe
B. etyolweni
C. emlanjeni
D. kwaMvubu
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. kwaMvubu

questions.text:
Ngubani owatya iintsane?
A. nguMvubu
B. nguHobe
C. nguDyakalashe
D. nguNgwenya
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. nguDyakalashe

questions.text:
UDyakalashe wayengumhlobo onjani?
A. okhohlakeleyo
B. onenimba
C. onobubelo
D. onobuqhophololo
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. okhohlakeleyo

questions.text:
Sifundo bani esifumaneka entsomini?
A. ungabothemba inoba ngubani
B. ungaboba nobubele kakhulu
C. ungabojija eqhingeni
D. ungabodinga umsebenzi
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. ungabothemba inoba ngubani — the story demonstrates that trust placed in the wrong person (uDyakalashe) leads to tragedy.

questions.text:
Kwenzakala ntoni kuHobe ekugqibeleni?
A. watyiwa nguDyakalashe
B. wawela emlanjeni
C. watyiwa ziinyosi
D. wangena etyolweni

questions.text:
Igama elisentsomini elintethonye nelithi 'wabagqiba' ngelithi
A. wakhawuleza.
B. wabaqhaphela.
C. waluphinda.
D. wabaqongqotha.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. wabaqongqotha — 'wabagqiba' means he finished/destroyed them all, and 'wabaqongqotha' (wiped them out) carries the same meaning in context.

questions.text:
Abantwana bakaHobe bathula _______ bebona uDyaka.
A. cwaka
B. krwe
C. dyumpu
D. cwe
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. cwaka — 'cwaka' is the ideophone for complete silence/stillness.

questions.text:
UHobe waxelela abantwana bakhe ukuthi kaloku esintwini, "___________ ibuzwa kwabaphambili."
A. Inyani
B. Inyosi
C. Ingwenya
D. Inyathi
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. Inyathi — the proverb is 'Inyathi ibuzwa kwabaphambili' (Ask those who have gone ahead / Experience is gained from elders).

questions.text:
UDyakalashe umke ________ Mvubu.
A. nge
B. ne
C. no
D. ngo
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. no — 'UDyakalashe umke noMvubu' (Dyakalashe left together with Mvubu). The conjunction 'no-' is used before a noun starting with a consonant to mean 'with'.

questions.text:
Chonga igama elipelwe ngokuchanekileyo.
A. umgquba
B. ugquba
C. umnquba
D. umqgubu
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. umgquba — correctly spelled with the click consonant 'gq' and the noun prefix 'um-'.

questions.text:
Nika igama elihloniphayo kweli elikrwelwe umgca ngaphatsi:
Inkosi yamaHlubi ifile.
A. itshabalele
B. ibhubhile
C. iswelekile
D. ikhotheme
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. ikhotheme — 'ukukhothama' is the respectful/royal term used when referring to the death of a king/chief.

questions.text:
Zintoni ezaziqhuma?
A. zizaqhwithi
B. ziinkabi
C. ziimvula
D. ziigusha
questions.aiModelAnswer: A. zizaqhwithi — the poem states 'Zaqhuma izaqhwithi kwabomvu' (dust-devils/whirlwinds erupted, turning red).

questions.text:
Ngobani ababebulisana ngemozulu?
A. ngoomama
B. ngootata
C. ngabantwana
D. Ngamaxhegwazana
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. ngootata — 'Babulisana ngemozulu ootata' (The fathers greeted each other about the weather).

questions.text:
Yintoni eyayikhalisa amaxhego namaxhegwazana?
A. yimvula eninzi
B. kukutshisa kwelanga
C. ngamafu emvula
D. kunqulwa kwizinyanya
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. kukutshisa kwelanga — the poem describes extreme heat and drought (imbalela); the elders lamented because of the scorching sun and the resulting drought.

questions.text:
Kwenziwa nzame bani ukusombulula iingxaki ezeza nembalela?
A. kwaqalwa iinkabi
B. kwabazwa izikeyi
C. kwanqulwa izinyanya
D. kwaphunguka iziphala
questions.aiModelAnswer: C. kwanqulwa izinyanya — among the solutions attempted was praying/appealing to ancestors ('Sayonqula kwizinyanya').

questions.text:
Ngobani ababizwa eembizweni?
A. ngootata
B. ngoomama
C. ngabantwana
D. ngamaxhego
questions.aiModelAnswer: D. ngamaxhego — 'Iinkosi zabizela iingwevu eembizweni' (The chiefs summoned the elders/grey-haired ones to council meetings).

questions.text:
Amanzi okunkcenkceshela ayezakuvelaphi?
A. emifuleni
B. emithonjeni
C. ezizibeni.
D. emadamu
questions.aiModelAnswer: B. emithonjeni — the poem advises 'Yenjiwe imithombo yamanzi. Kulinywe kunkcenkceshelwe' (Let water sources be established. Plant and irrigate).

questions.text:
Esincokweni kuthiwa mayiphiweni imfuyo?

questions.text:
Nika intsingiselo yebinzana elithi 'sixingile engxakini'.

B. Sivumelane singachasi imozulu.
C. Kulinywa izilimo zakudala.

questions.text:

questions.text:
Nika ubuninzi begama elikrwelwe umgca ngaphantsi:
Ixhego lixhele ibhokhwe.

questions.aiModelAnswer: C. iibhokhwe — 'ibhokhwe' (goat) forms its plural as 'iibhokhwe' (class 9/10 noun).

questions.text:
Iinkomo _________ zixingile odakeni.

B. yona

questions.aiModelAnswer: D. zona — 'iinkomo' (cattle) is a class 10 noun; the absolute pronoun/emphatic pronoun for class 10 is 'zona'.

questions.text:
Iingwevu bezihleli _________ komthi.

questions.text:

questions.text:
Abaxoxayo bathi amalahle embiwaphi?

Sesiphi isembiwa esisetyenziswa ukwenza ibhetri?

Ngokwengxoxo sesiphi isivakalisi esiyinyani ngezambiwa?

questions.text:
Ingxoxo kaBusi noMthuli ithetha
A. ngamaphephandaba
B. ngorhulumente
C. ngezembiwa
D. ngabafundi

questions.text:
Aba bahlobo bazakuphanda ngani malunga nezambiwa?
A. ngobubi bokwemba

(b) Monolithic floor construction: the foundation, floor slab and ground beam are all cast at the same time as one continuous unit/pour, forming a single integral structure. questions.topic: Freehand drawing, orthographic projection, and construction calculations (circular water tank)
questions.diagramNote: Figure 16(b) shows the plan of a circular brick water tank with an outer radius of R7000 (7000 mm) marked.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Award marks for: a recognisable freehand sketch of a traditional hut (circular or rectangular); inclusion of a window opening; a veranda shown; at least two important dimensions added.
(a)(ii) Award marks for: correct First Angle Orthographic projection layout (plan below front elevation, side elevation to the left of front elevation); correct floor plan showing walls, openings, veranda; correct front elevation showing wall height, roof, window, door, veranda; correct side elevation; correct projection lines; title/labels.

(b)(i) Volume of water when half full:
— Outer radius R = 7 000 mm = 7 m
— Wall thickness = 230 mm = 0.23 m
— Inner radius r = 7.000 − 0.230 = 6.770 m
— Inner diameter = 13.540 m
— Full height = 4 000 mm = 4 m; half height = 2 m
— Volume = π × r² × h = (22/7) × 6.770² × 2
= (22/7) × 45.8329 × 2
= (22/7) × 91.6658
= 3.142857 × 91.6658
≈ 288.1 m³

(b)(ii) Number of bricks for superstructure:
— Circumference of wall (use mean radius or outer surface area — typically outer circumference for brickwork):
— Outer circumference = 2πR = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 m
— Height = 4 m
— Surface area of outer wall = 44 × 4 = 176 m²
— Number of bricks = 176 × 104 = 18 304 bricks
(Note: if using mean radius = 7 − 0.115 = 6.885 m: circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 6.885 = 43.28 m; area = 43.28 × 4 = 173.1 m²; bricks = 173.1 × 104 ≈ 18 002 bricks. Accept either approach consistently applied.)

(a) Suggest and explain tools that you can use to attract customers.
(b) As a new business in the shoe market explain the pricing strategy you will adopt for your business.
(c) If the cost of making one pair of school shoes is $12 and the business wants to make a profit of 25% of cost. Calculate the selling price per pair of shoes.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Tools to attract customers (award 2 marks each — 1 for naming, 1 for explanation — up to 10 marks for 5 tools):
• Social media (Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram) – reaches a large audience quickly and cheaply
• Posters/flyers – visually communicate product details to the local community
• Word of mouth – satisfied customers recommend the product to others, building trust
• Discounts/promotions – attract price-sensitive customers and encourage first-time buyers
• Free samples/trials – allows potential customers to experience product quality
• Exhibitions/trade fairs – showcase products directly to schools and buyers
• Website/e-commerce – provides an online platform for customers to view and order products

(b) Appropriate pricing strategies for a new business:
• Penetration pricing – setting a low initial price to attract customers and gain market share quickly, then gradually increasing price once established. This is suitable as the business is new and needs to compete with existing shoe suppliers.
• Cost-plus pricing – adding a fixed percentage mark-up on top of the cost of production to ensure all costs are covered and profit is made.
Award marks for naming the strategy and providing a relevant explanation/justification in the context of a new shoe business.

(c) Cost price = $12
Profit = 25% of $12 = 0.25 × $12 = $3
Selling price = Cost price + Profit = $12 + $3 = $15
The selling price per pair of shoes is $15.

questions.text: What method of production would you recommend for producing shoes. Justify your answer.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Recommended method: Job Production or Mass/Flow Production (accept either with valid justification).

• Job Production: Producing shoes one pair at a time to meet specific customer orders. Justification: allows customisation to different shoe sizes and school requirements; suits a small/new business with limited capital; higher quality control per unit.

• Batch Production: Producing a set number of shoes of one size before switching to another size. Justification: allows flexibility to produce different sizes in batches; more efficient than job production; suits a growing business supplying multiple schools.

• Mass/Flow Production: Continuous large-scale production of identical shoes. Justification: lowers cost per unit; suitable if demand is very high and standardised; however, requires significant capital investment — less ideal for a new/small business.

Most appropriate recommendation for a new small business: Batch production — balances efficiency with flexibility to produce varying shoe sizes. Award marks for: correctly naming a method of production (2 marks), providing a clear and relevant justification linked to the shoe business context (up to 8 marks) covering factors such as scale of business, cost, flexibility, quality, and demand.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Solution: a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. [1]
Plasmolysis: the process by which a plant cell loses water by osmosis (when placed in a hypertonic/concentrated solution), causing the cell membrane/cytoplasm to shrink away from the cell wall. [2]

(b)(iv) Any two of: increase the concentration of the solution in the glass tube (increasing the osmotic gradient); increase the temperature (speeds up molecular movement); use a tube with a narrower bore (same volume of water entry causes a more visible/greater rise). [1+1]

questions.topic: Genetics – inheritance and sickle cell anaemia
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Cause: a mutation/change in the gene that codes for haemoglobin, resulting in abnormal (sickle-shaped) red blood cells. [1]
Any two effects: anaemia (reduced oxygen-carrying capacity); pain/blocked blood vessels (due to sickle cells clumping); organ damage; fatigue/weakness; increased susceptibility to infections; jaundice. [1 each, 2 marks]
(a)(ii) Explanation of one effect, e.g. Anaemia: sickle-shaped red blood cells have a shorter lifespan and are destroyed faster than they can be replaced, reducing the number of red blood cells and therefore less oxygen is carried to tissues, causing fatigue. OR Blocked blood vessels: sickle cells are rigid and sticky, they clump together and block capillaries, causing severe pain and depriving tissues of oxygen. [2]
(b)(i) A gene is a section/unit of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein/characteristic/trait. [1]
(b)(ii) Let B = light brown (dominant), b = white (recessive).
The offspring ratio of approximately 5 light brown : 2 white ≈ 3:1 suggests the light brown parent is heterozygous (Bb).
Parental phenotypes: Light brown (male) × White (female)
Parental genotypes: Bb × bb
Gametes: B or b (male); b (female)
Punnett square:
      b      b
B | Bb | Bb |
b | bb | bb |
Offspring genotypes: 50% Bb (light brown) : 50% bb (white)
Offspring phenotypes: approximately 1 light brown : 1 white (the actual 5:2 result is consistent with a 1:1 expected ratio due to chance).
Award marks for: correct parental genotypes [1]; correct gametes [1]; correct Punnett square or offspring genotypes [1]; correct phenotype ratio and conclusion [1]. [4]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) An enzyme is a biological catalyst (protein) that speeds up/catalyses chemical reactions in living organisms without being consumed/used up in the reaction. [2]
(a)(ii) Any four of: they are biological catalysts; they are proteins; they are specific (each enzyme acts on one substrate); they are reusable/not used up; they are affected by temperature (have an optimum temperature); they are affected by pH (have an optimum pH); they lower activation energy; they can be denatured by high temperatures or extreme pH. [1 each, 4 marks]
(b) Amylase (enzyme) has an active site with a specific/complementary shape to the starch molecule; starch (substrate) binds to the active site forming an enzyme-substrate complex; amylase breaks the glycosidic bonds in starch, hydrolysing it into maltose/glucose (sugars); the enzyme is released unchanged and can catalyse further reactions (lock-and-key or induced fit model accepted). [4]
(c)(i) At 60 °C the enzyme's activity will be reduced/significantly decreased or the enzyme may be denatured; the optimum temperature for most biological enzymes is around 37–40 °C; at 60 °C the high temperature causes the enzyme's active site to change shape (denaturation), so fewer/no enzyme-substrate complexes form and rate of conversion decreases. [2]
(c)(ii) Any two of: lower the temperature to the enzyme's optimum (approx. 37–40 °C); adjust pH to the optimum; use a more heat-stable/thermophilic amylase; increase enzyme concentration; ensure substrate (starch) concentration is adequate. [1 each, 2 marks]
(d)(i) Any two of: protease; lipase; amylase; cellulase. [1 each, 2 marks]
(d)(ii) Protease – breaks down/digests protein stains (e.g. blood, egg, grass) into amino acids so they can be washed away. Lipase – breaks down/digests fat/grease stains into fatty acids and glycerol so they dissolve in water. Amylase – breaks down starch-based stains into sugars. [1 mark per enzyme role, 2 marks]
(e) If other factors (e.g. pH, temperature, enzyme concentration, substrate concentration) are not kept constant, they may also affect enzyme activity; this would make results unreliable/invalid/confounding variables would prevent a fair test; only one variable should change at a time to establish a cause-and-effect relationship. [2]

questions.topic: Plant productivity, pests, and mineral nutrition
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Productivity (of plants) is the rate at which plants produce/accumulate organic matter/biomass through photosynthesis per unit area per unit time; or the total amount of organic material produced by plants in a given area and time. [2]
(a)(ii)
1. Temperature: enzymes involved in photosynthesis and respiration work faster at higher temperatures (up to optimum ~25–35 °C), increasing rate of photosynthesis and growth; above optimum, enzymes denature, reducing productivity; too low temperatures slow enzyme activity and reduce growth. [2]
2. Mineral salts: essential minerals (e.g. nitrates, phosphates) are needed for synthesis of proteins, chlorophyll, DNA, ATP; deficiency of minerals leads to poor growth, yellowing (chlorosis), and reduced productivity; adequate minerals increase photosynthesis efficiency and plant growth. [2]
3. Water: needed as a raw material for photosynthesis; maintains cell turgidity for support and growth; transports minerals and organic compounds; drought/water stress closes stomata (limiting CO₂ entry), reducing photosynthesis and productivity; excess water can cause waterlogging and root death. [2]
(b)(i) Two types of plant pests:
1. Animal/invertebrate pests – e.g. aphids, locusts, caterpillars, weevils, birds, rats (organisms that physically eat/damage plants).
2. Plant/pathogen pests (or microbial pests) – e.g. fungi (mildew, rust), bacteria, viruses, parasitic plants (striga/witchweed). [2 marks per type: name + example = 4 marks]
(b)(ii) Any three of: crop rotation (prevents build-up of pests); intercropping/mixed planting; proper spacing of plants; timely weeding; use of resistant varieties; proper disposal of crop residues; early planting/proper timing; physical removal of pests; use of biological control agents (e.g. introducing natural predators). [1 each, 3 marks]
(c)(i) Nitrogen: needed for synthesis of amino acids/proteins, chlorophyll, and nucleic acids (DNA/RNA); promotes leafy/vegetative growth. Phosphorus: needed for synthesis of ATP (energy transfer), DNA, RNA, and cell membranes (phospholipids); important for root development and energy metabolism. [1 each, 2 marks]
(c)(ii) Yellow leaves = nitrogen deficiency; brown leaf edges = potassium deficiency; weak stems = possibly potassium or calcium deficiency. Steps: (1) Apply nitrogenous fertiliser (e.g. ammonium nitrate/urea) to address yellowing; (2) Apply potassium-containing fertiliser (e.g. potash) to address browning/weak stems; (3) Ensure adequate watering to facilitate nutrient uptake; (4) Test/adjust soil pH to optimise mineral availability. Award 1 mark per valid, justified step, up to 3 marks. [3]

(c) An infectious disease is a disease caused by a pathogen (microorganism such as bacteria, virus, fungus, or parasite) that can be transmitted/passed from one person to another (directly or indirectly). [2]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Any four of: multicellular; eukaryotic (cells with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles); cells have a cell wall made of cellulose; contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis (autotrophic); store energy as starch; have no organs of locomotion/non-motile; reproduce by seeds, spores, or vegetative means; alternation of generations in life cycle. [1 each, 4 marks]
(a)(ii) Any three of: habitat destruction/deforestation; pollution (air, water, soil); climate change/global warming; overexploitation/overhunting/overfishing; introduction of invasive alien species; urbanisation/agriculture expansion; disease; poaching. [1 each, 3 marks]
(b)(i) An ecosystem is a community of living organisms (biotic factors) interacting with each other and with their non-living/physical environment (abiotic factors) in a specific area. [2]
(b)(ii) Comparison of clay soil vs sandy soil (award 1 mark per valid comparison point, up to 4):
- Clay soil has smaller/finer particles than sandy soil.
- Clay soil has a higher water-holding capacity; sandy soil drains quickly/has poor water retention.
- Clay soil has poor aeration/less air spaces; sandy soil has good aeration/larger air spaces.
- Clay soil is more fertile/has more mineral nutrients; sandy soil is less fertile.
- Clay soil becomes waterlogged easily; sandy soil does not become waterlogged.
- Clay soil is heavier/denser; sandy soil is lighter.
- Clay soil has smaller pore spaces; sandy soil has larger pore spaces. [4]
(c)(i) A valid food chain using the given organisms with exactly three trophic levels, e.g.:
Aphids → Ladybird beetles → Birds
OR Locusts → Spiders → Birds
OR Aphids → Spiders → Birds
(Award 1 mark for a correct producer implied/named or correct first consumer, 1 mark for correct arrow direction, 1 mark for three correct trophic levels.) [3]
(c)(ii) Credit any ONE organism chosen and a logical, detailed explanation. Example – Removing ladybird beetles: the population of aphids would increase (no predator control) causing greater damage to plants; bird populations may decrease due to reduced food source; the overall balance of the ecosystem/food web is disrupted. Example – Removing birds: spider or ladybird beetle populations may increase unchecked; eventually aphid/locust populations may also change; plant populations affected; loss of a top predator destabilises the food chain.
