questions.topic: Stone Age Craft and Khoisan Hunting
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Uses of craft during the Stone Age (any 5):
- Stone tools (hand axes, scrapers) were used to cut, chop and process food.
- Spears and arrow heads were crafted from stone for hunting animals.
- Bone needles were used to sew animal skin clothing.
- Pottery was made for storing food and water.
- Baskets and mats were woven from plant fibres for carrying and storing goods.
- Rock paintings/art were created for spiritual/ritual communication.
- Animal traps and snares were crafted for catching game.
- Grinding stones were used to process grain and seeds.
- Ornaments and beads were made for social/cultural identity and trade.

(b) Strategies to improve Khoisan hunting (any 5):
- Use of poisoned arrows to weaken and kill animals more effectively.
- Hunting in larger, organised groups (communal hunting) to trap more animals.
- Use of fire to drive animals into confined areas for easier killing.
- Construct animal traps, pit falls and snares for passive hunting.
- Develop better bows and spears with sharper, heavier stone tips.
- Study animal behaviour and migration patterns to anticipate locations.
- Train hunting dogs to track and corner prey.
- Collaborate with neighbouring communities to cover larger hunting areas.
- Specialise roles within the hunting party (trackers, ambushers, killers).

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five economic activities carried out in the prazos by the Portuguese. [15]

(b) Africans were exploited in Portuguese prazos. Propose, in essay form, any five methods that could have been used by the Mutapa people to resist economic domination. [10]

subParts.text: Describe any five economic activities carried out in the prazos by the Portuguese.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Africans were exploited in Portuguese prazos. Propose, in essay form, any five methods that could have been used by the Mutapa people to resist economic domination.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Economic activities in the prazos (any 5):
- Agriculture: cultivation of crops (maize, millet, sugarcane) using African labour.
- Cattle ranching: rearing of livestock for meat and trade.
- Trading in gold and ivory obtained from surrounding African communities.
- Slave trading: capturing and selling Africans as slaves for export.
- Collection of tribute (musamba) from African inhabitants on the prazo.
- Mining of gold and other minerals.
- Hunting of wild animals for ivory and skins.
- Fishing along major rivers such as the Zambezi.
- Craft production using forced African labour.

(b) Methods to resist economic domination (any 5):
- Form military alliances with neighbouring states to jointly resist Portuguese power.
- Use guerrilla warfare tactics to disrupt Portuguese trading operations.
- Refuse to pay tribute/boycott all trade with Portuguese traders.
- Establish alternative trade networks with Arab or other African traders.
- Strengthen political unity under a strong, centralised Mutapa leadership.
- Use diplomacy and treaties with other European powers against the Portuguese.
- Burn or destroy crops and resources to deny the Portuguese economic benefits.
- Educate and mobilise the population about the harms of Portuguese exploitation.
- Enforce traditional laws to limit Portuguese movement and land acquisition.

questions.text:
(a) Give an account of any five economic activities of the Portuguese in the Mutapa state. [15]

(b) The Mutapa king lost control of trade to the Portuguese. Recommend, in essay form, any five strategies the Mutapa could have employed to regain control of trade from the Portuguese. [10]

subParts.text: Give an account of any five economic activities of the Portuguese in the Mutapa state.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: The Mutapa king lost control of trade to the Portuguese. Recommend, in essay form, any five strategies the Mutapa could have employed to regain control of trade from the Portuguese.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Portuguese Economic Activities in the Mutapa State
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Portuguese economic activities in the Mutapa state (any 5):
- Gold trading: Portuguese established fairs (ferias) at Dambarare, Masapa and Luanze to trade for gold.
- Ivory trade: purchased ivory from Mutapa traders for export to Asia and Europe.
- Slave trade: captured and sold Africans into slavery.
- Mining: attempted direct involvement in gold and mineral extraction.
- Agriculture on prazos established within and near the Mutapa state.
- Imposition of tribute (curva) on the Mutapa king, extracting wealth.
- Monopolising trade routes to exclude Arab and Swahili traders.
- Establishing missions as economic/political bases of influence.
- Charging customs duties on goods passing through their controlled fairs.

(b) Strategies to regain control of trade (any 5):
- Re-establish direct trade relationships with Arab and Swahili merchants.
- Expel Portuguese traders from inland fairs and trade routes by force.
- Form military alliances with other kingdoms to confront Portuguese power.
- Introduce state-controlled trading systems monopolised by the king.
- Diversify exports to reduce dependency on Portuguese-controlled markets.
- Use diplomacy to negotiate fairer trade terms with the Portuguese Crown.
- Train and arm loyal soldiers to enforce trading laws and protect routes.
- Impose taxes and restrictions on Portuguese traders operating in the state.
- Strengthen the Mutapa army to resist Portuguese military pressure.

questions.text:
(a) Outline any five economic terms of the Rudd Concession. [15]

(b) Concession seekers were a problem to Lobengula. Suggest, in essay form, any five methods Lobengula could have used to protect his state from concession seekers. [10]

subParts.text: Outline any five economic terms of the Rudd Concession.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Concession seekers were a problem to Lobengula. Suggest, in essay form, any five methods Lobengula could have used to protect his state from concession seekers.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Economic terms of the Rudd Concession (any 5):
- Rhodes' representatives were granted exclusive mining rights throughout Lobengula's kingdom.
- Lobengula was to receive 100 pounds sterling per month in payment.
- He was promised 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles and 100,000 rounds of ammunition.
- A gunboat (steamboat) was to be provided on the Zambezi River.
- No more than ten white men were to dig or mine at any one time.
- The concession gave exclusive rights to minerals and metals in Matabeleland and Mashonaland.
- Rhodes gained the right to do all things necessary for mining operations.
- Lobengula could not grant similar concessions to other parties.
- The concession was used to obtain a Royal Charter giving the BSAC administrative control.

(b) Methods to protect the state from concession seekers (any 5):
- Seek legal advice from independent European advisers/missionaries before signing any documents.
- Establish a permanent committee of indunas to review and reject concession requests.
- Strengthen diplomatic ties with the British Crown directly to bypass company agents.
- Expel known concession seekers from the kingdom before negotiations began.
- Issue a public declaration (in writing) nullifying any previously signed concessions.
- Seek alliances with the Boer Republic (Transvaal) as a counterweight to British pressure.
- Limit contact between concession seekers and the king to formal, witnessed audiences.
- Develop the Ndebele military capacity to deter forced concession-seeking.
- Use missionaries as neutral intermediaries to communicate Lobengula's terms to the British government.

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five economic motives of the Pioneer column. [10]

(b) Africans became poorer due to loss of land to the Pioneer column. Propose, in essay form, any five ways that could have been used by the Africans to prevent land appropriation by the Pioneer white settlers. [15]

subParts.text: Describe any five economic motives of the Pioneer column.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Africans became poorer due to loss of land to the Pioneer column. Propose, in essay form, any five ways that could have been used by the Africans to prevent land appropriation by the Pioneer white settlers.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Pioneer Column – Economic Motives and Land Appropriation
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Economic motives of the Pioneer column (any 5):
- To access and exploit the mineral wealth (especially gold) believed to be abundant in Mashonaland.
- To acquire large tracts of fertile agricultural land for white settlement.
- To establish control of trade routes in the interior of southern Africa.
- Each Pioneer was promised 15 gold claims and a 3,000-acre farm as payment.
- To find a 'Second Rand' — a goldfield as rich as the Witwatersrand in South Africa.
- To open up markets for British manufactured goods in the interior.
- To exploit African labour for mining and agriculture.
- To pre-empt Boer (Transvaal) expansion northwards and secure the territory for Britain/BSAC.
- To develop infrastructure (roads, railways) that would open up the interior economically.

(b) Ways Africans could have prevented land appropriation (any 5):
- Form military alliances among different African groups (Shona and Ndebele) to jointly resist settlers.
- Use armed resistance/warfare to repel the Pioneer column before it established a foothold.
- Seek diplomatic intervention from the British Crown against BSAC land seizures.
- Destroy crops and food supplies to make the territory economically unattractive to settlers.
- Petition the British government and humanitarian organisations (like missionaries) to expose injustices.
- Avoid signing any land agreements or treaties with company representatives.
- Engage in guerrilla tactics to make settlement too costly and dangerous.
- Unite under a single strong political/military leadership to co-ordinate resistance.
- Establish clearly demarcated and defended land boundaries recognised by all African communities.

questions.text:
(a) Give an account of any five economic effects of the Land Apportionment Act of 1930. [15]

(b) Land Apportionment Act of 1930 impoverished Africans. Recommend, in essay form, any five solutions that could have been taken to deal with the negative effects of the Land Apportionment Act of 1930. [10]

subParts.text: Give an account of any five economic effects of the Land Apportionment Act of 1930.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Land Apportionment Act of 1930 impoverished Africans. Recommend, in essay form, any five solutions that could have been taken to deal with the negative effects of the Land Apportionment Act of 1930.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Economic effects of the Land Apportionment Act of 1930 (any 5):
- Africans were confined to infertile, overcrowded Tribal Trust Lands (TTLs), reducing agricultural output.
- Settlers acquired the most fertile land, boosting white commercial agriculture at African expense.
- Land overcrowding in reserves caused soil exhaustion and environmental degradation.
- Africans were forced into wage labour on white farms and mines due to loss of land.
- African peasant farming was undermined as productive land was lost.
- Urban Africans could not own property in towns, limiting their economic advancement.
- The Act entrenched a dual economy: a prosperous white sector and an impoverished African sector.
- Africans lost access to natural resources (forests, rivers, pastures) previously used for livelihood.
- Overcrowding in reserves led to food insecurity and poverty.

(b) Solutions to the negative effects (any 5):
- Repeal the Land Apportionment Act and redistribute land equitably among all races.
- Invest in improving the quality of soils in African reserves through irrigation and fertilisers.
- Provide agricultural training, credit and modern equipment to African farmers.
- Introduce fair wages and labour laws to improve conditions for African workers.
- Allow Africans to own urban property and engage in business freely.
- Open access to markets for African agricultural produce on equal terms with white farmers.
- Reduce overcrowding in reserves by opening new settlement areas for Africans.
- Establish cooperative farming schemes in reserves to pool resources.
- Lobby the British government and international community to pressure for legal reform.

questions.text:
(a) Outline any five economic reasons for the colonisation of Zimbabwe. [15]

(b) Disunity weakened African resistance to European occupation of their territories. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures African leaders could have employed to strengthen their resistance to European occupation. [10]

subParts.text: Outline any five economic reasons for the colonisation of Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Disunity weakened African resistance to European occupation of their territories. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures African leaders could have employed to strengthen their resistance to European occupation.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Colonisation of Zimbabwe – Economic Causes and African Resistance
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Economic reasons for the colonisation of Zimbabwe (any 5):
- Access to and exploitation of Zimbabwe's vast mineral wealth, especially gold.
- Acquisition of fertile agricultural land for white settler farming.
- Search for new markets for British and European manufactured goods.
- Need for cheap raw materials to feed European industrial factories.
- Desire to exploit cheap African labour for mines, farms and construction.
- Investment opportunities: European capitalists sought high returns in Africa.
- Perceived existence of a 'Second Rand' gold deposit in Mashonaland.
- Control of trade routes through the interior of Africa for commercial advantage.
- Resolution of economic depression in Europe by expanding overseas markets.

(b) Measures to strengthen African resistance (any 5):
- Form broad political and military alliances across different kingdoms and ethnic groups.
- Abandon internal wars and feuds to focus united military energy against Europeans.
- Adopt and learn to use modern European weapons to equalise military power.
- Establish a centralised command structure for co-ordinated military campaigns.
- Use diplomacy to exploit rivalries between European powers (British vs Boers vs Portuguese).
- Seek support from independent African states like Ethiopia or the Zulu kingdom.
- Employ guerrilla warfare tactics to compensate for inferior weapons.
- Use economic strategies (denying food and labour) to make colonisation costly.
- Train and maintain large, well-equipped standing armies.

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five measures that were taken by the settler government to improve settler agriculture between 1908 and 1951. [15]

(b) Settler agricultural policies weakened African peasant farming between 1908 and 1951. Propose in essay form, any five strategies peasants could have used to deal with negative effects of settler policies on their farming activities during this period. [10]

subParts.text: Describe any five measures that were taken by the settler government to improve settler agriculture between 1908 and 1951.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Settler agricultural policies weakened African peasant farming between 1908 and 1951. Propose in essay form, any five strategies peasants could have used to deal with negative effects of settler policies on their farming activities during this period.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Settler Agriculture and African Peasant Farming 1908–1951
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Measures to improve settler agriculture (any 5):
- Land Apportionment Act (1930) reserved the most fertile land exclusively for white settlers.
- Government provided subsidies, loans and grants to white farmers.
- Establishment of the Maize Control Act (1931) which guaranteed markets and high prices for settler maize.
- Development of railway and road infrastructure to transport settler produce to markets.
- Creation of the Cold Storage Commission to support settler beef and dairy farmers.
- Government funded research stations and extension services for white farmers.
- The Cattle Levy Act protected settler cattle industry from African competition.
- African production was deliberately undermined (through taxes, pass laws) to direct labour to white farms.
- Irrigation schemes were developed for exclusive settler use.

(b) Strategies peasants could have used (any 5):
- Form cooperative farming societies to pool resources, labour and capital.
- Lobby missionary and humanitarian organisations to advocate for fair agricultural policies.
- Seek legal redress through courts to challenge discriminatory laws.
- Diversify crops to reduce dependence on markets controlled by settlers.
- Develop informal/black market trade networks for agricultural produce.
- Engage in passive resistance — slow down labour on white farms.
- Organise political movements to demand fair treatment and access to resources.
- Seek education and training in modern farming techniques to improve yields on reserve land.
- Practise intensive farming and soil conservation on available TTL land.

questions.text:
(a) Give an account of any five methods that were used to recruit labour in colonial Zimbabwe between 1890 and 1930. [15]

(b) Colonial labour policies weakened African economies. Recommend, in essay form, any five ways Africans could have implemented to revive their economies. [10]

subParts.text: Give an account of any five methods that were used to recruit labour in colonial Zimbabwe between 1890 and 1930.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Colonial labour policies weakened African economies. Recommend, in essay form, any five ways Africans could have implemented to revive their economies.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Colonial Labour Recruitment and African Economies
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Methods of labour recruitment (any 5):
- Hut tax and poll tax: Africans were forced to earn cash wages to pay colonial taxes.
- Pass laws: Africans without proof of employment were arrested and forced into labour.
- Forced labour (chibaro): direct compulsion of Africans to work on mines and farms.
- Use of labour touts/recruiters (Wenela) who were paid commissions to bring workers.
- Land alienation: dispossessing Africans of land forced them into wage labour.
- Restricting African cash crop farming to eliminate alternatives to wage labour.
- The Native Registration Act required all African males to carry identity documents and be employed.
- Threat of imprisonment or beatings for those who refused to work.
- Reduction of cattle (destruction during rinderpest) eliminated an alternative livelihood, forcing labour.

(b) Ways Africans could have revived their economies (any 5):
- Re-establish and expand subsistence and commercial agriculture in reserves.
- Form savings and credit cooperatives to accumulate capital for investment.
- Develop small-scale industries and crafts for local trade.
- Invest in education and skills training to improve economic productivity.
- Create informal trade networks to exchange goods and services among Africans.
- Organise politically to lobby for removal of oppressive economic laws.
- Boycott products and services of exploitative settler businesses.
- Establish community-owned stores and businesses to retain wealth within African communities.
- Use remittances from migrant workers to invest in community development.

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five features of Industrial development in colonial Zimbabwe. [15]

(b) Settler exploitation of African resources led to forced labour. Suggest, in essay form, any five methods Africans could have used to resist forced labour. [10]

subParts.text: Describe any five features of Industrial development in colonial Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Settler exploitation of African resources led to forced labour. Suggest, in essay form, any five methods Africans could have used to resist forced labour.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Industrial Development in Colonial Zimbabwe and Forced Labour Resistance
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Features of industrial development in colonial Zimbabwe (any 5):
- Mining was the dominant industry; gold, chrome, asbestos and coal were the main minerals extracted.
- The railway network (built from 1890s) was the backbone of industrial transportation.
- Secondary industries (processing, manufacturing) grew mainly after World War II (import substitution).
- Industry was owned and managed almost exclusively by white settlers and foreign companies.
- African labour formed the majority of the industrial workforce but was paid very low wages.
- Industrial development was concentrated in urban centres (Salisbury, Bulawayo, Gwelo).
- The Industrial Conciliation Act excluded Africans from skilled trades, reserving them for whites.
- Growth of tobacco processing, cotton ginning and food processing industries.
- Federation (1953–1963) accelerated industrial growth through investment and a unified market.

(b) Methods to resist forced labour (any 5):
- Go-slow tactics: deliberately work slowly to reduce productivity and increase costs for employers.
- Desertion: leave farms or mines and return to rural areas to avoid forced labour.
- Sabotage: destroy equipment or property to disrupt production.
- Strikes and collective work stoppages to demand better conditions.
- Armed resistance: join uprisings (e.g., First Chimurenga/1896–97) against the colonial system.
- Petition missionaries and humanitarian organisations to publicise abuses.
- Flee to neighbouring territories (Mozambique, Bechuanaland) beyond colonial reach.
- Organise politically through early nationalist movements to challenge labour laws.
- Use the courts (where accessible) to challenge unlawful detention and forced labour orders.

questions.text:
(a) Outline any five economic factors for the formation of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland. [15]

(b) The Federation economically favoured Southern Rhodesia at the expense of Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland. Recommend, in essay form, any five methods Federal leaders could have introduced to ensure equal benefits for all territories. [10]

subParts.text: Outline any five economic factors for the formation of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: The Federation economically favoured Southern Rhodesia at the expense of Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland. Recommend, in essay form, any five methods Federal leaders could have introduced to ensure equal benefits for all territories.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland – Economic Factors and Inequalities
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Economic factors for the formation of the Federation (any 5):
- To pool the economic resources of the three territories — copper, tobacco, coal and hydro-power.
- To create a larger internal market for goods and services, stimulating trade and investment.
- Northern Rhodesia's copper revenues could fund development in all three territories.
- Southern Rhodesia sought access to Northern Rhodesian copper wealth and revenue.
- To build shared infrastructure (railways, roads, the Kariba Dam) more efficiently.
- To attract more foreign investment by presenting a larger, more stable economic unit.
- To develop the Kariba hydro-electric scheme for shared industrial power needs.
- To reduce tariff barriers and promote free movement of goods between territories.
- To provide a single currency and common fiscal policies for economic efficiency.

(b) Methods to ensure equal benefits (any 5):
- Establish a Federal development fund with equal per capita allocation to all three territories.
- Invest Federal revenues proportionally in infrastructure in Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
- Introduce policies to industrialise Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland, not just Southern Rhodesia.
- Ensure fair representation of all three territories in Federal economic decision-making bodies.
- Implement a common minimum wage applicable across all territories.
- Develop educational and technical training institutions equally in all territories.
- Extend the railway and road network to Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
- Introduce trade policies that promoted agricultural and mineral exports from all three territories equally.
- Audit Federal spending to ensure it was not disproportionately benefiting Southern Rhodesia.

questions.text:
(a) Give an account of any five effects of the Unilateral Declaration of Independence (UDI) on the economy of Rhodesia. [15]

(b) Sanctions weakened the economy of Rhodesia. Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Smith Regime could have taken to lessen the negative effects of sanctions on the Rhodesian economy? [10]

subParts.text: Give an account of any five effects of the Unilateral Declaration of Independence (UDI) on the economy of Rhodesia.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Sanctions weakened the economy of Rhodesia. Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Smith Regime could have taken to lessen the negative effects of sanctions on the Rhodesian economy?
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Unilateral Declaration of Independence (UDI) and Economic Sanctions
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Effects of UDI on the economy of Rhodesia (any 5):
- International economic sanctions (UN mandatory sanctions from 1968) cut off export markets for tobacco, chrome and other commodities.
- Import restrictions led to shortages of essential goods, machinery and fuel.
- The Rhodesian dollar was isolated from international financial systems.
- The country was forced to develop import-substitution industries to replace banned imports.
- Foreign investment declined sharply due to political isolation and risk.
- Trade was forced through clandestine channels via South Africa and Mozambique (Beira corridor), increasing costs.
- The cost of the liberation war (Chimurenga) escalated, draining state revenues.
- Tobacco exports collapsed initially as the main foreign currency earner was sanctioned.
- Brain drain occurred as skilled white professionals emigrated due to uncertainty.

(b) Measures to lessen the effects of sanctions (any 5):
- Develop and expand import-substitution industries to produce locally what could no longer be imported.
- Strengthen economic ties with South Africa and Portugal/Mozambique as sanctions-busting partners.
- Diversify the agricultural sector away from tobacco to crops less affected by sanctions.
- Develop domestic oil refining capacity and secure oil supplies via South Africa.
- Invest in the domestic mining sector to produce minerals for sale through third-party states.
- Introduce strict foreign exchange controls to protect dwindling currency reserves.
- Develop bilateral barter trade agreements with sympathetic countries.
- Encourage the white farming community to increase food self-sufficiency.
- Negotiate with international companies for covert trade arrangements to maintain key imports.

title: Family And Religious Studies O-Level 2025 Paper 2
subject: Family And Religious Studies

questions.text: Identify objects that show the importance of women in Indigenous Religion.
questions.topic: Indigenous Religion – Women and Sacred Objects
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should identify and explain objects/items that highlight the importance of women in Indigenous Religion. Key points include: 1) The grinding stone (mutswi) – symbolises the woman's central role in food preparation and sustaining the family. 2) The clay pot (hari) – associated with women as providers of water and food; also used in rituals and ceremonies. 3) The nhava/nhanga (winnowing basket) – used by women in grain processing, showing their economic role. 4) The ngozi/spirit medium's regalia – some female spirit mediums (svikiro) hold important positions; their beads, white cloth and other adornments show women's spiritual authority. 5) Beads (huriro) – worn by women during ceremonies to signify fertility, womanhood and spiritual connection. 6) The mortar and pestle (mutswi nechoto) – tools used exclusively by women, underlining their domestic and ritual importance. 7) Calabash/gourd (muzembe) – used by women to serve beer during ceremonies, signifying their role as hosts. 8) Ceremonial pots used during puberty/initiation rites that mark a girl's transition to womanhood. Candidates should explain how each object demonstrates or symbolises the importance of women. Award marks for identification (1 mark each) and explanation (1 mark each), up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Describe values that shape unhu / ubuntu / vumunhu in Indigenous Religion.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should describe the core values that underpin unhu/ubuntu/vumunhu. Key points include: 1) Respect (kuremekedza) – showing reverence to elders, ancestors and fellow human beings. 2) Hospitality (uneni/ukaribishana) – welcoming strangers and sharing food, shelter and resources. 3) Communalism/Togetherness (kubatana) – the belief that 'I am because we are'; prioritising the community over the individual. 4) Compassion (ngoni/tsitsi) – caring for the poor, sick and vulnerable in society. 5) Honesty and integrity (kuvimbika) – telling the truth and being trustworthy. 6) Responsibility (basa) – fulfilling one's duties to family and community. 7) Sharing (kugoveranawo) – distributing resources and wealth within the community. 8) Hard work (kushingirira) – diligence in all tasks as a contribution to the community. 9) Forgiveness (ruregerero) – resolving conflicts and restoring harmony. 10) Love (rudo) – genuine care and affection for others. Each value should be identified and described clearly. Award 2–3 marks per value (identification + description), up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Discuss activities that encourage teamwork in Indigenous Religion.
questions.topic: Indigenous Religion – Teamwork and Community Activities
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should discuss activities in Indigenous Religion that foster teamwork. Key points include: 1) Nhimbe/ilima (communal work parties) – community members gather to help one another with farming, building or harvesting; promotes cooperation and solidarity. 2) Rain-making ceremonies (mukwerera/njele) – the whole community participates in rituals to appease ancestors for rain; requires collective effort and unity. 3) Burial and funeral rites – community members come together to dig graves, prepare food and comfort the bereaved family. 4) Initiation ceremonies – the community collectively trains and guides initiates into adulthood. 5) Communal hunting (chibondo) – groups of men hunt together, sharing roles and the spoils, teaching cooperation. 6) Building of homes (kuvaka imba) – neighbours and relatives collectively assist in constructing houses. 7) Spiritual ceremonies and bira – families and communities unite to appease ancestral spirits, share food and drink, and perform dances together. 8) Dispute resolution/dare/inkundla – community elders and members participate jointly in resolving conflicts. Each activity should be identified and its role in promoting teamwork discussed. Award marks for identification and discussion, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Explain how Jews distinguish themselves from the rest of the people.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should explain practices, beliefs and symbols that set Jews apart. Key points include: 1) Circumcision (brit milah) – performed on the eighth day for male infants as a sign of the covenant with God. 2) Dietary laws (kashrut/kosher) – Jews follow strict rules about permitted (kosher) and forbidden (treif) foods, e.g. no pork or shellfish, separation of meat and dairy. 3) Sabbath observance (Shabbat) – Jews rest from sunset Friday to Saturday night, attending synagogue and refraining from work. 4) Wearing of distinctive clothing/symbols – e.g. kippah (head covering), tallit (prayer shawl), tzitzit (fringes). 5) Mezuzah – a scroll fixed to doorposts of Jewish homes as a sign of identity and faith. 6) Torah study and adherence to the 613 commandments (mitzvot). 7) Jewish festivals – Passover, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Hanukkah etc. distinguish the Jewish calendar. 8) Language – Hebrew used in prayer and study. 9) Synagogue worship – regular communal prayer distinguishes Jewish religious life. 10) The concept of being a 'chosen people' (Am Segulah) – a special covenant relationship with God. Award marks for each point identified and explained, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Show the difference between roles of men and women in Judaism.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should contrast the roles of men and women across different aspects of Jewish life. Key points include: MEN – 1) Obligated to observe all time-bound commandments (mitzvot). 2) Traditionally lead synagogue services and are counted in the minyan (quorum of 10 for prayer). 3) Responsible for Torah study as a primary religious duty. 4) Role of Rabbi traditionally held by men (in Orthodox Judaism). 5) Perform circumcision covenant as recipients. 6) Required to wear tallit and tefillin. 7) Provider/breadwinner role in traditional families. WOMEN – 1) Exempt from many time-bound positive commandments. 2) Central role in the home – lighting Shabbat candles, keeping a kosher kitchen. 3) Responsible for passing on Jewish identity (Jewish identity passes through the mother). 4) In Progressive/Reform Judaism, women may lead services, become rabbis and be counted in the minyan. 5) Traditionally responsible for raising and educating children in the faith. 6) Attend synagogue but may be seated separately (Orthodox – mechitza). Candidates should clearly contrast the roles rather than simply listing. Award marks for relevant identified differences and explanation, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Identify Jewish practices that promote hygiene in the Jewish community.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should identify and explain Jewish practices that contribute to hygiene and health. Key points include: 1) Kosher dietary laws (kashrut) – prohibition of certain foods (e.g. pork, shellfish) that may carry disease; separation of meat and dairy prevents cross-contamination. 2) Ritual handwashing (netilat yadayim) – washing hands before meals and after using the toilet promotes cleanliness. 3) Mikveh (ritual bath) – immersion in the mikveh for purification after menstruation (niddah), childbirth, and conversion; promotes bodily cleanliness. 4) Circumcision (brit milah) – associated with health benefits including reduced risk of certain infections. 5) Prohibition of eating blood – draining blood from meat (melicha/salting) reduces bacterial contamination. 6) Laws of family purity (taharat hamishpacha) – periods of sexual abstinence and purification promote reproductive health. 7) Sabbath rest – mandatory rest one day a week promotes mental and physical well-being. 8) Slaughter laws (shechita) – humane and hygienic method of animal slaughter minimises suffering and contamination. 9) Laws regarding bodily discharges (tzaraat) – biblical quarantine laws for skin diseases protected the community. Award marks for identification and explanation of each practice, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: To what extent is freedom of worship of benefit to your community?
questions.topic: Christianity – Freedom of Worship and Community Benefits
questions.aiModelAnswer: This is a discursive/evaluative question. Candidates should present both the benefits and possible limitations, then reach a balanced conclusion. BENEFITS: 1) Promotes peace and tolerance – people of different faiths coexist without persecution, reducing religious conflict. 2) Encourages spiritual growth – individuals can choose the faith that best meets their spiritual needs, leading to personal development. 3) Social welfare – churches and religious organisations provide schools, hospitals, orphanages and feeding programmes benefiting the whole community. 4) Moral guidance – religious teachings on honesty, respect and love promote good citizenship. 5) Community cohesion – religious communities provide social support networks. 6) Economic contribution – religious organisations create employment and drive development projects. 7) Cultural enrichment – diverse religious practices enrich community culture. LIMITATIONS/CHALLENGES: 1) Risk of proliferation of false prophets/cults that exploit members. 2) Religious differences can sometimes cause division or conflict. 3) Some groups may engage in anti-social or harmful practices under the guise of religion. 4) Can lead to fragmentation of community values. CONCLUSION: Freedom of worship is largely beneficial, provided there is adequate regulation to prevent abuse. Award marks for relevant points of benefit and limitation, and quality of argument/conclusion, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Discuss activities that Christians do to earn a living.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should discuss various lawful and ethical economic activities undertaken by Christians, linking them to Christian values. Key points include: 1) Farming/agriculture – many Christians farm as a dignified means of livelihood; stewardship of the land as a God-given resource. 2) Trade and commerce – running businesses ethically, honesty in buying and selling reflecting Christian integrity. 3) Teaching/education – Christian teachers serve in schools, inspired by the Great Commission to educate and uplift communities. 4) Healthcare – Christian nurses, doctors and community health workers serve others as an expression of love and compassion. 5) Crafts and artisanship – carpentry (echoing Jesus as a carpenter), pottery, sewing etc. as dignified work. 6) Pastoral/ministry work – pastors, priests and evangelists earn a living through full-time ministry. 7) Non-Governmental Organisation (NGO) work – Christians working in development and humanitarian organisations. 8) Construction and building – Christians involved in the built environment, contributing to community development. 9) Information technology and professional services. 10) The theological basis: 2 Thessalonians 3:10 ('if a man will not work, he shall not eat'); the Protestant work ethic; work as a calling (vocation). Award marks for activity identification, discussion and any theological linkage, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Explain how Christians manage risks in Zimbabwe.
questions.topic: Christianity – Risk Management and Christian Practice
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should explain strategies Christians use to manage personal, community, spiritual and financial risks. Key points include: 1) Prayer and faith – Christians trust in God's protection and provision, reducing anxiety about uncertain futures (Philippians 4:6–7). 2) Church welfare/support systems – churches provide support to members facing illness, poverty or bereavement (e.g. funeral funds, benevolence committees). 3) Savings and investment groups – many church groups (e.g. women's guilds) run rotating savings clubs (rounds/chamas) to manage financial risk. 4) Tithing and offerings – regular giving to the church creates a communal fund that can be used to assist those in need. 5) Education and life skills – churches run programmes that equip members with skills to handle risks (e.g. HIV/AIDS awareness, financial literacy). 6) Insurance – Christians are encouraged to take out insurance (life, health, property) as responsible stewardship. 7) Avoidance of risky behaviour – Christian moral teaching discourages alcohol abuse, promiscuity and gambling, thus reducing associated risks. 8) Disaster preparedness – some churches participate in disaster risk reduction programmes and community resilience building. 9) Counselling and pastoral care – pastors provide guidance to help members navigate crises. 10) Bible-based principles of planning, e.g. the example of Joseph storing grain in Genesis 41. Award marks for each strategy identified and explained, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Discuss the contribution of Islam to development in Zimbabwe.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should discuss specific contributions Islam and Muslims have made to Zimbabwe's development. Key points include: 1) Education – establishment of Islamic schools, madrassas and colleges (e.g. Islamic Education Trust schools); promoting literacy and numeracy. 2) Healthcare – Islamic organisations run clinics and hospitals, contributing to public health. 3) Economic development – Muslim traders and entrepreneurs have contributed significantly to commerce; halal industries create employment. 4) Social welfare – Zakat (obligatory almsgiving) and Sadaqah (voluntary charity) fund poverty relief, orphan care and support for the needy. 5) Infrastructure – mosques built across Zimbabwe serve as community centres; Islamic organisations have funded boreholes, roads and community halls. 6) Moral development – Islamic teachings on honesty, hard work and family values contribute to good citizenship. 7) Inter-faith dialogue – Muslim organisations participate in national interfaith initiatives promoting peace and national unity. 8) Waqf (endowments) – Islamic charitable endowments fund sustainable development projects. 9) Agricultural support – some Islamic NGOs assist farmers with inputs and training. 10) Disaster relief – Islamic Relief and similar organisations respond to floods, droughts and other disasters in Zimbabwe. Award marks for each contribution identified and discussed, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Explain how the pillars of Islam encourage unity among youths.
questions.topic: Islam – Five Pillars and Youth Unity
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should explain each of the Five Pillars of Islam and link each to the promotion of unity among young people. Key points include: 1) Shahada (Declaration of Faith) – all Muslims share the same declaration 'There is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His messenger'; creates a shared identity and brotherhood/sisterhood among youth regardless of race or background. 2) Salah (Prayer) – Muslims pray five times daily, often in congregation at the mosque; youth standing shoulder to shoulder in prayer dissolves class and racial distinctions, fostering equality and unity. 3) Zakat (Almsgiving) – obligatory giving of 2.5% of savings to the poor; reduces inequality among youth, creating a spirit of solidarity and shared responsibility. 4) Sawm (Fasting during Ramadan) – all Muslim youth fast together during Ramadan, sharing the same experience of hunger, self-discipline and breaking fast (iftar) together, building bonds of empathy and community. 5) Hajj (Pilgrimage to Mecca) – millions of Muslims from around the world including youth gather in Mecca; demonstrates the ultimate unity of the Ummah (global Muslim community) beyond nationality, language and race. Additional points: the concept of the Ummah itself as a unifying framework; Islamic youth organisations and activities centred on the pillars. Award marks for identification of each pillar and clear explanation of its unifying effect on youth, up to 25 marks.

questions.text: Describe the significance of marriage in Islam.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Candidates should describe the importance and meaning of marriage (nikah) in Islam from multiple perspectives. Key points include: 1) Religious obligation/Sunnah – marriage is strongly recommended (sunnah mu'akkadah) as it follows the example of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH); it is described as 'half of one's deen (faith)'. 2) Procreation – marriage is the legitimate framework for having children and continuing the human race and the Muslim community. 3) Companionship and emotional fulfilment – Allah created spouses as sources of comfort and love (Quran 30:21 – 'He created for you mates from among yourselves that you may dwell in tranquillity'). 4) Protection of morality – marriage channels sexual desire lawfully, preventing zina (fornication/adultery) and its social consequences. 5) Social stability – the family unit formed through marriage is the foundation of a stable, ordered society. 6) Legal contract (aqd) – nikah is a formal contract with mahr (bridewealth/dower) paid to the bride, protecting her rights. 7) Rights and responsibilities – marriage defines clear roles: the husband as provider (qawwam) and the wife's rights to maintenance (nafaqah), respect and kindness. 8) Spiritual partnership – spouses support each other in worship and the fulfilment of religious duties. 9) Expansion of family ties – marriage joins two families, strengthening community bonds. 10) Conditions of valid nikah – consent of both parties, wali (guardian), witnesses, mahr. Award marks for each point of significance identified and described, up to 25 marks.

questions.diagramNote: Student must draw well-labelled diagrams illustrating the process of exfoliation weathering.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Any three of: quartz, feldspar, mica, hornblende, biotite. [1 mark each, max 3]

(a)(ii) Sedimentary rocks are formed through: weathering and erosion of existing rocks producing fragments/sediments; transportation of sediments by wind, water or ice to a basin/sea; deposition of sediments in layers (strata); compaction under the weight of overlying layers; cementation where minerals bind particles together; lithification produces sedimentary rock. [5 marks for well-described process]

(b)(i) Any two of:
• Traction/rolling – large boulders/pebbles rolled along the river bed by the force of water.
• Saltation – smaller stones/pebbles bounced along the river bed in a leaping motion.
• Suspension – fine silt and clay particles carried within the water flow.
• Solution – soluble minerals dissolved in the water and carried invisibly.
[2 marks each, max 4]

(b)(ii) Exfoliation weathering (onion-skin weathering):
• Occurs in hot desert/semi-arid regions with high diurnal temperature ranges.
• Daytime: intense solar heating causes outer rock layers to expand.
• Night-time: rapid cooling causes contraction.
• Repeated expansion and contraction causes surface layers to crack and peel off like onion skins.
• Diagram should show: a rock with concentric curved cracks parallel to the surface, peeling outer layers, and labels for 'expansion crack', 'peeling layer', 'solid rock core'.
[Content: 4 marks; Diagrams: 4 marks]

(c) Benefits of Chinhoyi Caves to local people:
• Tourism income – entrance fees, craft sales, guiding services generate revenue.
• Employment – tour guides, security, hospitality workers.
• Cultural/heritage significance – education and pride.
• Diving/recreation attraction boosts local economy.
• Infrastructure development (roads, accommodation) benefits community.
[1 mark per valid explained point, max 5]

questions.topic: Weather Instruments, Station Models and Flooding
questions.diagramNote: Fig. 2 shows a model of a weather instrument (rain gauge). Student must also draw a station model for Gweru's weather conditions. The temperature table for Bulawayo is required for the calculation.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Rain gauge (hyetometer). [1 mark]

(a)(ii) Any three of: plastic bottle, ruler/measuring scale, funnel, container/tin, tape, marker pen. [1 mark each, max 3]

(a)(iii) Improvements: use transparent materials so readings can be taken without opening; add a clearly graduated scale in millimetres; attach a funnel of standard diameter to prevent evaporation and catch more rain; place on a stable flat surface at an agreed standard height; add a label in local language for community use. [1 mark per valid explained point, max 4]

(b)(i) Station model for Gweru should show:
• Circle filled/fully covered (overcast sky – 8 oktas)
• Cumulonimbus cloud symbol/notation
• Thunderstorm symbol (lightning bolt or TS)
• Wind barb pointing from NE with 25 knots (2 full barbs + 1 half barb)
• Temperature 20°C written to upper left of circle
• Pressure 980 mb written to upper right (as 980)
• Precipitation symbol for heavy rain shower
[1 mark per correctly drawn/labelled element, max 7]

(b)(ii) Diurnal temperature range (Tuesday) = Max – Min = 18°C – 14°C = 4°C. [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for correct answer]

(b)(iii) Friday max temp = 34°C (very hot). Precautions: stay hydrated/drink plenty of water; wear light, loose, light-coloured clothing; seek shade/avoid direct sun during peak hours; apply sunscreen; avoid strenuous outdoor activity in midday heat; use a hat/umbrella. [1 mark each, max 3]

(c) Family protection against flooding:
• Build house on elevated ground away from flood plains.
• Construct sandbag barriers around property.
• Have an emergency evacuation plan and designated meeting point.
• Store important documents and valuables at height.
• Keep an emergency kit (food, water, torch, first aid).
• Monitor weather forecasts and heed early warning systems.
• Avoid building near rivers or drainage channels.
[1 mark per valid point, max 5]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) A wetland is an area of land that is permanently or seasonally saturated with water, supporting vegetation and wildlife adapted to waterlogged conditions. [2 marks: 1 for water-saturated land, 1 for supporting unique ecosystems/flora and fauna]

(a)(ii) Any three of: swamps, marshes, bogs, vleis (dambos), mangroves, floodplains, peatlands, estuaries. [1 mark each, max 3]

(a)(iii) Any three of: source of water for irrigation and domestic use; fishing for food and income; grazing land for livestock; collection of medicinal plants; brick-making/clay; dry-season gardening (winter cropping); biodiversity conservation. [1 mark each, max 3]

(b)(i) Characteristics of wetland ecosystems:
• Hydric (waterlogged) soils with poor drainage.
• Presence of water-tolerant (hydrophytic) vegetation e.g. reeds, papyrus, sedges.
• High biodiversity – home to amphibians, birds, fish, insects.
• Act as water filters/purifiers removing pollutants.
• High organic matter content due to slow decomposition.
• Seasonal flooding/water level fluctuations.
• Act as carbon sinks storing organic carbon.
[1 mark per valid described characteristic, max 6]

(b)(ii) Human activities negatively affecting wetlands:
• Urban expansion/settlement – draining wetlands for housing construction.
• Agriculture – conversion to farmland, use of agrochemicals/pesticides.
• Deforestation of surrounding vegetation causing siltation.
• Brick moulding – excavation and disturbance of wetland soils.
• Illegal gold panning – use of chemicals (mercury) and digging.
• Waste dumping/pollution from industries and households.
• Over-abstraction of water reducing wetland extent.
[1 mark per valid described activity, max 6]

(c) Sustainable solutions:
• Enforce urban planning laws that protect wetland buffer zones.
• Relocate informal settlements away from wetlands.
• Public education and awareness campaigns on wetland value.
• Rehabilitate degraded wetlands by replanting indigenous vegetation.
• Establish legal protected status for urban wetlands.
• Promote eco-friendly waste management to reduce pollution.
• Engage local communities in wetland stewardship programmes.
[1 mark per valid suggestion, max 5]

questions.topic: Sustainable Use of Resources and CAMPFIRE Programme
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Sustainable use of resources means using natural resources in a way that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; managing resources so they are not depleted or permanently damaged. [2 marks]

(a)(ii) Renewable: Mopane worms, river, fish. Non-renewable: coal, sand, lithium. [1 mark each correct classification, max 6]

(b)(i) Three objectives of CAMPFIRE:
• To encourage and promote wildlife conservation.
• To generate income for local communities through sustainable use of natural resources and tourism.
• To reduce human-wildlife conflict.
• To empower local communities to manage their own natural resources.
[1 mark each, max 3]

(b)(ii) Three problems before CAMPFIRE:
• Human-wildlife conflict – elephants damaging crops and destroying houses.
• Lack of income/economic opportunities in rural areas.
• Lack of social services such as schools and healthcare.
• Poaching of wildlife due to lack of community benefit from conservation.
[1 mark each, max 3]

(b)(iii) Evaluation of CAMPFIRE's role (must address both positive and negative/limitations):
Positive contributions:
• Generated income from tourism and trophy hunting shared with communities.
• Funded construction of schools and clinics – improved education and healthcare.
• Fencing of fields reduced crop damage – improved food security.
• Created employment (game rangers, guides, camp staff).
• Promoted wildlife conservation and biodiversity.
Limitations/challenges:
• Benefits may not be evenly distributed among community members.
• Wildlife conflict still occurs despite fencing.
• Revenue dependent on fluctuating tourism numbers.
• Some communities may feel excluded from decision-making.
[Award up to 3 marks for positive points and up to 3 marks for limitations/evaluation, max 6]

(c) Other strategies to solve human-wildlife conflict:
• Construction of electric fences along national park boundaries.
• Compensation schemes for farmers who lose crops/livestock to wildlife.
• Community wildlife scouts and early warning systems.
• Relocation of settlements away from wildlife corridors.
• Use of chilli pepper/beehive fences to deter elephants.
• Education and awareness programmes for communities.
• Introduction of more CAMPFIRE-type benefit-sharing programmes.
[1 mark per valid strategy, max 5]

questions.topic: Mining in Zimbabwe – Gold Panning and Indigenous Knowledge
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Any four of: gold, platinum, chrome, coal, diamonds, iron ore, lithium, nickel, copper, asbestos, emeralds, granite. [1 mark each, max 4]

(a)(ii) Any four of: availability of capital/investment; availability of mineral deposits/geology; labour supply; technology and equipment; government policy/legislation; infrastructure (roads, rail, energy); market demand and prices; environmental regulations. [1 mark each, max 4]

(b)(i) Panning is a small-scale, manual method of mining where gold particles are separated from gravel and sand by washing them in a shallow pan using water and a swirling/shaking motion, allowing heavier gold to settle at the bottom. [2 marks]

(b)(ii) Characteristics of panning:
• Simple/low technology – uses a shallow metal or wooden pan.
• Labour-intensive – done manually by individuals or small groups.
• Low capital investment – requires minimal equipment.
• Carried out near rivers, streams or alluvial deposits.
• Small-scale in nature.
• Environmentally disruptive – disturbs riverbanks and stream beds.
• Produces small quantities of gold at a time.
• Predominantly done in informal/artisanal sector.
[1 mark per valid described characteristic, max 6]

(b)(iii) Indigenous knowledge in gold prospecting:
• Observing the colour of soil/rock – reddish/iron-stained soils may indicate gold-bearing reefs.
• Presence of certain plants (bio-indicators) known to grow in gold-rich soils.
• Elders pass down knowledge of locations where gold was historically found.
• Reading of stream sediment colours and patterns.
• Use of traditional divining/spiritual practices to locate deposits.
[1 mark per valid described method, max 4]

(c) How gold panning can increase GNP:
• Foreign currency earnings when gold is sold on international markets.
• Government earns royalties and taxes from registered panners.
• Stimulates local economic activity – buying of equipment, food, services.
• Reduces unemployment, increasing household incomes and spending.
• Encourages development of small and medium enterprises around mining areas.
[1 mark per valid point, max 5]

questions.topic: Types of Industry – Location, Health and Environmental Impacts
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i)
• Mining – primary industry
• Insurance – tertiary industry
• Car assembly – secondary industry
• Farming – primary industry
• Research and development – quaternary industry
[1 mark each, max 5]

(a)(ii) Any three of: textiles/clothing manufacturing, food processing, steel/iron manufacturing, cement production, furniture making, vehicle assembly, chemical manufacturing, beverage production (e.g. Delta). [1 mark each, max 3]

(b)(i) Any three factors (2 marks each for explanation):
• Raw materials – industries locate near sources of raw materials to reduce transport costs (e.g. sugar mills near cane fields).
• Labour supply – industries need skilled and unskilled workers, so locate near populated areas or towns.
• Transport/infrastructure – good road, rail links needed to receive inputs and distribute products.
• Market – industries locate near consumers/large population centres to reduce distribution costs.
• Energy supply – reliable electricity or fuel needed; industries locate near power sources.
• Government policy – industrial zones, tax incentives attract industries to certain areas.
• Water supply – some industries require large volumes of water and locate near rivers.
[2 marks per well-explained factor, max 6]

(b)(ii) Health and environmental problems:
Health: air pollution from emissions causing respiratory diseases; water pollution from effluent causing waterborne diseases; noise pollution causing hearing loss; exposure to toxic chemicals causing cancer/poisoning; work-related injuries.
Environmental: deforestation to supply raw materials; water contamination of rivers and groundwater; air pollution/smog from factory emissions; soil degradation from chemical waste; habitat destruction; greenhouse gas emissions contributing to climate change.
[1 mark per valid outlined problem, max 6]

(c) Environmental health checklist (award marks for a structured, logical checklist):
• Are fire extinguishers present and regularly serviced? ✓/✗
• Is there adequate ventilation in the workplace? ✓/✗
• Are workers provided with Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)? ✓/✗
• Is waste disposed of safely and in designated areas? ✓/✗
• Are chemical/hazardous material storage areas clearly labelled? ✓/✗
• Is there a first aid kit and trained first-aider on site? ✓/✗
• Are emergency exits clearly marked and accessible? ✓/✗
• Is noise within acceptable limits? ✓/✗
• Is there clean drinking water available for workers? ✓/✗
• Are effluent/waste water systems functional and not polluting? ✓/✗
[1 mark per valid checklist item, presented as a checklist format, max 5]

questions.topic: Settlements – Rural vs Urban, Concentric Land Use Model
questions.diagramNote: Student must draw a labelled diagram of the urban concentric (Burgess) land use model showing concentric rings/zones.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) A settlement is a place where people establish homes and live, ranging from a single dwelling to a large city; any place where human habitation is established permanently or semi-permanently. [2 marks]

(a)(ii) Differences between rural and urban settlements (award 1 mark per valid contrast, max 6):
• Population density: rural – low; urban – high.
• Economic activities: rural – farming/agriculture dominant; urban – manufacturing, trade, services.
• Infrastructure: rural – limited roads, services; urban – well-developed roads, utilities, services.
• Building types: rural – low density, spread out; urban – high density, tall buildings.
• Land use: rural – mostly agricultural; urban – residential, commercial, industrial.
• Access to services: rural – limited schools, hospitals; urban – better access to social amenities.
• Settlement size: rural – small villages/hamlets; urban – large towns/cities.

(b)(i) Concentric land use model (Burgess Model) diagram:
Zone 1 (centre): Central Business District (CBD) – shops, offices, banks.
Zone 2: Transition/twilight zone – old factories, warehouses, low-quality housing.
Zone 3: Low-class residential – working class housing.
Zone 4: Medium-class residential – better housing.
Zone 5 (outer): High-class residential/suburbs – large houses, gardens.
[Diagram: 3 marks for correct concentric rings; Labels: 1 mark each correct zone label, max 4; Total 7 marks]

(b)(ii) Applicability to Harare:
• Harare has a clearly defined CBD at its centre (First Street, Samora Machel Ave) with shops, banks and offices.
• Surrounding the CBD are industrial/commercial areas e.g. Workington, Msasa.
• Low-density high-income suburbs (Borrowdale, Highlands) exist on the urban fringe.
• High-density/low-income suburbs (Mbare, Kuwadzana, Glen Norah) form inner residential rings.
• Model is partially applicable but informal settlements (e.g. Epworth) do not always follow concentric patterns.
[1 mark per valid applied point, max 5]

(c) Measures to deal with environmental degradation:
• Enforce waste management policies and increase refuse collection frequency.
• Establish more sewage treatment plants to prevent river pollution.
• Plant trees and create urban green spaces.
• Regulate informal traders and settlements to prevent unplanned development.
• Educate residents on proper waste disposal and recycling.
• Rehabilitate quarried/degraded land.
• Enforce industrial emission standards.
[1 mark per valid suggested measure, max 5]

questions.topic: Energy Sources, Solar Energy and Agricultural Energy Use
questions.diagramNote: A table showing economic importance of energy use in agriculture (Fertilizer 25%, Farm equipment 30%, Water abstraction 15%, Transportation 10%, Processing 13%, Packaging 7%) is provided and must be studied to answer (b)(i).
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i)
• Biogas – organic waste/animal manure/decomposing plant matter (anaerobic digestion).
• Nuclear – uranium (nuclear fission).
• Hydroelectric – flowing/falling water (rivers, dams).
• Geothermal – heat from within the Earth (volcanic/geothermal activity).
[1 mark each, max 4]

(a)(ii) Advantages of solar energy:
• Renewable and inexhaustible – sunlight is freely available.
• Environmentally friendly – no greenhouse gas emissions.
• Low running/maintenance costs once installed.
• Can be used in remote areas off the national grid.
• Reduces electricity bills.
• Long lifespan of solar panels.
[1 mark each, max 4]

(b)(i) How the table helps farmers in planning:
• Farm equipment (30%) is the highest energy cost – farmers should prioritise fuel budgets for tractors and machinery or invest in fuel-efficient equipment.
• Fertilizer (25%) – plan for energy used in fertilizer production/procurement; consider organic alternatives.
• Water abstraction (15%) – invest in solar-powered pumps to reduce energy costs for irrigation.
• Processing (13%) – plan for post-harvest energy needs; could use renewable energy for mills.
• Transportation (10%) – plan logistics efficiently to cut fuel costs.
• Packaging (7%) – least energy-intensive; less financial priority.
• Overall: farmers can identify where most energy is spent and prioritise energy-saving technologies or budgets accordingly.
[1 mark per valid explained planning implication, max 7]

(b)(ii) Problems facing communal farmers using renewable energy:
• High initial capital cost of solar panels and equipment.
• Lack of technical knowledge and skills to install/maintain systems.
• Theft/vandalism of solar equipment in rural areas.
• Limited access to credit/financing for purchase.
• Unreliable supply of spare parts in rural areas.
• Low awareness of available technologies.
[1 mark each, max 5]

(c) Ways to solve Zimbabwe's energy crisis:
• Invest in expanding hydroelectric capacity (e.g. expand Kariba).
• Develop solar energy farms and incentivise household solar installation.
• Introduce/expand wind energy projects.
• Rehabilitate ageing thermal power stations (Hwange).
• Promote biogas use in rural households.
• Reduce transmission line losses through infrastructure investment.
• Implement energy conservation/efficiency programmes.
• Import electricity from neighbouring countries as short-term measure.
[1 mark per valid suggestion, max 5]

questions.topic: Transport – Road Accidents, Pipelines and Government Response
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Causes of road accidents in Zimbabwe:
• Speeding – driving above permitted speed limits.
• Drunk driving – alcohol impairs judgment and reaction time.
• Driver fatigue – long-distance drivers falling asleep at the wheel.
• Overloading – overloaded vehicles, especially public transport.
• Poor road conditions – potholes, lack of road markings, poor signage.
• Mechanical failure – unroadworthy vehicles with defective brakes/tyres.
• Reckless overtaking on blind corners or hills.
• Use of mobile phones while driving (distraction).
• Pedestrians jaywalking/walking on the road.
• Inexperienced/unlicensed drivers.
[1 mark per valid outlined cause, max 6]

(a)(ii) Challenges facing pipeline development:
• High capital cost of construction and laying pipes over long distances.
• Risk of leakages and environmental pollution.
• Vandalism and illegal tapping of pipelines.
• Difficult terrain (mountains, rivers) increases construction complexity.
[1 mark each, max 2]

(b)(i) How road accidents can be reduced:
• Strict enforcement of traffic laws and speed limits by police.
• Regular roadblocks to check vehicle roadworthiness and sobriety.
• Public education and road safety awareness campaigns.
• Improving road infrastructure – repair potholes, improve signage and road markings.
• Banning overloading of public transport vehicles.
• Mandatory use of seatbelts and helmets.
• Increasing penalties/fines for traffic offences.
• Installation of speed bumps in accident-prone areas.
[1 mark per valid explained measure, max 6]

(b)(ii) Problems government faces in eliminating road accidents:
• Insufficient funding to repair and maintain all roads.
• Shortage of traffic police for effective enforcement.
• High levels of corruption – offenders bribing police.
• Continued use of unroadworthy vehicles due to poverty.
• Difficulty enforcing laws in rural/remote areas.
• Lack of public compliance with traffic laws and education.
• High cost of replacing aged public transport fleet.
[1 mark per valid problem, max 6]

(c) Evaluation of government efforts to help road accident victims (must address both strengths and weaknesses):
Positive efforts:
• Establishment of Vehicle Inspection Department (VID) to ensure roadworthiness.
• Traffic Safety Council of Zimbabwe (TSCZ) runs road safety campaigns.
• Government hospitals provide emergency treatment to accident victims.
• Victim Support Unit (VSU) in police assists victims.
• Periodic blitz operations to enforce road safety.
Limitations:
• Public hospitals are underfunded and lack equipment for trauma care.
• Ambulance services are inadequate – slow response times.
• Compensation for victims is often delayed or insufficient.
• Road safety education campaigns have limited reach in rural areas.
[Award up to 3 marks for positive efforts and up to 2 marks for limitations/evaluation, max 5]

questions.text:
Which drainage pattern is formed by Mucheke river and its tributaries?

C Radial

questions.text:

B Crop farming

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:

A wind rose is a diagram that displays the frequency of wind from different directions; the Beaufort scale measures wind speed; the Mercalli scale measures earthquake intensity.

questions.text:
Predicting weather is called
A weather monitoring.
B weather forecasting.
C weather evaluating.

questions.aiModelAnswer: B – weather forecasting. Weather forecasting is the application of science and technology to predict atmospheric conditions for a future time and location.

questions.text:
Month: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec
Temperature (℃): 21 21 20 19 17 15 14 16 18 22 23 21
Rainfall (mm): 130 110 70 25 10 0 0 0 0 20 95 120
Which climate is represented by this station?
A Mediterranean in northern hemisphere.
B Mediterranean in southern hemisphere.
C Savanna in northern hemisphere.
D Savanna in southern hemisphere.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – Mediterranean in southern hemisphere. The data shows: rainfall concentrated in the cooler months (winter rainfall: June–August = 0 mm, summer months Jan–Mar = highest rainfall) — wait, re-examining: rain falls Oct–Apr (summer) and dry Jun–Aug; temperatures peak Oct–Nov. This is actually a summer rainfall pattern with a dry winter, which is Savanna. However, temperatures are moderate (14–23°C) and the dry season is absolute. The rainfall pattern (summer maximum, dry winter, moderate temperatures) and the fact that the coolest months have the most rain upon closer inspection — Jan=130mm (hottest) suggests summer rainfall → Savanna. Peak rainfall in summer (Jan/Feb/Mar/Nov/Dec) and dry winter (Jun/Jul/Aug) with temperatures ranging 14–23°C fits Savanna in southern hemisphere (D). Correct answer: D – Savanna in southern hemisphere. The summer (Dec–Feb) rainfall maximum and dry winter, with temperatures peaking in October–November (spring in southern hemisphere), confirms a southern hemisphere savanna climate.

questions.text:
Which weather hazard can affect subsistence farmers in Zimbabwe between June and July?
A Dew
B frost
C Hail
D Lightning
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – frost. June and July are the coldest months in Zimbabwe (winter). Temperatures can drop to near or below freezing at night, especially on high-altitude plateaus, causing frost which damages crops.

questions.text:
What is the effect of river siltation to communities near large rivers such as Save?
A Drought

questions.text:
Which process changes nitrogen and ammonia into nitrates and nitrites?
A Denitrification
B Eutrophication

questions.aiModelAnswer: D – Nitrification. Nitrification is the biological process by which bacteria (e.g., Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter) convert ammonia/ammonium into nitrites and then into nitrates in the soil.

questions.text:
Which activity increases the amount of rainfall?
A afforestation
B damming
C Panning
