questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Afforestation. Planting trees (afforestation) increases transpiration and evapo-transpiration, which adds moisture to the atmosphere and promotes convectional rainfall. Trees also intercept rainfall and contribute to the water cycle.

questions.text:
"Wild pigs destroy crops and attack people. On the other hand, people hunt wildlife and chase them away from their fields."
The situation above describes
A culling of wildlife.
B human wildlife conflict.
C wildlife conflict.
D wildlife poaching.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – human wildlife conflict. The scenario describes a two-way conflict between humans and wildlife — animals damaging human livelihoods and humans retaliating — which is the definition of human-wildlife conflict.

questions.text:
Which mineral is mined at Sengwa in Gokwe?
A Lithium
B Iron
C Copper
D Coal
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – Coal. Sengwa in Gokwe district is known for its large coal deposits. The Sengwa Colliery is one of Zimbabwe's significant coal mining areas.

questions.text:
Which type of pollution is caused by panning?
A Air pollution
B deforestation
C visual pollution
D water pollution
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – water pollution. Panning (artisanal gold panning) involves washing gravel and sediment in rivers, releasing mercury and other chemicals into waterways, causing water pollution. Note: deforestation is not a type of pollution.

questions.text:
Chirinda forest is under which type of industry?
A Primary
B Quaternary
C Secondary
D Tertiary
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Primary. Chirinda forest involves forestry, which is the extraction of natural resources (timber) directly from the environment. Forestry is classified as a primary industry.

questions.text:
Poaching is
A culling of wild animals.
B conservation of wild animals.
C illegal hunting of wild animals.
D legal hunting of wild animals.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – illegal hunting of wild animals. Poaching is defined as the illegal hunting, killing, or capturing of wild animals, in violation of wildlife protection laws.

questions.text:
Urban agriculture is expanding in Zimbabwe due to the need to
A reduce robberies.
B improve food security.
C generate foreign currency.
D clear the land.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – improve food security. Urban agriculture expands primarily because city residents need to grow their own food to supplement income and ensure household food availability, especially during economic hardships.

questions.text:
Market gardening and dairy farming are both characterised by
A low capital input.
B low labour input.
C high capital input.
D high labour input.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – high labour input. Both market gardening (intensive horticulture) and dairy farming require significant amounts of labour for planting/harvesting/processing and milking/feeding respectively. They are both intensive farming systems requiring high labour inputs.

questions.text:
The fall in Zimbabwe's agriculture production between 2023 and 2024 could have been due to
A pests.
B floods.
C drought.
D heat.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – drought. The 2023–2024 El Niño event caused severe drought across southern Africa, including Zimbabwe, significantly reducing agricultural output.

questions.text:
Farmers in drought prone communities can reduce the risk of losses by practising
A basin irrigation.
B drip irrigation.
C sprinkler irrigation.
D siphon irrigation.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – drip irrigation. Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone of plants in small quantities, minimising water wastage through evaporation and run-off. It is the most water-efficient irrigation method, making it ideal for drought-prone areas.

questions.text:
How can life expectancy be increased?
A good diet
B reduce birth rate
C increase leisure time
D improve health care
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – improve health care. Improving healthcare (access to hospitals, medicines, doctors, vaccinations) directly reduces mortality rates and increases life expectancy. While a good diet also helps, improved healthcare is the most comprehensive and direct answer.

questions.text:
The implementation of women empowerment policies corresponds to
A stage 1 of the Demographic Transition model
B stage 2 of the Demographic Transition model
C stage 3 of the Demographic Transition model
D stage 4 of the Demographic Transition model
questions.diagramNote: A Demographic Transition Model diagram is provided showing 4 stages with birth rate and death rate curves.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – stage 3 of the Demographic Transition model. In Stage 3, birth rates begin to fall rapidly due to factors including women's empowerment, increased education of women, access to family planning, and greater female participation in the workforce.

questions.text:
How can the problem of housing shortages in Zimbabwe's cities be addressed?
A constructing garden flats.
B constructing hybrid cities.
C constructing multi storey flats.
D constructing underground bunkers.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – constructing multi storey flats. Multi-storey flats (high-rise residential buildings) maximise the use of limited urban land by housing many families vertically, making them the most practical solution to housing shortages in cities.

questions.text:
The exchange of goods and services between Zimbabwe and Botswana is
A bilateral trade.
B invisible trade.
C multilateral trade.
D visible trade.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – bilateral trade. Bilateral trade refers to the exchange of goods and services between two countries — in this case Zimbabwe and Botswana. Multilateral trade involves more than two countries.

questions.text:
Which method helps to solve traffic congestion during peak hours?
A one way roads
B round abouts
C spaghetti roads
D traffic lights
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – one way roads. One-way road systems improve traffic flow by eliminating opposing traffic streams, reducing conflict points and increasing throughput, thereby alleviating congestion during peak hours.

questions.text:
Environmental management is the responsibility of
A all citizens.
B community leaders.
C school children.
D the government.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – all citizens. Environmental management is a shared responsibility that involves every member of society — individuals, communities, businesses, and government — not just one group.

questions.text:
Which type of energy can be produced at a local level in Zimbabwe?
A nuclear
B thermal
C geothermal
D biogas
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – biogas. Biogas can be produced locally at household or community level using organic waste (animal dung, crop residues) in small biodigesters. Nuclear and thermal require large-scale infrastructure; geothermal requires specific geological conditions not widely available in Zimbabwe.

questions.text:
The use of renewable energy resources in the community helps to
A control climate change.
B reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
C reduce exposure to diseases.
D reduce occurrence of natural disasters.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydro, biogas) produce little or no greenhouse gases during operation, unlike fossil fuels. This directly reduces GHG emissions. While this contributes to climate change mitigation, the most direct and immediate benefit is the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions.

questions.text:
THE FAST TRACK LAND REFORM PROGRAMME

Carefully study the following sources and answer all the questions which follow.

SOURCE A
Flash-back: Angry Svosve villagers, led by war veterans flooded to White commercial farms in what became known as the Third Chimurenga.
(Adapted from a book written by Zimbabwean writer published 2012).

SOURCE B
People will seize the land if we do not proceed with the Bill and we will not be able to move them. We have to proceed in an orderly manner. Aid or no aid we will proceed. This is a do or die matter for us. We will not brook threats from any quarter.
(Adapted from a book by a Zimbabwean historian published in 2012).

SOURCE C
It is widely considered that land is best held by those people who are best qualified to promote sustainable production. Qualification is not a piece of paper to say I have a Diploma in Agriculture, its part thereof. Education is not the end. It's a nice start. Unless you have resources, you can't afford to go farming. Accordingly, one needs to be resourceful, have ability, experience, initiative and integrity. The little things which you can't explain.
(Adapted from a book by a Zimbabwean historian published in 2010).

subParts.text: Read Source A. What evidence in the source shows that the people were determined to get land?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Read Source B. How reliable is this source on the state of things at that time?
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Read Source C. Is source accurate on the qualifications of resettled farmers? Explain your answer.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Read Source B and Source C. How do these sources differ as historical evidence on land acquisition and resettlement in Zimbabwe?
subParts.label: (d)

subParts.text: Read Source A. What do you think were the feelings of the people in Zimbabwe who witnessed land occupations?
subParts.label: (e)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [4 marks] Evidence of determination: The villagers are described as 'angry', showing emotional urgency; they 'flooded' the farms, indicating large numbers acting with force/momentum; they were 'led by war veterans', showing organised leadership and resolve; the event is compared to the 'Third Chimurenga', linking it to a historic liberation struggle, implying ideological commitment and determination. Award 1 mark per valid point up to 4.

(b) [5 marks] Reliability assessment: The source is reliable because it reflects the political urgency of the time — the government faced pressure from the masses and had to act; the language 'do or die' reflects genuine resolve that aligns with historical events of land invasions. However, it is from a secondary source (a book, 2012) and may reflect the author's bias; it only presents the government's viewpoint and does not include perspectives of farm owners or farm workers; it may be politically motivated. Award marks for both supporting and questioning reliability with explanation. Up to 3 marks for one side if the other is not addressed.

(c) [5 marks] Accuracy of Source C on qualifications: Source C is partially accurate — it correctly argues that farming requires more than academic qualifications; it highlights resources, experience, initiative and integrity as key. However, it may be inaccurate in implying resettled farmers were unqualified — many had farming experience as farm labourers or peasant farmers; it could be seen as biased against the land reform beneficiaries. Award marks for agreeing and disagreeing with evidence/explanation.

(d) [5 marks] Differences between Source B and Source C: Source B supports rapid land redistribution regardless of qualifications or international pressure ('Aid or no aid we will proceed'), focusing on political urgency; Source C emphasises the importance of qualifications, resources and experience for productive land use, implying the process should be selective and orderly. Source B reflects a pro-government/nationalist stance; Source C reflects a more cautious, productivity-focused perspective. Award 1 mark per valid point of difference up to 5.

(e) [6 marks] Feelings of Zimbabweans who witnessed land occupations: Supporters felt jubilation, pride and a sense of justice/liberation — land was being returned to the indigenous majority; war veterans and the rural poor felt empowered. Opposition/white farmers and farm workers felt fear, anxiety, insecurity and loss. Urban Zimbabweans may have felt concern about economic consequences. International observers felt alarm at the breakdown of rule of law. Award marks for a range of feelings with explanation; accept any well-reasoned response.

questions.text:
(a) Outline any five ideas of Marxist-Leninist thought.
(b) Exploitation of workers has intensified over the years worldwide. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures workers can take to free themselves from persistent economic exploitation.

subParts.text: Outline any five ideas of Marxist-Leninist thought.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Exploitation of workers has intensified over the years worldwide. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures workers can take to free themselves from persistent economic exploitation.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point, up to 5 points] Ideas of Marxist-Leninist thought:
1. Class struggle — society is divided into the bourgeoisie (owners of means of production) and the proletariat (workers); history is driven by conflict between these classes.
2. Dictatorship of the proletariat — after a revolution, the working class must seize state power to suppress the former ruling class.
3. Vanguard Party — a disciplined revolutionary party (the Communist Party) must lead the working class to revolution.
4. Imperialism as the highest stage of capitalism — capitalism expands through colonialism and imperialism to exploit developing nations.
5. Nationalisation/socialisation of means of production — factories, land and resources should be owned collectively/by the state, not private individuals.
6. Withering away of the state — ultimately, the state becomes unnecessary as a classless communist society is achieved.
7. Surplus value — capitalists exploit workers by paying wages less than the value workers produce.
Award 3 marks per well-explained point: 1 mark identification, 2 marks explanation.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point, up to 5 points] Measures workers can take:
1. Form and join strong trade unions to collectively bargain for better wages and conditions.
2. Go on strike to pressurise employers into meeting worker demands.
3. Political organisation — workers can vote for or join worker-friendly political parties.
4. Workers can co-operate and establish worker-owned cooperatives, removing the capitalist employer.
5. Workers can use litigation/legal channels to challenge unfair labour practices.
6. International solidarity — affiliate with global worker organisations (e.g. International Labour Organisation) to gain support.
7. Workers can educate themselves about their rights through worker education programmes.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five problems faced by industrial workers since independence in Zimbabwe.
(b) Zimbabwe has experienced progressive closure of its key industries since 1980. Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can take to revive its once flourishing industries.

subParts.text: Describe any five problems faced by industrial workers since independence in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Zimbabwe has experienced progressive closure of its key industries since 1980. Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can take to revive its once flourishing industries.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Industrial Workers and Industrial Decline in Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Problems faced by industrial workers:
1. Retrenchment/unemployment — mass job losses due to de-industrialisation and company closures.
2. Low wages — hyperinflation, especially post-2000, eroded real wages making workers unable to afford basic goods.
3. Poor working conditions — many workers faced unsafe environments, long hours and lack of protective equipment.
4. Suppression of trade union activity — government at times restricted union activity, limiting collective bargaining.
5. Casualisation of labour — workers employed on short-term contracts with no benefits or job security.
6. Hyperinflation (2007–2008) — wages became worthless almost immediately after payment.
7. Sanctions and economic crisis — foreign currency shortages led to factory shutdowns and layoffs.
Award 3 marks per well-described point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to revive industry:
1. Government investment in industry through industrial development banks and incentives.
2. Attracting foreign direct investment by creating a stable, investor-friendly environment.
3. Providing cheap/subsidised electricity to reduce production costs.
4. Implementing protectionist policies (tariffs, import substitution) to shield local industries from cheap imports.
5. Re-equipping/modernising factories through loans and technology transfer.
6. Removing or reducing sanctions/diplomatic engagement to unlock international trade.
7. Training skilled workers to meet industrial demands.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Give any account of any five post-colonial industrial developments in Zimbabwe between 1980 and 1990.
(b) Gold-panning has cost the country millions in potential revenue. Recommend, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can implement to regulate mining activities in Zimbabwe.

subParts.text: Give any account of any five post-colonial industrial developments in Zimbabwe between 1980 and 1990.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Gold-panning has cost the country millions in potential revenue. Recommend, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can implement to regulate mining activities in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Post-Colonial Industrial Development and Mining Regulation
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Post-colonial industrial developments 1980–1990:
1. Expansion of manufacturing — the government promoted import substitution industrialisation; industries producing consumer goods, textiles and food processing expanded.
2. Growth of the Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Company (ZISCO) — government invested in steel production as a cornerstone of industrial development.
3. Development of agro-processing industries — sugar, cotton and tobacco processing industries grew, linked to agricultural expansion.
4. Establishment of the Zimbabwe Development Bank (ZDB) — to finance industrial projects.
5. Growth of the construction industry — massive government spending on infrastructure (schools, hospitals, roads) stimulated the construction sector.
6. Expansion of the National Railways of Zimbabwe (NRZ) — to support industrial transport needs.
7. Growth of the mining sector — platinum, gold and coal production expanded under government oversight.
Award 3 marks per well-described point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to regulate mining:
1. Enforce and strengthen the Mines and Minerals Act — ensure all miners are licensed and comply with regulations.
2. Increase the deployment of the Zimbabwe Republic Police (ZRP) and Environmental Management Agency (EMA) officers in mining areas.
3. Introduce formalisation programmes for artisanal/small-scale miners, bringing them into the formal economy.
4. Use technology (drones, GIS) to monitor and detect illegal mining operations.
5. Impose heavy fines and penalties on illegal gold-panners and buyers of illegal gold.
6. Educate communities on the economic and environmental costs of illegal gold-panning.
7. Channel small-scale miners into recognised cooperatives under FIDELITY/RBZ frameworks.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five reasons for the introduction of the Zimbabwe Programme for Economic and Social Transformation [ZIMPREST].
(b) Indigenisation has not been embraced by all Zimbabweans. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can take to enlighten people on the benefits of indigenisation.

subParts.text: Describe any five reasons for the introduction of the Zimbabwe Programme for Economic and Social Transformation [ZIMPREST].
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Indigenisation has not been embraced by all Zimbabweans. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can take to enlighten people on the benefits of indigenisation.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Reasons for introduction of ZIMPREST (1996–2000):
1. Failure of ESAP — the Economic Structural Adjustment Programme (1991–1995) had worsened poverty, unemployment and inequality; ZIMPREST was meant to correct these failures.
2. Need to stimulate economic growth — GDP growth had stagnated and the government needed a new economic blueprint.
3. Reduction of poverty — ZIMPREST aimed to address social inequalities and improve living standards for the majority.
4. Unemployment — the government needed to create jobs following retrenchments under ESAP.
5. Budget deficit — the government sought to reduce fiscal deficit and public debt.
6. Need to attract foreign investment — through economic stability and reform, Zimbabwe hoped to attract investors.
7. Pressure from international donors/IMF/World Bank — to implement a follow-up programme to ESAP to continue accessing credit.
Award 3 marks per well-described point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to promote indigenisation:
1. Public awareness campaigns through radio, TV and print media explaining the benefits of indigenisation.
2. Government roadshows and community meetings to explain the indigenisation policy at grassroots level.
3. Showcasing success stories of indigenised companies to inspire confidence.
4. Simplifying the indigenisation process to make it accessible and less bureaucratic.
5. Engaging schools and universities to incorporate indigenisation education in curricula.
6. Partnering with business chambers to promote indigenisation benefits to the private sector.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Outline any five achievements of the Zimbabwe Agenda for Sustainable Social and Economic Transformation [ZIMASSET] of 2013.
(b) Local Industries are exposed to unfair competition from powerful foreign companies. Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can implement to protect local industries from unfair foreign competition.

subParts.text: Outline any five achievements of the Zimbabwe Agenda for Sustainable Social and Economic Transformation [ZIMASSET] of 2013.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Local Industries are exposed to unfair competition from powerful foreign companies. Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can implement to protect local industries from unfair foreign competition.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: ZIMASSET and Protection of Local Industries
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Achievements of ZIMASSET:
1. Food security and nutrition — government promoted agricultural production, including Command Agriculture later linked to ZIMASSET goals, improving food availability.
2. Infrastructure development — roads, airports and public buildings were rehabilitated and upgraded.
3. Social services delivery — improvements in health and education delivery, including construction/rehabilitation of schools and hospitals.
4. Value addition and beneficiation — some progress in processing minerals locally rather than exporting raw materials.
5. Job creation — public sector employment expanded and some private sector initiatives were supported.
6. Energy development — investment in energy infrastructure including Kariba South Power Station expansion.
7. Housing development — some urban housing projects were initiated under ZIMASSET.
Award 3 marks per well-outlined point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to protect local industries:
1. Impose tariffs and import duties on foreign goods that compete directly with local products.
2. Enforce anti-dumping laws against foreign companies selling below production cost.
3. Provide subsidies and tax incentives to local manufacturers to reduce their cost of production.
4. Implement 'Buy Zimbabwe' campaigns to encourage consumers to choose local products.
5. Set local content requirements in government procurement.
6. Negotiate favourable trade agreements that protect Zimbabwean industries.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Give account of any five challenges faced in the implementation of the Community Share Ownership Trusts (CSOTs).
(b) Communities lack commitment towards the Community Share Ownership Trusts (CSOTs). Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can introduce to ensure maximum participation by these communities.

subParts.text: Give account of any five challenges faced in the implementation of the Community Share Ownership Trusts (CSOTs).
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Communities lack commitment towards the Community Share Ownership Trusts (CSOTs). Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can introduce to ensure maximum participation by these communities.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Challenges in CSOTs implementation:
1. Corruption and mismanagement — funds meant for communities were misappropriated by officials and trust administrators.
2. Lack of transparency — communities were not adequately informed about how funds were being used, breeding mistrust.
3. Non-compliance by mining companies — some companies resisted or delayed making the required contributions to CSOTs.
4. Lack of capacity — community trust members lacked business management and financial skills to run trusts effectively.
5. Political interference — CSOTs were sometimes used for political patronage rather than genuine community development.
6. Inadequate legal framework — initial legislation was vague making enforcement difficult.
7. Conflict within communities — disputes over beneficiaries and leadership undermined effective functioning.
Award 3 marks per well-explained point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to ensure maximum community participation:
1. Conduct community education and awareness programmes on the purpose and benefits of CSOTs.
2. Ensure transparent and democratic election of community trust representatives.
3. Establish independent oversight/audit committees to build community confidence.
4. Involve community leaders (chiefs, headmen) as stakeholders in CSOT governance.
5. Create regular community feedback meetings so residents can see results of CSOT investments.
6. Capacity-building training for CSOT trustees and community members.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five reasons behind the Land Reform Program in Zimbabwe.
(b) Newly settled farmers are facing acute shortages of inputs for effective farming. Recommend, in essay form, any five measures the government of Zimbabwe can put in place to ensure the viability of farming for the newly settled farmers.

subParts.text: Describe any five reasons behind the Land Reform Program in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Newly settled farmers are facing acute shortages of inputs for effective farming. Recommend, in essay form, any five measures the government of Zimbabwe can put in place to ensure the viability of farming for the newly settled farmers.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Reasons for Land Reform:
1. Colonial land alienation — colonial governments dispossessed indigenous Africans of fertile land and confined them to overcrowded, infertile reserves (Tribal Trust Lands).
2. Overcrowding in communal areas — post-independence population pressure in communal areas made land redistribution necessary.
3. Fulfilment of liberation war promises — ZANU-PF had promised land redistribution during the liberation struggle (Chimurenga).
4. Racial land imbalance — a small white minority owned the majority of prime agricultural land.
5. Poverty alleviation — land was seen as a means to empower the black majority and reduce poverty.
6. Political pressure from war veterans — war veterans and landless peasants put political pressure on the government to speed up redistribution.
7. Failure of willing-seller willing-buyer model — the Lancaster House Agreement limited land acquisition; after 1990 when provisions expired, the government moved to compulsory acquisition.
Award 3 marks per well-described point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to ensure viability for new farmers:
1. Government-subsidised input schemes (seeds, fertilisers, chemicals) such as Command Agriculture.
2. Establishment of farmer support centres to provide extension services and technical advice.
3. Provision of affordable farm mechanisation (tractors, equipment) through hire-purchase or subsidised loans.
4. Irrigation infrastructure development to reduce reliance on rainfall.
5. Accessible credit and microfinance facilities specifically for resettled farmers.
6. Guaranteed market access — government offtake/contracts to give farmers assured buyers.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Outline any five reasons for the decline of tourist arrivals in Zimbabwe.
(b) Locals hardly visit Zimbabwe's tourist attractions. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures the Ministry of Tourism and Hospitality can take to promote local tourism.

subParts.text: Outline any five reasons for the decline of tourist arrivals in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Locals hardly visit Zimbabwe's tourist attractions. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures the Ministry of Tourism and Hospitality can take to promote local tourism.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Reasons for decline in tourist arrivals:
1. Political instability — the political crisis post-2000, including farm invasions and election violence, created a negative international image deterring tourists.
2. Economic sanctions/travel advisories — Western governments issued travel warnings against Zimbabwe, discouraging their citizens from visiting.
3. Hyperinflation (2007–2008) — economic collapse undermined infrastructure, hospitality and services that support tourism.
4. Poor infrastructure — deteriorating roads, airports and hotels reduced Zimbabwe's attractiveness as a destination.
5. Negative international media coverage — Zimbabwe received overwhelmingly negative global press, damaging its tourism brand.
6. Competition from regional destinations — South Africa, Botswana and Zambia invested heavily in tourism marketing, drawing visitors away.
7. Security concerns — reports of crime and instability deterred international visitors.
Award 3 marks per well-outlined point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to promote local tourism:
1. Subsidise entry fees to national parks and heritage sites to make them affordable for locals.
2. Introduce school tourism programmes — arrange educational trips for students to visit attractions.
3. Market tourist attractions through social media and local broadcast media in local languages.
4. Develop domestic tourism packages in partnership with local travel agencies and tour operators.
5. Introduce 'Explore Zimbabwe' campaigns and public holidays linked to tourism activities.
6. Improve road infrastructure and transport links to major tourist sites.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Give account of any five aims of the Indigenisation Programme in Zimbabwe.
(b) Corruption has derailed the Indigenisation Programme in Zimbabwe. Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can take to curb corruption.

subParts.text: Give account of any five aims of the Indigenisation Programme in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Corruption has derailed the Indigenisation Programme in Zimbabwe. Propose, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can take to curb corruption.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Aims of the Indigenisation Programme:
1. Economic empowerment of indigenous Zimbabweans — transfer ownership of businesses and resources to the black majority who had been historically excluded.
2. Wealth redistribution — reduce economic inequalities stemming from colonial dispossession.
3. Job creation for locals — encourage indigenous-owned businesses to employ Zimbabweans.
4. Transfer of skills and technology — through partnerships with foreign firms, Zimbabweans would gain business and technical skills.
5. Increase local ownership of natural resources — ensure that revenue from mining and other resources benefits local communities (e.g. via CSOTs, Employee Share Ownership Trusts).
6. Promote entrepreneurship — encourage indigenous Zimbabweans to start and grow their own businesses.
7. Achieve economic sovereignty — reduce foreign dominance of the Zimbabwean economy.
Award 3 marks per well-described point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to curb corruption:
1. Strengthen and empower the Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission (ZACC) with independent investigative powers.
2. Enforce strict whistleblower protection laws to encourage reporting of corrupt practices.
3. Ensure transparency in government procurement and indigenisation deal approvals.
4. Introduce and enforce severe penalties (imprisonment, asset forfeiture) for corrupt officials.
5. Promote e-governance to reduce face-to-face transactions that facilitate bribery.
6. Conduct public awareness campaigns on the harm caused by corruption.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five problems faced by the informal sector in Zimbabwe.
(b) Informal traders have been unfairly victimised by local authorities in Zimbabwe. Recommend in essay form, any five measures the government can introduce to regulate the activities of the informal traders.

subParts.text: Describe any five problems faced by the informal sector in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Informal traders have been unfairly victimised by local authorities in Zimbabwe. Recommend in essay form, any five measures the government can introduce to regulate the activities of the informal traders.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Problems faced by the informal sector:
1. Harassment by local authorities — police and municipal police regularly raid and confiscate goods from informal traders.
2. Lack of access to credit/finance — banks consider informal operators too risky and most lack collateral for loans.
3. Lack of business premises — traders operate in congested and often unsafe spaces without secure shelter.
4. Competition from formal retailers and cheap imports — informal traders struggle to compete with supermarkets and imported goods.
5. Limited market access — informal traders are often excluded from large contracts or formal supply chains.
6. Poor record-keeping and business skills — lack of financial literacy limits business growth.
7. Vulnerability to economic shocks — hyperinflation, currency changes and economic instability disproportionately affect informal operators.
Award 3 marks per well-described point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to regulate informal traders:
1. Designate and develop formal trading spaces/markets for informal traders in urban areas.
2. Introduce a simple, affordable licensing system for informal traders to formalise their activities.
3. Provide training in business management, financial literacy and record-keeping.
4. Create microfinance schemes specifically for informal traders.
5. Establish clear legal protection for informal traders against unlawful raids and confiscation.
6. Engage informal trader associations in policy-making to ensure regulations are practical.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Outline any five problems faced by women in Zimbabwe since independence.
(b) Discrimination against women at the workplace is on the increase. Suggest, in essay form, any five ways the government can implement to improve the status of women at the workplace.

subParts.text: Outline any five problems faced by women in Zimbabwe since independence.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Discrimination against women at the workplace is on the increase. Suggest, in essay form, any five ways the government can implement to improve the status of women at the workplace.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Women's Rights and Gender Equality in Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Problems faced by women since independence:
1. Unequal access to education — girls were historically less likely to complete secondary or tertiary education due to cultural attitudes and early marriages.
2. Gender-based violence — women face high rates of domestic violence, rape and sexual harassment.
3. Discrimination in employment — women are often paid less than men and denied promotions to senior positions (glass ceiling).
4. Property rights — cultural and legal barriers prevented women from inheriting or owning property, especially under customary law.
5. Early/forced marriages — young women removed from school for marriage, limiting economic independence.
6. Burden of unpaid care work — women bear the primary responsibility for domestic labour and child-rearing, limiting time for economic activity.
7. Limited political representation — women are underrepresented in parliament and government decision-making bodies.
Award 3 marks per well-outlined point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to improve women's status at the workplace:
1. Enact and enforce equal pay legislation to close the gender pay gap.
2. Introduce gender quotas in recruitment and promotion to senior positions.
3. Provide maternity/paternity leave and childcare support so women are not penalised for having children.
4. Establish workplace anti-harassment policies and independent complaints mechanisms.
5. Promote women's entrepreneurship through access to business loans and mentorship.
6. Invest in girls' education and vocational training to build a skilled female workforce.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Give an account of any five areas of economic cooperation between Zimbabwe and South Africa.
(b) Border jumping has led to the problem of economic refugees in some SADC states. Propose, in essay form, any five measures SADC can introduce to reduce border-jumping.

subParts.text: Give an account of any five areas of economic cooperation between Zimbabwe and South Africa.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Border jumping has led to the problem of economic refugees in some SADC states. Propose, in essay form, any five measures SADC can introduce to reduce border-jumping.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Zimbabwe–South Africa Economic Relations and SADC
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Areas of economic cooperation between Zimbabwe and South Africa:
1. Trade — South Africa is Zimbabwe's largest trading partner; Zimbabwe exports tobacco, minerals and manufactured goods; imports machinery, fuel and consumer goods from South Africa.
2. Energy/electricity — South Africa (ESKOM) has supplied electricity to Zimbabwe through ZESA during periods of power shortage.
3. Transport and transit — Zimbabwe uses South African ports (Durban, Richards Bay) for imports and exports; the rail and road links are critical trade routes.
4. Banking and finance — South African banks (Standard Bank, FNB, ABSA) operate in Zimbabwe and facilitate investment and financial services.
5. Labour migration — Zimbabweans have worked in South African mines, farms and industries, with remittances forming a significant inflow into Zimbabwe.
6. Tourism — there are significant tourist flows between the two countries, especially to Victoria Falls and Kruger National Park.
7. Investment — South African companies have invested heavily in Zimbabwean retail, mining and agriculture sectors.
Award 3 marks per well-described point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] SADC measures to reduce border-jumping:
1. Harmonise immigration policies and simplify legal migration procedures across SADC to make legal entry easier.
2. Invest in regional economic development to reduce poverty and inequality that drives migration.
3. Strengthen border security infrastructure (fencing, surveillance, border posts).
4. Establish SADC-wide refugee/asylum frameworks to legally process and protect genuine refugees.
5. Bilateral labour agreements — allow legal temporary migration for workers between countries.
6. Promote regional integration and free movement of persons within a regulated SADC framework.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Describe any five challenges faced by Zimbabweans as a result of economic sanctions imposed by the West since 2000.
(b) Sanctions have retarded economic development in Zimbabwe. Recommend, in essay form, any five measures that can be implemented to counter the negative effects of sanctions.

subParts.text: Describe any five challenges faced by Zimbabweans as a result of economic sanctions imposed by the West since 2000.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Sanctions have retarded economic development in Zimbabwe. Recommend, in essay form, any five measures that can be implemented to counter the negative effects of sanctions.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Economic Sanctions and Their Impact on Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Challenges due to sanctions:
1. Reduced foreign direct investment — sanctions created an uncertain business environment, deterring foreign investors.
2. Exclusion from international financial institutions — Zimbabwe was cut off from IMF and World Bank loans, limiting access to development finance.
3. Shortages of foreign currency — sanctions restricted Zimbabwe's ability to trade internationally, causing acute foreign currency shortages.
4. Collapse of industry — without access to imported machinery, spare parts and raw materials, industries shut down.
5. Hyperinflation — economic collapse linked partly to sanctions contributed to the world's worst recorded hyperinflation (2007–2008).
6. Brain drain/emigration — economic hardship caused millions of skilled Zimbabweans to emigrate, hollowing out the labour force.
7. Shortages of medicines and essential goods — import restrictions caused humanitarian shortfalls in health and food.
Award 3 marks per well-described point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to counter negative effects of sanctions:
1. Diplomatic engagement — negotiate with Western governments for removal or easing of sanctions.
2. Look East Policy — diversify trade and investment partnerships to China, Russia and other non-Western economies.
3. Regional trade integration — deepen SADC and COMESA trade relationships to replace lost Western trade.
4. Domestic production — invest in import substitution industries to reduce dependence on sanctioned trade.
5. Mobilise diaspora remittances — formalise remittance channels to boost foreign currency inflows.
6. Pursue investment from non-Western multilateral institutions (BRICS New Development Bank, African Development Bank).
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
(a) Outline any five economic reasons for the adoption of the Look East Policy (L.E.P) by the Zimbabwe Government.
(b) Zimbabwe has become a dumping ground for Chinese products. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can introduce to regulate the movement of foreign goods into the country.

subParts.text: Outline any five economic reasons for the adoption of the Look East Policy (L.E.P) by the Zimbabwe Government.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Zimbabwe has become a dumping ground for Chinese products. Suggest, in essay form, any five measures the Zimbabwe Government can introduce to regulate the movement of foreign goods into the country.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.topic: Look East Policy and Trade Regulation
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) [15 marks — 3 marks per point] Economic reasons for Look East Policy:
1. Western sanctions — Zimbabwe was cut off from Western trade, aid and investment; the Look East Policy sought to replace these with Asian alternatives.
2. Access to Chinese investment — China offered loans and investment without political conditions, funding infrastructure such as roads, government buildings and energy projects.
3. Access to cheap goods and technology — trade with China and other Asian economies provided affordable manufactured goods and machinery.
4. Alternative markets for Zimbabwean exports — minerals such as chrome and tobacco could be exported to China in place of Western markets.
5. Need for foreign currency — engaging with Eastern economies helped Zimbabwe generate foreign exchange earnings.
6. Access to development finance — China's EXIM Bank and other Asian financial institutions provided credit lines unavailable from the West.
7. Technology transfer — partnerships with Chinese and Malaysian companies aimed to modernise Zimbabwean industries.
Award 3 marks per well-outlined point.

(b) [10 marks — 2 marks per point] Measures to regulate movement of foreign goods:
1. Impose tariffs and import duties on foreign (especially Chinese) products to make local goods price-competitive.
2. Enforce anti-dumping legislation to prevent goods being sold in Zimbabwe below their production cost.
3. Strengthen border control and customs enforcement to prevent smuggling and under-invoicing.
4. Establish and enforce product quality and safety standards through ZABS (Zimbabwe Bureau of Standards) to bar substandard imports.
5. Require import licences for certain categories of goods, especially those competing with local products.
6. Negotiate bilateral trade agreements with China that include clauses protecting Zimbabwean industries from dumping.
Award 2 marks per well-explained point in essay form.

questions.text:
Write a composition on one of the following guided compositions.

Answer either 1(a) or (b).

(a) There has been an outbreak of bedbugs in your community. As a News Reporter for one of the local newspapers, you carried out an interview with the Councillor of the community to find out the extent of the problem. Write an interview script between yourself and the Councillor. Include the following points and any other relevant points of your own in your interview script.
- when the problem started.
- signs of infestation
- how the bugs spread
- area affected
- measures taken to curb the spread of bugs
- how to curb future outbreaks

(b) Imagine that you are the Head of Blue Mountain High School. You received the following letter from a concerned parent after you held a fund raising show at your school. Write a response, suggesting measures you will take to deal with the issues raised.

120 Magaba Drive
Skyline Extension
Gutu
20 May 2026

The Head
Blue Mountain High School
P O Box 31
Gutu

Dear Sir

Re: COMPLAINT ABOUT LEANERS' BEHAVIOUR AT THE RECENT FUND-RAISING SHOW.

I write to register my complaint about the unbecoming behaviour by students at the recent fund-raising show held at your school. I witnessed a group of girls who were skimpily dressed, loitering at the local shopping centre. The girls were wearing short skirts. I presumed that was meant to attract the attention of gold panners who were at the township. On the other hand, boys from your school were visibly drunk and some hurled insults at the local vendors who tried to reprimand them. They had satchels which appeared to be loaded with alcoholic drinks and cigarettes. I wonder how they skipped school and managed to buy alcohol.

As a concerned parent, I am also worried about the number of fundraising activities being conducted at your school. Week after week, there is one fundraising activity after another. The school is milking us dry through these activities and, as parents, we feel the school is being inconsiderate. We are struggling to raise funds for school fees. What is more disturbing is the fact that there is no development taking place at the school. How are these funds being used?

I would appreciate if you could highlight measures that will be taken to limit disruptions to learning as a result of countless fundraising activities. I am very much interested in knowing what actions you will take, as a school, to instil discipline during fund raising events at the school. I also feel that funds collected should be accounted for.

Concerned parent
Mrs Sipho Moyo.

questions.topic: Guided Composition – Interview Script / Formal Letter Response
questions.aiModelAnswer:
EITHER (a) OR (b) — maximum 20 marks. Marks are typically awarded across: Content (10 marks) + Language/Expression (10 marks).

--- MODEL ANSWER GUIDE FOR 1(a): Interview Script ---
Format: Must follow interview script conventions — reporter's name/designation introduced, questions and responses clearly labelled (e.g., Reporter: / Councillor:), formal yet accessible tone.
Content points (award marks for inclusion and development of each):
1. When the problem started – e.g., 'The outbreak was first reported about three months ago in the high-density suburbs.'
2. Signs of infestation – e.g., red itchy bites on skin, blood stains on bedding, musty odour, visible bugs in mattress seams.
3. How the bugs spread – e.g., through second-hand furniture, shared bedding, travellers' luggage, overcrowded housing.
4. Area affected – e.g., specific wards/suburbs, schools, lodges, and homes.
5. Measures taken – e.g., fumigation drives, public awareness campaigns, distribution of insecticides, condemning infested furniture.
6. Curbing future outbreaks – e.g., regular inspections, public education, avoiding second-hand mattresses, reporting early signs.
Language: Correct use of question-and-answer format, varied vocabulary, grammatical accuracy, appropriate register.

--- MODEL ANSWER GUIDE FOR 1(b): Formal Letter of Response ---
Format: Must be a formal letter — sender's address (school letterhead/address), date, recipient's address, salutation (Dear Mrs Moyo), subject heading, body paragraphs, complimentary close, signature.
Content points (addressing all three issues raised by Mrs Moyo):
1. Acknowledging the complaint courteously and thanking the parent for bringing concerns to attention.
2. Addressing learner behaviour – e.g., measures such as: strict dress code enforcement, chaperones/teachers on duty during events, disciplinary hearings for students involved, counselling sessions, parental involvement meetings.
3. Addressing excessive fundraising – e.g., reviewing and limiting the number of fundraising activities per term, consulting parents/SDA before organising events, ensuring activities do not disrupt learning.
4. Addressing financial accountability – e.g., publishing financial statements, involving the School Development Association (SDA) in auditing funds, displaying projects funded by collections.
5. Closing: Reassurance that the school values the parent's partnership and will act decisively.
Tone: Professional, conciliatory, action-oriented. Avoid being defensive.

questions.text:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.

"Son, I want to talk to you," my father barged in on me as I was staring at Penny's picture. "Yes, father," I sat up on the bed and put the phone on the side. "It's not good that a girl buys a boy stuff," he had always been blunt. I did not try to sieve his words and try to figure out what he was trying to say. "Sorry, what do you mean?" I tried to act dumb instead; I knew he was talking about the phone and the drop off. "That girl, she is not your class," he blatantly said it. The words I had been dreading came rolling off his tongue. "We are only friends, Father," I lied. My heart knew that I wanted to be more than a friend to Penny. "My son, I hope so. Girls like her do not know how to respect a man," he spoke. His words rang in my head, I never imagined Penny to be like that. She was perfect in my eyes; she was not the type to disrespect me. "They will control you and buy your submission. Find a girl like your mother. Your class, our class." He continued and I sat on the bed, staring quietly at my father. Somehow, he spoke some sense. A part of my day that I spent with Penny replayed in my head; she did not ask me what I wanted to eat, she only followed what she thought was right in her head. Maybe that was her favourite food or she had pre-ordered it. I loved Penny; I think she liked me. Would she disrespect me? My father left the room and left a huge void in my heart. I was a way out of Penny's league and my father confirmed it for me, but was I going to listen to him?

- Tension and anxiety as Jabu fears his father's reaction to his relationship.
- Sadness/void felt by Jabu when his father leaves, as he is left conflicted.

Candidates should make personal responses and anchor each emotion to specific lines in the passage.

(b) Ways Penny proves to be controlling (award up to 6 marks, 2 marks per valid point with textual support):
- She bought Jabu a phone, effectively 'buying his submission' as the father warns.
- She gave Jabu a drop-off/lift, reinforcing her financial dominance in the relationship.

(c) Relationship between Jabu and his father (award up to 9 marks):
- The relationship is close yet tense; the father feels free to intrude and give unsolicited advice ("barged in").
- The father is blunt and authoritative; Jabu listens respectfully but internally resists.
- There is a generational divide: the father holds traditional, patriarchal views about gender roles and class.
- Jabu respects his father enough to consider his words ("Somehow, he spoke some sense") yet lies to protect his feelings for Penny.
- Elsewhere in the novel the father continues to guide Jabu on issues of manhood, class, and relationships, suggesting a protective but domineering parental dynamic.

questions.text: Discuss the theme of love in the novel, Jabu.

Candidates should write a well-structured essay discussing how love is presented in the novel.

Key marking points:
- Romantic love: Jabu's feelings for Penny – genuine affection, admiration ('She was perfect in my eyes'), and longing, despite social and family obstacles.
- Parental love: Jabu's father's intervention is motivated by concern for his son's wellbeing, even if expressed harshly.
- Love and class/social barriers: the novel explores how love is complicated by social class and family expectations.
- Love and power: Penny's material generosity blurs the lines between love and control.

Read the following poem and answer the questions that follow.

Tears of a princess

Thou art my prince
Thy princess is on
A quest for her majesty
Thy knight in shining armour rescue thy
Damsel in distress
I know not your name
Neither do I need to know your face
All I need is your heart
A heart rich in love
A royal heart is all I need
Hear my cry
A cry from the heart
A heart tainted with
Nothing but tears
My time with commoners is due
Commoners who know not that
Loyalty is royalty
Come hither my prince
Your royal heart is all I need
Thy heart is an empty space.

questions.topic: Poetry analysis and comparison – New Voices, Diversity Dawns
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Style in 'Tears of a princess' (up to 10 marks; award 2 marks per well-explained stylistic device):
- Archaic/medieval language ('Thou art', 'Thy', 'Come hither') creates a fairy-tale/royal tone and underscores the speaker's yearning for an idealised love.
- Metaphor: 'knight in shining armour' – the ideal man is portrayed as a protector and rescuer.
- Repetition: 'A royal heart is all I need' / 'Your royal heart is all I need' emphasises the speaker's longing for genuine love over material wealth.
- Imagery: 'A heart tainted with nothing but tears' – vivid emotional imagery conveying heartbreak and loneliness.
- Contrast: 'commoners' vs 'royalty' – juxtaposes unworthy suitors with the idealised prince.
- Oxymoron/paradox: 'Loyalty is royalty' – suggests that true love is defined by faithfulness, not status.
- Apostrophe: the speaker addresses an absent 'prince', heightening the sense of longing.
- Free verse: no strict rhyme scheme, reflecting the spontaneous, emotional nature of the plea.

(b) 'My plight' and problems faced by women (up to 15 marks):
- Candidates must draw on the poem 'My plight' from the anthology.
- Expected points include: oppression by men/society, emotional suffering, lack of voice/agency, domestic hardship, societal expectations, and the quest for recognition and dignity.

questions.text:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.

PASI (pinning down the Scout's head with his boot) So you are a Selous Scout! You kill innocent people, priests, nuns, teachers and businessmen to confuse the povo. You poison wells, shoot cattle, burn down villages.
SELOUS SCOUT Kill me please. Finish me off.
(PASI raises his bayonet, hesitates, lowers it. He searches through the Scout's pockets, appropriating watch, money, cigarettes, twists of marijuana, etc.)
SELOUS SCOUT Won't you finish me off? Please.
PASI I won't waste a bullet on a Smithie dog like you. Or stain my bayonet with your evil blood.
SELOUS SCOUT (Hoarsely) Dear Lord … forgive me –
PASI Forgive yourself, mate.
SELOUS SCOUT So … so stupid …. Stupid to die…(shudders and dies)
(NKAZANA screams)
PASI Quiet, Nkazana. (He drags the red cloth from the pulpit and covers the dead man with it)
NKAZANA (crossing herself and peering at the wrapped body) Is he – dead?
PASI Yeah. Lifeless as a drowned rat. (philosophically) Isn't it so easy, dying.
NKAZANA Bantu beNkosi! Or God!
PASI He's just one more of them down. There are hundreds of them out there, haunting the countryside. It's they who are the terrorists, not us.
NKAZANA Abanye bakhe bazabuya hini ukhuzomuthatha? Will they come for him?
PASI I guess so. Maybe they'll send a chopper in the morning. (sardonically) Meantime he can get ready to meet with his Maker, undisturbed.
(NKAZANA crosses herself again and mumbles a prayer)
PASI A prayer? For him? Let him stew in hell. If ever there is a heaven or hell.
NKAZANA Comrade Pasi. Please –
PASI It was going to be either him, or me. Us and them. Wrestling this wretched piece of the Earth from each other. Every day. Watering this soil with our dear blood. And where do you think God is looking while we butcher each other like this?

(a) Aspects of culture shown in the passage (up to 10 marks; award 2 marks per well-explained cultural aspect):
- Religion/spirituality: Nkazana crosses herself (Christian tradition) and mumbles a prayer, showing Christian faith even in a war context.
- Language/multilingualism: Nkazana speaks in isiNdebele ('Bantu beNkosi', 'Abanye bakhe bazabuya hini ukhuzomuthatha?'), reflecting Zimbabwe's multilingual cultural identity.
- African spiritual belief: Pasi questions the existence of heaven and hell, reflecting tension between Christianity and indigenous worldviews.
- Warrior/combatant culture: the liberation war ethos of 'us and them', sacrifice ('watering this soil with our dear blood'), and justifying killing in the name of freedom.
- Respect for the dead: covering the Selous Scout's body with a cloth shows a cultural impulse to treat the dead with some dignity, even in war.
- Gender roles in wartime: Nkazana's emotional response (screaming, praying) contrasts with Pasi's hardened, philosophical stance.

(b) The comrades' visit to the spirit medium (up to 15 marks):
- Candidates should recount events from the play where the comrades (including Pasi) visit a spirit medium (svikiro/isangoma) for guidance, protection, and blessing before military operations.
- Key points: the spirit medium channels ancestral spirits; comrades seek spiritual protection (e.g., medicines/charms); the medium gives warnings or instructions about conduct during the struggle; rituals are performed; the visit reinforces the connection between the liberation struggle and ancestral/spiritual authority.
- Award 3 marks per well-developed and accurate point with reference to the play (up to 5 points).

questions.text: Examine the presentation of freedom fighters in the play, Harvest of Thorns Classic: A Play.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
Candidates should write a well-structured essay examining how freedom fighters are presented throughout the play.

Key marking points:
- Freedom fighters (comrades) are presented as both heroic and flawed/human.
- Heroic/patriotic dimension: dedication to the liberation cause, willingness to sacrifice their lives, belief in justice ('It's they who are the terrorists, not us').
- Human/flawed dimension: Pasi's ruthlessness, looting of the Selous Scout's possessions, moral questioning about God and the value of life.
- Pasi's philosophical reflection on death and war humanises freedom fighters beyond mere propaganda figures.
- The play presents their psychological toll: violence, moral ambiguity, and disillusionment.
- Solidarity and camaraderie among comrades.
- Relationship with the civilian population (povo): protectors but also a burden on villagers.
- Use of specific scenes, dialogue, and stage directions to support arguments.

subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any ONE of:
• Regularly clear swarf/chips from the hole to prevent tap breakage.
• Use a bottoming tap last and apply cutting lubricant.
• Back off the tap frequently (half turn back for every full turn forward) to break and clear chips.
• Do not force the tap to the bottom of the hole; leave clearance.

(b) Temporary joining: components can be assembled and disassembled without damage (e.g., nuts and bolts, screws). Permanent joining: components cannot be separated without damaging the joint or the parts (e.g., riveting, welding, soldering).

(c) Formula for snap head rivet overall length:
• Grip length = sum of plate thicknesses = 6 + 6 = 12 mm
• Length of rivet tail to form snap head = 1.5 × diameter = 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 mm
• Overall length = grip length + tail length = 12 + 7.5 = 19.5 mm
(Award marks: 1 mark for grip = 12 mm; 1 mark for correct formula for tail; 1 mark for tail = 7.5 mm; 1 mark for final answer 19.5 mm)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any THREE (1 mark each):
• Cuts from swarf/flying metal chips
• Entanglement of clothing/hair in rotating parts
• Eye injuries from flying debris
• Crush injuries from workpiece/chuck
• Electrical shock
• Burns from hot workpiece or coolant splashes

(b)(i) A = Live/revolving centre (or driving plate/carrier/catch plate); B = Dead centre (or: A = Dead centre, B = Live centre — accept either logical assignment with correct names)
(1 mark each for correct name, 1 mark for both correctly identified)

(b)(ii) Live centre: rotates with the workpiece to support the tailstock end without friction/overheating. Dead centre: fixed support in the tailstock, used to support long workpieces (lubrication needed). (1 mark each)

(c) Sketch should show: workpiece held in chuck; boring bar/tool mounted in tool post or boring head; tool feeding into a pre-drilled hole to enlarge/true it. Credit for correct labelling of boring bar, workpiece, and direction of feed. (3 marks for clear, labelled sketch showing correct setup)

(d) Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Face milling / slab milling
• Slot/groove cutting
• Gear cutting
• Drilling
• Boring
• Angular/chamfer milling

(e)(i) Main drive clutch: engages or disengages the power from the motor to the milling spindle/cutter, allowing the spindle to be started or stopped without switching off the motor.

(e)(ii) Table: holds and supports the workpiece (via vise or clamps); can be moved in X, Y and Z directions to position the workpiece relative to the cutter.

(e)(iii) Feed selector lever: used to select the rate (speed) at which the table feeds the workpiece into the cutter, controlling the depth and quality of cut.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Leather apron/welding jacket
• Leather gloves/gauntlets
• Leather spats/boots
• Flame-resistant overalls/sleeves

(b) Typical welding positions (1 mark each):
(i) Flat/Downhand position
(ii) Horizontal position
(iii) Vertical position
(iv) Overhead position

(c) Differences (2 marks each side, up to 4 marks):
• Welding blowpipe: has a single nozzle/tip designed to mix oxygen and acetylene to produce a flame for melting/fusing metal; no additional oxygen jet.
• Gas cutting blowpipe: has an additional high-pressure oxygen lever/valve that releases a jet of pure oxygen to oxidise and blow away the molten metal, enabling cutting; has a cutting attachment with a central oxygen jet and surrounding preheat flames.

(d) Shutdown procedure (1 mark per correct step, up to 5 marks):
1. Close the acetylene blowpipe valve first, then the oxygen blowpipe valve (to extinguish the flame).
2. Close the acetylene cylinder valve.
3. Close the oxygen cylinder valve.
4. Re-open the acetylene blowpipe valve to release pressure from the hose, then close it.
5. Re-open the oxygen blowpipe valve to release pressure from the hose, then close it.
6. Unscrew/release both regulator adjusting screws (pressure adjusters) until slack.
7. Coil hoses and store equipment safely.

questions.topic: Sheet Metal and Beaten Metal Technology
questions.diagramNote: Fig. 5 – diagram showing a range of sheet metal stakes labelled P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, W (e.g., hatchet stake, bick iron, funnel stake, creasing iron, etc.).
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Any THREE from the stakes shown (accept correct names for the stakes depicted, e.g.):
• Hatchet stake – for making sharp bends and folds
• Bick iron (Beck iron) – for forming cylindrical or curved shapes
• Funnel/Cone stake – for making conical/funnel shapes
• Creasing iron – for forming grooves/seams
• Half-moon stake – for hollowing curved forms
• Flat stake – for general planishing/flattening
(1 mark each for any 3 correctly named)

(a)(ii) Use of each stake (1 mark each, matched to identified stake):
• Hatchet stake: forming right-angle bends and sharp folds in sheet metal.
• Bick iron: shaping cylindrical, conical or curved pieces; forming tubes.
• Funnel stake: shaping conical/funnel forms.
• Creasing iron: forming wired edges or grooves/seams.
• Half-moon stake: hollowing/dishing curved forms.
• Flat stake: planishing and flattening sheet metal.

(b) Any THREE reasons (1 mark each):
• To remove sharp edges that could cause cuts/injuries to users.
• To strengthen/stiffen the edges of the article.
• To improve the appearance/finish of the article.
• To prevent the edges from splitting or cracking over time.
• To provide a neat, professional finish.

(c) Beaten metalwork is the process of shaping metal (usually sheet or plate) into three-dimensional forms by hammering it over stakes or formers, without the use of heat or casting.

(d) Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Decorative bowls/trays
• Vases
• Jugs/pitchers
• Wall plaques/panels
• Candleholders

(e) Raising process (3 marks for explanation + sketches):
• Start with a flat disc of annealed sheet metal.
• Place the disc over a raising stake (or sandbag) and strike with a raising hammer in concentric circles working from the edge towards the centre, causing the metal to compress and rise up.
• Anneal the metal frequently to restore ductility as work hardening occurs.
• Continue hammering in successive courses, gradually building the wall height and reducing the diameter.
• Sketches should show: flat disc → progressive stages of raised form → final hollow vessel shape, with hammer blows indicated working from rim inward.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any TWO hazards (1 mark each):
• Burns from hot metal/fire/sparks
• Eye injuries from flying scale/sparks
• Respiratory problems from fumes/smoke/coal dust
• Noise-induced hearing loss
• Muscular injuries from heavy hammering
• Fire hazard from forge/hot metal

(b)(i) Chisels in forge technology: used to cut/split hot metal on the anvil (hot chisels) or cold metal (cold chisels); also used for making decorative cuts.

(b)(ii) Tongs: used to hold/grip hot metal securely while it is being worked on the anvil or moved in and out of the fire/hearth.

(c) Design of a flower-hanging item (6 marks):
Expected response: A freehand sketch/design drawing of a decorative wall bracket or hanging hook for flower pots, incorporating AT LEAST THREE of the following forge processes:
• Drawing down (tapering ends)
• Bending/curling (hooks, scrolls)
• Upsetting (thickening sections)
• Punching (holes for fixing)
• Twisting (decorative twisted sections)
• Riveting (joining parts)
Mark allocation: 2 marks for a clear, appropriate design sketch; 2 marks for labelling/identifying at least 3 forge processes on the design; 2 marks for design suitability/creativity/aesthetics.

(d) Sand casting: uses a mould made of sand which is broken away after casting; used for large/complex shapes; low tooling cost; rough surface finish. Die casting: uses a permanent metal mould (die); produces smooth surface finish; suitable for high-volume production of small/medium parts; higher tooling cost. (1 mark for a valid distinguishing point)

(e)(i)
• Porosity: the presence of small holes/voids (pores) within the casting caused by trapped gases in the solidifying metal.
• Inclusion: the presence of foreign materials (e.g., sand, slag, oxide particles) embedded within the casting.

(e)(ii) Causes:
• Porosity: caused by gases dissolved in the molten metal that are released during solidification; insufficient venting of the mould; moisture in the mould/sand; excessively high pouring temperature.
• Inclusion: caused by sand particles breaking away from the mould walls; slag/dross not skimmed from the molten metal before pouring; dirty/contaminated scrap metal used; turbulent pouring.

questions.topic: Engineering Design – Mechanisms and Locking Devices
questions.diagramNote: Fig 9 – detailed dimensioned drawing of the Light Duty Press Stand (not to scale), showing Part A (table, 50×20), Part B (column, 30×600), Part C (sliding collar, 40×20), Part D (press ram, 30×25), with key dimensions including 300 mm (centre of Part C above table), 400, 250, 50, 40, 20, 275, 40, 30, 25 mm. Arrow F indicates front elevation direction.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Safety locking Part C on column Part B (5 marks):
Acceptable solutions (mark for clarity of sketch + correct function):
• Clamping bolt/locking screw: A bolt/thumb screw passing through a tapped hole in Part C that bears against Part B to clamp it at any height. Sketch should show the bolt arrangement, direction of clamping, and Part C on Part B.
• Rack and pawl/pin lock: Holes drilled along Part B at intervals; a spring-loaded pin in Part C engages a hole to lock position.
• Cam-action clamp: A cam lever on Part C that when rotated tightens the collar against Part B.
Mark scheme: 2 marks for appropriate design concept; 2 marks for clear, labelled sketch; 1 mark for explanation of how it locks at ANY point.

(b) Quick release mechanism for Part D (5 marks):
Acceptable solutions:
• Spring return: A compression spring around Part D (or inside Part C) that pushes Part D back upward once downward force is removed. Sketch should show spring position, retaining collar, and direction of action.
• Cam/toggle quick release: A lever-operated cam that releases the drive and allows Part D to spring back.
• Ball-catch detent: Not ideal for quick release — spring is preferred.
Mark scheme: 2 marks for appropriate mechanism concept; 2 marks for clear, labelled sketch showing spring/Part D/Part C relationship; 1 mark for correct explanation of release action.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
Part (a)(i): Students must form words using each of the given noun prefixes: ba-, bu-, lu-, zwi-, li-, ku-, mu-. One valid word per prefix is required. Examples: ba-nhu (people), bu-hle (beauty), lu-gwana (basket), zwi-nhu (things), li-bwe (stone), ku-enda (going), mu-nhu (person). Award 1 mark per correct word formed [7 marks].

Part (a)(ii): Students choose six of the words formed and write grammatically correct sentences. Award 1 mark per correct sentence [6 marks].

Part (b)(i): A noun (zina) is a word that names a person, place, thing, or idea. In Kalanga, nouns are identified by their class prefixes. [1 mark]

Part (b)(ii): Five types/classes of nouns in Kalanga, e.g.: (1) Mazina ebanhu (nouns for people), (2) Mazina ezvinhu (nouns for objects/things), (3) Mazina enzvimbo (nouns for places), (4) Mazina ezvikalo (abstract nouns), (5) Mazina emibvunzo (interrogative nouns). Award 1 mark per correct class [5 marks].

Part (b)(iii): Correct plural forms of the nouns listed. Award 1 mark per correct plural form [5 marks].

Part (b)(iv): Two grammatically correct, extended/complex sentences using the chosen nouns. Award 1 mark per correct sentence [2 marks].

questions.aiModelAnswer:
Part (a)(i): Identify which noun class the adjective concord (isubvu) comes from for each adjective stem listed. Examples: -bgwelele = describes a noun of a particular class (e.g., li- class), -yose = all, used with various classes, -nunga = round, -zipa = long, -moto = warm/hot, -inyoka = snake-like. Students should identify the noun class prefix that agrees with each adjective concord. Award 1 mark per correct identification [6 marks].

Part (a)(ii): Adjective stems (zwisubvu zwetjibaluli) can be used to: (1) describe nouns directly, (2) take concord prefixes agreeing with the noun class, (3) appear predicatively after a copula, (4) be modified by intensifiers, (5) appear in comparative constructions, (6) qualify pronouns. Award 1 mark per correct and relevant point [6 marks].

Part (b)(i): Three types of pronouns (tjizinana) in Kalanga, e.g.: (1) Mazwizinana ekutanga (personal/subject pronouns), (2) Mazwizinana ekugadziridzwa (object pronouns), (3) Mazwizinana edzwibvunzo (interrogative pronouns) / possessive pronouns / demonstrative pronouns. Award 2 marks per correct type with explanation [6 marks].

Part (b)(ii): Identify the pronoun type in each sentence:
(a) Ngubo dzedu — possessive pronoun (dzedu = of us)
(b) Mbisana unlefu — demonstrative or adjective qualifier
(c) Ndabona nhema — subject pronoun (Nda- = I)
(d) Izwezwi zwanana zohiya — demonstrative pronoun (izwezwi = these things)
(e) Iye watumwa kutolo — personal/subject pronoun (iye = he/she)
(f) Hingisa lugwana gogu — demonstrative pronoun (gogu = this)
Award 1 mark per correct identification [6 marks].

questions.aiModelAnswer:
This question is from the play 'Gombalume Pedzani' by Belthazor Mlalazi (Kalanga Heritage Press). Students are asked to analyse the character of Sandlana (a character with a Western/English name) and discuss the tension and conflict regarding the manhood/masculinity of the father figure. They must also explain what the play says about people who are confused about their identity (bekamanikana — those who are caught between two worlds/cultures).

Marking guide (25 marks):
- Content/Argument (15 marks): Identification and analysis of Sandlana as a character; discussion of the conflict between traditional and modern/Western values; reference to specific scenes, dialogue, and events; analysis of masculinity and identity themes; what the playwright is saying about cultural identity confusion.

5. Specific dramatic scenes/dialogue that illustrate the conflict.
Award marks proportionally for depth, accuracy, and textual support.
