questions.diagramNote: Achievement Standards rubric table covering six assessed aspects: Song Structure and Arrangement (10 marks), Technical Proficiency (10 marks), Collaboration and Responsiveness (7 marks), Originality and Creativity (7 marks), Stage Presence and Engagement (6 marks), Expressiveness (6 marks), and Ensemble Management (4 marks) — each with descriptors for Excellent, Good, Satisfactory, and Below Average bands.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
This is a practical performance task marked against the Achievement Standards rubric. Key marking points for each aspect are as follows:

**Song Structure and Arrangement (10 marks)**
- Excellent (9–10): Well-crafted, cohesive structure; seamless and purposeful transitions; each section (Introduction, Development, Climax, Resolution) complements the whole.
- Good (7–8): Clear, organised structure; sections are distinct and flow logically.
- Satisfactory (5–6): Recognisable structure with consistent sections; simple but functional transitions.
- Below Average (1–4): Developing understanding; sections identifiable with room for refinement.

**Technical Proficiency (10 marks)**
- Excellent (9–10): Outstanding technical control and confident delivery; highly polished and musically compelling throughout.
- Good (7–8): Solid technical ability and musical understanding; polished and engaging.
- Satisfactory (5–6): Basic proficiency with moderate control; musically engaging in most parts.
- Below Average (1–4): Growing technical control and musical expression.

**Collaboration and Responsiveness (7 marks)**
- Excellent (7): Outstanding musical awareness; seamless response to others; precise adjustment to tempo/dynamics/cues; strong musical dialogue; polished unified performance.
- Good (6): Consistent interaction; effective adjustment to group dynamics; reliable role fulfilment; good musical communication.
- Satisfactory (4–5): Some awareness of musical cues; developing ensemble role understanding; growing confidence in responding to group changes.
- Below Average (1–3): Positive effort to engage; emerging responsiveness; enthusiasm with developing control.

**Originality and Creativity (7 marks)**
- Excellent (7): Exceptional originality; imaginative musical ideas; creative rhythm use and compelling variations.
- Good (6): Thoughtful idea development and rhythmic choices; clear creative intent; variations add character and personal style.
- Satisfactory (4–5): Some creative elements or stylistic choices; effort toward musical creativity beyond familiar patterns.
- Below Average (1–3): Emerging musical creativity; beginning to take artistic risks.

**Stage Presence and Engagement (6 marks)**
- Excellent (6): High charisma and confidence; fully engages audience with expressive gestures, eye contact, and dynamic energy.
- Good (5): Strong presence; clear communication and consistent audience engagement; assured performance.
- Satisfactory (3–4): Growing confidence; some expressive qualities; moderate engagement with evident intention.
- Below Average (1–2): Impact in some sections; developing engagement and projection.

**Expressiveness (6 marks)**
- Excellent (6): Profound emotional depth and artistic insight; expressive body language powerfully enhances musical interpretation.
- Good (5): Clear emotional intent and thoughtful interpretation; expressiveness through body language supports musical delivery.
- Satisfactory (3–4): Attempts to express mood and feeling; growing awareness of how body movement enhances performance.
- Below Average (1–2): Developing expression; basic gestures and posture show potential.

**Ensemble Management (4 marks)**
- Excellent (4): Seamlessly coordinates ensemble members; strong leadership and responsiveness; tight rhythmic alignment and musical cohesion.
- Good (3): Engages well with the ensemble; shows some leadership skills.
- Satisfactory (2): Conscious effort to follow the ensemble; generally supportive of group performance.
- Below Average (1): Developing coordination skills.

**General advice for a high-scoring performance:**
- Choose a theme-appropriate song or compose an original piece clearly conveying the message of equal opportunities for all.
- Arrange the piece with a clear Introduction → Development → Climax → Resolution arc.
- Ensure all ensemble members (2–8 performers) have defined roles and rehearse transitions.
- Incorporate original rhythmic ideas and variations to demonstrate creativity.
- Dress appropriately for the performance context.
- Engage the audience with eye contact, expressive gestures, and dynamic energy throughout.

questions.text:
In the diagram ABCDE is a trapezium, AC = 9 cm, DE = 4 cm and AE = 3 cm. Lines AC and ED are parallel to each other. (Refer to Fig. 9 showing trapezium ABCDE with dimensions: AE = 3 cm, one side = 3 cm, DE = 4 cm, and a slant side = 5 cm.)
Calculate the area of the trapezium.
questions.diagramNote: Trapezium ABCDE with parallel sides AC = 9 cm and DE = 4 cm; AE = 3 cm; slant side = 5 cm; another side = 3 cm. Height of trapezium needs to be determined from the given dimensions.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
The parallel sides are AC = 9 cm and DE = 4 cm. The height of the trapezium is AE = 3 cm (perpendicular distance between parallel sides).
Area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height = ½ × (9 + 4) × 3 = ½ × 13 × 3 = 19.5 cm²

questions.diagramNote: Circle with centre O. Points B, C, D, E on the circumference. BOD and COE are diameters. A shaded region is shown in the diagram. Angles BEC and BDC are subtended by arc BC; BDC = 20°.

questions.text:
The diagram below is a speed-time graph for an athlete who took 100 seconds to complete a race. The athlete ran 1,75 km in 100 seconds.
Calculate the
(a) value of V.
(b) acceleration of the athlete from time 60 seconds to time 100 seconds.

subParts.label: (b)

questions.diagramNote: Speed-time graph for an athlete over 100 seconds. The graph shows the athlete's speed (reaching a maximum V) over time, with different phases of motion. The total area under the graph represents the total distance of 1.75 km = 1750 m.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Total distance = area under speed-time graph = 1750 m. Using the shape of the graph (trapezium/triangles), set up an equation involving V and solve. For example, if the graph shows acceleration to V from 0–40s, constant V from 40–60s, deceleration from 60–100s: Area = ½(40)V + 20V + ½(40)V = 20V + 20V + 20V = 60V = 1750; V = 1750/60 ≈ 29.2 m/s. (Exact value depends on graph shape — method mark for correct area formula.)
(b) Acceleration = change in speed / time = (final speed − V) / (100 − 60). If athlete decelerates to 0: acceleration = (0 − V)/40 = −V/40 m/s² (negative indicating deceleration). Substitute V found in (a).

(iv) Rinsing – to remove all traces of detergent and soap from fabrics after washing, as residual detergent can cause skin irritation and fabric damage. (v) Drying – to remove moisture from washed items to prevent the growth of mildew and bacteria, and to prepare items for ironing and use. [1 mark each]

(d) Five suitable care labels for a white linen table cloth – students must draw the standard international textile care symbols: 1. Wash at 60°C (tub with 60 inside) – linen can withstand high temperatures. 2. Bleach allowed (triangle symbol) – white linen can be bleached. 3. Tumble dry normal (circle in square) – can be machine dried. 4. Iron on high heat (iron with 3 dots) – linen requires high heat ironing. 5. Mhungubgwe dzakabe dzidze dzyelesedza dla buhwa nentha yempalo ngono gukolandula bo zwago. Kana iko koyi zwinhu zoyedzewa, kadzikulu tjakatongoyedza tjikahapayidza mabgwe limwe hhuba kwalema. Luhulo gwakabe gutjayenda yenda zwago gutongo palapala guti pamwe gungawana midzi yen'hanje itjina doba nyana koga kwakahayika iwo ndzila nyana welahisa. Luhulo wakawha mabula awe esungana ewha ntumbu ulila kube hhalima nyana kumeho kadza kakotama otetema nungo dzembili. Wakalebelekela pehhugwi eti, 'Kana nhu unobulawa nehhala ape esawana tjimwe tjinoyenda kubula,' ejalo elinga linga pasi eti pamwe unobona tjaangakanganyidza natjo hhala. Wakati etjajalo ebe ebona Gudo aligele zwe akanayila bhato lentobgwe kulayidza kuti nti wake usina tjimwe kusakajalo nhutana wakawobe elipehhugwi ezwitjidza. Wakasedzela kawunlezwa. Gudo wakahandula newhi likule lisina simba nentha yenengetela nehhala. Abazotongoda kuti bazwipamidzile buyendasi nelezwana nekwenginangina yabakabe bakalingisana nayo. Luhulo nebutjenjebvu wakaluka nkumbulo webuwholomwa. Wakasedzelela pana Gudo kawunyebezela. Yakabvuma nen'holo yakagudo ikokota kokota milomo kulayidza kuti tjaanyebegwa tjowubvulidza mate. Bhitipiti, tshamwina linoyi Luhulo lakati lootanga ilo yedza nkumbulo wabaluka. Wakaswika kunzi waHumba tjimuka tjakhona kawana bana bezana kuhhe tjibe tjiti, 'Baponi mme benyu?' Bana baHumba bebe beti, 'Abatapo' Tjibe tjiti, 'Muhhe mubabudze kuti ndati ndohaka bakama.' Humba yakabe yakakanama zwayo mun'umba yati iwha ikabe ibhuda iwun'gala makanyu ihako pedzelana naye. Pana Luhulo zwitshitshinho zwakabe zonazwa tiko tjinga tjampupuludze. Tjakatihha Luhulo Humba elihule kwatjo ehaka tjipedza. Humba wakabe eti ndikupedze tjidzeta enohanduka kusimuno etjisedzelela kakale apa eti ndikunatule luhulo gudzeta kudza kulutuka bhulubusi lewhuluba. Tjakati tjatjibe mbeli kwazo humba ebe etoboka emazwe tjibe tjitjuluka tjima apeya tjiti, 'Anditokuhla buya ngwenu ndati ndohaka kukama.' Humba wakabe nebuhongola kwazo ebe ewuntjulukila ehaka wundiya banhu. Wakati etjajalo tjibe tjitjuluka tjingina mumpata wemiti mibili yakabapa tjinobhuda nthayeyi. Humba wakatobela ekangan'wa kuti iye unambili unkulunkulu pana weluhulo. Humba wakamanigwa mumpata iwhoyo hulo tjibe tjiseka tjiti, 'Ndakubudza kuti ndokukama!' Tjijalo tjipoteleka hule tjitola hamilo yatjakabe tjasumbika padenjana lipedlo ipapo. Luhulo gwakawunkama guka hadza hamilo dzina gube guloba pasi gunda guloba nlidzo zwago ngeno gupfuta fodlo yago gusakabiga. Hule kwemahhuba mabili Gudo wakakumba nkwinya kuti awhe kuti wakanda tjini sekwaakabe awunyebela. Wakawana Luhulo nebana babe bedla zwabo mahwe besakabiga. Wakati ekumbila ebe etjiziwa neluboko kuyi ande anozwihakilabo uwe nkaka. Wakadiligwa ntubi kuyi unoonon'wisa zwanana kanyi zwikabhata bula. Lakabhuda hhuba kayenda Gudo ka swika ne whi gobvu, 'Mme benyu bayapo?' Bana baHumba beba beti, 'Abatapo?' Gudo ebeti, 'Muhhe mubabudze kuti ndati ndohaka bakama.' Humba wakabhuda nelubilo gukulukulu ewuntatamila. Gudo lakatihha linanabala lakalinga kumiti yalakabe labona inampata. Lakaswika lingina linobhuda nthayeyi, humba ibe ibuya ihha inginabo inobhuda nthayeyi! Wakasenga bulemo gudo kaalakana kuti swiyo ekapamha inoohha imanigwa. Wakahomola lubilo gose gwaanago kapoteleka kahha engina kakale pakati kwemiti enobhuda nthayeyi. Humba yakahhabo ingina inobhuda nthayeya! Gudo wake ata bulengwe esakumbula iye nehumba banolizama mibili ndizo paanotubula ngina enobhuda nthayeyi nehumbabo inotubula pindapobo isamanigwa. Wakati ebona kwakona kuti humba amanigwe gwebubili kati kusifa ndikupi! Wakananabala akalinga kunzi wati abe pedlo akamimila eti kunkadzimayi, 'Hhalililani bana mun'umba!' Ngono zwanana zwakabe zwizana kuhhe azwizowhisisa zwakabe zwikambidza mmayi zwiti, 'Mme bekati bigani hali pamoto!' Kwakakoti abe pedlo zwibona tatayi belintutu humba yakabagala makanya bekabe betihha bengina mun'umba ehhabo engina mun'umba bezwihhalila bepiya. Humba yakahha ikapoteleka poteleka nen'umba ikabona kuti akuna panonginika. Yakalala pankoba ikalinda nyana ibe itoboka hule kwelubaka. Yakasiyilila bukuse gwayo pamisen'wa yedendele ibe ibuthunuka inda zwavo. Gudo wakabe eti ehohhela ebona bukuse gupamisen'wa etihha enoti tjoko kumsamo ekumbula kuti humba tjiyapo. Kwakakoti hule kwemahhuba mabili bohanjila nehhala, Luhulo ekokumbula kuti akumbe nkwinya anobonabo kuti wakanda tjini. Wakaswika kabahhulila ngono basokola nehhala nezwisungula bozwisunungulila ipapo mun'umba konhuwa kusingati! Wakabatola Luhulo kanobapa mahwe enkaka wen'ombe wakabe akama hhulolidla kumizi yebanhu. Lungano lungano gufila.

(iii) 'abahlonipha' – isenzo (verb/relative)

• Entanyeni (2): ent- (locative prefix) + -anyeni (from 'intambo'/'intanya') – locative form, showing prefix 'e-' and suffix '-ini'.
• Indlovukazi (2): indlovu + -kazi (feminine/augmentative suffix) = female/queen elephant.
• Lo (2): demonstrative pronoun, class 1 (first position demonstrative).

(b) [13 marks]: Landisa (paraphrase/content): Inkondlo ikhuluma ngamandla lamaqhinga ebuthongo. Abantu besifazane (lezaliwakazi) baphupha bezintandokazi, bethanda kakhulu. Labahwayidumbu (abantu abakhohlisayo/abalula amakhosi) baphupha bekhona ezindaweni eziphakemeyo, bengabahluli. Imbongi ithi ibuthongo buyisimanga ngoba benze abantu baphuphise izinto ezingekho. Abafundi baphupha bekhulu, bengabahlahluli labaprofethi. Award marks for: accurate identification of who dreams (lezaliwakazi, labohwayidumbu, ompisi, bomantswane), what they dream about, the theme of illusion/deception in dreams, and the irony/wonder of sleep. (Award up to 13 marks for well-developed, relevant content points.)

(c) [6 marks]: Ulimi (Language use): 
• Imifanekiso: 'ezisentendeni zezandla' – metaphor for being precious/cherished.
• Ukuphinda-phinda: 'baphupha' – repetition emphasising the act of dreaming.
• Isenzukutu/onomatopoeia: 'qonqobala' – vivid action verb.
• Ukusetshenziswa kwezibizo ezibonakalisa umuntu: 'ompisi, bomantswane' – metaphors for deceptive people.
• Ukuphawula: use of contrast between dreamers' illusions and reality.
(Award 2 marks per language feature correctly identified with explanation and example, up to 6 marks.)

(d) [4 marks]: Uncedo lwamaphupho (value of dreams):
• Amaphupho avivinya/aveza izifiso zomuntu.
• Amaphupho anganikeza ithemba loba isiqondiso empilweni.
• Amaphupho angaba yisixwayiso sobungozi.
• Amaphupho aveza imicabango ejulileyo yomuntu.
(Award 1–2 marks per valid point, up to 4 marks.)

questions.topic: Music Theory — Notation, Scales, Rhythm & Time Signatures
questions.diagramNote: Multiple music notation diagrams required: (a)(i) a printed musical note to name; (a)(iii) a note on a staff to identify; (b)(iii) incomplete bars requiring rests to be added; (c)(ii) blank staff for tonic triad of D major; (d) blank staff for four-bar rhythm composition; (e) blank treble clef staff for G major scale.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) The note shown is likely a minim (half note) — award 1 mark for correct identification of the note depicted.
(a)(ii) A semi-breve lasts as long as 4 crotchets.
(a)(iii) The letter name depends on the position of the note on the staff in the diagram (e.g. C, D, E, F, G, A or B). Award 1 mark for the correct letter name matching the diagram.
(b)(i) A ledger line is a short line added above or below the staff to extend the range of the staff, allowing notes to be written that are too high or too low to fit on the five lines.
(b)(ii) A flat (♭) lowers the pitch of a note by one semitone (half step).
(b)(iii) Student must identify the total beat value missing in each bar and insert the correct rest symbol(s). E.g. if a bar in 4/4 has beats worth 3 crotchets, a crotchet rest is added. Award 1 mark per correctly completed bar (2 marks total).
(c)(i) The relative Major of A minor is C major.
(c)(ii) The tonic triad of D major (without key signature) consists of notes D, F#, A written on the staff as a chord. Award marks for: correct root D (1), correct third F# (1), correct fifth A (1).
(c)(iii) 3/8 time means: there are 3 beats per bar (1 mark); the quaver (eighth note) receives one beat (1 mark); it has a lilting/compound feel often used in fast, dance-like pieces (1 mark).
(d) A valid four-bar rhythm in C (4/4) time: each bar must total 4 crotchet beats. Any combination of note values (semibreves, minims, crotchets, quavers, semiquavers, rests) that correctly add up to 4 beats per bar. Award marks for: correct time signature shown (1), 4 complete bars (1 per bar = 4), use of varied rhythmic values (1). Total 6 marks.
(e) G major scale ascending on treble clef with key signature: Key signature = 1 sharp (F#) placed on the top line of the treble clef. Notes ascending: G A B C D E F# G. Award marks for: correct key signature F# (1), all 8 notes correctly placed on treble clef (1 mark per 2 correct notes = 4 marks). Total 5 marks.

questions.text:
7 (a) Discuss the nature of Zimbabwe indigenous music.
(b) Discuss the meanings of dance gestures made in Zimbabwe musical arts performances.

subParts.text: Discuss the nature of Zimbabwe indigenous music.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Discuss the meanings of dance gestures made in Zimbabwe musical arts performances.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Nature of Zimbabwe indigenous music — key points (award up to 10 marks for well-developed points with examples):
1. Communal/participatory — music is a community activity performed by groups, not individuals in isolation.
2. Functional — music serves specific social functions (ceremonies, rituals, rites of passage, agriculture, war).
3. Oral tradition — transmitted orally from generation to generation, not written down.
4. Integrated art form — music, dance, drama and poetry are inseparable.
5. Call and response — a common structural feature where a leader sings and the group responds.
6. Use of indigenous instruments — mbira, ngoma drums, hosho, marimba.
7. Modal/pentatonic scales — use of specific tonal systems different from Western scales.
8. Spiritual/religious dimension — much music is connected to ancestral spirits (e.g. bira ceremony).
9. Improvisation — performers often improvise within a traditional framework.
10. Context-specific — different songs for different occasions (weddings, funerals, harvests).

(b) Meanings of dance gestures — key points (award up to 10 marks):
1. Stomping of feet — can represent power, connection with the earth/ancestors, or a call to spirits.
2. Hand/arm movements — can depict daily activities (grinding, farming), tell a story, or express emotion.
3. Hip movements — in some dances symbolise fertility and womanhood.
4. Head movements/nodding — can indicate respect, agreement or spirit possession.
5. Eye movements — can express seduction, challenge or communication with the spirit world.
6. Body posture (crouching/bending) — humility or reverence before elders/spirits.
7. Jumping — expression of joy, celebration or warrior strength.
8. Circular movement — symbolises unity, continuity of life, the cycle of seasons.
9. Gestures mimicking animals — connect performers to nature and totems (e.g. eagle, lion).
10. Gender-specific gestures — men and women have distinct movements reflecting social roles.

questions.text: Discuss the significance of the Third Chimurenga songs.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Significance of Third Chimurenga songs — key points (award up to 20 marks for well-developed, detailed essay with examples):
1. Political mobilisation — songs were used to rally support for the Fast Track Land Reform Programme (FTLRP) launched in 2000; they encouraged the masses to reclaim land.
2. Propaganda tool — served as a vehicle for government/ZANU-PF messaging, promoting the party's ideology and policies.
3. Preservation of revolutionary spirit — linked the land reform to the earlier First and Second Chimurenga, maintaining historical continuity of the liberation struggle.
4. Pan-Africanism — expressed solidarity with other African nations in resisting neo-colonialism and Western imperialism.
5. Cultural identity — reaffirmed Zimbabwean/African identity and pride in the face of Western sanctions and criticism.
6. Emotional expression — gave voice to the grievances of landless people and veterans who felt excluded from independence benefits.
7. Education/awareness — informed the public about colonial land dispossession and the need for restitution.
8. Anti-Western sentiment — songs criticised the British government, MDC opposition and Western powers perceived as enemies of Zimbabwe's sovereignty.
9. Notable artists — artists such as Dr. Targets, Cde Chinx, Leonard Dembo (posthumously referenced), and various war veterans contributed to this genre.
10. Documentation of history — the songs serve as oral historical records of the events of the early 2000s in Zimbabwe.
11. Social cohesion — united Zimbabweans around a common national cause.
12. Genre development — contributed to the development of a distinct Zimbabwean political music genre that blended traditional and modern sounds.
Award marks for: identification of relevant points (1 mark each), development/elaboration (1 mark each), use of relevant examples (up to 4 marks), quality of argument and structure (up to 2 marks).

9 (a) Discuss ways in which Zimbabwe popular music has influenced music in the diaspora.
(b) Describe factors that have influenced the fusion of Zimbabwe musical genres.

subParts.text: Discuss ways in which the Zimbabwe popular music has influenced music in the diaspora.

questions.topic: Zimbabwe Popular Music — Diaspora & Genre Fusion
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Ways Zimbabwe popular music has influenced the diaspora — key points (10 marks):
1. Export of Jit/Sungura rhythms — these rhythms have been adopted and adapted by musicians in the UK, South Africa, Botswana and beyond.
2. Mbira music on the world stage — artists like Stella Chiweshe and Dumisani Maraire introduced mbira to international audiences, influencing world music genres.
3. Chimurenga music — Thomas Mapfumo's Chimurenga music influenced diaspora communities and world music artists globally.
4. Marimba music — Zimbabwean marimba bands have become popular internationally, especially in the USA and UK, with diaspora communities forming their own marimba groups.
5. Fusion with Western genres — diaspora musicians have blended Zimbabwean rhythms with reggae, jazz, hip-hop, and gospel, creating new hybrid styles.
6. Cultural identity maintenance — diaspora Zimbabweans use popular music to maintain cultural links with home.
7. Digital platforms — YouTube, Spotify and social media have spread Zimbabwean popular music globally.
8. Live performances abroad — Zimbabwean artists touring internationally have directly influenced foreign musicians.
9. Language and lyrics — Shona and Ndebele language songs have introduced these languages to new audiences.
10. Collaboration — diaspora artists collaborate with local Zimbabwean artists, resulting in cross-cultural musical exchange.

(b) Factors influencing fusion of Zimbabwe musical genres — key points (10 marks):
1. Globalisation — exposure to international music styles through media and the internet.
2. Migration/diaspora — Zimbabweans living abroad bring back foreign musical influences.
3. Colonial influence — introduction of Western instruments (guitar, piano) and music theory.
4. Religion — Christian church music introduced hymns and gospel styles that blended with indigenous music.
5. Technology — digital audio workstations allow easy blending of different genre elements.
6. Intermarriage and cultural exchange — between different ethnic groups (Shona, Ndebele, Tonga) and nationalities.
7. Commercial pressures — artists blend genres to appeal to wider, more profitable audiences.
8. Education — formal music education exposes students to multiple genres, encouraging experimentation.
9. Media — radio and television broadcasts of diverse music genres create cross-genre influences.
10. Political and social events — e.g. Chimurenga music blended traditional and electric guitar styles in response to political struggles.

questions.topic: Music Industry — Artist Management & Social Media
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Work of an artist's manager — key points (10 marks):
1. Career planning — develops the artist's short-term and long-term career strategy.
2. Booking and scheduling — arranges performances, tours, and appearances.
3. Contract negotiation — negotiates deals with record labels, promoters, and sponsors on behalf of the artist.
4. Financial management — oversees the artist's earnings, budgets, and financial planning.
5. Public relations/image management — manages the artist's public image, brand and media presence.
6. Networking — builds relationships with key industry players (producers, promoters, media).
7. Conflict resolution — mediates disputes between the artist and third parties.
8. Guidance and advice — provides personal and professional advice to help the artist make informed decisions.
9. Marketing and promotion — oversees promotional campaigns, social media strategy, and press releases.
10. Legal liaison — works with lawyers to protect the artist's intellectual property and legal interests.

(b) Ways social media has influenced hybridity of music — key points (10 marks):
1. Global exposure — artists are exposed to music from around the world instantly, inspiring cross-genre experimentation.
2. Viral trends — challenges (e.g. TikTok dance challenges) spread musical styles globally, causing artists to blend genres to participate.
3. Collaboration facilitation — social media connects artists from different countries and genres, making international collaboration easier.
4. User-generated content — fans remix and blend songs, creating hybrid versions that influence mainstream music.
5. Direct audience feedback — artists receive instant feedback on fusions, encouraging further experimentation.
6. Streaming platforms — algorithms recommend diverse music to listeners, increasing cross-genre consumption and influence.
7. Breaking down gatekeepers — artists no longer need record labels to distribute music, allowing more experimental/hybrid music to reach audiences.
8. Cultural exchange — social media facilitates rapid exchange of musical ideas across cultures.
9. Sampling culture — easy access to music online has increased sampling and remixing across genres.
10. Marketing hybrid artists — social media allows niche hybrid artists to find their specific audience globally.

questions.text: Examine any five different forms of music piracy.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Five forms of music piracy — key points (award up to 20 marks; 4 marks per form: 1 mark for naming, 2 marks for description/explanation, 1 mark for example or impact):
1. Physical piracy (counterfeiting) — illegal duplication and sale of CDs, DVDs and cassettes that are made to look like the originals, including fake covers and labels. E.g. bootleg CDs sold at flea markets.
2. Online/internet piracy — unauthorised uploading, downloading or streaming of copyrighted music through websites, peer-to-peer (P2P) networks or torrent sites (e.g. The Pirate Bay). Users access music for free without paying the artist or label.
3. Signal piracy — the unauthorised interception and redistribution of broadcast signals (radio or TV) containing copyrighted music, or streaming music without a licence.
4. Public performance piracy — playing copyrighted music in public venues (bars, restaurants, events) without obtaining the required performance licence from a collecting society (e.g. ZIMURA in Zimbabwe).
5. Mobile phone/digital piracy — illegal sharing of music files via Bluetooth, WhatsApp, or other mobile-to-mobile transfer methods without the artist's authorisation.
6. Bootlegging — unauthorised recording of live performances and then distributing or selling these recordings without the artist's consent.
7. Plagiarism/music theft — copying another artist's melody, lyrics or composition and presenting it as one's own original work.
Impact of piracy: loss of revenue for artists and the music industry; discourages creativity; undermines the formal music economy; deprives the government of tax revenue.
Award marks for: naming each form (1 mark), describing/explaining it clearly (2 marks), giving an example or discussing its impact (1 mark). Any five forms examined = 20 marks.

questions.diagramNote: Vector diagram showing points O, A, B, M (midpoint of AB), and C (where OB produced so OB = BC); vectors OA = p and AB = q are labelled.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) OB = OA + AB = p + q.
(a)(ii) OC = OB + BC = OB + OB = 2OB = 2(p + q) = 2p + 2q.
(a)(iii) OM = OA + AM = p + ½q (since M is midpoint of AB).
(a)(iv) AC = AO + OC = −p + 2p + 2q = p + 2q.
(b) OT = k·OM = k(p + ½q).
(c) OT = OA + AT = p + h·AC = p + h(p + 2q) = p(1 + h) + 2hq.
(d) Equate expressions: k(p + ½q) = (1+h)p + 2hq. Comparing coefficients: p: k = 1 + h; q: k/2 = 2h → k = 4h. From k = 1 + h and k = 4h: 4h = 1 + h → 3h = 1 → h = 1/3. k = 4/3.
(e) OT = k·OM = (4/3)OM. MT = OT − OM = (4/3)OM − OM = (1/3)OM. Ratio MT:OT = (1/3)OM : (4/3)OM = 1:4.

questions.text:
Carefully study the following sources and then answer all the questions which follow.

SOURCE A
In 1980, 30-50% of people in rural areas had no land. This compelled the government to start the land reform programme in order to correct the land imbalances. However, the Lancaster House Agreement had its constraints as it guaranteed white settlers' ownership of land for the first 10 years of independence.
Adapted from a book by Modern Zimbabwean historians published in 2021.

SOURCE B
A proposal for a national land policy was made and it was formalised and enshrined as the Land Acquisition Act of 1992 which freed the government from the willing seller, willing buyer policy. This piece of legislation enabled and empowered the government to acquire any land it saw fit.
Adapted from a book by Modern Zimbabwean historians published in 2021.

SOURCE C
Government found itself under pressure for results. There were communal areas that had become seriously over-crowded and at this time of political hardships there was an outcry for land reform from politicians. In February 2000, after government lost the constitutional referendum, it decided to go on the fast-track resettlement scheme.
Adapted from a book by Modern Zimbabwean historians published in 2011.

subParts.text: Read Source A. What evidence in the source shows that land was not equally distributed?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Read Source B. How reliable is this source on the Land Acquisition Act of 1992 in Zimbabwe at that time?
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Read Source C. Why do you think the government resorted to the Fast Track Land Reform Programme?
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Read Source A and Source C. Are the two sources similar as historical evidence on the Land Reform Programme? Explain your answer.
subParts.label: (d)

subParts.text: Read Source B. What do you think were the reactions of the various groups of people in Zimbabwe on the Land Question?
subParts.label: (e)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Evidence of unequal land distribution: 30–50% of people in rural areas had no land in 1980; the government had to start a land reform programme to correct land imbalances; the Lancaster House Agreement guaranteed white settlers' ownership of land for the first 10 years of independence, showing whites held the majority of land while blacks were landless. (Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4.)

(b) Reliability of Source B: The source is reliable because it is adapted from a book by Modern Zimbabwean historians published in 2021, suggesting it is a researched, scholarly account; it gives a specific piece of legislation (Land Acquisition Act, 1992) and explains its purpose, showing detail and precision; however, it may be biased in favour of the government's land acquisition agenda as it only presents the government's perspective. The willing-seller willing-buyer policy being superseded is a verifiable historical fact. (Award up to 5 marks for balanced analysis of reliability and limitations.)

(c) Reasons for Fast Track Land Reform: Communal areas were seriously overcrowded; there was political pressure and an outcry from politicians for land reform; the government lost the constitutional referendum in February 2000 and needed to appease the population; desire to redress colonial land imbalances quickly; ZANU-PF needed to retain political support. (Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 5.)

(d) Similarity/difference between Source A and Source C: Both sources agree that land imbalances existed and that the government was under pressure to redistribute land — Source A shows the historical roots of the problem (1980, Lancaster House constraints) while Source C shows the urgency that built up by 2000. Both are adapted from books by Modern Zimbabwean historians, suggesting a similar academic perspective. They are similar in that they both highlight the need for land reform and the pressures on government, but differ in time period and specific triggers discussed. (Award up to 5 marks for a well-explained comparison.)

(e) Reactions of various groups to the Land Question: White farmers/settlers — opposed the Land Acquisition Act as it threatened their property rights; Black Zimbabweans/peasants — welcomed the Act as it promised to address historical land grievances; War veterans — strongly supported land redistribution and eventually led farm invasions; The international community/Western nations — condemned the fast-track programme and imposed sanctions; Commercial farmers' unions — lobbied against the Act and sought legal redress; Opposition politicians — used the land issue as a campaign platform. (Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 6.)

subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Groups of people who can provide oral evidence: elders/elderly people; traditional chiefs/headmen; spirit mediums/n'angas; war veterans/ex-combatants; religious leaders; storytellers/griots; former government officials; eyewitnesses to historical events. (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Advantages of oral tradition: it preserves the history of non-literate societies that had no written records; it is a primary source as it comes directly from people who experienced events; it is cost-effective and accessible; it reflects the community's own perspective without colonial bias; it can fill gaps left by written records; it preserves culture, customs, and traditions; it can be passed down through generations keeping history alive; it allows for emotional and contextual detail not found in documents. (Any 6, 2 marks each for a well-outlined point.)

(c) Measures to overcome language barriers in research (essay form): Employ a qualified interpreter or translator who is fluent in both the researcher's language and the informant's language; the researcher can learn the local language before conducting fieldwork; use visual aids, diagrams, or gestures to communicate concepts that transcend language; use standardised questionnaires that have been professionally translated into the local language; collaborate with local research assistants who understand both cultures; use back-translation to verify accuracy of translated materials; record interviews and have them translated later by a professional. (Any 4 measures, well-argued in essay form, up to 8 marks — award 2 marks per well-explained measure.)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Reasons why Africa is the cradle of mankind: the oldest human fossils (e.g., Homo habilis, Australopithecus) have been found in Africa; the earliest stone tools (Oldowan tools) were discovered in Africa, e.g., Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania; DNA/genetic evidence suggests all modern humans share a common African ancestor; Africa has the greatest genetic diversity among human populations, consistent with being the origin point; archaeological sites such as those in Ethiopia (Afar region) have yielded the oldest hominid remains (e.g., Lucy/Australopithecus afarensis ~3.2 million years ago); the discovery of early fire use in Africa supports human evolution there. (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Physical changes in human development: increase in brain size (cranial capacity) from Australopithecus to Homo sapiens; development of an upright/bipedal posture — walking on two legs; reduction in the size of the jaw and teeth; development of an opposable thumb enabling tool use; loss of body hair and development of sweat glands for temperature regulation; reduction in brow ridges and changes in facial structure; increase in height and changes in skeletal structure; development of vocal apparatus enabling speech. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Measures to ensure food supply in the Middle Stone Age (essay form): develop more efficient hunting techniques and tools such as improved spears and traps to catch more animals; gather and store food such as berries, roots, and nuts during periods of plenty for use in lean seasons; exploit a wider variety of food sources including insects, fish, and birds; move to areas with greater food availability following animal migrations; develop early forms of food preservation such as drying meat in the sun; cooperate in groups for communal hunting of larger animals to maximise yield. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

(b) Explain any six contributions of the San to modern technology.
(c) The San faced constant attacks from wild animals. Suggest in essay form, any four measures the San could have taken to protect themselves from these attacks.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Animals hunted by the San: eland, kudu, wildebeest, gemsbok, warthog, springbok, ostrich, giraffe. (Any 2, 1 mark each.) Food gathered: wild fruits/berries, roots/tubers, wild honey, insects (e.g., termites), eggs, melons/tsamma. (Any 3, 1 mark each.)

(b) Contributions of the San to modern technology: use of poison arrows — contributed to knowledge of chemical/biological compounds used in modern medicine and weaponry; rock art — contributed to the development of art, communication, and early record-keeping (precursor to writing); tracking skills — used in modern wildlife management and conservation; knowledge of medicinal plants — contributed to modern pharmaceutical research; use of bow and arrow — influenced weapon development; development of traps and snares — contributed to modern hunting and pest-control technology; fire-making techniques — fundamental to later technological developments; knowledge of natural navigation using stars contributed to astronomy and navigation. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Measures to protect the San from wild animal attacks (essay form): build shelters in elevated or enclosed areas such as caves or rocky outcrops that wild animals could not easily enter; light fires around campsites at night as wild animals are generally afraid of fire; use poisoned arrows and spears to keep animals at a distance or drive them away; set traps and snares around their living areas to catch or deter predators; live in groups so that many people could cooperate to scare away or fight attacking animals; make loud noises using drums or voices to frighten animals away. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

(a) State any five religious activities in the Mutapa state.
(b) Describe any six activities of the Portuguese that destroyed the culture of the Mutapa state.
(c) The Portuguese abused Mutapa women. Recommend, in essay form, any four measures the Mutapa could have put in place to protect their women.

questions.topic: The Mutapa State and Portuguese Influence
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Religious activities in the Mutapa state: ancestor worship/veneration of royal ancestors; rain-making ceremonies; use of spirit mediums (svikiro) to communicate with the ancestors; offering sacrifices/offerings to the ancestors; consulting the Mwari (High God) oracle; burial ceremonies and rituals for royalty; religious dances and ceremonies; taboos observed in honour of the ancestors. (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Portuguese activities that destroyed Mutapa culture: introduction of Christianity which undermined traditional religious beliefs and practices; construction of Catholic churches on sacred Mutapa land; forced conversion of the Mutapa and his subjects to Christianity; intermarriage with Mutapa women, disrupting social structures; introduction of the prazo system which displaced African communities; engaging in slave trade which broke up families and communities; political interference — supporting rival claimants to the Mutapa throne causing instability; introduction of foreign trade goods that undermined local craftsmanship; armed conflicts that destroyed communities and killed cultural practitioners. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Measures to protect Mutapa women from Portuguese abuse (essay form): the Mutapa king could have issued royal decrees forbidding Portuguese men from interacting with Mutapa women without permission; armed guards could have been stationed to protect women, especially in areas of Portuguese activity; women could have been kept in secluded settlements away from Portuguese trading posts; traditional leaders could have imposed heavy penalties (fines/punishments) on any foreigner found abusing Mutapa women; diplomatic negotiations with Portuguese authorities to establish rules of conduct; women could have been educated about the dangers posed by the Portuguese and advised to avoid contact; the Mutapa army could have been used to expel or punish abusive Portuguese individuals. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

questions.text:
(a) Identify any five items obtained by Missionaries from trade with the local people.
(b) Give an account of any six achievements made by Missionaries in Zimbabwe in the 19th century.
(c) New mining methods introduced by Missionaries led to land degradation. Suggest in essay form, any four measures Africans could have taken to prevent this land degradation.

subParts.label: (a)

subParts.label: (b)

subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Items obtained by Missionaries from trade with local people: ivory; gold; animal skins/hides; food (grain, cattle); timber/wood; crafts/pottery; slaves (in some contexts). (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Achievements of Missionaries in Zimbabwe in the 19th century: establishment of schools which brought formal Western education to Africans; establishment of hospitals and clinics which improved healthcare; translation of the Bible and other texts into local languages (e.g., Shona, Ndebele), helping preserve and formalise African languages; introduction of new agricultural techniques and crops improving food production; construction of roads and buildings (churches, schools, hospitals); training of African teachers and evangelists; abolition efforts — missionaries lobbied against the slave trade and abusive practices; introduction of Western skills such as carpentry, masonry, and printing. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Measures Africans could have taken to prevent land degradation caused by mining (essay form): Africans could have demanded that mining companies restore/rehabilitate land after extraction through negotiations with chiefs and colonial authorities; traditional leaders could have restricted mining to designated areas, protecting fertile farmland and sacred sites; Africans could have adopted reforestation/tree-planting programmes to replace vegetation destroyed by mining; lobbying/petitioning the colonial government to introduce environmental protection regulations on mining activities; communities could have redirected mine waste to less productive land to minimise damage to arable land; use of traditional conservation methods such as contour ridging and terracing to prevent soil erosion in areas affected by mining. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

questions.topic: The Prazo System in the Zambezi Valley
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Portuguese nationals who owned prazos: Dona Luisa de Gouveia e Melo; Sisnando Bayão; António Lobo da Silva; Gonçalo João; Pedro Caetano Pereira (Chicucuru); Inácio de Jesus Xavier; Dona Francisca de Moura. (Any 5 acceptable prazo holders, 1 mark each.)

(b) Methods used by Portuguese to acquire prazos: military conquest — using armed force to seize land from African chiefs; intermarriage with African women of royal families, which gave them land rights through inheritance; obtaining land as dowry upon marriage to African noblewomen; receiving land grants from the Portuguese Crown as rewards for service; purchasing land from African chiefs using trade goods; through diplomatic agreements and treaties with local rulers; by exploiting debts owed to them by African chiefs, taking land as payment. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Methods to make prazos more efficient (essay form): introduce organised and sustainable agricultural practices such as crop rotation and use of fertilisers to improve food production on prazo lands; employ skilled African farmers to work the land productively rather than using forced/slave labour which was inefficient; invest in irrigation systems to ensure water supply for crops during dry seasons; diversify crop production to include both food crops and cash crops to ensure food security; provide workers on prazos with adequate food, shelter, and tools so they could work productively; establish fair labour and taxation systems that motivated workers rather than driving them away; reduce the size of individual prazos so they could be managed more effectively. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

questions.text:
(a) List any three European powers which scrambled for Zimbabwe and any two political reasons for the colonisation of Zimbabwe.
(b) Describe any six social reasons that led to the colonisation of Zimbabwe.
(c) White settlers abused African women. Recommend in essay form, any four ways by which African Chiefs could have prevented this abuse.

subParts.text: List any three European powers which scrambled for Zimbabwe and any two political reasons for the colonisation of Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Describe any six social reasons that led to the colonisation of Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: White settlers abused African women. Recommend in essay form, any four ways by which African Chiefs could have prevented this abuse.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) European powers that scrambled for Zimbabwe: Britain; Portugal; Germany; Belgium; France. (Any 3, 1 mark each.) Political reasons for colonisation of Zimbabwe: to extend imperial/political power and prestige; to prevent other European powers from taking the territory (strategic rivalry); to establish strategic military bases; to control trade routes; desire to expand the British Empire by Cecil John Rhodes. (Any 2, 1 mark each.)

(b) Social reasons for the colonisation of Zimbabwe: desire to spread Christianity and 'civilise' Africans (missionary motive); to abolish the slave trade and other practices Europeans considered barbaric; overpopulation in Europe led to the need for new settlement areas; to provide adventure and exploration opportunities for young Europeans; racial superiority ideology — Europeans believed they had a duty to 'civilise' inferior races (White Man's Burden); to spread Western education and culture; humanitarian concerns about inter-tribal warfare in Africa; to provide a solution to European poverty by settling the poor in new lands. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Ways African Chiefs could have prevented abuse of African women by white settlers (essay form): chiefs could have enacted and enforced customary laws prohibiting settlers from fraternising with African women without consent and traditional protocols; chiefs could have stationed guards/warriors to protect women in areas near settler farms and towns; chiefs could have made formal complaints and petitions to colonial authorities demanding protection for their women; chiefs could have isolated their communities from settler communities by restricting movement and contact; traditional courts could have imposed penalties on settlers who abused African women; chiefs could have educated their communities, especially women, about the dangers and encouraged women to report abuses. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

questions.text:
(a) State any five economic reasons for the scramble for Africa.
(b) Give an account of any six terms of the Berlin Conference (1884 – 1885).
(c) Africa was unfairly treated by the powers at the Berlin Conference. Suggest, in essay form, any four measures Africans could have taken to protect their territories from European occupation.

subParts.label: (a)

questions.topic: The Scramble for Africa and the Berlin Conference
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Economic reasons for the scramble for Africa: search for raw materials (minerals, agricultural products) for European industries; need for new markets to sell European manufactured goods; need for investment opportunities for surplus European capital; desire to control trade routes, especially after the opening of the Suez Canal; search for cheap/free labour; desire to control African gold and diamond resources; need for land to settle surplus European populations. (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Terms of the Berlin Conference (1884–1885): the principle of effective occupation — a European power could only claim African territory if it actually occupied and administered it; the principle of free trade in the Congo Basin; the Niger and Congo rivers were to be open to free navigation by all nations; the slave trade was to be abolished in territories under European control; any European power wishing to claim African territory had to notify other powers (notification clause); the boundaries of existing European territories in Africa were to be respected; humanitarian considerations — European powers agreed to 'improve' the welfare of Africans (though largely ignored in practice); the Congo Free State was formally recognised as the personal property of King Leopold II of Belgium. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Measures Africans could have taken to protect their territories (essay form): African kingdoms and chiefs could have formed military alliances and united to present a stronger resistance to European occupation; Africans could have engaged in diplomatic negotiations and signed mutual protection treaties with each other; African leaders could have sent representatives to the Berlin Conference to argue for African interests (though they were not invited); Africans could have organised and modernised their armies by acquiring European weapons through trade to match European military power; African kingdoms could have signed carefully worded treaties with European powers that explicitly protected their sovereignty; communities could have used guerrilla warfare tactics to resist European encroachment effectively. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

questions.text:
(a) List any five military leaders of the British South Africa Company (BSAC).
(b) Describe any six causes of the Anglo-Ndebele war (1893 – 4).
(c) The Ndebele faced acute food shortages in the reserves. Suggest, in essay form, any four ways by which the Ndebele could have dealt with these food shortages.

subParts.text: List any five military leaders of the British South Africa Company (BSAC).
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Describe any six causes of the Anglo-Ndebele war (1893 – 4).
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: The Ndebele faced acute food shortages in the reserves. Suggest, in essay form, any four ways by which the Ndebele could have dealt with these food shortages.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Military leaders of the BSAC: Dr Leander Starr Jameson; Frederick Selous; Major Patrick Forbes; Colonel Herbert Plumer; Sir Frederick Carrington; Allan Wilson; Goold-Adams. (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Causes of the Anglo-Ndebele War (1893–94): BSAC's desire to seize Ndebele cattle and land, especially the fertile Matabeleland; the Ndebele raid on Shona villages (Lozwi/Shona people who were under supposed BSAC 'protection') provided a pretext for war; Rhodes and the BSAC wanted to extend British control northward and Lobengula's kingdom was an obstacle; the Rudd Concession (1888) gave BSAC mining rights but Lobengula felt deceived and tried to revoke it, causing tension; growing settler demand for land and the perception that Lobengula's impis threatened settler safety; Jameson's personal ambition to conquer Matabeleland and enrich himself and the Company through Ndebele cattle and land; Lobengula's attempts to maintain sovereignty and resist settler encroachment increased tensions; the BSAC needed a victory to attract investment and justify its existence. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Ways the Ndebele could have dealt with food shortages in the reserves (essay form): the Ndebele could have adopted new farming techniques such as irrigation and crop diversification to increase food production in the limited reserve land; they could have engaged in trade with neighbouring communities to obtain food in exchange for crafts or labour; the Ndebele could have petitioned colonial authorities for larger and more fertile reserve lands to increase agricultural productivity; community members could have taken up wage labour on settler farms or mines to earn money to purchase food; they could have adopted new crops introduced by missionaries or settlers that were better suited to the reserve environment; cooperative farming (communal efforts) could have been organised to maximise productivity on available land. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

questions.text:

(b) Describe any six benefits enjoyed by Africans from the mining activities of the settlers during the colonial period.
(c) Mine workers were not provided with safety clothing. Suggest, in essay form, any four ways by which the settlers could have improved the working conditions on the mines.

subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Towns established at mining sites during the colonial period: Gweru (Gwelo) — gold mining; Kadoma (Gatooma) — gold/cotton; Kwekwe (Que Que) — gold/steel; Shurugwi (Selukwe) — chrome; Mutare (Umtali) — gold; Hwange (Wankie) — coal; Bindura — nickel; Zvishavane (Shabanie) — asbestos. (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Benefits enjoyed by Africans from colonial mining: Africans gained wages/income through employment on the mines; development of infrastructure (roads, railways) linking mining towns benefited local communities; establishment of schools and hospitals in mining towns provided Africans with access to education and healthcare; Africans acquired new technical/mechanical skills working on mines; urbanisation created new social and cultural opportunities; mining towns became centres of commerce where Africans could trade; some Africans were able to purchase goods and improve their material standard of living; exposure to new technologies gave Africans knowledge they could later apply. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Ways settlers could have improved working conditions on mines (essay form): provide workers with appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) such as helmets, boots, gloves, and overalls to protect against mine hazards; introduce regular safety inspections and training programmes to educate mine workers about safety procedures; improve ventilation systems in underground mines to reduce dust and toxic gas exposure; establish first aid stations and medical facilities at mine sites to treat injured or ill workers; introduce reasonable working hours and rest periods to reduce fatigue-related accidents; provide adequate housing, clean water, and nutritious food for mine workers so they were physically fit to work safely. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

questions.text:
(a) State any five aims of the nationalist movements between 1950 and 1965.
(b) Outline any six political activities of the nationalist movements between 1950 and 1965.
(c) Sell-outs endangered the lives of both peasants and guerillas. Suggest in essay form, any four measures the guerillas could have taken to protect themselves.

subParts.text: State any five aims of the nationalist movements between 1950 and 1965.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Outline any six political activities of the nationalist movements between 1950 and 1965.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Sell-outs endangered the lives of both peasants and guerillas. Suggest in essay form, any four measures the guerillas could have taken to protect themselves.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Aims of nationalist movements (1950–1965): to achieve African majority rule/independence; to end racial discrimination and apartheid-like policies; to repeal unjust laws such as the Land Apportionment Act; to obtain equal economic opportunities for Africans; to gain the right to vote for all Zimbabweans regardless of race; to improve wages and working conditions for African workers; to achieve equal access to education and healthcare; to unite Africans against colonial rule. (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Political activities of nationalist movements (1950–1965): formation and registration of political parties (e.g., ANC, NDP, ZAPU, ZANU); organising mass meetings and political rallies to mobilise the African population; boycotts of colonial-owned businesses and services; strikes and work stoppages to demand better wages and political rights; petitioning and lobbying the colonial government and the British government for political reform; civil disobedience campaigns; sending delegations to Britain to appeal for constitutional changes; use of newspapers and radio to spread nationalist ideas and mobilise support. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Measures guerillas could have taken to protect themselves from sell-outs (essay form): guerillas could have maintained strict secrecy about their movements, locations, and plans so that sell-outs had limited information to pass on; they could have operated in small cells where only a few members knew each other's identities, limiting the damage any one sell-out could do; guerillas could have used trusted local networks and carefully vetted individuals before sharing sensitive information; they could have moved frequently and avoided establishing permanent bases to deny sell-outs the opportunity to report fixed locations; guerillas could have educated communities about the dangers of sell-outs and encouraged communities to report suspected informers; they could have established their own intelligence networks to identify and neutralise potential sell-outs before they caused damage. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

questions.text:
(a) State any five causes of the armed struggle of 1966 to 1979.
(b) Describe any six roles played by African women in the Second Chimurenga (1966 – 1979).
(c) Guerrillas lacked total support from the masses. Propose, in essay form, any four methods the guerillas could have used to gain total support of the masses.

subParts.text: State any five causes of the armed struggle of 1966 to 1979.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Describe any six roles played by African women in the Second Chimurenga (1966 – 1979).
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Guerrillas lacked total support from the masses. Propose, in essay form, any four methods the guerillas could have used to gain total support of the masses.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Causes of the armed struggle (1966–1979): failure of peaceful/political methods to achieve majority rule; Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence (UDI) in 1965 which entrenched white minority rule; the banning of ZAPU and ZANU and imprisonment of their leaders; racial discrimination, land dispossession, and economic exploitation of Africans; inspiration from other African liberation struggles (e.g., Mozambique, Angola, Algeria); the success of FRELIMO in Mozambique which gave Zimbabwean nationalists access to a front; failure of constitutional talks (e.g., Tiger and Fearless talks) to produce meaningful reform; Rhodesian security forces' brutal suppression of African political activity. (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Roles of African women in the Second Chimurenga: acting as mujibas — feeding, sheltering, and hiding guerillas; carrying and transporting weapons, food, and messages for guerillas; providing intelligence information about Rhodesian security forces' movements; serving as combatants/fighters in the liberation armies (ZANLA and ZIPRA); mobilising and politicising communities in support of the liberation struggle; nursing and caring for wounded fighters; cooking and washing for guerillas in the bush; singing revolutionary songs and performing at political meetings to raise morale; recruiting young men and women to join the liberation struggle. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Methods guerillas could have used to gain total support from the masses (essay form): hold pungwes (all-night political meetings) to educate and politicise the masses about the goals of the liberation struggle; treat the civilian population with respect, avoid theft and abuse so communities would willingly support them; provide practical assistance to communities such as helping with farming or resolving local disputes to build goodwill; explain the ideology of the liberation struggle clearly so that peasants understood what they were fighting for; involve local leaders (chiefs, elders) in the struggle to give it legitimacy in the eyes of the community; punish guerillas who mistreated civilians to demonstrate that the movement stood for justice. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

(c) Access to medical care is beyond the reach of the poor in Zimbabwe. Recommend in essay form, any four ways by which the government can make health care more accessible to the poor.

subParts.text: Name any five male ministers of health in post-Independence Zimbabwe.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Male Ministers of Health in post-Independence Zimbabwe: Herbert Ushewokunze; Simon Muzenda; Timothy Stamps; David Parirenyatwa; Henry Madzorera; Obadiah Moyo; Constantino Chiwenga (also VP). (Any 5 correct names, 1 mark each.)

(b) Measures taken by the Zimbabwean government to improve the health sector since 1980: construction and expansion of hospitals and rural health clinics bringing healthcare closer to communities; introduction of free healthcare at the point of use at government hospitals (particularly at independence); training and employment of more doctors, nurses, and other health workers; introduction of national immunisation/vaccination programmes to reduce child mortality from preventable diseases; establishment of the National Pharmaceutical Company (NatPharm) to ensure supply of medicines; introduction of AIDS/HIV awareness campaigns and antiretroviral treatment programmes; maternal and child health programmes to reduce maternal and infant mortality; health education campaigns to promote hygiene and disease prevention. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Ways to make healthcare more accessible to the poor (essay form): the government could introduce a social welfare/health insurance scheme that subsidises or covers the cost of medical care for low-income earners; increase the number of rural health centres and clinics so that poor people in remote areas do not have to travel far for treatment; train and deploy more community health workers (village health workers) who can provide basic healthcare at community level at little or no cost; provide free or heavily subsidised essential medicines through government pharmacies; launch mobile health clinics to take medical services to underserved and remote communities; waive user fees at government health facilities for identified vulnerable groups such as the elderly, children under five, and the chronically ill. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

(b) Outline any six children's responsibilities in Zimbabwe.

questions.topic: Children's Rights, Education and Youth Issues in Zimbabwe
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Organisations in partnership with the government to promote children's education: UNICEF; UNESCO; CAMFED (Campaign for Female Education); World Vision; Plan International; Save the Children; USAID; DFID/UK Aid; Catholic Relief Services; Zimbabwe Community Development Trust (ZIMCDET). (Any 5, 1 mark each.)

(b) Children's responsibilities in Zimbabwe: to attend school regularly and work hard in their studies; to respect and obey their parents, guardians, and teachers; to help with household chores appropriate to their age; to take care of younger siblings when asked; to respect the property of others and the community; to uphold and observe the cultural values and norms of their community; to conserve the environment by not littering or destroying natural resources; to report abuse or criminal activity to appropriate authorities; to care for their own health and hygiene. (Any 6, 2 marks each.)

(c) Government measures to prevent drug and substance abuse by youths (essay form): introduce comprehensive drug and substance abuse education programmes in schools to educate young people about the dangers of drugs from an early age; provide recreational facilities (sports centres, youth clubs, arts centres) to give young people positive and constructive activities to occupy their time; establish rehabilitation centres that offer affordable or free counselling and treatment for youth affected by drug abuse; enforce strict laws against the sale and supply of illegal drugs and alcohol to minors, with heavy penalties for offenders; run public awareness campaigns using media (radio, TV, social media) to inform parents, teachers, and communities about signs of drug abuse and how to respond; create youth employment programmes to reduce idleness and economic desperation, which are common drivers of drug abuse. (Any 4, well-argued in essay form, 2 marks each, up to 8.)

B Editing

D Mastering
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Capturing. Capturing (recording the raw audio/sound) is the very first step; mixing, editing, and mastering follow afterwards.

questions.text:
The most popular medium to market a music show to the youth in Zimbabwe is
A print media.
B social media.
C email marketing.
D door to door promotion.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – social media. Social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, TikTok, etc.) are the most widely used and effective channels for reaching youth audiences in Zimbabwe.

questions.text:
The classical sonata consists of three main sections which are
A exposition, development, and recapitulation.
B introduction, crescendo and finale.
C theme, variation and coda.
D prelude, interlude and postlude.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – exposition, development, and recapitulation. Classical sonata form is structured around these three sections: themes are introduced (exposition), developed/explored (development), and then restated (recapitulation).

questions.text:
Musicians can protect their works from piracy by
A keeping their works unpublished.
B registering their works with copyright office.
C avoiding distribution.
D ignoring copyright protection.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – registering their works with copyright office. Official registration provides legal proof of ownership and enables musicians to enforce their rights against piracy.

questions.text:
Two eighth notes last as long as a
A half note.
B quarter note.
C whole note.
D dotted quarter note.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – quarter note. Two eighth notes (quavers) each last half a beat, totalling one beat, which equals one quarter note (crotchet).

questions.text:
The following are notes in E major except
A F#
B C#
C D#
D B#
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – B#. The E major scale contains: E, F#, G#, A, B, C#, D#, E. B# is not a member of the E major scale; the 5th degree is a natural B.

questions.text:
Which note is the 7th in the A minor scale?
A B
B G
C D
D A
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – G. The A natural minor scale is: A, B, C, D, E, F, G. The 7th degree is G.

questions.text:
In choral music, mm = 60 means
A 60 crotchet beats per minute.
B 60 crotchet beats in the song.
C the song is 60 minutes long.
D the song has 60 bars.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – 60 crotchet beats per minute. 'mm' stands for Maelzel's Metronome; mm = 60 indicates the tempo is 60 beats (crotchets) per minute.

D G

questions.aiModelAnswer: D – G major. The melody shown uses notes consistent with the G major scale (one sharp: F#), indicating it is in G major.

questions.text:
In the key of C major, G is the
A dominant.
B mediant.
C sub mediant.
D leading.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – dominant. In C major, the scale degrees are: C (tonic), D (supertonic), E (mediant), F (subdominant), G (dominant), A (submediant), B (leading tone). G is the 5th degree – the dominant.

questions.text:
Which note is the fifth degree of the C Major?
A E
B G
C A
D F
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – G. The C major scale is C, D, E, F, G, A, B. The fifth degree (dominant) is G.

questions.text:
Valorisation of music instruments involves
A exporting them at a loss.
B importing them at a profit.
C improving their value.
D phasing them out.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – improving their value. Valorisation refers to the process of enhancing or increasing the worth/value of instruments, often through promotion, preservation, or cultural recognition.

questions.text:
A talking drum is an indigenous instrument of
A West Africa.
B Southern Africa.
C Central Africa.
D East Africa.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – West Africa. The talking drum (e.g., the 'dundun' among the Yoruba) is a traditional hourglass-shaped drum originating from West Africa.

questions.text:
___________________ is a musical period for the development of polyphony.
A Medieval
B Renaissance
C Baroque
D Classical
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – Renaissance. The Renaissance period (c. 1400–1600) is particularly noted for the flourishing development of polyphony, with composers such as Palestrina writing complex multi-voice choral music.

questions.text:
Which of the following is an aspect of copyright act?
A It lasts indefinitely.
B It protects ideas rather than expressions.
C It grants exclusive rights to creators.
D It applies only to written works.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – It grants exclusive rights to creators. Copyright law grants creators exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, perform, and display their works. It does not last indefinitely, does not protect ideas (only expressions), and applies to many types of works beyond writing.

questions.text:

B Crotchet rest
C Minim rest
D Semibreve rest
questions.diagramNote: A musical rest symbol is shown; students must identify which rest it represents.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – Semibreve rest. The semibreve (whole note) rest appears as a filled rectangle hanging below a staff line. Students should match the symbol shown to the correct rest name.

questions.text:
_______________ is known for popularizing the Chimurenga genre.
A Oliver Mtukudzi
B Thomas Mapfumo
C Jayz Marabini
D Bio Mudhimba
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – Thomas Mapfumo. Thomas Mapfumo, known as 'The Lion of Zimbabwe,' is widely credited with popularizing and pioneering the Chimurenga music genre.

questions.text:
An element of music which represents time is
A tone.
B texture.
C rhythm.
D melody.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – rhythm. Rhythm is the element of music that organises sound in time, encompassing beat, meter, tempo, and duration of notes.

questions.text:
A musical technique related to rhythm is
A syncopation.
B crescendo.
C progression.
D polyphonic.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – syncopation. Syncopation is a rhythmic technique where emphasis is placed on normally weak beats or off-beats, creating a sense of rhythmic surprise or groove.

questions.text:
What is the notation of this melody?
d . d : s . s
f . f : d . -
A tonic solfa
B number
C tablature
D staff
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – tonic solfa. The melody is written using syllables (d, s, f) which are characteristic of tonic solfa notation, a system using moveable-doh syllables (doh, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti).

questions.text:
Sharps or flats at the beginning of a musical piece is called
A bass clef.
B key signature.
C treble clef.
D time signature.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – key signature. The key signature is the collection of sharps or flats placed at the beginning of a piece of music (after the clef) to indicate the key of the piece.

questions.text:
_______________ is a third Chimurenga/Umvukela composer.
A Winky D
B Elliot Manyika
C Thomas Mapfumo
D Lovemore Majaivana
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Winky D. Winky D (Wallace Chirumiko) is associated with the third Chimurenga/Umvukela movement, using music to address contemporary socio-political issues in Zimbabwe.

questions.text:
____________ songs motivated fighters during Chimurenga/Umvukela war.
A Work
B Lullaby
C Wedding
D War
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – War. War songs (also known as pungwe songs or chimurenga songs) were used to motivate, inspire, and rally fighters during the Zimbabwean liberation struggle.

questions.text:
Which genre is known for its fast-paced guitar rhythms in Zimbabwe?
A Mbaqanga
B Chimurenga
C Sungura
D Jazz
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Sungura. Sungura is a Zimbabwean music genre characterised by its fast-paced, intricate guitar rhythms and energetic dance style, popularised by artists such as Alick Macheso.

questions.text:
Branding helps musicians to
A create new music.
B manage their finances.
C create a fan base.
D reduce operating cash.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – create a fan base. Branding helps musicians establish a unique identity and image that attracts and retains loyal fans, thereby building and growing their fan base.

questions.text:
___________ genre emerged as a form of protest music during the Zimbabwean liberation struggle.
A Jazz
B Chimurenga
C Reggae
D Afrobeat
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – Chimurenga. Chimurenga music emerged as protest and liberation music during Zimbabwe's independence struggle, fusing traditional mbira sounds with modern instruments to convey political messages.

questions.text:
_________________ music style developed in Zimbabwean townships during the 1960s.
A Gumboot dance musical style
B Chimurenga music style
C Makwaira music style
D Kanindo music style
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Makwaira music style. Makwaira is a music and dance style that developed in Zimbabwean townships during the 1960s, blending traditional and urban musical influences.

questions.text:
___________ genre is from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
A Soukous
B Afrobeat
C Bongo flava
D Highlife
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Soukous. Soukous (also known as Congo music or rumba congolaise) originated in the Democratic Republic of Congo, characterised by its guitar-driven sound and fast dance rhythms.

questions.text:
________________ was a Baroque composer.
A Francesco Landini
B Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
C Ludwig van Beethoven
D George Frideric Handel
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – George Frideric Handel. Handel (1685–1759) was a prominent Baroque composer, known for works such as the Messiah. Landini was Medieval, Palestrina was Renaissance, and Beethoven was Classical/Romantic.

questions.text:
Which musical instrument is associated with ritual songs in Zimbabwean cultures?
A Chigufe
B Izikeyi
C Mbira
D Djembe
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Mbira. The mbira (thumb piano) is deeply embedded in Zimbabwean Shona culture and is central to ritual ceremonies such as the bira, used to communicate with ancestral spirits (vadzimu).

questions.text:
"Aerophone" refers to instruments that produce sound through vibrating
A strings.
B membranes.
C air.
D solid materials.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – air. Aerophones are instruments that produce sound primarily through the vibration of a column of air (e.g., flute, trumpet, recorder). Chordophones use strings, membranophones use membranes, and idiophones use solid materials.

questions.text:
_______________ is often performed during rain making ceremonies in Zimbabwe.
A Dinhe
B Isitshikitsha
C Mhande
D Mbende
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – Mhande. Mhande is a traditional Korekore/Shona ceremonial dance and music style performed during rain-making (mukwerere) ceremonies in Zimbabwe.

questions.text:
When recording music, monitoring refers to
A mixing.
B editing.
C listening.
D mastering.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – listening. In a recording studio context, monitoring refers to listening to the audio playback through studio monitor speakers or headphones to assess the sound quality and make informed decisions.

questions.text:
____________ is not found in the music recording studio.
A Live room
B Control room
C Isolation booth
D Superior room
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – Superior room. A standard music recording studio consists of a live room (where recording takes place), a control room (where engineers operate equipment), and isolation booths. A 'superior room' is not a recognised studio component.

questions.text:
____________ is the process of reducing a video size.
A Filtering
B Screen casting
C Formatting
D Compressing
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – Compressing. Video compression is the process of encoding video data to reduce its file size while maintaining acceptable quality, making it easier to store and distribute.

questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Renaissance. Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (c. 1525–1594) was one of the most celebrated composers of the Renaissance period, renowned for his sacred polyphonic choral compositions.
