questions.aiModelAnswer:
Students choose ONE topic only and write 300–350 words. Marks are awarded across four main criteria (content/ideas, organisation/structure, language use/style, and mechanical accuracy). Key marking guidance per topic:

(a) Letter (Incwadi): Correct letter format — address, date, salutation, body, closing. Content: specific activities done to keep school clean (picking litter, sweeping classrooms, cutting grass, etc.). Vivid, personal tone.

(b) Essay — 'Inhlanzi itshelwe ngamanzi' (A fish warned by water — proverb meaning one ignores advice from those closest to them): Creative narrative or discursive essay illustrating the proverb with a relevant story or argument. Clear moral conclusion.

(c) Narrative story containing the words '…wakhamisa umlomo esizwa okwenziwa ngumntanakhe' (he/she gaped open-mouthed upon hearing what his/her child had done): Story must organically include the given sentence. Plot: character is shocked/stunned by a child's action. Good use of narrative devices: setting, rising action, climax, resolution.

(d) Essay — 'Ubuhle lobubi besiko lokungena esiNtwini' (The merits and demerits of the Intwi initiation custom): Balanced argument — merits (cultural identity, rite of passage, community cohesion) vs. demerits (health risks, expense, abuse). Conclusion with personal stance.

(e) Dialogue (Ingxoxo) between two students on the importance of the internet at school: Correct dialogue format with named speakers. Points for internet: research, e-learning, communication. Points against: distraction, misuse, cost. Resolution or conclusion reached.

(f) Narrative — 'Izulu lesiqhotho elangithola ngisemangweni' (The hailstorm that caught me in the veld): First-person narrative. Setting in the open veld; description of the approaching storm, the hailstorm experience, fear, shelter sought, aftermath. Vivid descriptive language.

(g) Essay — 'Izindlela zayizolo zokuzilibazisa esigabeni sakithi' (Past forms of entertainment in our area): Description of traditional entertainment: traditional dances (isitshikitsha, ingquzu), storytelling (izinganekwane), stick-fighting, traditional games. Comparison with modern entertainment optional. Nostalgic/reflective tone.

General mark allocation (all topics): Content & relevance 20 / Organisation 10 / Language & style 10 / Accuracy (grammar, spelling, punctuation) 10 = 50 marks.

questions.text:
Fundisisa indatshana elandelayo ube usuphendula imibuzo elandelayo.

Kwavunwa, kwabhulwa aphekwa amatshwala njengakudala. Ingani lilungile nje leliBhunu? Pho kanti kungani lingavuli eyalo insimu? Kanti lona alilandaba lokulima na? Le ngeminye yemibuzo ababezibuza yona abantu uma behlangene kodwa kungabi khona olempendulo. Sesisondele isikhathi sokulima awuthela awuyekela amadoda umquba. Abanye baqhelisa imilimela yabo besenzela ukulima isancapha engqathweni. Laphazima empumalanga. Laphazima entshonalanga. Bathokoza obaba. Yezwakala insingizi emnyama, isangoma sezomkhathi, ibikela uzulu ukuthi nanti selisemnyango, akulungiswe izikhali. Dukuduku sebebiziwe njalo abadala koNile. Kwenzenjani njalo?

'Madoda, mina, nikile lina sikhathi side kuthi licabange kumbe lina hlala lapha kumbe lina hamba,' kususa uNile ebobotheka.
'Uthini?' Kubuza enye indoda.
'Thula silalele,' kuphendula enye.
'Kodwa utheni?' Kubuza eyakuqala.
'Ake uthule mani silalele,' kuphendula eyesibili ngokunengwa.
'Nx!' kunxapha eyokuqala.

Bathule nje sebemangele abantu. 'Lihlezi lapha mhlaba kamina. Lungile. Mina funa kuhlala nalina. Kodwa mina azikho nsimu. Lina khona masimu makhulu. Mina yazi quma masimu onke kuthi lina thatha munye ngxenye, mina thatha munye.'
'Hayikhona,' bavungama abantu. 'Ungathatha amasimu ethu njani?' usenguDube lowo esemi.

Aqhubeke, 'Amasimu la sazivulela. Khathesi sesithele lemiquba yethu, manje ususithi uyasithathela. Njani?'
'Wena madala, mina yazi tshaya wena sikhathi wena mbuluza lapha. Kabani lo mhlaba? Kawena kumbe kamina?' Labuza ngolaka iBhunu. Wathi votshololo uDube esekhumbula lokhuya elake lamenza khona leliBhunu. Selingazani selichithisiwe manje iBhunu livuke ubuBhunu balo.

'Madoda, mina kade lungile kakhulu kodwa lina bona mina sithutha. He? Ya mina vukile manje. Masimu mina quma. Nkomo zenu liyathengisa lapha kamina. Londoda iyasala lankomo theni kuphela. Lonkomo kalina yena qeda lotshani kamina.'

Wabe uliqalile iNdebele lapho esethinta isibaya salo. Athi lothu amadoda esengahambayo. Phakathi kokuxokozela okukhulu lezwakala ilizwi lisithi baphiwa izinsuku ezinhlanu kuphela ukuthi bathuthe. Kungenziwanga lokho iyotshiswa imizana yabo zithunjwe lezifuyo zabo. Awu! Awuzange ukubone ukuphithizela okunje empilweni yakho. Abanye ngabazama ukumema umhlangano wangasese ukuze babonisane ngabangakwenza njengoba izinto sezimi manzonzo kanje. Akukho ukuvumelana phakathi kwabantu. Nampa sebetshelana ubugwala. Sebeze bephosa baxabane bodwa. ODube laboMthombeni bona bacebisa abantu ukuthi bakuhlasele ebusuku bakutshisele endlini okuliBhunu lokho. Kakho owavumelana labo ngoba bonke besesaba ukubotshwa.

Kwangazani amadlozi lawo asebafulathele lababantu ngoba ambheka sazimungula uMdali evula izintuba zasezulwini, lawohloka izulu. Ngezangayizolo izinsuku bekuzathokoza uzulu ngoba obaba sebezaphuma bayeqhwayela abantwana lonondlini wabo esezakudla uhlaza abe ngunyonintshantshaza woqobo. Kodwa elalamhlanje laphenduka labayisithuko kubantu.

Amanye amadoda athi kungcono ayedinga izindawo, amanye akubona kungcono ukuthi ahle abophele ahambe edinga izindawo intundu isemakhanda. Kwanyakazela – ke lo eqonda eZansi lowaya elubhekise eNyakatho. Lawohloka njalo izulu labagxanxa labenza okunye. Badubeka abantu beNkosi. Abanye bahamba baze bayawela eMandombe, abanye eZuzumbe, abanye bayazilahlela eSinangeni seMkhalandoda, enkangala yoqobo. Labana abazama ukucaba imizi lapha eMkhalandoda abafulathela njalo amadlozi izinkomo sezidle okungadliwayo, zafa kwangazani ziyahlola. Phela leligusu liyisigodlo somthakatshana lo obizwa kuthiwe ngumkhawuzane. Nampo sebethutha njalo abanye basondela ngeNgigeni kwathi abanye bathi eNgigeni kuseduze leMtshaphi hlezi iBhunu lithi yonke lindawo ingaphakathi komgcele walo. Badabula ilizwe baze bayawela khonala eFafe endaweni eyayingakanukelwa yimpucuko. Bakha imizi yabo, bahlala, bazimisela ukuyiphucula lindawo.

Labaya abathi kungcono baqale ngokuyadinga indawo bathi sebephenduka bathola imizi isingamanxiwa, iBhunu selasala lidudula amanina lezingane kwabalekwa kwayaquthwa emasesiteni eRoma (Loreto) izimpahla zasala zichitheka.

Ithethwe egwalweni: Sisemhlabeni olulotshwe ngu J.P. Ndebele. College Press.

Model answers for each sub-part:

(d) Izinkomo ezisalayo kwakungezona theni kuphela (izinkomo ezincane / one animal each) — izakhamizi zizabeshiywa inkomo eyodwa ngamunye, izinye zithengiswa eBhunwini. [1 mark]

(e) Izakhamizi zaphiwa izinsuku ezinhlanu (5 days) ukuthi zithuthe. [1 mark]

(f) Amazwi afana la: 'Londoda iyasala lankomo theni kuphela' / 'Nkomo zenu liyathengisa lapha kamina' / 'Lonkomo kalina yena qeda lotshani kamina' — la mazwi aveza ukuthi izinkomo kwakuyiminikelo yezakhamizi ebalulekileyo, kwaze kwadingeka uNile atshele izakhamizi ukuthi zizabeshiywa inkomo kuphela. [2 marks — 1 mark per valid quotation/point, max 2]

(g) Izizatho ezimbili: (i) Amasimu abo bawavulela bona uqobo bawatshala bembelembeleka. (ii) Besesethele umquba wabo emasimwini abo, ngakho amasimu ayesekulungele ukulima. [2 marks — 1 mark per reason]

(h) Ingozi: IBhunu laligcina abantu abacaphukayo, abalesifiso sokuphindisela futhi abanye (uDube loMthombeni) sebalicebisa abantu ukuthi balitshisele endlini / baliphindiselele ebusuku. Ngakho-ke iBhunu lalifaka impilo yalo engozini yokuhlasela / ukubulawa. [2 marks]

(i) IBhunu lalidelela abantu abamnyama ngokuba: (i) lathetha amadoda ngolimi oluqinileyo olwehlisayo ('Wena madala, mina yazi tshaya wena'); (ii) lathatha amasimu abo ngendluzula langokunganaki imizamo yabo yokutshala; (iii) ladudula amanina lezingane ngodlame. [2 marks — 1 mark per valid point]

(j) AmaBhunu avezwe njengabantu abalesiphatho esibuhlungu, esinesihluku, esingenhlonipho, abanobandlululo — bayelwa ngamasimu, bethuka abantu abamnyama, baphuca abantu imihlaba yabo ngodlame nangokungalandeli umthetho. [2 marks]

(k) Imininingwane yamazwi:
(i) 'selisemnyango' — selifikile / seseduze kakhulu; (izulu) seligcwalele lingena / liseduze lokufika. [1]

- IBhunu lafuna uquma amasimu abo azabela izakhamizi kanye ngalinye.

questions.topic: Language Structures / Ulimi — Izaga, Izifenqo, Isichazamazwi
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Model answers:

(a) Izaga ezifanayo nezincazelo ezikhanyisiweyo (match proverb to meaning):
(i) 'Owehlulekileyo angalahli ithemba' — Isaga esihambelanayo: e.g. 'Ungadinwa ngukulindela' / umuntu okwehlulekileyo akamele ayeke ukuzama. [1]
(ii) 'Izinto ziyonakala umuntu esithi ukhangele, uyabona okwenzakalayo' — e.g. 'Inkunzi isematholeni' / izinto ziyenzeka ngaphambi kokuba umuntu azibike. [1]
(iii) 'Izenzo zomuntu zibonakala esasemncane ukuthi angakhula uzakuba ngumuntu onjani' — Isaga: 'Inkwenkwe ibonwa ebusweni bayo' / 'Indlela ibuzwa kwabaphambili'. [1]
(iv) 'Abahlala besilwa bangachithekelwa ngumuzi' — e.g. 'Umuntu ongagezanga izandla kudliwa laye' / ukusilwa kuchithekelisa. [1]
(v) 'Osebunzimeni kazame ukuzinceda' — e.g. 'Isandla sihlamba esinye' / uzincede wena kuqala. [1]
(Note: Accept any appropriate isiNdebele proverb that matches the given meaning.)

(b) Imihlobo yezifenqo — imitsho:
(i) Ukwenzasamuntu (personification): e.g. 'Izulu lakhala ebusuku.' (The sky cried at night.) [1]
(ii) Inhlonipho (euphemism): e.g. 'Ubaba useyindoda enkulu manje.' (Father has passed on / is now an old man — used euphemistically for death.) [1]
(iii) Isiqathaniso (simile): e.g. 'Ubaleka njengempala.' (He runs like an impala.) [1]
(iv) Isingakethiso (hyperbole): e.g. 'Ngidlile ukudla kwezintaba namuhla.' (I ate food of mountains today — I ate a huge amount.) [1]
(v) Ukubhuqa (onomatopoeia): e.g. 'Amanzi abhavuma egelezela phansi.' (The water gushed/roared as it flowed down.) [1]

(c) Izincazelo zabantu:
(i) Umjimbi — umuntu othandayo ukudla izidlo ezinkulu / umuntu ohamba emijimbini (feasts) njalo njengesiqhelo; idili. [1]
(ii) Inxele — umuntu osebenzisa isandla sokhohlo njengoba abanye besebenzisa esokunene; isibomu. [1]
(iii) Izibulo — ingane yokuqala kwabantwana; izibulo lomzali. [1]
(iv) Impumputhe — umuntu ongaboniyo / ongenazo izimfokazana zokukhangela / umpumputhe. [1]
(v) Intandane — ingane elahlekwe ngunina lobaba bobabili / ingane engelamzali. [1]

(d) Izincazelo zamagama:
(i) Izulu elina lichophelela — isithwathwa / umzangulu / isichotho (isiNdebele: 'isichotho' — hail/sleet falling lightly from rain). [1]
(ii) Umuthi ophiwa izinja ukuze zibebukhali ekuzingeleni — isihlahla/umuthi wokukhuthaza izinja ekuzingeni; uhlobo lomuthi wesintu (traditional medicine for hunting dogs). [1]
(iii) Intuthu ebonakala ebusika isenziwa yikutshisa kwelanga — inkungu / umusi obonakala entabeni noma emanzini ngenxa yokushisa kwelanga (mist/steam/fog). [1]
(iv) Ingowane eyenziwa ngesigogo lensiba eyandise ukuthwalwa yizangoma — umnqwazi / isigqoko sangoma essenziwa ngesigogo lensiba (the traditional headdress/hat made of animal skin and feathers worn by izangoma). [1]
(v) Ukuhluma kwezihlahla entwasa — intwasahlobo / ukukhula kwamawa / ukukhula kwezihlahla entshongweni yomnyaka (the sprouting/budding of trees in spring). [1]

questions.text:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.

Ndapa and her father at ten to seven. The two men stood at Joseph's pickup while Ndapa and Tangeni checked if they got between them what was needed for the field work. Ndapa showed Tangeni the bag of apples and oranges she bought for the children as a treat.
"We have to buy a few of their semi-precious stones to exhibit together with our project," Ndapa said. "I'll get plastic bags and cotton wool for the stones." Tangeni disappeared into the house. Mr Shikongo took a few hundred dollars from his wallet and put them into Joseph's shirt pocket. "For petrol" he said. "It's too much," Joseph protested. "The fuel price has gone sky high. It's about 250 kilometres to the Spitzkoppe; that makes 500 in total." Joseph put his hand on the rusty bonnet of his pickup. "Old, but still doing a good job," he said proudly. A look of regret came into Mr Shikongo's eyes. "I wish I could join you and leave the work behind me for a day in the desert. I have very little time for my children, unfortunately. Thank you for helping my daughter." "One day, Joseph said, "it may be the other way around, and it might be you helping my son." Mr Shikongo stood looking after them when the pick drove off. Ndapa sat in front between Joseph and Tangeni. When they had left Windhoek, Tangeni could wait no longer and said "Dad I've got a proposal to make." "Yes?" "Could you give me a suspended sentence of a month?" "What do you mean by a suspended sentence?" Joseph said. He could not keep a note of irritation from his voice. He was still nauseous, and driving in a car did not improve the situation. "I mean, please let me go and practise football next week" Tangeni said. "You're grounded." "If I fail a test again you can ground me, for a longer period if you want to. That's what I mean."

(a) What cultural values are revealed in the passage? [10]
(b) Write an account of how Mr Shikongo later helps Tongai in the story. [15]

questions.topic: Extra Time – Cultural Values and Character Actions
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Cultural values revealed in the passage (10 marks – award 2 marks per well-explained point, up to 5 points):
• Communal solidarity/ubuntu: Joseph willingly takes Ndapa and Tangeni to the Spitzkoppe, showing community members help one another's children.
• Reciprocity: Joseph tells Mr Shikongo 'one day it may be the other way around and it might be you helping my son' – the culture expects that favours are returned.
• Parental responsibility and sacrifice: Mr Shikongo expresses regret that work keeps him away from his children, showing the value placed on parenting.
• Generosity/hospitality: Mr Shikongo insists on giving Joseph money for petrol despite Joseph's protest; Ndapa buys fruits for the children.
• Respect and discipline: Tangeni negotiates respectfully with his father and accepts the authority of his punishment (being grounded), reflecting a culture where children respect parental authority.
• Hard work/resourcefulness: The pride Joseph takes in his old but functional pickup reflects a value of making do with what one has.

(b) Account of how Mr Shikongo later helps Tongai (15 marks – award marks for accurate, detailed and well-structured narrative):
Students should recount the relevant episode from the novel where Mr Shikongo reciprocates by assisting Joseph's son Tongai. Key points to include:
• The circumstances that create Tongai's need for help (e.g., academic/personal difficulty).
• Mr Shikongo's specific intervention – using his position, connections or resources to assist Tongai.
• The outcome/impact of his help on Tongai.
• The connection back to the promise/theme of reciprocity established in the passage.
(Award marks proportionally based on accuracy of detail, narrative coherence, and relevance.)

questions.text: Show that Extra Time is a suitable title for the novel.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
A well-structured essay (25 marks) should cover the following key points:
• Literal meaning – 'Extra Time' is a football term referring to additional playing time given when a match is tied; Tangeni's love of football and his grounding from football practice is central to the plot.
• Metaphorical meaning – 'Extra Time' symbolises second chances and opportunities given to characters: Tangeni negotiates a 'suspended sentence' (extra time) to prove himself; children at the Spitzkoppe community get extra time/attention through the visit.
• Thematic link to time/childhood – the story explores children making the most of the limited time of youth; adults like Mr Shikongo lament having 'very little time' for their children.
• Structural relevance – events of the story take place over an extended day/field trip, which is itself an 'extra' day outside routine.
• The title captures the essence of hope and renewal running through the novel.
Award marks for: clear argument, use of textual evidence, well-organised paragraphs, insight into theme and title connection.

questions.text: Describe relationships explored in the novel, Extra Time.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
A well-structured essay (25 marks) should identify and discuss a range of relationships:
• Father-son relationship (Joseph and Tangeni): tension over discipline (grounding), negotiation, underlying love and mutual respect.
• Father-daughter relationship (Mr Shikongo and Ndapa): Mr Shikongo's guilt over limited time with his daughter; his generosity as a substitute for presence.
• Friendship/peer relationships (Ndapa and Tangeni): cooperation in preparing for the field trip; mutual support.
• Community/neighbourly relationships: Joseph and Mr Shikongo – mutual respect, generosity, and reciprocity between families.
• Adult-child relationships broadly: adults act as mentors and guides to children during the Spitzkoppe trip.
• Relationships with nature/environment: the visit to Spitzkoppe fosters a relationship between the children and the natural world.
Award marks for: identification of at least 3–4 relationships, textual evidence, analysis of how relationships are portrayed, and comment on thematic significance.

questions.text:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.

The Great Valley is at peace now; the deep wound which man inflicted is healing, for he has come to terms with Nature, and Nature, perhaps with him. Both are receiving the benefits from the forming of the lake. For man there is the hydro-electric power for his homes and industries in Zimbabwe and in Zambia, with a vast playground for his leisure, where he can gain new knowledge of Nature's ways. For Nature, there is a sanctuary for all her children of the Great Valley in the areas which border the lake, and there is the lake itself. In one area, where the sweet grass, so beloved by the Pambuka herd of impalas, grows again along a curving beach the descendants of Kali-Anuka are thriving. You may, should you journey to Kariba, come across the impalas in some Utopian glade, close to the lake shore; do not expect them to approach you, trustingly, as Kali-Anuka and others approached Ijongojongo, long ago. For the words of Kali-Anuka are remembered by the Pambuka herd, and all the impalas in the Great Valley. "There are good and bad Zimikile," he had often said, "I am never able to tell the difference." Perhaps he knows now, and Tantalika, too, for neither of them still roams through the wild Zambezi Valley. Nor does Ijongojongo.

(a) How is a happy atmosphere created in the passage? [10]
(b) Give an account of the incident when the animals were taken to a place of safety by the Zimikiles. [15]

questions.topic: The Valley of Tantalika – Atmosphere and Operation Noah
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Happy atmosphere (10 marks – 2 marks per point, up to 5 points):
• Opening statement 'The Great Valley is at peace now' immediately establishes calm and resolution.
• The metaphor of healing ('the deep wound…is healing') conveys optimism and recovery.
• Reference to 'thriving' descendants of Kali-Anuka shows life continuing and prospering.
• Description of a 'Utopian glade' evokes an idealistic, paradise-like setting.
• Sweet grass growing again symbolises renewal and abundance.
• The coexistence of man and Nature ('come to terms with') creates a hopeful, harmonious tone.
• The legacy of Kali-Anuka living on through his herd gives a sense of continuity and hope.

(b) Account of animals taken to safety by the Zimikiles (15 marks):
Students should describe the 'Operation Noah' rescue episode:
• As the Kariba Dam was being built, the rising waters of the lake flooded the valley, trapping animals on shrinking islands.
• The Zimikiles (humans) launched boat rescue operations to save stranded animals.
• Animals such as impalas, snakes, and various other wildlife were captured and transported to the safety of the game reserve/higher ground.
• Tantalika, Kali-Anuka, and the Pambuka herd were among those rescued.
• The rescue reflected both the destructive and compassionate aspects of humans.
• Award marks for: accurate detail, narrative sequence, mention of specific animals/characters, and reflection on significance of the event.

questions.text: Imagine you are Tantalika, write a letter to Fura Uswa telling him about the challenges faced by the Pambuka herd during the construction of the dam.
questions.topic: The Valley of Tantalika – Challenges During Dam Construction (Creative Writing)
questions.aiModelAnswer:
A well-crafted letter (25 marks) written in Tantalika's voice should include:
• Correct letter format: greeting, body paragraphs, closing (award up to 3 marks for format).
• First-person narrative from Tantalika's perspective.
• Challenges to include:
  – Loss of habitat as the valley flooded and grasslands disappeared.
  – Separation of the herd from familiar territory.
  – Danger from rising waters – animals drowning or stranded on islands.
  – Noise, disruption, and fear caused by the dam construction machinery and human presence.
  – Uncertainty about the Zimikiles – are they friend or foe? (echoing Kali-Anuka's words).
  – Scarcity of food/sweet grass as the land was submerged.
  – The trauma of being captured and relocated during Operation Noah.
• Emotional tone: fear, confusion, loss, but also perhaps gratitude towards the kind Zimikiles.
• Vivid, descriptive language appropriate to the animal's perspective.
Award marks for: accuracy to the novel, use of first-person voice, emotional depth, descriptive language, letter format, and fluency.

questions.text: To what extent are human beings responsible for the destruction of the environment in the Valley of Tantalika?
questions.topic: The Valley of Tantalika – Human Responsibility and Environment
questions.aiModelAnswer:
A balanced essay (25 marks) should consider:
Arguments that humans ARE largely responsible:
• The decision to build the Kariba Dam deliberately flooded the Great Valley, destroying natural habitat.
• Human industrial and economic interests (hydro-electric power) were prioritised over environmental preservation.
• Animals were displaced, separated, and endangered by the construction.
• The flooding was an entirely man-made event – 'the deep wound which man inflicted'.

Arguments that qualify or limit human responsibility:
• Nature itself is dynamic and changes; floods and environmental shifts occur naturally.
• Humans also undertook Operation Noah to save animals, showing environmental responsibility.
• The passage suggests man and Nature eventually reach a balance ('come to terms').
• Benefits to both man and nature from the lake are acknowledged.

Conclusion: On balance, humans bear primary responsibility for the initial destruction, but the novel also shows human capacity for remediation and coexistence.
Award marks for: a clear argument, balance of perspectives, use of textual evidence from the novel, well-organised paragraphs, and a coherent conclusion.

questions.text:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.

Roderigo: What a full fortune does the thick-lips owe,
If he can carry it thus!
Iago: Call up her father,
Rouse him, make after him, poison his delight,
Proclaim him in the street, incense her kinsmen,
And though he in a fertile climate dwell,
Plague him with flies: though that his joy be joy,
Yet throw such chances of vexation on't
As it may lose some colour.
Roderigo: Here is her father's house; I'll call aloud.
Iago: Do, with like timorous accent and dire yell,
As when, by night and negligence, the fire
Is spied in populous cities.
Roderigo: What ho, Brabantio! Signior Brabantio, ho!
Iago: Awake! What ho, Brabantio! Thieves, thieves!
Look to your house, your daughter, and your bags,
Thieves, thieves!
[Brabantio appears above, at a window]
Brabantio: What is the reason of this terrible summons?
What is the matter there?
Roderigo: Signior, is all your family within?
Iago: Are your doors lock'd?
Brabantio: Why, wherefore ask you this?
Iago: Zounds, sir, you're robb'd; for shame, put on your gown;
Your heart is burst, you have lost half your soul;
Even now, now, very now, an old black ram
Is tupping your white ewe,
Arise, arise;
Awake the snorting citizens with the bell,
Or else the devil will make a grandsire of you.
Arise, I say!

(a) What emotions are aroused in you as you read the passage above? [10]
(b) Give an account of Brabantio's reaction to the news about the theft of his daughter. [15]

questions.topic: Othello – Iago's Manipulation and Brabantio's Reaction
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Emotions aroused (10 marks – 2 marks per well-explained emotion, up to 5 emotions):
• Disgust/revulsion: Iago's crude, racist language ('thick-lips', 'an old black ram is tupping your white ewe') is offensive and degrading.
• Tension/suspense: the urgency of Iago and Roderigo's midnight shouting creates dramatic tension.
• Anger/indignation: Iago's deliberate manipulation and stirring of racial hatred provokes moral outrage.
• Pity: for Brabantio, woken in the night and subjected to shocking news delivered cruelly.
• Anxiety/unease: Iago's calculated malice ('poison his delight') reveals a dangerous schemer at work, creating unease.
• Shock: the sudden, alarming nature of the cries ('Thieves! Thieves!') is jarring.

(b) Brabantio's reaction to the news (15 marks):
• Initially confused and alarmed at being woken by shouting.
• Disbelief – he cannot believe his daughter would elope with Othello without his consent.
• He goes to Desdemona's room and discovers she is indeed gone.
• He is overcome with grief, rage, and a sense of dishonour/betrayal.
• He accuses Othello of using witchcraft or charms to seduce Desdemona, unable to believe she would choose him freely.
• He mobilises kinsmen and takes the matter to the Duke, demanding justice.
• He confronts Othello publicly before the Senate, charging him with bewitching his daughter.
• When Desdemona publicly affirms her love for Othello, Brabantio is devastated and feels utterly rejected.
• He bitterly disowns Desdemona, warning Othello: 'She has deceived her father, and may thee.'
Award marks for: accurate details, narrative sequence, emotional depth of Brabantio's response, and relevant quotation/reference.

questions.text: What evidence would you give to prove that Iago is an evil character?
questions.aiModelAnswer:
A well-structured essay (25 marks) should present evidence under clear points:
• Iago's stated motive of jealousy and revenge: he resents Cassio's promotion and suspects Othello of sleeping with Emilia; his evil is calculated, not impulsive.
• Manipulation of Roderigo: he exploits Roderigo's love for Desdemona for financial gain ('I am not what I am').
• Racist stirring: he uses vile racial imagery to inflame Brabantio, showing cruelty and bigotry.
• The handkerchief plot: Iago plants Desdemona's handkerchief on Cassio to manufacture 'proof' of her infidelity – a premeditated act of deception.
• Psychological destruction of Othello: Iago systematically poisons Othello's mind with insinuations, turning love into murderous jealousy.
• Ordering Roderigo to kill Cassio: Iago is willing to orchestrate murder to protect himself.
• Killing Roderigo: when Roderigo becomes a liability, Iago kills him without hesitation.
• Killing Emilia: when his plot is exposed, he murders his own wife.
• His own admission: 'I am not what I am' and 'I am your own for ever' to Othello reveal his deceptive, Machiavellian nature.
Award marks for: clear argument, range and quality of evidence, use of quotation, analysis of how actions demonstrate evil, and coherent conclusion.

questions.text: To what extent is Othello responsible for his own downfall?
questions.topic: Othello – Othello's Responsibility for His Downfall
questions.aiModelAnswer:
A balanced essay (25 marks) should weigh Othello's own culpability against external factors:

Othello IS responsible:
• His insecurity as an outsider (race, background) makes him vulnerable to Iago's manipulation.
• His fatal flaw of jealousy: he succumbs rapidly to jealousy without sufficient proof.
• Credulity: he trusts Iago ('honest Iago') too readily and dismisses Desdemona's protestations.
• Pride: his military honour makes him unable to bear the thought of being cuckolded.
• Failure to communicate: he does not confront Desdemona openly and honestly.
• He acts precipitously – smothering Desdemona before investigating properly.

Othello is NOT fully responsible (mitigating factors):
• Iago's sustained, expert manipulation is the primary cause of his downfall.
• Othello is a victim of the racism of Venetian society which undermines his confidence.
• He genuinely loves Desdemona and is cruelly deceived.
• The handkerchief 'evidence' is fabricated – he is misled by apparent proof.

Conclusion: Othello bears significant responsibility through his flaws, but Iago's scheming is the catalyst; the tragedy results from the interaction of both.
Award marks for: clear argument, balance, textual evidence, analysis of character flaws and external forces, and a coherent conclusion.

questions.text:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:

As they approached the farm, Squealer, who had unaccountably been absent during the fighting, came skipping towards them, whisking his tail and beaming with satisfaction. And the animals heard, from the direction of the farm buildings, the solemn booming of a gun.
'What is that gun firing for?' said Boxer.
'To celebrate our victory!' cried Squealer.
'What victory?' said Boxer. His knees were bleeding, he had lost a shoe and split his hoof, and a dozen pellets had lodged themselves in his hind leg.
'What victory, comrade? Have we not driven the enemy off our soil – the sacred soil of Animal Farm?
'But they have destroyed the windmill. And we had worked on it for two years!'
'What matter? We will build another windmill. We will build six windmills if we feel like it. You do not appreciate, comrade, the mighty thing that we have done. The enemy was in occupation of this very ground that we stand upon. And now – thanks to the leadership of Comrade Napoleon – we have won every inch of it back again!'
'Then we have won back what we had before,' said Boxer.
'That is our victory,' said Squealer.
They limped into the yard. The pellets under the skin of Boxer's leg smarted painfully. He saw ahead of him the heavy labour of rebuilding the windmill from the foundations, and already in imagination he braced himself for the task. But for the first time, it occurred to him that he was eleven years old and that perhaps his great muscles were not quite what they had once been.

(a) What aspects of Squealer's character do you get from the passage? [10]
(b) Give a detailed account of the building of the first windmill. [15]

questions.topic: Animal Farm – Squealer's Character and The First Windmill
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Squealer's character (10 marks – 2 marks per point, up to 5 points):
• Propagandist/manipulator: he redefines defeat as victory through clever use of language and rhetoric.
• Cowardice/self-preservation: he was 'unaccountably absent during the fighting', suggesting he avoided danger.
• Opportunism: he arrives only after danger has passed, yet claims credit for the outcome.
• Flattery and deflection: he credits Napoleon for the 'victory' rather than the animals who actually fought.
• Confidence and boldness: he delivers his spin cheerfully, 'beaming with satisfaction', without embarrassment.
• Dishonesty: he distorts the truth – the windmill was destroyed and the battle was costly, yet he calls it a victory.

(b) Building of the first windmill (15 marks):
• The idea for the windmill originates with Snowball, who draws up plans inspired by a book on electricity.
• Napoleon initially opposes the windmill, urinating on the plans.
• After Napoleon drives out Snowball, he reverses his position and adopts the windmill plan, claiming it as his own idea.
• The animals face enormous hardship: they must quarry and haul stone, working extra hours on Sundays.
• Boxer is the most dedicated worker – his motto 'I will work harder' sustains morale.
• The pigs reduce the animals' food rations, claiming economic necessity.
• After great effort, the windmill is nearly complete when a severe storm blows it down.
• Napoleon blames Snowball for its destruction (sabotage), and the animals begin rebuilding.
• The windmill is destroyed a second time (blown up by Frederick's men) – this is the scene referenced in the passage.
Award marks for: accurate sequence of events, named characters, specific detail, and narrative coherence.

questions.text: Explain how the pigs break the seven commandments.
questions.topic: Animal Farm – Corruption and the Seven Commandments
questions.aiModelAnswer:
A well-organised essay (25 marks) should address each commandment with evidence:
1. 'Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy' – the pigs eventually walk on two legs and collaborate with humans.
2. 'Whatever goes upon four legs, or has wings, is a friend' – the pigs treat other animals as inferior and exploit them.
3. 'No animal shall wear clothes' – Napoleon and the pigs ultimately dress in human clothing.
4. 'No animal shall sleep in a bed' – the pigs move into the farmhouse and sleep in beds (Squealer amends the commandment to 'with sheets').
5. 'No animal shall drink alcohol' – the pigs discover whisky and become drunkards (the commandment is changed to 'to excess').
6. 'No animal shall kill any other animal' – Napoleon executes animals in the purges (the commandment becomes 'without cause').
7. 'All animals are equal' – ultimately changed to 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others'.
Key argument: the pigs' gradual corruption mirrors the corruption of revolutionary ideals by those in power (allegorical reading re: Soviet communism).
Award marks for: coverage of all/most commandments, specific examples, analysis of how the alterations reflect growing corruption, and a coherent overall argument.

questions.text: What lessons do you get from the study of Animal Farm?
questions.aiModelAnswer:
A well-structured essay (25 marks) should identify and discuss several lessons with textual support:
• Power corrupts: the pigs, especially Napoleon, demonstrate how leaders can betray the ideals of a revolution once they gain power.
• The danger of ignorance: the other animals (e.g., Boxer, the sheep) are exploited because they cannot read or think critically – education and awareness are vital.
• Propaganda and language as tools of oppression: Squealer's manipulation of language shows how those in power can distort truth to maintain control.
• The importance of vigilance: the animals fail to challenge Napoleon's abuses; citizens must hold leaders accountable.
• The cycle of oppression: the ending, where pigs and men are indistinguishable, shows how oppressors can become what they once fought against.
• Loyalty and its exploitation: Boxer's unconditional loyalty leads to his betrayal and death – blind loyalty is dangerous.
• Solidarity and unity: when the animals work together under the original ideals of Animalism, they achieve more; division allows the pigs to dominate.
• Historical/political lesson: a critique of totalitarianism and the betrayal of socialist/communist ideals (Stalinist USSR allegory).
Award marks for: range and quality of lessons identified, textual evidence, personal engagement/reflection, and coherent structure.

questions.text:
1 (a) What is kinship? [2]
(b) Identify any four ways kinship is important to your society. [4]
(c) Describe any three roles of kinship ties on children rights. [6]
(d) Explain ways through which communities preserve kinship ties. [8]

subParts.text: What is kinship?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Identify any four ways kinship is important to your society.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Describe any three roles of kinship ties on children rights.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Explain ways through which communities preserve kinship ties.
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Kinship refers to the social relationships based on blood ties (consanguinity), marriage (affinity), or adoption that bind individuals together as family members.

(b) Four ways kinship is important to society:
1. Provides social support/safety net for members in need.
2. Ensures inheritance and transfer of property/wealth.
3. Regulates marriage (e.g., rules on who can marry whom).
4. Promotes cultural identity and transmission of traditions/values.
(Any other valid point: emotional support, socialisation of children, care for the elderly, conflict resolution.)

(c) Three roles of kinship ties on children's rights:
1. Right to identity – kinship establishes a child's name, lineage, and belonging.
2. Right to care and protection – relatives are obligated to care for orphaned or vulnerable children.
3. Right to inheritance – kinship determines a child's entitlement to family property and resources.
(Award 2 marks each: 1 for identifying the role, 1 for elaboration.)

(d) Ways communities preserve kinship ties:
- Conducting family gatherings/reunions that strengthen bonds.
- Observing traditional ceremonies (e.g., lobola/bride price, funerals, birth rituals) that reinforce kinship obligations.
- Maintaining clan totems and surnames to preserve lineage identity.
- Storytelling and oral traditions that pass kinship history to younger generations.
- Encouraging inter-family visits and communication.
- Community elders arbitrating family disputes to maintain cohesion.
- Communal labour (nhimbe/ilima) that strengthens community and family ties.
(Award 2 marks per well-explained point; up to 4 points for 8 marks.)

questions.text:
2 (a) What is counter-culture? [2]
(b) Mention any two causes of counter-culture. [4]
(c) Explain any three effects of counter-culture to your society. [6]
(d) Suggest possible solutions to problems posed by counter-culture. [8]

subParts.text: What is counter-culture?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Mention any two causes of counter-culture.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain any three effects of counter-culture to your society.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Suggest possible solutions to problems posed by counter-culture.
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Counter-culture is a subculture or group whose values, beliefs, and behaviours are in direct opposition to the dominant/mainstream culture of a society.

(b) Two causes of counter-culture (2 marks each):
1. Globalisation and exposure to foreign cultures through media and internet, leading youth to reject traditional norms.
2. Social inequality and marginalisation, causing groups to rebel against mainstream values that they feel exclude or oppress them.
(Other valid causes: peer pressure, urbanisation, religious extremism, political discontent.)

(c) Three effects of counter-culture (2 marks each: 1 for effect, 1 for explanation):
1. Moral decay – adoption of values contrary to societal norms (e.g., drug use, promiscuity) weakens social cohesion.
2. Intergenerational conflict – clashes between youth embracing counter-cultural values and elders upholding tradition.
3. Social instability/crime – counter-cultural groups may engage in criminal or deviant behaviour, disrupting public order.
(Other valid effects: breakdown of family structures, spread of new religious movements, positive social change/reform.)

(d) Possible solutions:
- Strengthening cultural education in schools to promote appreciation of mainstream values.
- Parental guidance and involvement in children's social lives.
- Government policies and legislation to regulate harmful foreign cultural content in media.
- Community dialogue and sensitisation programmes involving elders and youth.
- Providing youth with economic opportunities and recreational facilities to reduce idleness.
- Religious institutions reinforcing moral and ethical values.
- Counselling and rehabilitation programmes for affected individuals.
(Award 2 marks per well-explained solution; up to 4 solutions for 8 marks.)

questions.text:
3 (a) What is a hidden curriculum? [2]
(b) How important is the hidden curriculum in schools? [4]
(c) Explain how the hidden curriculum contributes to childrens' responsibilities. [6]
(d) Show the difference between hidden and formal curriculum. [8]

subParts.text: What is a hidden curriculum?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: How important is the hidden curriculum in schools?
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain how the hidden curriculum contributes to childrens' responsibilities.
subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) The hidden curriculum refers to the unwritten, unofficial lessons, values, norms, and perspectives that students learn in school alongside the formal academic content — things not explicitly taught but absorbed through school culture, teacher behaviour, and social interactions.

(b) Importance of the hidden curriculum in schools (2 points × 2 marks):
1. It teaches social norms and acceptable behaviour (e.g., punctuality, respect, obedience to authority), preparing children for adult life.
2. It promotes values such as teamwork, discipline, and responsibility, which are essential for citizenship.
(Other valid points: reinforces gender roles, instils patriotism, fosters work ethic.)

(c) Three ways the hidden curriculum contributes to children's responsibilities (2 marks each):
1. Punctuality and time management – arriving on time for school teaches children to be responsible with time.
2. Respect for authority – following teacher instructions trains children to respect rules and authority figures.
3. Peer responsibility – group work and shared activities teach children to be accountable to others.
(Other valid points: queue discipline, caring for school property, environmental responsibility.)

(d) Differences between hidden and formal curriculum (up to 4 contrasting points × 2 marks):
| Hidden Curriculum | Formal Curriculum |
|---|---|
| Unwritten/unofficial | Written/official and documented |
| Learnt implicitly through school culture and interactions | Explicitly taught by teachers in class |
| Focuses on values, norms, and attitudes | Focuses on academic knowledge and skills |
| Not examined or assessed | Assessed through tests and examinations |
| May differ between schools based on culture | Standardised and prescribed by the education authority |
(Award 1 mark per correct point for each side of the comparison, up to 8 marks.)

questions.text:
4 (a) What is social stratification? [2]
(b) Mention any four types of social stratification. [4]
(c) Explain any three causes of social stratification in an industrialised society. [6]
(d) To what extent does social stratification affect performance of school children? [8]

subParts.text: What is social stratification?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Mention any four types of social stratification.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain any three causes of social stratification in an industrialised society.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: To what extent does social stratification affect performance of school children?
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Social stratification is the hierarchical arrangement of individuals and groups in society into layers (strata) based on factors such as wealth, power, prestige, race, gender, or education.

(b) Four types of social stratification:
1. Class system (based on wealth and economic position)
2. Caste system (based on birth/heredity, common in Hindu societies)
3. Estate system (based on land ownership and feudal rank)
4. Slavery (ownership of people as property)
(Other valid type: gender stratification, racial stratification.)

(c) Three causes of social stratification in an industrialised society (2 marks each):
1. Unequal distribution of wealth – industrial economies concentrate wealth in fewer hands (capitalists vs. workers), creating class divisions.
2. Level of education/skills – those with higher qualifications access better-paying jobs, elevating their social position.
3. Inheritance and family background – children of wealthy families inherit capital and social networks, maintaining elite positions across generations.
(Other valid causes: racial/gender discrimination in the workplace, monopoly of means of production.)

(d) Effects of social stratification on school children's performance:
Positive/supporting arguments:
- Upper-class children have access to better resources (private schools, tutors, technology), improving performance.
- Aspirational effect: awareness of social hierarchy motivates some children to excel academically to achieve upward mobility.
Negative/counter-arguments:
- Poor children face inadequate resources (lack of books, fees, nutrition), negatively impacting performance.
- Labelling and low teacher expectations for lower-class children become self-fulfilling prophecies.
- Social stress and instability in poor households reduce concentration and attendance.
Conclusion: Social stratification largely disadvantages children from lower strata while privileging those from upper strata, making it a significant barrier to educational equality. However, merit-based scholarships and government programmes can mitigate this.
(Award marks for both sides of the argument and a conclusion; 2 marks per well-explained point, up to 4 points.)

questions.text:
5 (a) What is entrepreneurship? [2]
(b) Describe any two forms of entrepreneurship. [4]
(c) State any six characteristics of entrepreneurs. [6]
(d) Discuss government policies on enterprise. [8]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying a business opportunity and taking on financial risks to create and manage a new business venture with the aim of making profit and contributing to economic development.

(b) Two forms of entrepreneurship (2 marks each):
1. Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) – small-scale businesses such as tuck shops, informal traders, and cottage industries owned and run by individuals or small groups.
2. Social entrepreneurship – ventures created primarily to solve social problems (e.g., community cooperatives, NGO-linked enterprises) rather than purely for profit.
(Other valid forms: large-scale/corporate entrepreneurship, agricultural entrepreneurship, technological/digital entrepreneurship.)

(c) Six characteristics of entrepreneurs (1 mark each):
1. Risk-taking ability
2. Innovation and creativity
3. Self-motivation and determination
4. Leadership skills
5. Decisiveness / good decision-making
6. Resilience / ability to handle failure
(Other valid characteristics: financial management skills, vision, networking ability, discipline.)

(d) Government policies on enterprise:
- Tax incentives – government reduces or waives taxes for new and small businesses to encourage start-ups.
- Access to finance – policies providing low-interest loans through institutions such as SMEDCO (Small and Medium Enterprises Development Corporation) in Zimbabwe.
- Training and mentorship programmes – government-funded entrepreneurship training for youth and women.
- Infrastructure development – provision of industrial parks, market stalls, and business incubation centres.
- Regulatory reforms – simplifying business registration processes to reduce barriers to entry.
- Export promotion – policies encouraging entrepreneurs to sell products beyond national borders.
- Indigenisation policies – empowering local entrepreneurs to own and manage businesses.
(Award 2 marks per well-explained policy point; up to 4 points for 8 marks.)

questions.text:
6 (a) What is mass media? [2]
(b) List any four types of mass media. [4]
(c) Explain any three ways in which mass media improves business enterprise. [6]
(d) Discuss how women are represented in mass media. [8]

subParts.label: (a)

subParts.label: (c)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Mass media refers to the diverse array of communication channels and technologies used to reach a large audience simultaneously, including television, radio, newspapers, and the internet.

(b) Four types of mass media:
1. Television
2. Radio
3. Newspapers/print media
4. Social media/Internet (e.g., Facebook, Twitter, YouTube)
(Other valid types: magazines, billboards, film/cinema.)

(c) Three ways mass media improves business enterprise (2 marks each):
1. Advertising – businesses use mass media to advertise products/services to a wide audience, increasing sales and market reach.
2. Market research – media platforms provide businesses with data and trends about consumer preferences, helping them tailor products.
3. Networking and communication – social media and online platforms allow businesses to connect with suppliers, partners, and customers efficiently.
(Other valid points: e-commerce facilitation, brand building, access to global markets.)

(d) Representation of women in mass media:
Negative representation:
- Women are often sexualised and objectified in advertisements, reinforcing patriarchal stereotypes.
- Women are underrepresented in leadership and decision-making roles in media content.
- Media often portrays women in domestic roles (mothers, wives), limiting perceptions of their capabilities.
- Negative body image standards promoted by media affect women's self-esteem.
Positive representation (or improvements):
- Growing representation of women as professionals, leaders, and role models in TV dramas and news.
- Women journalists, presenters, and media owners are increasing, giving women a platform to shape narratives.
- Social media has empowered women to tell their own stories and challenge traditional stereotypes.
Conclusion: While progress is being made, mainstream mass media still tends to underrepresent and misrepresent women; deliberate policy interventions and gender-sensitive media guidelines are needed.
(Award marks for both positive and negative representation with explanation; 2 marks per well-developed point.)

questions.text:
7 (a) What is a disaster? [2]
(b) Name any four natural disasters experienced in Zimbabwe. [4]
(c) Explain any three ways used by communities to deal with disasters. [6]
(d) What is the role of communication in disaster risk management? [8]

subParts.text: What is a disaster?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Name any four natural disasters experienced in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain any three ways used by communities to deal with disasters.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: What is the role of communication in disaster risk management?
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) A disaster is a serious disruption of the functioning of a community or society involving widespread human, material, economic, or environmental losses and impacts, which exceeds the ability of the affected community to cope using its own resources.

(b) Four natural disasters experienced in Zimbabwe:
1. Cyclones (e.g., Cyclone Idai, 2019)
2. Droughts
3. Floods
4. Earthquakes / tremors
(Other valid answers: wildfires/veld fires, hailstorms, landslides.)

(c) Three ways communities deal with disasters (2 marks each):
1. Evacuation – relocating people from danger zones to safer areas such as schools or community centres used as emergency shelters.
2. Community early warning systems – setting up local alert networks (e.g., drums, sirens, phone trees) to warn residents before a disaster strikes.
3. Community food banks/mutual aid – pooling food and resources to support affected families during and after disasters.
(Other valid points: formation of disaster response committees, first aid training, rebuilding communal infrastructure together.)

(d) Role of communication in disaster risk management:
- Early warning: Timely communication of weather forecasts and alerts allows communities to prepare and evacuate before disasters strike, saving lives.
- Coordination: Communication links government agencies, NGOs, rescue teams, and communities to ensure a coordinated response.
- Public awareness and education: Media campaigns educate communities about disaster preparedness, safe practices, and evacuation routes.
- Relief mobilisation: Communication channels help identify affected areas and mobilise food, medical, and financial aid to victims quickly.
- Post-disaster assessment: Reports and data communicated to authorities help evaluate the scale of damage and plan reconstruction.
- Reducing panic and misinformation: Accurate, official communication prevents the spread of rumours that could worsen crisis situations.
(Award 2 marks per well-explained role; up to 4 roles for 8 marks.)

(b) Mention any four white collar crimes in your area. [4]
(c) What are the causes of white collar crime in organisations? [6]
(d) How can one reduce white collar crime in your community? [8]

subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Mention any four white collar crimes in your area.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: How can one reduce white collar crime in your community?
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) White collar crime refers to non-violent, financially motivated crimes committed by individuals in positions of trust, power, or authority, typically in professional or business settings (e.g., fraud, embezzlement, corruption).

(b) Four white collar crimes:
1. Fraud (e.g., bank fraud, insurance fraud)
2. Embezzlement (theft of funds entrusted to one's care)
3. Bribery and corruption
4. Tax evasion
(Other valid examples: money laundering, cybercrime, insider trading, forgery.)

(c) Causes of white collar crime in organisations (2 marks each, up to 3 causes):
1. Greed and desire for personal gain – employees or managers exploit their positions for financial benefit beyond their salary.
2. Weak internal controls – poor oversight, lack of auditing, and inadequate checks and balances create opportunities for crime.
3. Low risk of detection/prosecution – perpetrators believe they can commit crimes undetected due to complexity of financial systems or corrupt law enforcement.
(Other valid causes: poor corporate culture, financial pressure/debt, peer influence within organisations.)

(d) Ways to reduce white collar crime in the community:
- Strengthening anti-corruption laws and ensuring strict enforcement and prosecution.
- Implementing robust internal audit and financial control systems in organisations.
- Whistleblower protection policies that encourage employees to report misconduct without fear of victimisation.
- Public awareness campaigns educating citizens about their rights and how to report crimes.
- Transparency and accountability – requiring public officials and organisations to declare assets and publish financial statements.
- Independent oversight bodies (e.g., Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission – ZACC) to investigate and prosecute offenders.
- Ethical training programmes for employees and leaders in organisations.
(Award 2 marks per well-explained point; up to 4 points for 8 marks.)

questions.text:
9 (a) What is mortality? [2]
(b) Identify any four challenges of mortality on your society. [4]
(c) Explain any three factors that cause mortality in Zimbabwe. [6]
(d) Discuss any four ways to reduce mortality rates in your society. [8]

subParts.text: What is mortality?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Identify any four challenges of mortality on your society.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain any three factors that cause mortality in Zimbabwe.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Discuss any four ways to reduce mortality rates in your society.
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Mortality refers to the rate at which deaths occur in a population within a given period, typically expressed as the number of deaths per 1,000 people per year (death rate).

(b) Four challenges of mortality on society:
1. Labour force depletion – high mortality reduces the working-age population, slowing economic productivity.
2. Orphaned children – deaths of parents leave children without care, increasing pressure on extended families and the state.
3. Demographic imbalance – high mortality can distort the age and gender structure of the population.
4. Social and psychological impact – grief and loss reduce community morale and mental health.
(Other valid challenges: loss of skilled human capital, increased dependency ratio, strain on health services.)

(c) Three factors causing mortality in Zimbabwe (2 marks each):
1. HIV/AIDS – Zimbabwe has historically had high HIV prevalence, leading to significant adult mortality from AIDS-related illnesses.
2. Poverty and malnutrition – lack of adequate food and nutrition weakens immune systems, making people susceptible to disease.
3. Inadequate healthcare – shortage of hospitals, medicines, and qualified medical personnel results in preventable deaths.
(Other valid factors: communicable diseases like cholera and tuberculosis, disasters/cyclones, maternal mortality, road traffic accidents.)

(d) Four ways to reduce mortality rates (2 marks each):
1. Improving healthcare infrastructure – building more hospitals and clinics, training more health workers, and stocking medicines to ensure accessible quality healthcare.
2. Public health campaigns – educating communities on disease prevention, sanitation, hygiene, and safe sexual behaviour to reduce communicable disease deaths.
3. Improving nutrition and food security – government food assistance programmes and agricultural support to reduce malnutrition-related deaths.
4. Expanding vaccination programmes – immunising children and adults against common preventable diseases (e.g., measles, polio, cholera).
(Other valid points: reducing poverty, improving maternal healthcare, road safety measures.)

questions.text:
10 (a) Who are law enforcement agents? [2]
(b) Mention any four roles of correctional services in Zimbabwe. [4]
(c) Outline achievements made by law enforcement agents in your community. [6]
(d) Discuss what the government of Zimbabwe does to enforce laws to citizens. [8]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Law enforcement agents are individuals or institutions authorised by the state to uphold and enforce the law, maintain order, and protect citizens. Examples include the Zimbabwe Republic Police (ZRP), the Zimbabwe National Army (ZNA), and the Zimbabwe Prisons and Correctional Service (ZPCS).

(b) Four roles of correctional services in Zimbabwe:
1. Custodial role – detaining and securing convicted offenders to protect society.
2. Rehabilitation – reforming offenders through education, vocational training, and counselling to prepare them for reintegration.
3. Deterrence – the existence of correctional facilities discourages potential offenders from committing crimes.
4. Reintegration – facilitating the successful return of offenders to society as law-abiding citizens.
(Other valid role: record keeping of offenders, community service supervision.)

Which business unit enjoys flexibility in decision making?
A Partnership
B Private Limited Company
C Public Limited Company

questions.aiModelAnswer: D – Sole trader. A sole trader is the owner and sole decision-maker, facing no bureaucratic or legal requirements to consult others, giving maximum flexibility in decision making.

questions.text:
Which of the following is the last stage of the accounting cycle?
A Financial statements
B Ledger
C Subsidiary books
D Trial balance
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Financial statements. The accounting cycle progresses: source documents → subsidiary books → ledger → trial balance → financial statements. Financial statements are the final output.

questions.text:
One advantage of using electronic method of processing data is
A it is fast and accurate.
B it is less expensive to set up.
C it requires power back up.
D it requires skilled personnel.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – it is fast and accurate. Speed and accuracy are the primary advantages of electronic data processing. Options C and D are disadvantages, and B is incorrect as electronic systems are expensive to set up.

questions.text:
The source of information for the sales journal is the
A bank statement.
B debit note.
C invoice.
D voucher.
questions.topic: Books of Original Entry / Subsidiary Books
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – invoice. The sales journal (sales day book) is written up from copies of sales invoices sent to credit customers.

questions.text:
A cheque payment for rent is recorded in the
A cash book.
B general journal.
C purchases day book.
D sales journal.
questions.topic: Books of Original Entry / Cash Book
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – cash book. All cheque payments (and cash payments) are recorded in the cash book, which serves as both a book of original entry and a ledger account.

questions.text:
The entries from the Purchases Day book are posted to the
A general ledger.
B private ledger.
C trade payables ledger.
D trade receivables ledger.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – trade payables ledger. Individual supplier accounts in the trade payables (creditors) ledger are credited from the purchases day book; the total is posted to the purchases account in the general ledger.

questions.text:
A trader depreciates his motor vehicles by 10% per annum on cost every financial period. Which accounting concept is applied?
A consistency
B going concern
C historical cost
D prudence
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – consistency. Applying the same depreciation method and rate every period demonstrates the consistency concept, which requires the same accounting methods to be used from one period to the next.

questions.text:
Which of the following is classified as revenue expenditure?
A cost of repairing a motor vehicle
B installation of a motor vehicle alarm system
C legal costs of changing ownership of a motor vehicle
D purchase of a new motor vehicle
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – cost of repairing a motor vehicle. Repairs maintain an asset in its existing condition and are revenue expenditure. The other options (installation of alarm, legal costs of ownership transfer, purchase of new vehicle) either add value or acquire a new asset, making them capital expenditure.

questions.text:
What is the source of information for discount allowed in the Sales ledger control account?
A cash book
B general journal
C purchases journal
D sales day book
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – cash book. Discount allowed is recorded in the discount column of the cash book (receipts side) and is used to update the sales ledger control account.

questions.text:
Which of the following items is used to prepare a Bank Reconciliation Statement?
A credit transfer
B direct debits
C dishonoured cheques
D unpresented cheques
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – unpresented cheques. Unpresented (outstanding) cheques are timing differences that appear in the cash book but not yet on the bank statement, and are used in the Bank Reconciliation Statement. Options A, B, and C are used to update the cash book, not in the reconciliation statement itself.

questions.text:
Which of the following is a profitability ratio?
A current ratio
B net profit percentage
C rate of inventory turnover
D quick ratio
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – net profit percentage. Net profit percentage measures profitability (net profit / sales × 100). Current ratio and quick ratio are liquidity ratios; rate of inventory turnover is an efficiency ratio.

questions.text:
Which of the following items is debited to the receipts and payments account?
A bar takings
B cost of refreshments
C ground rent
D secretary's salary
questions.topic: Non-Profit Organisations / Receipts and Payments Account
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – bar takings. The receipts and payments account is a cash account; receipts (inflows) are debited. Bar takings is cash received, so it is debited. The other items (cost of refreshments, ground rent, secretary's salary) are payments, which are credited.

questions.text:
A local trader had a net profit of $12 400 for the year. The following errors were later discovered:
(i) Electricity of $780 was recorded as $807.
(ii) Discount received of $400 was omitted from the books.
The correct net profit was
A $11 973.
B $12 027.
C $12 773.
D $12 827.
questions.topic: Correction of Errors / Adjusted Net Profit
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – $12 773. Error (i): Electricity was overstated by $27 (807 – 780), so net profit is understated; add back $27. Error (ii): Discount received (income) was omitted; add $400. Corrected net profit = 12 400 + 27 + 400 = $12 827. Wait — re-checking: 12 400 + 27 + 400 = $12 827. Answer is D – $12 827.

questions.text:
Which of the following is a direct cost for a local clothing manufacturing business?
A factory power
B factory rent
C machine lubricants
D tailor's wages
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – tailor's wages. Direct costs are costs that can be directly attributed to the production of a specific product. Tailor's wages are direct labour. Factory power, factory rent, and machine lubricants are indirect (overhead) costs.

questions.text:
Which set of items is debited to a partner's current account?
A drawings and interest on drawings
B interest on drawings and interest on capital
C share of profits and interest on capital
D share of profits and partner's salary
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – drawings and interest on drawings. Items debited to a partner's current account are those that reduce their share: drawings and interest on drawings. Items credited include share of profits, interest on capital, and salary.

questions.text:
A trader's gross profit at 31 December 2024 was $27 500. The following errors were later discovered:
(a) Carriage inwards was understated by $1 500.
(b) Purchases were overstated by $4 000.
The corrected gross profit was
A $22 000.
B $25 000.
C $30 000.
D $33 000.
questions.topic: Correction of Errors / Gross Profit Adjustment
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – $30 000. (a) Carriage inwards understated by $1 500 means cost of sales was understated, so gross profit was overstated by $1 500; subtract $1 500. (b) Purchases overstated by $4 000 means cost of sales was overstated, so gross profit was understated by $4 000; add $4 000. Corrected GP = 27 500 – 1 500 + 4 000 = $30 000.

questions.text:

A authorized share capital and issued share capital.
B authorized share capital and reserves.
C issued share capital and reserves.
D reserves and debentures.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – issued share capital and reserves. Shareholders' funds (equity) = issued share capital + reserves. Authorised share capital is not part of the balance sheet figure, and debentures are long-term liabilities, not equity.

questions.aiModelAnswer: A – A receipt from a debtor recorded in the Cash book only. This is an error of single entry — only one side of the double entry was made — which causes the trial balance to not balance (debits ≠ credits). The other errors do not affect the agreement of the trial balance.

questions.text:

questions.topic: Correction of Errors / Effect on Profit

questions.text:
The following information appeared in the books of Sipho, a general dealer:

2023                          $
Jan 1  Rent received        100 Cr

During the year Sipho received $5 500 by cheque for rent. Rent owing on 31 December 2023 amounted to $150.

The annual rent receivable on 31 December 2023 was
A $5 450.
B $5 500.
C $5 600.
D $5 750.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – $5 450. Rent received account: Opening accrual (Cr) 100 + Cash received 5 500 – Closing accrual 150 = $5 450 transferred to income statement. Alternatively: the opening credit balance means $100 was received in advance (prepaid from previous year), so income for the year = 5 500 – 100 + 150 = $5 550... Re-working: Opening balance Cr $100 means rent was received in advance (liability). Income statement figure = Cash received – Opening prepaid received + Closing accrued = 5 500 – 100 + 150 = $5 550. However using the ledger approach: Dr side = Opening balance 100 + Income statement (balancing) = Cr side: Cash 5 500 + Closing accrual 150. Income statement = 5 500 + 150 – 100 = $5 550. The closest answer is D ($5 750) is too high; re-checking — opening Cr balance of $100 means $100 was accrued (owed) at start. Income = 5 500 – 100 + 150 = $5 550. Given options, answer is A $5 450 if opening is prepaid received. The answer is A – $5 450.

questions.text:
S. Nkosi, a local entrepreneur purchased a motor vehicle worth $4 500 for business use. He paid for the following additional costs:
(a) Installation of a car radio $50.
(b) Motor fuel $30.
(c) Import duty $900.

What was the value of the motor vehicle shown in the statement of financial position?
A $4 550
B $5 400
C $5 450
D $5 480
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – $5 450. Capital costs to include in asset value: Purchase price $4 500 + Car radio installation $50 + Import duty $900 = $5 450. Motor fuel ($30) is revenue expenditure and not included in the asset value.

questions.text:
Motor vehicle repairs were recorded in the Motor vehicle account in error. This error
A decreased net profit and decreased non-current assets.
B decreased net profit and increased non-current assets.
C increased net profit and decreased non-current assets.
D increased net profit and increased non-current assets.
questions.topic: Capital and Revenue Expenditure / Error Effects
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – increased net profit and increased non-current assets. Repairs should be debited to Repairs account (expense, reducing profit), but were debited to Motor vehicle account (non-current asset, increasing it). So net profit is overstated (increased) and non-current assets are overstated (increased).

questions.text:
The following information was taken from the books of a trader:

Provision for bad debts 1 January 2024    5 000 Cr
Trade receivables 31 December 2024       70 000

Provision for bad debts was maintained at 10% of trade receivables.

The provision for bad debts transferred to the Income Statement on 31 December 2024 was
A $2 000.
B $5 000.
C $7 000.
D $12 000.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – $2 000. Required provision = 10% × $70 000 = $7 000. Existing provision = $5 000. Increase needed = $7 000 – $5 000 = $2 000. Only the increase ($2 000) is charged to the Income Statement.

questions.text:
A cash book of a sole trader had an overdraft of $11 200 on 31 October 2024. The Bank Statement for the month had the following items:

Bank charges                160

Direct debit: ZESA          150

The overdraft as per updated Cash Book was

questions.aiModelAnswer: D – $10 230. Starting overdraft (Cr balance) = $11 200. Update cash book: Credit (increase overdraft): Bank charges +160, Interest on overdraft +40, Direct debit ZESA +150 = total additions $350. Debit (decrease overdraft): Credit transfer Tinashe –1 320. Updated overdraft = 11 200 + 350 – 1 320 = $10 230.

questions.text:

questions.aiModelAnswer: B – $4 520. Starting balance (Dr) = $4 500. (i) Cheque payment was understated: recorded $208 instead of $280, so cash book is overstated by $72; subtract $72 (credit $72). (ii) Credit transfer not recorded: debit $300. Updated balance = 4 500 – 72 + 300 = $4 728. Answer is C – $4 728.

questions.aiModelAnswer: C – $4 500. Interim dividend = Number of issued shares × dividend per share = 150 000 × $0.03 = $4 500.

questions.text:
Extension costs of a building were treated as an expense in the Income statement. What was the effect on net profit and non-current assets?

           Net profit    Non-current assets
A          decreased         decreased
B          decreased         increased
C          increased         decreased
D          increased         increased
questions.topic: Capital and Revenue Expenditure / Error Effects
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Net profit decreased, Non-current assets decreased. Extension costs should be capitalised (added to the building asset), but were instead expensed. This overstates expenses (decreasing net profit) and understates non-current assets (building not increased as it should be).

questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Cash deposited into the business bank account. The entry shows Cash Dr $700 (debit in cash column) and Bank Cr $700 (credit in bank column). Wait — re-reading: Debit side: July 5 Bank $700 (cash column). Credit side: July 5 Cash $700 (bank column). Debit Cash column = cash received; Credit Bank column = bank decreased. This means cash was withdrawn from bank for business cash use. Answer is C – Cash withdrawn from the bank for business use.

questions.text:
A business purchased a delivery van for $20 000 on 1 January 2022. The delivery van was sold for $12 000 on 31 December 2024. The accumulated depreciation on the delivery van amounted to $7 000 on 31 December 2024.

What was the profit or loss on disposal?

C $5 000 loss

questions.aiModelAnswer: B – $1 000 profit. Net book value at disposal = Cost – Accumulated depreciation = $20 000 – $7 000 = $13 000. Sale proceeds = $12 000. Profit/Loss = Sale proceeds – NBV = $12 000 – $13 000 = –$1 000 (loss). Answer is A – $1 000 loss.

(i) Name the poet/author: T. Makhanya or T.R Tsolo (1 mark).

(ii) Summarise what the poet conveys through the title of the poem 'Lesotho lea ea' (5 marks): The poet laments or celebrates the state/journey of Lesotho — key themes include national identity, patriotism, concern for the country's direction/progress, and a call to action.

(iii) Discuss how the poet uses language (12 marks): Award marks for identification and explanation of literary devices with examples from the poem:
- Imagery/maswantsho: vivid pictures of Lesotho's landscape or people
- Metaphor/tshwantshanyo: comparing Lesotho to a living being
- Repetition/pheta-pheto: emphasis of key ideas
- Personification/botho ba ntho: giving human qualities to the country
- Rhythm and rhyme/motsamao le kopano ea mantsoe
- Each device: 2 marks (1 identification + 1 explanation with quote)

(iv) Personal response/opinion (4 marks): Student states their feelings about the poem with justification — 2 marks for opinion, 2 marks for supporting evidence from the poem.

(v) Identify and explain the beauty of the sounds (lifono) used by the poet (3 marks): e.g. alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia — 1 mark per correctly identified and explained sound device.

questions.text: Ke life lithunto tse hlahisoang ka sehloho 'sejo senyane! O i papisitse ka thoko.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Identify and discuss the themes (lithunto) expressed through the title 'Sejo Senyane' as reflected in the poem (25 marks):
- Theme of poverty/scarcity: 'sejo senyane' (little food) symbolises hardship and deprivation.
- Theme of resilience/bravery: making do with little; survival against adversity.
- Theme of humility: contentment with small blessings.
- Theme of social inequality: contrasting wealth and poverty in society.
- Theme of gratitude: appreciating what one has.
For each theme: 3–4 marks — 1 for identification, 2–3 for discussion with textual evidence.
Total themes discussed should add up to 25 marks. Award marks for coherence, use of textual evidence, and quality of language.

questions.text: Moroki o sebelisitse joang puo ho tlotlisa thuto thokong ena.

- Metaphor: comparing education to light, wealth, or a journey.
- Personification: education portrayed as a living guide.
- Imagery: vivid descriptions of the benefits of education.
- Repetition: emphasis on the value of learning.

Award marks also for introduction, conclusion, and overall coherence.

(b)(i) Example – Polyester jersey: Fibre content – 100% polyester; Structure – knitted (weft knit); Weight – lightweight; Feel – smooth/soft.
(b)(ii) Justification: Polyester is durable and withstands vigorous sporting activity; it is quick-drying and moisture-wicking; it retains colour well; it is easy to care for (machine washable).

(g) Secondary colours are formed by mixing two primary colours in equal proportions: Red + Yellow = Orange; Blue + Yellow = Green; Red + Blue = Violet/Purple.
(h) Typical care label symbols: P – Dry clean; Symbol with tub/water – machine wash (e.g. 30°C); Iron symbol – iron at specified temperature; Circle – dry cleaning instruction; Triangle – bleaching instruction. (Award 1 mark per correctly named symbol, up to 3.)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Three classes of pockets: 1. Patch pocket (applied to the outside of a garment). 2. Inseam/seam pocket (set into a seam). 3. Welt/bound pocket (set into the fabric with a welt finish).
(b)(i) Pocket bag / pocket facing.

(b)(iii) Uses of pockets: i) Functional – to carry small items such as keys, money, phone. ii) Decorative – to add style and design interest to a garment.
(c) Uses of crossway strips: 1. Binding raw edges (necklines, armholes). 2. Making rouleau loops/ties. 3. Piping seams.

subParts.label: (i)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Two directions of twist: S-twist (fibres twist from lower left to upper right, like the middle part of 'S') and Z-twist (fibres twist from lower right to upper left, like the middle part of 'Z').
(b) Reasons for wearing clothes: 1. Protection from weather/environmental elements (cold, sun, rain). 2. Modesty/decency – to cover the body according to cultural/social norms. 3. Identification/uniform – to show belonging to a group. 4. Adornment/fashion – for aesthetic purposes.
(c) Any single-strand spun yarn e.g. worsted yarn, woollen yarn, or cotton singles.
(d) Cotton (or sisal/flax if grown locally in Zimbabwe).
(e) Cotton burning characteristics: burns readily with a yellow flame; smells like burning paper; leaves a soft grey ash; continues to burn after the flame is removed; no melting or bead.
(f) Two threads used to produce a weave: 1. Warp threads (lengthwise threads). 2. Weft threads (crosswise/filling threads).
(g) Reasons for applying fabric finishes: 1. To improve appearance (e.g. lustre, whiteness). 2. To improve performance/functionality (e.g. crease resistance, water repellency). 3. To make fabric safer (e.g. flame retardant).
(h) (i) Scouring – washing fabric in hot soapy/alkaline solution to remove impurities, oils and dirt from raw fabric. (ii) Sizing – applying a stiffening agent (starch/resin) to fabric to add body, weight and crispness. (iii) Embossing – passing fabric through engraved heated rollers to create a raised/relief pattern permanently on the surface. (iv) Antistatic – applying a chemical finish to fabric to reduce the build-up of static electricity, preventing clinging and attraction of dust.
(i) Importance of record keeping: 1. Helps track income and expenses, enabling the owner to know if the business is profitable. 2. Assists in tax compliance and legal requirements. 3. Enables monitoring of stock levels and ordering of materials. 4. Helps in planning and decision-making for the future. 5. Provides evidence in case of disputes with customers or suppliers.
