questions.aiModelAnswer:
Model answers for each sub-part:

(a) Hosi ya Xihlayamagoza i Maluleke. (1 mark)

(b) Xikongomelonkulu xa ku hlengeleta a xi ri xa ku twanana ni ku ya hi moya wun'we hi hehleni ka vuvabyi bya Xisandzhaku / ku amukela xileriso xa muvabyi xo yisiwa exibedhlele xa Madonoro eGolodivhiya. (1 mark)

(c) Muvabyi a a lava ku yisiwa exibedhlele xa Madonoro eGolodivhiya. (1 mark)

(d) Khapakhapa (n'wana wa muvabyi / Xisandzhaku) a a tsaleliwa papila hi Thicara Cauke. (1 mark)

(e) 
(i) ruu! – maencisi ya ku hlengeleta ka vanhu vo tala hi ku tsakela / ku vitaniwa hi nkoka; sound of people gathering in large numbers all at once. (1 mark)
(ii) rwee, rwee! – maencisi ya ku rirhimela ka xifuva; sound of the chest rattling/wheezing continuously. (1 mark)

(f) Swivulwahava (idiomatic expressions):
(i) hi va nyandza yin'we – hi twana, hi pfunana eka matimba/vuvabyi byin'we; to share the same suffering/stand together in one burden. (1 mark)
(ii) ku bisana huwa – ku lwana, ku xanisana, ku nga twanani; to quarrel / be in conflict with each other. (1 mark)
(iii) hi nga tidlayi matihlo – hi nga titlhavisi hi ku vona swilo swo olova; do not deceive/delude ourselves / do not blind ourselves to the truth. (1 mark)
(iv) hi banana hi rhanga ro hisa – hi ta sala hi pfukile, hi humisiwile; we will end up regretting / left with nothing / in an awkward/burning situation. (1 mark)

(g) Swivulwa (proverbs/figurative expressions):
(i) 'munhu i ndlopfu a nga hanyi hi murhi wun'we' – Ndlopfu i nyama yo kulukumba, yi lava miri yo tala ku khorwisiwa; swi vula leswaku munhu u lava mpfuno wa van'wana a nga koti ku tshama hi yena ndzexe – no one is self-sufficient; a person needs others for survival, just as an elephant cannot be satisfied by a single tree. (2 marks)
(ii) 'rikari va lavela ematini' – Rikari (ndlopfu) ri lava mati yo tala; swi vula leswaku munhu loyi a kulukumba / a ni nkoka u lava nchumu wo kulukumba / a lava mpfuno wo kulukumba – a great/important person has great needs; one of high status requires much care and support. (2 marks)

(h) Swilo swimbirhi leswi nga endla leswaku N'wa-Khazamula a nga lavi nuna a yisiwa exibedhlele:
1. A swi twisisi leswaku nuna wa yena a yisiwa eGolodivhiya a vhiyiwa kona – a nga tshembeli xibedhele / a pfumelelana na ku yisiwa kule. (1 mark)
2. U navela ku sungula hi mungoma a lavisise leswo dlaya nuna wa yena hi tinhlolo/vutlhari bya xintu, a twa hi mani a dlawa kona va lava tin'anga. (1 mark)

(i) Swivulwa swimbirhi:
- N'wa-Khazamula (xintu): 'Mina n'wini wakwe, ndzi ri xo sungula hi fanele ku huma mungoma, hi famba hi vutisisa na ku lavisisa eka lava va swi tivaka' – u tshembela mungoma/xintu. (1 mark)
- N'wa-Yingwani (xilungu): 'Leswi yena a navelaka ku yisiwa exibedhlele swi fanerile leswaku swi va tano ehandle ka ku phikizana' – u pfumelelana na ku yisiwa exibedhlele / xilungu. (1 mark)

(j) N'wa-Yingwani u kombisa vumunhu lebyi: U tlhela u na ntlhelo/timfanelo – a nga ngheni mutini hi xikhongelo kambe u tile hi tihomu, a kombisa ku xixima. U na vukheta bya ku tshikelela miehleketo ya van'wana byi nga ri na ku nghenela / ku dyoha miehleketo ya van'wana. U na wutivi bya swikombelo swa ngoma kambe u pfumelelana na vutsunguri bya xilungu hi hehleni ka mavabyi. U tshembeka, a nga lavi swixangu, u lava ku tsundzuxa lava va Maluleke hi ntlhelo. (2 marks – any 2 valid points)

(k) Vumbhoni: N'wa-Khazamula a a vulisiwa na ku twa rito ra yena hi ku kombisiwa embyeni (a nga yisiwa exibedhlele nuna wa yena); N'wa-Yingwani naye a a yingisiwa a twa rito ra yena; va Maluleke va hlengeleta va twa leswi vavasati va swi vula, va va xixima – swi kombisa ku xixima vavasati emutini wa Maluleke. (1 mark)

(l) Nkomiso (Summary ~80 words): Award up to 10 marks. Key points to include:
- Xisandzhaku u kombela ku yisiwa exibedhlele hikuva a kala ku antswisiwa. (1)
- Xihlayamagoza u pfumelela u kombela leswaku nuna a yisiwa eGolodivhiya. (1)
- Va ka Maluleke va hlengeleta ku twanana hi mhaka leyi. (1)
- N'wa-Khazamula a pfumelelani na xileriso xa nuna; u navela mungoma wa xintu. (1)
- N'wa-Yingwani u pfumelelana na ku yisiwa exibedhlele, a ri rito ri huma eka muvabyi ndzexe. (1)
- Ku hambana ka miehleketo: xintu (mungoma) vs xilungu (xibedhele). (2)
- Language/expression: correct Xichangana, coherent summary form. (2)
- Word count approximately 80 words. (1)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
Model answers:

(a) Maencisi (Ideophones/Interjections) – choose ANY 5 for 5 marks (1 each):
(i) gaa! – ku vula ku etlela/ku anama ka ntsena, e.g. ku anama ka nkuku; ideophone for spreading wide/flat (as a bird spreading wings).
(ii) n'walala! – ku vula ku etlela/ku rhama ka ntsena; ideophone for lying flat/sprawled out.
(iii) n'wee! – ku vula rirhimelo/ku lila ka ntswa kumbe nkuku; ideophone for a thin, high-pitched cry/sound.
(iv) bulumuku! – ku vula ku wa ka nchumu wo kulukumba/ko kurhi; ideophone for a heavy thud/fall.
(v) phatsa! – ku vula ku khoma hi matimba kumbe ku pfurheka hi ku tshaxeka; ideophone for a sudden sharp slap/snap.
(vi) ngirr! – ku vula ku rhurhuma ka mhisi kumbe swiharhi; ideophone for growling/purring of an animal.
(vii) kakatsuku! – ku vula ku rhurhuma/ku khutama ka swiharhi swa le henhla; ideophone for the sound of a bird or small creature fluttering/scurrying.

(b) Swivuriso (Proverbs from animal names) – choose ANY 5 (1 each):
(i) mhala – Mhala wu byeliwa hi ribye (a duiker is caught/warned by a stone) – swi vula ku lulamiseriwa hi ntlhelo wo karhi.
(ii) nyarhi – Nyarhi a yi khomi mhunti (a rhino does not catch a mouse) – swi vula munhu wo kulukumba a nga wi swin'wana/ku nga tshami u xiximana na van'wana va ka hansi.
(iii) mhisi – Mhisi yi dlaya leswi yi swi vonaka (a hyena kills what it sees) – swi vula ku tirhela leswi ku nga emahlweni ka wena.
(iv) ngwenya – Ngwenya yi dlaya exibyeni xa yona (a crocodile kills in its own river) – swi vula munhu u na matimba etikweni ra yena.
(v) nyoka – Nyoka yi tshembaniwa hi nhloko (a snake is trusted/watched by its head) – swi vula ku languta nchumu wo ngana hi ntlhelo.
(vi) mhunti – Mhunti a yi endli ndhawu leyi yi tirhaka kona yo nkoka (a mouse/rat does not neglect where it works) – swi vula ku xixima ndhawu ya wena.
(vii) ndlopfu – Ndlopfu a yi khali hi maribye (an elephant does not tire from stones/carrying its tusks) – swi vula munhu wo kulukumba a papalata swisiwana.

(c) Maritofularha (antonyms) – choose ANY 5 (1 each):
(i) tsakile → a tsakanga / u khumbekile / u swekile (unhappy/sad)
(ii) endzhaku → emahlweni (forward/front)
(iii) mundzuku → namuntlha / xikati lexi / tolo (today / yesterday)
(iv) mona → rhandzo / ku tsakela van'wana (love/goodwill, opposite of jealousy)
(v) pfupfula → tirhela / siya (leave / keep)
(vi) rilile → u tsandzehile / u hlamule (laughed / answered back without crying)
(vii) soleka → tsakisa / antswa (pleasing/good)

(d) Tinomboro hi Xichangana – choose ANY 5 (1 each):
(i) 8 – mune na va nharhu / nhungu
(ii) 27 – makume mambirhi na ntlhanu na vambirhi / nkarhi wa ntlhanu na vambirhi
(iii) 66 – makume ya rhondzweni na ntlhanu na n'we / makume ya rhondzweni na ntsevu
(iv) 430 – tikhume ta mune na makume ya ntlhanu
(v) 575 – tikhume ta ntlhanu na makume ya ntlhanu na ntlhanu na ntlhanu
(vi) 907 – tikhume ta kaye na ntlhanu na vambirhi
(vii) 1 320 – lukume ra n'we na tikhume ta ntlhanu na makume ya mbirhi

questions.text:
In local home industries, built-up materials are mainly used because of their advantages over solid timber. Complete the diagram in Figure 2 to show:
(a) stout heart in A,
(b) lamin board in B.

subParts.text: Complete the diagram to show stout heart in A.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Complete the diagram to show lamin board in B.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.diagramNote: Figure 2 shows two blank cross-section boxes labelled A and B representing built-up/manufactured board sections that the student must complete to illustrate stout heart (A) and lamin board (B).
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Stout heart (also called stout-heart board): cross-section should show a thick central core of solid timber (staves/blocks laid edge-to-edge with grain running in one direction) sandwiched between two thin veneer layers on each face. The core strips are wider/thicker than in blockboard.
(b) Lamin board: cross-section should show a core made up of very thin strips of timber (narrow laminations, typically under 7 mm wide) glued together with alternating grain, then faced with veneer on both sides. Strips are narrower than blockboard or stout heart.

questions.diagramNote: Figure 3 shows an image of a common woodworking workshop machine/equipment that students must identify and evaluate.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) The equipment is a Band Saw (or other common woodworking machine as depicted in the figure, e.g. scroll saw / bench drill / mortising machine).

Doors can be classified based on materials used to construct them.
(a) Identify one material apart from timber which can be used to make a door.
(b) On a ledged braced and battened door, state the function of the braces.

subParts.text: Identify one material apart from timber which can be used to make a door.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: On a ledged braced and battened door, state the function of the braces.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any ONE of: steel/metal; aluminium; glass; UPVC/plastic; fibreglass.
(b) The braces prevent the door from sagging/racking (distorting out of square). They run diagonally from the bottom of the hanging (hinge) side to the top of the opposite side, transferring the load and keeping the door rigid/square.

questions.text:

(b) Explain the use of water when grinding a tool.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any ONE of: glasspaper; garnet paper; aluminium oxide paper; silicon carbide (wet-and-dry) paper; emery paper.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) The bridge guard covers/guards the cutterblock (cutter head) to prevent the operator's hands from coming into contact with the rotating cutters, protecting against serious injury. It bridges over the cutterblock while allowing the workpiece to pass through.

questions.text:
(a) Felling timber is done in winter. Evaluate this statement.
(b) Give one example of thermoplastics.

subParts.text: Felling timber is done in winter. Evaluate this statement.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Give one example of thermoplastics.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) The statement is TRUE/valid. In winter, trees have less sap/moisture content because growth is minimal (dormant period). This means less risk of sap staining/fungal attack, the timber seasons more uniformly, and it is easier to work with. Also, the reduced sap content makes the timber lighter to transport.
(b) Any ONE of: polyethylene (polythene/PE); polypropylene (PP); polyvinyl chloride (PVC); polystyrene (PS); acrylic (Perspex/PMMA); nylon (polyamide).

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Recycling is the process of converting/reprocessing used or waste materials into new products or raw materials so they can be used again, thereby reducing waste sent to landfill and conserving natural resources.
(b) Any ONE of: incineration releases harmful/toxic gases (e.g. carbon monoxide, dioxins) into the atmosphere causing air pollution; it contributes to greenhouse gas emissions/climate change; the ash residue may still be toxic and require safe disposal; high initial cost of incinerators; not all materials can be incinerated safely.

questions.text:
Etula creations is a furniture company in Gokwe that offers a wide range of stylish and functional furniture pieces for homes and offices. The enterprise wants to increase its market share and sales.
(a) Define the concept of marketing. [2]
(b) List three marketing strategies that Etula Creations can use to increase its market share. [3]
(c) Explain each of the three components of the marketing mix that Etula Creations can make use of to boost its sales. [6]
(d) Outline any two challenges that may be faced when marketing products. [4]

subParts.text: Define the concept of marketing.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: List three marketing strategies that Etula Creations can use to increase its market share.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain each of the three components of the marketing mix that Etula Creations can make use of to boost its sales.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Outline any two challenges that may be faced when marketing products.
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Marketing is the process of identifying, anticipating and satisfying customer needs and wants profitably through activities such as research, promotion, distribution and pricing of goods and services. (Award 2 marks for a complete definition covering the process and customer satisfaction/profit element.)

(b) Any THREE of: social media advertising; attending trade fairs/exhibitions; offering discounts/promotions; word-of-mouth/referrals; creating a website/online store; collaborating with interior designers; door-to-door selling; product catalogues/brochures; loyalty programmes.

(c) The three components of the marketing mix (3Ps or 4Ps — Product, Price, Place, Promotion):
- Product: The furniture items offered must meet customer needs — quality, design, range of styles, durability. Etula should ensure products are stylish and functional as stated.
- Price: The price set must be competitive and affordable yet profitable. Etula can use penetration pricing, skimming, or competitive pricing strategies.
- Place: The channels through which products reach customers — showroom, online platform, delivery services, partnerships with retailers.
- Promotion: How the product is communicated to customers — advertising, social media, exhibitions, special offers. (Award 2 marks per component explained: 1 mark for naming, 1 mark for explanation.)

(d) Any TWO of (2 marks each):
- High cost of advertising/limited marketing budget.
- Strong competition from established furniture companies.
- Limited access to the target market in remote areas.
- Lack of skilled marketing personnel.
- Changing consumer tastes and preferences.
- Economic challenges such as inflation reducing consumer purchasing power.
- Difficulty in reaching customers in rural areas due to poor infrastructure.

Mr Moyo, a timber retailer in Mutare sells both hardwood and softwood timber boards.
(a) State three characteristics of hardwood timber board. [3]
(b) Describe the causes of:
(i) heart rot, [3]
(ii) wet rot. [3]
(c) Illustrate any three growth defects in timber. [6]

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Any THREE characteristics of hardwood (1 mark each):
- Generally denser/heavier than softwood.
- Has a more complex cellular structure (contains vessel cells/pores — ring porous or diffuse porous).
- Usually slower growing, producing tighter grain.
- More durable and harder-wearing.
- Generally more expensive than softwood.
- Comes from broad-leaved/deciduous trees (angiosperms).
- Often has more attractive grain patterns and figure.

(b)(i) Heart rot — causes (3 marks):
- Caused by fungi (wood-rotting fungi) that attack the heartwood at the centre of the tree.
- The fungus gains entry through wounds, broken branches, or damage to the bark.
- The fungus breaks down the lignin and cellulose in the heartwood cells, causing the wood to decay and become soft and discoloured.
- Favoured by moisture and poor growing conditions.

(b)(ii) Wet rot — causes (3 marks):
- Caused by specific fungi (e.g. Coniophora puteana — cellar fungus) that require very high moisture content in the timber (typically above 50%).
- Occurs when timber is persistently wet due to poor drainage, rain penetration, or lack of ventilation.
- The fungi break down the cellulose in the wood causing it to become soft, darkened and fibrous.
- Stops progressing if timber is dried out — less destructive than dry rot once moisture is removed.

(c) Any THREE growth defects illustrated (2 marks each — 1 mark for sketch, 1 mark for label):
- Knot: where a branch joined the trunk; shows as a circular hard area of different grain direction.
- Shakes (heart shake, ring shake, star shake): splits or cracks along the grain caused by growth stresses.
- Reaction wood (tension wood in hardwood / compression wood in softwood): abnormal wood formed on one side of a leaning tree.
- Irregular/sloping grain: grain runs at an angle to the length of the board.
- Burr: abnormal rounded outgrowth on the trunk caused by bud growth.
- Resin pockets/pitch pockets: cavities in softwood containing resin.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Four ways of terminating dimension lines: 1. Arrow heads (open or filled triangular arrowheads pointing to the extension lines); 2. Oblique/diagonal tick strokes (45° short lines at termination points); 3. Dots (filled circles at the termination points); 4. Open circles/rings at the termination points. [1 mark each, any four clearly illustrated with a sketch or labelled description]

(b)(i) Datum: A fixed reference point or level from which all heights/elevations on a site are measured. It is usually an assumed or known Ordnance Bench Mark (OBM) value assigned a specific reduced level (RL), e.g. 100.000 m.

(b)(ii) Back-sight (BS): The first staff reading taken after the instrument has been set up at a new station, always taken to a point of known reduced level (e.g. the benchmark or a change point). It is used to determine the height of the instrument (HI).

(b)(iii) Rise: The positive difference in reduced level between a preceding staff station and a succeeding staff station, i.e. when the new point is higher than the previous point. Rise = previous foresight/intermediate sight − current reading (when the result is positive).

(a) Five causes of ill-health in the building industry (any five, 1 mark each):
1. Exposure to hazardous/toxic substances (e.g. asbestos, lead, silica dust, chemicals).
2. Prolonged exposure to excessive noise causing hearing loss.
3. Vibration from tools/machinery causing hand-arm vibration syndrome (HAVS).

8. Biological hazards (e.g. leptospirosis from rodents on site).

(b) Five effects of accidents at a building site (any five, 1 mark each):

3. Financial loss to the contractor (compensation claims, fines, delays).

(a)(i) Two provisions of site security (any two, 1 mark each):
1. Perimeter fencing/hoarding around the site boundary.
2. Security lighting at access points and around the site.
3. Manned security guard/watchman at entrance/exit.
4. Controlled access gates with a visitors' log/register.
5. CCTV surveillance cameras.

(a)(ii) Justification for site security control (2 marks):
- To prevent theft/vandalism of materials, tools, and equipment.
- To restrict unauthorised entry, thereby protecting the public and workers from injury and the contractor from liability.
- To safeguard sensitive design documents and plans.
- To protect against sabotage or malicious damage.

(b)(i) Recycling: The process of converting waste materials into new usable products or raw materials to prevent waste of potentially useful materials, reduce consumption of fresh raw materials, and lower energy usage. E.g., crushed concrete reused as hardcore; scrap metal melted down and reformed.

(b)(ii) Composting: A biological process whereby organic/biodegradable waste (e.g. vegetation, food scraps, timber offcuts) is decomposed by microorganisms under controlled conditions to produce compost/humus, which can be used as a soil conditioner or fertiliser on site or gardens.

(b)(iii) Reclaiming: The process of salvaging/recovering materials from demolished or disused structures so they can be reused in their original or near-original form. E.g., reclaimed bricks cleaned and reused, reclaimed timber reused as structural members or flooring, reclaimed roof tiles reused.

questions.text:
(a) Explain the relationship between retention fee and defects liability period.
(b) Describe the procedure of patenting.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Relationship between retention fee and defects liability period (4 marks):
- The retention fee (retention money) is a percentage (typically 5–10%) of each interim payment withheld by the employer/client from the contractor during the construction period.
- Half the retention is released at Practical Completion (issue of the Certificate of Practical Completion).
- The remaining half is held throughout the Defects Liability Period (DLP), which is a specified period (usually 6–12 months) after practical completion during which the contractor is obliged to return and rectify any defects that appear.
- At the end of the DLP, when the architect/engineer is satisfied that all defects have been made good, a Certificate of Making Good Defects is issued and the remaining retention money is released to the contractor.
- Therefore, retention money acts as financial security/incentive to ensure the contractor fulfils their obligations during the DLP.

(b) Procedure of patenting (6 marks, 1 mark per step):
1. Conceive and document the invention clearly, describing how it works.
2. Conduct a prior art search to confirm the invention is novel and does not already exist.
3. Prepare and file a patent application with the relevant Patents Office (including claims, description, drawings, and abstract).
4. The application is examined by a patent examiner to check novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability.
5. Publication of the application (usually 18 months after filing) so the public can view it.
6. Substantive examination and any objections/oppositions are addressed.
7. Grant of patent if requirements are met; the inventor pays the required fees.
8. The granted patent gives the inventor exclusive rights for a specified period (usually 20 years), subject to annual renewal fees.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Renovation vs Replacement (2 marks):
- Renovation: The process of restoring, improving, or updating an existing structure/element to a better or original condition without completely removing and substituting it (e.g. repainting, refurbishing, repairing). The original element is retained.
- Replacement: The complete removal of an existing element/component that is beyond repair and substituting it with a new one (e.g. replacing a rotten window frame with a new one). The original element is discarded.

(b)(i) Planning Permission: Ensures that proposed development is in line with local/national land use plans and zoning regulations. It controls the type, scale, and location of development to prevent inappropriate use of land, protect the environment, and ensure orderly urban/rural development.

(b)(ii) Building Regulations: Set minimum standards for the design, construction, and alteration of buildings to ensure the health, safety, welfare, and convenience of people in and around buildings. They cover structural stability, fire safety, drainage, energy efficiency, accessibility, etc.

(b)(iii) Health and Safety Control: Ensures that workplaces (including construction sites) comply with legal requirements to protect workers and the public from injury, illness, and death. It mandates risk assessments, provision of PPE, safe working practices, and accident reporting.

(c) Architects nominate subcontractors (any two valid reasons, 1 mark each):
- When specialist work is required (e.g. lift installation, specialist glazing) that requires expertise/equipment the main contractor may not possess.
- To ensure quality control by specifying a subcontractor with a proven track record for specialist work.
- To maintain design intent by using a supplier/installer already involved in the design process.
- To comply with a client's specific requirements or preferences for a particular specialist firm.

(i) wet state,
(ii) hardened state.
(d) Outline the procedure of carrying out a cube test on concrete.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Bulking of sand: The increase in volume of sand due to the presence of moisture (water film) on the surface of the sand particles. The surface tension of the thin water film holds the particles apart, causing the sand to bulk up (increase in volume). Bulking can increase the apparent volume of sand by up to 20–30%, meaning a batch measured by volume could contain less sand than intended, leading to a weaker mix. Bulking does not occur in bone-dry or fully saturated (flooded) sand.

(b) Justification for testing building materials (any two points, 1 mark each):
- To verify that materials meet required specifications/standards before incorporation into the works.
- To prevent use of sub-standard/defective materials that could compromise structural integrity and safety.
- To ensure value for money and that materials are fit for purpose.
- To comply with building regulations and contract requirements.
- To identify potential problems early and avoid costly remedial works.

(c)(i) Properties of concrete in wet/fresh state (any three, 1 mark each):
1. Workability – ease with which fresh concrete can be mixed, transported, placed, and compacted.
2. Consistency/flowability – ability to flow into formwork and fill spaces.
3. Cohesiveness/plasticity – ability to hold together without segregation or bleeding.
4. Setting time – time taken for the mix to begin stiffening.
5. Air content – amount of entrained/entrapped air in fresh mix.

(c)(ii) Properties of concrete in hardened state (any three, 1 mark each):
1. Compressive strength – ability to resist crushing/compressive loads.
2. Durability – resistance to weathering, chemical attack, and abrasion.
3. Permeability – resistance to water/liquid penetration.
4. Tensile strength – resistance to tensile/pulling forces (relatively low).
5. Shrinkage – reduction in volume as concrete dries/cures.
6. Thermal conductivity – ability to conduct heat.

(d) Procedure for cube test on concrete (5 marks):
1. Obtain a representative sample of fresh concrete from the mix (during pouring).
2. Lightly oil the inside of the steel cube moulds (usually 150 mm × 150 mm × 150 mm) to prevent adhesion.
3. Fill the mould in three equal layers, compacting each layer with 35 blows of a tamping rod (or using a vibrating table) to remove air voids.
4. Strike off the top surface level with the mould using a trowel and mark/label the mould with mix details, date, and sample reference.
5. Cover with a damp cloth/polythene sheet and leave undisturbed for 24 hours at room temperature.
6. After 24 hours, demould the cubes and immerse in a curing tank of water at 20°C.
7. Cure for the required period (commonly 7 days and/or 28 days).
8. Remove cubes, wipe dry, and weigh. Place centrally in the compression testing machine.
9. Apply load continuously at a rate of 0.2–0.4 MPa/s until failure.
10. Record the maximum load at failure; calculate compressive strength = Load (N) ÷ Area (mm²).
11. Compare result against the specified characteristic strength.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
Open Tendering Procedure (15 marks – award marks for each clearly described step, approximately 1–2 marks each):
1. Decision to build: The client/employer decides to proceed with a project and appoints consultants (architect, quantity surveyor, engineers).
2. Preparation of tender documents: Full tender documents are prepared, including drawings, specification, bills of quantities (BoQ), conditions of contract, and form of tender.
3. Public advertisement: An open invitation to tender is advertised in newspapers, government gazettes, or official procurement portals, stating the nature of the project, conditions for obtaining documents, and closing date.
4. Issue of tender documents: Interested contractors purchase or collect tender documents upon payment of a deposit (refundable or non-refundable).
5. Pre-tender meeting / site visit: A compulsory or voluntary site visit/briefing is arranged for all prospective tenderers to inspect the site and seek clarifications.
6. Clarification and addenda: Any queries from tenderers are answered and issued as addenda to all tenderers simultaneously to ensure fairness.
7. Submission of tenders: Contractors prepare and submit their priced tenders in sealed envelopes by the stated deadline; late tenders are rejected.
8. Opening of tenders: Tenders are opened publicly (or formally) at the stated time and date; a register of all submitted prices is prepared.
9. Evaluation/analysis of tenders: The quantity surveyor checks and analyses all tenders for arithmetic errors, qualifications, and compliance; a tender report is prepared.
10. Recommendation: The lowest compliant tender is normally recommended, but assessment also considers contractor competence, experience, and financial standing.
11. Award of contract: The client approves and the successful contractor is notified; a Letter of Intent may be issued.
12. Signing of contract: Both parties sign the formal contract documents before work commences.
13. Unsuccessful tenderers are notified and deposits may be refunded.

questions.text: Discuss any five characteristics of Zimbabwean architecture.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Five characteristics of Zimbabwean architecture (3 marks each = 15 marks):

1. Use of local/natural materials: Traditional Zimbabwean architecture makes extensive use of locally available materials such as granite stone (dry-stone walling as seen at Great Zimbabwe), pole-and-dagga (mud/earth), thatch grass for roofing, and burnt clay bricks. This reflects adaptation to the natural environment and available resources.

2. Circular/round plan forms: Traditional homesteads (musha) typically feature round huts (rondavels) with circular walls and conical thatched roofs. The circular form is culturally and structurally significant – it is efficient in material use, aerodynamically stable, and reflects communal cultural values.

3. Dry-stone walling technique: Exemplified by Great Zimbabwe (c. 11th–15th century), the sophisticated technique of stacking granite stones without mortar in carefully coursed patterns demonstrates advanced craft knowledge. Walls feature decorative chevron and herringbone patterns.

4. Courtyard/compound spatial organisation: Buildings are arranged around a central open courtyard (dare for men, court for women and children), reflecting social hierarchy and communal living. The spatial layout encodes cultural norms regarding gender, age, and status.

5. Climatic responsiveness/passive design: Architecture is adapted to the local climate – thick earth/stone walls provide thermal mass to keep interiors cool during hot days and warm at night. Small openings limit solar heat gain and dust infiltration. Overhanging thatched eaves provide shade and weather protection.

6. Integration with landscape: Structures are sited to blend with the natural topography, using natural rock outcrops as building platforms or incorporating them into walls, demonstrating a harmonious relationship between the built and natural environment.

7. Symbolic and spiritual elements: Spatial organisation often has symbolic meaning – the position of the dare (men's meeting place), granaries, and spirit huts reflects beliefs about ancestry, community governance, and spiritual protection.

questions.text:
(a) With reference to structural design work of built structures, write brief notes on footing and support your answer with a neatly labelled diagram.
(b) Compare using any five points, concrete and steel as structural materials of the built environment.

subParts.text: With reference to structural design work of built structures, write brief notes on footing and support your answer with a neatly labelled diagram.
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Compare using any five points, concrete and steel as structural materials of the built environment.
subParts.label: (b)

questions.diagramNote: A neatly labelled diagram of a footing (foundation type, e.g. strip or pad footing) is required for part (a), showing components such as the base, depth, width, ground level, and column/wall above.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Footing (5 marks):
- A footing is the lowest part of a foundation that is in direct contact with the ground/soil. It distributes the load from the superstructure over a sufficiently large area of soil to prevent excessive settlement or shear failure.
- Types include: strip footings (under continuous walls), pad/isolated footings (under individual columns), raft footings (covering the entire building footprint), and combined/cantilever footings.
- Key design considerations: bearing capacity of soil, depth below ground (below frost line and topsoil), size of footing base (determined by load and safe bearing capacity), reinforcement (for reinforced concrete footings).
- Diagram should show: ground level, depth of footing, footing base width, column/wall, concrete pad, soil below, and labels for each component.

(b) Comparison of Concrete and Steel as structural materials (any five points, 2 marks each):

| Point | Concrete | Steel |
|---|---|---|  
| 1. Compressive/Tensile strength | High compressive strength but low tensile strength | High in both compressive and tensile strength |
| 2. Weight/Density | Heavy (approx. 2400 kg/m³); increases dead load | Lighter relative to its strength; reduces dead load |
| 3. Fire resistance | Naturally fire-resistant; does not combust | Poor fire resistance; loses strength rapidly at high temperatures; requires fire protection |
| 4. Corrosion resistance | Durable and resistant to corrosion/weathering if well made | Susceptible to corrosion/rust; requires protective coatings or maintenance |
| 5. Workability/Fabrication | Can be cast into any shape on site; economical for complex shapes | Fabricated off-site to precise dimensions; limited shapes but connections are versatile |
| 6. Maintenance | Low maintenance once cast | Requires regular maintenance (painting, galvanising) to prevent corrosion |
| 7. Cost | Generally cheaper in material and labour cost locally | More expensive, especially where imported |
| 8. Speed of construction | Slower – requires curing time and formwork | Faster – prefabricated and quickly assembled on site |
| 9. Sustainability/Recyclability | Not easily recycled; uses large amounts of aggregate and cement | Highly recyclable; scrap steel can be fully remelted |
| 10. Span capability | Limited spans without heavy sections | Can achieve long spans with lightweight sections (e.g. trusses, beams) |

questions.text: With the aid of a diagram explain the production of biogas in the biogas digester.
questions.diagramNote: A labelled diagram of a biogas digester is required, showing components such as the inlet, digester chamber/tank, slurry, gas holder/dome, outlet/effluent pipe, and gas outlet pipe.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Biogas Production in a Biogas Digester (15 marks):

Diagram description (award marks for a correctly labelled diagram showing): inlet pipe, digester tank/chamber, slurry/substrate, floating drum or fixed dome gas holder, gas outlet pipe, overflow/effluent outlet, and manure/organic feed. [Up to 5 marks for diagram]

Explanation [Up to 10 marks]:
1. Feedstock/input: Organic material such as animal dung (cattle, pig manure), food waste, or crop residues is mixed with water to form slurry and fed into the digester through the inlet pipe.
2. Anaerobic digestion: Inside the sealed digester tank, in the absence of oxygen (anaerobic conditions), microorganisms (bacteria) break down the organic matter through a four-stage process: hydrolysis → acidogenesis → acetogenesis → methanogenesis.
3. Gas production: During methanogenesis, methanogenic bacteria convert acetic acid, hydrogen, and carbon dioxide into biogas, which is approximately 55–70% methane (CH₄) and 30–45% carbon dioxide (CO₂), with trace amounts of other gases.
4. Gas collection: The biogas rises and is collected in the gas holder (fixed dome or floating drum) above the slurry. Pressure builds up and the gas is piped out through the gas outlet for use in cooking, lighting, or electricity generation.
5. Effluent output: The digested slurry (digestate) that remains is nutrient-rich and flows out through the overflow/effluent outlet. It can be used as organic fertiliser (bioslurry) for agriculture.
6. Temperature and pH: Optimal digestion occurs at mesophilic temperatures (30–40°C) and a pH of 6.5–7.5. Maintaining these conditions maximises gas yield.
7. Retention time: The organic material typically remains in the digester for 20–40 days (hydraulic retention time) to allow complete digestion.

Marking guidance for the site layout drawing (20 marks total):

Security [3 marks]: Perimeter hoarding/fence around entire site boundary (1); controlled access gate(s) with gatehouse/security hut (1); indication of security lighting positions or CCTV (1).

Services [3 marks]: Temporary site electricity supply/distribution board indicated (1); temporary water supply pipe/tap indicated on layout (1); temporary drainage/waste disposal point or site toilet drainage indicated (1).

Hutments [2 marks]: Site offices/contractor's hut clearly labelled and positioned away from construction activity/danger zones, near site entrance (1); drawing office or clerk of works hut shown (1).

Welfare facilities [3 marks]: Canteen/mess room (1); toilets/sanitary facilities/WCs (1); first aid room/medical post or drying room/changing room (1).

Material storage [3 marks]: Open storage area for bulk materials (sand, aggregates) positioned for easy delivery access (1); covered/locked storage shed for valuable/sensitive materials (cement, tools) (1); appropriate positioning away from building works to avoid obstruction but close enough for efficient use (1).

Plant and equipment [3 marks]: Concrete mixer positioned centrally or near material storage (1); tower crane or scaffold shown if applicable (1); vehicle parking/turning area or site roads/hardstanding for plant movement shown (1).

Informative signs [2 marks]: Site name/project signboard at entrance (1); safety/warning signs (PPE required, danger, no unauthorised entry) shown at gate or around site (1).

Overall dimensions [1 mark]: Overall dimensions of the site/layout plan clearly marked/annotated on the drawing (1).

questions.text:
The following are foreign musical instruments in Zimbabwe except
A keyboard.
B mbira.
C guitar.
D recorder.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – mbira. The mbira is an indigenous Zimbabwean instrument, not a foreign one. Keyboard, guitar, and recorder are all foreign/Western instruments.

questions.text:
Which materials were used to make rock painting in Zimbabwe?
A pencils
B fibres
C beads
D animal blood
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – animal blood. Rock paintings in Zimbabwe were made using natural pigments including animal blood, ochre, and other organic materials.

questions.text:
In theatre, what name is given to clay pots, knobkerries and animal tails?
A costumes
B instruments
C props
D sets
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – props. Props (properties) are objects used on stage during a performance, such as clay pots, knobkerries, and animal tails.

questions.text:
The importance of suspense during a play is
A bringing uneasiness to the audience.
B keep the audience anxious.
C making acting interesting.
D making the performance enjoyable.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – keep the audience anxious. Suspense in theatre is primarily used to keep the audience in a state of anticipation and anxiety about what will happen next.

questions.text:
The following are examples of principles of dance except
A weight.
B intent.
C coordination.
D balance.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – coordination. Coordination is an element/skill of movement but not a principle of dance. Weight, intent, and balance are recognised principles of dance.

questions.text:

questions.text:
The making of artworks using stone and chisel is called
A computer art.
B weaving.
C pottery.
D sculpturing.
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – sculpturing. Sculpturing involves carving or shaping materials such as stone using tools like a chisel to create three-dimensional artworks.

questions.text:

A focus
B force
C time
D space
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – focus. The main elements of dance are body, space, time, and force/energy. Focus is a performance quality/skill but is not classified as a core element of dance.

questions.text:
Which one is a common colour on rock painting in Zimbabwe?
A green
B pink
C purple
D brown
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – brown. Rock paintings in Zimbabwe predominantly feature earth tones, especially brown and red ochre, derived from natural pigments available to the San people.

questions.text:
Which of the following place is known for stone sculpture in Zimbabwe?
A Tengenenge
B Gwai

questions.aiModelAnswer: A – Tengenenge. Tengenenge is a famous stone sculpture community in Zimbabwe, known as one of the leading centres for Zimbabwean stone sculpture art.

questions.text:
IYASA is a theatre group found in
A Zambia.
B Zimbabwe.

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.text:
Activities done before the main exercise are called
A cool down.
B warm up.

questions.aiModelAnswer: B – warm up. A warm up consists of preparatory exercises performed before the main activity to gradually increase heart rate, loosen muscles, and reduce the risk of injury.

questions.text:
The technique of holding a striking equipment is
A aiming.
B footwork.
C grip.
D stance.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – grip. A grip is the specific technique used to hold striking equipment such as a bat, racket, or hockey stick.

questions.text:
How can people locate new places and objects?
A maps and compass
B maps and lines
C maps and strings
D strings and lines
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – maps and compass. Maps and a compass are the standard tools used in orienteering and navigation to locate new places and objects.

questions.text:
The following are locomotion activities except
A galloping.
B rolling.
C twisting.
D walking.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – twisting. Twisting is a non-locomotor (axial) movement performed on the spot. Galloping, rolling, and walking are all locomotor activities that move the body from one place to another.

questions.text:
Which of the following is an injury prevention measure?
A lack of exercise
B age cheating
C use of appropriate equipment
D use oversized attire
questions.topic: Physical Education – Safety and Injury Prevention
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – use of appropriate equipment. Using appropriate and correctly fitted equipment is a key injury prevention measure in physical activity and sport.

questions.text:
The following are apparatus in gymnastics except
A hoops.
B hurdles.
C metal bars.
D ropes.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – hurdles. Hurdles are athletics/track and field equipment, not gymnastics apparatus. Hoops, metal bars, and ropes are all standard gymnastics apparatus.

questions.text:
In which category does netball and basketball fall?
A adventure games
B invasion games
C net games
D target games
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – invasion games. Netball and basketball are invasion games because players must invade the opponent's territory/court to score in a goal or basket.

questions.text:
Which equipment is used in one of the vertical jumps?
A take off board
B shot
C pole
D pole vault
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – pole. A pole is used in the pole vault, which is a vertical jump event in athletics where athletes use a flexible pole to propel themselves over a bar.

questions.text:
Select a health-related component of fitness.
A agility
B speed
C coordination
D muscular endurance
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – muscular endurance. Muscular endurance is a health-related component of fitness. Agility, speed, and coordination are skill-related (performance-related) components of fitness.

questions.text:
Triple jump has three stages which are
A go, step and jump.
B hop, step and jump.
C hop, jump and go.
D jump, step and hop.
questions.aiModelAnswer: B – hop, step and jump. The triple jump consists of three phases: a hop (landing on the same foot), a step (landing on the opposite foot), and a jump (landing in the sand pit).

questions.text:
Flexibility is tested using
A beep test.
B skin folds.
C sit and reach test.
D Illinois test.
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – sit and reach test. The sit and reach test measures flexibility, particularly of the lower back and hamstring muscles. The beep test measures cardiovascular endurance, skin folds measure body composition, and the Illinois test measures agility.

questions.text:
Gaseous exchange takes place in the
A alveoli.
B bronchi.
C bronchioles.
D diaphragm.
questions.topic: Physical Education – Anatomy and Physiology (Respiratory System)
questions.aiModelAnswer: A – alveoli. Gaseous exchange (oxygen entering the blood and carbon dioxide leaving) takes place in the alveoli, which are tiny air sacs in the lungs with thin walls and a rich blood supply.

questions.text:
Which injury is caused by overworking muscles?
A fracture
B dislocation
C strain
D sprain
questions.aiModelAnswer: C – strain. A strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon caused by overstretching or overworking the muscle. A sprain affects ligaments, a fracture is a broken bone, and a dislocation is a joint injury.

questions.text:

A sweets
B fatty fresh chips
C salty braai meat
D fruits
questions.aiModelAnswer: D – fruits. Fruits are healthy foods rich in vitamins, minerals, and fibre. Sweets, fatty chips, and salty braai meat are unhealthy options high in sugar, fat, and salt respectively.

questions.text:

questions.aiModelAnswer: B – Modified sit and reach test. The modified sit and reach test is adapted for people living with disabilities and those who cannot perform the standard sit and reach test, making it more inclusive and accessible.

D heart – breaks food

questions.text: Explain the role of your father's sister in a family set up.
questions.aiModelAnswer: The father's sister (paternal aunt / 'tete' in Shona / 'isisi' in Ndebele) plays several key roles in a family set up. Key points include: 1. **Cultural advisor**: She guides nieces and nephews on cultural norms, traditions, and values (e.g., teaching girls about womanhood, marriage preparation). 2. **Marriage negotiations**: She plays a central role in lobola/roora (bride price) negotiations, representing her brother's family. 3. **Disciplinarian**: She corrects bad behaviour in nephews and nieces and instils discipline. 4. **Mediator**: She resolves conflicts between couples or within the extended family. 5. **Counsellor**: She provides guidance on personal issues such as relationships, sexuality, and life challenges. 6. **Caretaker**: She looks after children when parents are absent or deceased. 7. **Spiritual intermediary**: She connects the family to ancestral spirits and performs certain rituals. 8. **Role model**: She sets an example of womanhood and family responsibility. Award marks for any well-explained relevant points (approximately 5 points fully explained = 25 marks).

questions.text: What is the importance of guidance and counselling to people living with H.I.V?
questions.aiModelAnswer: Guidance and counselling is vital to people living with HIV (PLHIV) in the following ways: 1. **Emotional support**: Helps individuals cope with shock, denial, fear, anger, and depression following diagnosis. 2. **Acceptance**: Counselling assists PLHIV to accept their status and live positively. 3. **Adherence to medication**: Counsellors encourage compliance with ARV treatment regimens. 4. **Reducing stigma and discrimination**: Equips PLHIV with skills to handle societal stigma and maintain self-worth. 5. **Behaviour change**: Encourages safer sexual practices to prevent re-infection and transmission. 6. **Disclosure support**: Guides PLHIV on how and when to disclose their status to partners, family, and employers. 7. **Nutritional guidance**: Advises on healthy living and diet to boost immunity. 8. **Family counselling**: Helps families understand and support PLHIV. 9. **Prevention of suicide/mental health**: Addresses suicidal ideation and promotes mental wellness. 10. **Linkage to services**: Connects PLHIV to support groups, social services, and health facilities. Award marks for any well-explained relevant points.

questions.text: Show how Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu can reduce gender based violence in your community.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu (the philosophy of humaneness and communal living) can reduce gender-based violence (GBV) in the following ways: 1. **Respect for others**: Ubuntu promotes respect for all people regardless of gender, discouraging violent behaviour. 2. **Community responsibility**: Encourages community members to speak out against GBV rather than remaining silent. 3. **Empathy and compassion**: Instils empathy so perpetrators understand the pain they cause victims. 4. **Conflict resolution**: Traditional Ubuntu values encourage peaceful resolution of disputes rather than violence. 5. **Collective upbringing/discipline**: Communities collectively raise and discipline children, teaching them non-violent behaviour from an early age. 6. **Role of elders**: Elders guided by Ubuntu principles counsel and reprimand those who perpetrate GBV. 7. **Dignity and equality**: Ubuntu affirms the dignity of every person, promoting gender equality and discouraging patriarchal dominance. 8. **Social accountability**: Ubuntu's emphasis on 'I am because we are' creates social accountability that deters violent acts. 9. **Support for survivors**: Communities guided by Ubuntu support and shelter GBV survivors. Award marks for any well-explained relevant points.

questions.text: Examine challenges facing adolescence in Zimbabwe.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Challenges facing adolescents in Zimbabwe include: 1. **Peer pressure**: Pressure from peers to engage in substance abuse, early sex, or criminal activities. 2. **Substance abuse**: Abuse of alcohol, drugs, and substance use (e.g., crystal meth/mutoriro) is widespread among adolescents. 3. **Early pregnancy/child marriage**: Girls face risk of early pregnancy, dropping out of school and child marriage. 4. **Identity crisis**: Adolescents struggle to define who they are, leading to confusion and risky behaviours. 5. **Unemployment/poverty**: Limited economic opportunities lead to despair and risky coping mechanisms. 6. **HIV/AIDS and STIs**: Risky sexual behaviour exposes adolescents to HIV and other STIs. 7. **Mental health challenges**: Depression, anxiety, and low self-esteem are common. 8. **School dropout**: Economic pressures, pregnancy, and lack of fees cause many adolescents to drop out. 9. **Cyberbullying and social media influence**: Negative online content and cyberbullying affect mental health. 10. **Physical changes**: Difficulty coping with puberty-related physical and emotional changes. 11. **Gender-based violence**: Adolescent girls are especially vulnerable to sexual and physical violence. Award marks for any well-explained relevant challenges.

questions.text: How does low self-esteem affect learners' performance?
questions.aiModelAnswer: Low self-esteem affects learners' performance in the following ways: 1. **Lack of confidence**: Learners with low self-esteem doubt their abilities and are unwilling to attempt tasks or answer questions in class. 2. **Poor academic results**: Lack of belief in themselves leads to underperformance in tests and exams. 3. **Withdrawal/social isolation**: Learners may withdraw from class participation, group work, and social interactions. 4. **Fear of failure**: Excessive fear of making mistakes discourages learners from trying, leading to learned helplessness. 5. **Susceptibility to bullying**: Low self-esteem makes learners easy targets for bullies, further affecting concentration and attendance. 6. **Depression and anxiety**: Low self-esteem is linked to mental health issues that impair learning and memory. 7. **Negative self-talk**: Constant internal negative messages ('I am stupid', 'I can't do it') reduce motivation and effort. 8. **School absenteeism/dropout**: Some learners avoid school altogether to escape feelings of inadequacy. 9. **Poor relationships with teachers and peers**: Difficulty forming positive relationships affects the learning environment. 10. **Substance abuse**: Some learners turn to substances to cope, further impairing academic performance. Award marks for any well-explained relevant points.

questions.text: Suggest ways to prevent child abuse in society.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Ways to prevent child abuse in society include: 1. **Education and awareness**: Educate parents, children, and communities about the forms, signs, and effects of child abuse. 2. **Teaching children body safety**: Teach children about personal boundaries, the difference between appropriate and inappropriate touch. 3. **Strong legal frameworks**: Enforce existing child protection laws (e.g., Children's Act) and ensure perpetrators are prosecuted. 4. **Reporting mechanisms**: Establish accessible, confidential reporting systems (hotlines, community structures) so abuse is reported promptly. 5. **Parenting programmes**: Offer parenting skills training to reduce frustration-driven abuse at home. 6. **Community vigilance**: Encourage communities to watch out for signs of abuse and intervene or report. 7. **Support for vulnerable families**: Provide social support (food, economic assistance) to families under stress to reduce neglect. 8. **School-based programmes**: Integrate child rights and safety education into school curricula. 9. **Training professionals**: Train teachers, health workers, and police to identify and respond to child abuse. 10. **Reducing poverty**: Address poverty and inequality, which are root causes of neglect and exploitation. 11. **Media campaigns**: Use radio, TV, and social media to sensitise the public against child abuse. Award marks for any well-explained relevant suggestions.

questions.text: Write a job application letter to a company of your choice.
questions.aiModelAnswer: A well-written job application letter should include the following elements (award marks accordingly): 1. **Sender's address** (top right): Candidate's full address and date. 2. **Recipient's address** (left): Name/title of the addressee, company name, and address. 3. **Salutation**: 'Dear Sir/Madam' or 'Dear Mr/Mrs [Name]'. 4. **Subject line**: Clear reference to the position being applied for e.g., 'RE: APPLICATION FOR THE POST OF ACCOUNTS CLERK'. 5. **Opening paragraph**: State the position applied for and where it was advertised. 6. **Body paragraphs**: Highlight relevant qualifications, skills, and experience that make the candidate suitable for the role. 7. **Personal qualities**: Mention relevant personal attributes (hardworking, team player, etc.). 8. **Closing paragraph**: Express willingness for an interview, state that documents are enclosed/attached. 9. **Complimentary close**: 'Yours faithfully' (if salutation was Dear Sir/Madam) or 'Yours sincerely' (if a name was used). 10. **Signature and full name**. Mark for: correct format, appropriate tone, relevance of content, grammar and language use. Deduct marks for major format errors or irrelevant content.

questions.text: To what extent are youths in Zimbabwe patriotic?
questions.aiModelAnswer: This is a discursive question requiring a balanced argument. Key points: **Evidence of patriotism among Zimbabwean youth**: 1. Participation in national events (Independence Day, Heroes Day celebrations). 2. Involvement in national development programmes (e.g., NYICC, Border Gezi training). 3. Youth volunteering in community service and clean-up campaigns. 4. Talented youth representing Zimbabwe in sports, arts, and academia internationally. 5. Youth participation in elections and civic processes. **Evidence of lack of patriotism**: 1. Brain drain — many skilled youths emigrate in search of better opportunities ('Jecha' phenomenon). 2. Disregard for national symbols (flag, anthem, national monuments). 3. Low participation in national development initiatives. 4. Drug abuse and criminal behaviour undermining national fabric. 5. Apathy towards civic and political processes. **Conclusion**: Patriotism among Zimbabwean youth is partial — while some display strong national pride, economic hardship and disillusionment drive others to disengage. Award marks for balanced arguments with evidence, plus a reasoned conclusion. Reward any well-supported stance.

questions.text: Discuss methods of waste disposal in your society.
questions.aiModelAnswer: Methods of waste disposal in society include: 1. **Landfill**: Waste is buried in designated sites; common but can lead to soil and water contamination. 2. **Incineration/burning**: Waste is burned at high temperatures; reduces volume but may cause air pollution. 3. **Composting**: Organic waste is decomposed to produce manure/fertiliser; environmentally friendly. 4. **Recycling**: Materials such as paper, glass, plastic, and metals are processed and reused; reduces raw material use. 5. **Pit latrines/pit disposal**: Organic waste including human waste is disposed of in pits; common in rural Zimbabwe. 6. **Sewage treatment**: Liquid waste is treated in sewage plants before being released; reduces water pollution. 7. **Open dumping**: Waste is dumped in open spaces; widespread but harmful — causes disease, pollution. 8. **Biogas production**: Organic waste is used to produce energy through anaerobic digestion. 9. **Littering awareness/waste bins**: Community waste bins and education campaigns reduce indiscriminate waste disposal. 10. **Hazardous waste management**: Special disposal for chemicals, medical waste, and e-waste to prevent environmental contamination. Award marks for description of each method and discussion of advantages/disadvantages.

questions.text: How does your country benefit from international relationships?
questions.aiModelAnswer: Zimbabwe benefits from international relationships in the following ways: 1. **Trade and investment**: International relationships open markets for Zimbabwean goods (tobacco, minerals) and attract foreign direct investment. 2. **Foreign aid and grants**: Zimbabwe receives financial, humanitarian, and technical aid from international bodies (UN, IMF, World Bank, bilateral donors). 3. **Technology transfer**: Partnerships with developed nations facilitate access to modern technology and innovation. 4. **Diplomatic support**: International allies support Zimbabwe's interests in global forums (AU, UN, SADC). 5. **Tourism**: Good international relations promote Zimbabwe as a tourist destination, generating foreign currency. 6. **Education and scholarships**: International relationships provide scholarships and academic exchange programmes for Zimbabwean students. 7. **Peace and security**: Membership in international bodies (SADC, AU, UN) supports regional peace and collective security. 8. **Cultural exchange**: Promotes sharing of cultural values, arts, and heritage between nations. 9. **Health support**: Access to international health programmes (WHO, PEPFAR) for disease control and healthcare strengthening. 10. **Remittances**: Zimbabweans in the diaspora (facilitated by open international relations) send remittances that support the economy. Award marks for any well-explained relevant benefits.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Mongo (Theme/Central Message) – 5 marks:
The poem 'Nsimbi a yi si chaya' (The bell has not yet rung) by T.P. Magaisa explores themes of time, patience, hope, and anticipation. The central message concerns waiting for the right moment — that things must happen in due course and one should not rush. Credit clear identification of the main theme (2 marks) plus supporting explanation with reference to the poem (3 marks).

(b) Nkoka wa swigaririmi (Role/Effect of five poetic devices) – 20 marks (4 marks each):
Students must identify and explain the effect of five devices used in the poem. Expected devices include (any five):
1. Xifaniso (Simile) – comparison using 'tanihi/nga' to create vivid imagery.
2. Swifananiso (Metaphor) – direct comparison to deepen meaning.
3. Ritiho / Xitlhangi (Personification) – giving human qualities to non-human things.
4. Ku phindha-phindha (Repetition/Refrain) – emphasises key ideas and creates rhythm.
5. Nkulumo yo sungula (Alliteration) – repetition of initial sounds for musical effect.
6. Nkulumo ya ntlawa (Onomatopoeia) – words that imitate sound.
7. Xivumbeko xa xitlhokovetselo (Stanza/Structure) – how stanzas shape meaning.
For each device: 1 mark for correct identification + 1 mark for quotation/example from the poem + 2 marks for explanation of its effect = 4 marks each × 5 = 20 marks.

questions.text: Pimanisa switlhokovetselo swa Vurhongo bya makumu na Xihambanyisi u karhi u kombisa ku fana na ku hambana ka swona.
questions.topic: Vutlhokovetseri – Ku Pimanisa Switlhokovetselo (Comparative Poetry Analysis)
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Students must compare and contrast the two poems 'Vurhongo bya makumu' and 'Xihambanyisi' by T.P. Magaisa. A well-structured response should include:

Ku fana (Similarities) – up to ~12 marks:
- Both poems are written by the same poet (T.P. Magaisa) and share a Xichangana cultural context.
- Both may deal with themes of change, transition, or social commentary.
- Both use poetic devices such as imagery and repetition.
- Similar tonal qualities or emotional appeal.

Ku hambana (Differences) – up to ~12 marks:
- Themes may differ: e.g. one focuses on death/endings ('Vurhongo bya makumu' – the last sleep/death) while the other may address a journey or departure ('Xihambanyisi' – the passer-by/traveller).
- Tone, mood, and setting differ between the two poems.
- Structure/stanza organisation may vary.
- Use of specific poetic devices and imagery differs.

Presentation/organisation of comparison – 1 mark.

Marking guide: Award marks for: identification of similarities (up to 12), identification of differences (up to 12), evidence/quotation from poems (integrated throughout), overall presentation (1 mark). Total = 25 marks.

questions.topic: CAD, Quality Assurance and Quality Control
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Advantages of CAD (any 2): 1. Easy to edit/modify designs without redrawing. 2. Produces accurate and precise drawings. 3. Designs can be stored and retrieved electronically. 4. Enables 3D visualisation of products. 5. Saves time in producing multiple copies.
Disadvantages of CAD (any 2): 1. High initial cost of software and hardware. 2. Requires specialist training. 3. Risk of data loss due to technical faults. 4. Over-reliance on technology/power dependency.

(b)(i) Quality Assurance: A proactive, systematic process or set of planned activities implemented throughout the production process to ensure that a product will meet specified quality standards before, during and after production. It focuses on preventing defects.

(b)(ii) Quality Control: A reactive process involving inspection, testing and checking of finished products or components at specific stages to identify and eliminate defects. It focuses on identifying defects in products.

(c) Purpose of Quality Staff: To monitor and enforce quality standards throughout production; to carry out inspections and testing; to ensure products meet customer requirements and specifications; to reduce waste and reject rates; to maintain and improve production processes and standards.

(a) A patent is a legal right granted by a government authority to an inventor, giving them the exclusive right to make, use, sell, or licence their invention for a specified period (usually 20 years), in exchange for public disclosure of the invention.

(b) Five procedures for patent registration (any 5):
1. Conduct a prior art/patent search to ensure the invention is new.
2. Prepare/document a full description of the invention including drawings.
3. File a patent application with the relevant patent office/authority.
4. Pay the required application fees.
5. Examination of the application by the patent office for novelty and inventiveness.
6. Publication of the patent application.
7. Grant/issuance of the patent certificate upon approval.
8. Respond to any objections raised by the patent examiner.

(c) Three benefits of patents to a Wood Technologist (any 3):
1. Provides exclusive rights to profit from the invention, preventing others from copying it.
2. Can license the invention to others and earn royalties/income.
3. Protects investment in research and development.

5. Enhances the reputation and credibility of the technologist.

questions.topic: Health and Safety / Disaster Management in the Workshop
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Disaster management refers to the organised process of preparing for, responding to, and recovering from disasters (accidents, fires, injuries, etc.) in order to minimise their impact on people, property and the environment. It involves prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery.

(b) Effective management of disasters in the workshop (any 6 points):
1. Conduct regular risk assessments to identify potential hazards.
2. Ensure all fire extinguishers and first aid kits are available and accessible.
3. Train all staff and students in emergency procedures and first aid.
4. Maintain clear and unobstructed emergency exits and escape routes.
5. Carry out regular safety drills (fire drills, evacuation drills).
6. Ensure proper storage and labelling of flammable/hazardous materials.
7. Install smoke detectors, fire alarms and sprinkler systems.
8. Keep machinery well maintained and guarded to prevent accidents.
9. Display emergency contact numbers and evacuation plans clearly.
10. Ensure proper housekeeping — keep floors and walkways clear of debris.

(c)(i) Precautions for dust: Wear appropriate dust masks/respirators (PPE); ensure adequate ventilation/dust extraction systems are in use; wear safety goggles to protect eyes.

(c)(ii) Precautions for toxic fumes: Work in a well-ventilated area or use fume extraction systems; wear appropriate respiratory protection (respirator/gas mask); wear protective clothing and gloves; avoid prolonged exposure.

questions.topic: Material Properties – Static Stress and Manufactured Boards
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Three types of static stress (any 3, each with identification and explanation):
(i) Tension/Tensile stress: A pulling or stretching force applied to a material along its length, tending to elongate or pull it apart. e.g., a rope under load.
(ii) Compression/Compressive stress: A pushing or squeezing force applied to a material, tending to shorten or crush it. e.g., a column supporting a load.
(iii) Shear stress: A force applied parallel or tangential to a surface, causing one part of the material to slide over an adjacent part. e.g., scissors cutting a material.
(iv) Bending/Flexural stress: A combination of tensile and compressive stresses caused by a transverse load applied to a beam, causing it to bend.
(v) Torsion/Torsional stress: A twisting force applied to a material about its longitudinal axis.

(b)(i) Suitable manufactured board: Medium Density Fibreboard (MDF) / Chipboard / Plywood / Blockboard.

(b)(ii) Reason: MDF – has a smooth, uniform surface suitable for laminating or painting; uniform thickness; no grain direction issues; stable and resistant to warping. Plywood – strong, rigid, resistant to splitting; available in large sheets. Chipboard – relatively cheap and widely available in large stable sheets.

(b)(iii) Production of MDF (example): Wood fibres are produced by breaking down wood chips using heat and pressure (thermomechanical refining). The fibres are mixed with resin binders and wax, then formed into a mat. The mat is pressed under high temperature and pressure in a hot press to bond the fibres and form a dense, uniform board of the required thickness. The board is then trimmed and sanded to final dimensions.
For Chipboard: Wood chips/shavings are mixed with resin adhesive, spread into a mat, and pressed under heat and pressure to form sheets.

questions.topic: Design, Mechanisms and Working Drawings – Folding Table Tennis Table
questions.diagramNote: Candidate must produce freehand design sketches, folding mechanism, locking mechanism, knock-down fitting detail, front view and sectional end elevation working drawings of the folding table tennis table on A2 paper.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Design (8 marks): Sketches should show a table tennis table (standard dimensions approx. 2740 mm × 1525 mm × 760 mm) that folds in half along the length/width and has detachable legs or a folding underframe. Credit for: clear proportions, labelled parts, foldable top (hinged at centre), detachable/folding legs, compactness when stored.

(b)(i) Folding mechanism (10 marks): Detailed sketch showing a piano/continuous hinge or butterfly hinge along the centre line of the table top allowing the two halves to fold upward/together. Folded unit should stand vertically for storage. Award marks for: clarity of mechanism, correct hinge placement, folded position shown, annotations/labels.

(b)(ii) Locking mechanism (2 marks): A latch, hook-and-eye, barrel bolt, or positive locking pin/clip that holds the two halves open flat during play. Sketch and label required.

(c) Knock-down (KD) fitting (4 marks): Suitable KD fittings include: cam lock and bolt, barrel nut and bolt, or confirmat screw. Sketch should show how the fitting connects the table top to the underframe/leg assembly and allows disassembly. Labels, exploded view, and material awarded marks.

(d) Three important design factors (any 3):
1. Size/dimensions – must conform to standard table tennis dimensions or be compact enough to store.
2. Stability – the table must be rigid and stable during play.
3. Ease of folding/storage – the mechanism must be simple and quick to operate.
4. Strength and durability of materials used.
5. Safety – no sharp edges; locking mechanism must prevent accidental collapse.
6. Cost/affordability of materials and construction.
7. Portability/weight – light enough to move.

(e) Working drawings (10 marks): Front view – orthographic projection showing overall height, width, leg position, hinge centre line, drawn to indicated scale. Sectional end elevation – section through the table showing internal construction, thickness of top, leg cross-section, hinge detail, knock-down fitting. Award marks for: correct projection, dimensions, section lines, labels, title block.

(f) Two other materials (any 2): 1. Metal (steel/aluminium) – for hinges, brackets, legs, KD fittings. 2. Plastic – for feet/caps, edge banding, locking clips. 3. MDF/plywood surface laminate. 4. Rubber – for feet to prevent slipping.

(g) Suitable finish: Polyurethane varnish / paint (white or green as per table tennis standards) / lacquer / melamine laminate.

questions.topic: Applied Mathematics – Machining Calculations and Business/Costing
questions.diagramNote: Fig. 1 shows a bar to be machined to a sharp (tapered/pointed) end. Dimensions given: overall label A = 87.00 mm, sections labelled B and C, centre line O-O, with dimensions 25 mm, 60 mm, and 8 mm marked on the diagram.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Minimum length of bar (using Fig. 1 dimensions — 87.00 mm total, with 25 mm, 60 mm, 8 mm sub-dimensions and a tapered/pointed end):
The minimum length of bar = sum of all linear segments along the axis.
Based on the given dimensions: Length = 87.00 mm (as dimension A represents the full required length including the machined sharp end). Workings must account for the tapered section geometry. Using Pythagoras if the taper involves a diagonal: the sharp end taper adds to the straight length. With the given values (25 mm body + 60 mm taper section + allowance), minimum bar length ≈ 87.00 mm. Full marks for correct application of geometry and clear working.

(a)(ii) Work done = Force × Distance = mass × g × height
= 20 kg × 9.81 m/s² × 8 m
= 20 × 9.81 × 8
= 1 569.6 J ≈ 1 570 J (or 1.57 kJ)
(Accept g = 10 m/s²: W = 20 × 10 × 8 = 1 600 J)

(b)(i)
1. Revenue (Total Revenue) = Selling price per unit × Number of units sold
= $600 × 30 000 = $18 000 000

2. Total Cost = Variable (Direct) Costs + Fixed Costs
Variable cost per unit = Labour + Materials = $200 + $175 = $375
Total Variable Cost = $375 × 30 000 = $11 250 000
Total Cost = $11 250 000 + $2 000 000 = $13 250 000

3. Profit = Total Revenue − Total Cost
= $18 000 000 − $13 250 000 = $4 750 000

(b)(ii) Adjusted figures:
New sales = 30 000 × (1 − 0.20) = 24 000 units
New selling price = $600 × (1 + 0.15) = $690
New Revenue = $690 × 24 000 = $16 560 000
Total Variable Cost = $375 × 24 000 = $9 000 000
Total Cost = $9 000 000 + $2 000 000 = $11 000 000
New Profit = $16 560 000 − $11 000 000 = $5 560 000

questions.topic: Structural Calculations – Roofing Trusses and Angle Irons
questions.diagramNote: Fig. 2 shows a roofing truss diagram with labelled members: rafters (R), tie-beam, king post, queen posts (A and B), and struts (C and D). The truss has a symmetrical pitch roof profile. Members A, B, C, D and R are labelled on the diagram.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a)(i) Length of tie-beam:
Tie-beam = width of block + front verandah overlap + back verandah overlap
= 8.2 m + 0.8 m + 0.4 m = 9.4 m

(a)(ii) Length of rafter R:
The half-span of the building (excluding verandahs) = 8.2 ÷ 2 = 4.1 m
King post height = 1.8 m
Using Pythagoras: R = √(4.1² + 1.8²) = √(16.81 + 3.24) = √20.05 ≈ 4.478 m ≈ 4.48 m
(Note: the rafter extends over the verandah; if the full half including verandah overhang is used: half tie-beam = 9.4/2 = 4.7 m; R = √(4.7² + 1.8²) = √(22.09 + 3.24) = √25.33 ≈ 5.03 m — accept either based on truss geometry interpreted from Fig. 2.)

(a)(iii) Members using 50 × 50 × 5 mm angle iron (per truss):
- 2 rafters: 2 × 4.48 m = 8.96 m (or per calculated R)
- 1 tie-beam: 9.4 m
- 1 king post: 1.8 m
- Queen posts A (×2): 2 × 1.2 m = 2.4 m
- Queen posts B (×2): 2 × 0.9 m = 1.8 m
Total per truss = 8.96 + 9.4 + 1.8 + 2.4 + 1.8 = 24.36 m
Number of 6 m lengths = 24.36 ÷ 6 = 4.06 → 5 full lengths per truss (round up to next whole number).

(a)(iv) Struts using 30 × 30 × 5 mm angle iron (per truss):
- Struts C (×2): 2 × 1.5 m = 3.0 m
- Struts D (×2): 2 × 1.2 m = 2.4 m
Total strut length per truss = 3.0 + 2.4 = 5.4 m
Number of 6 m lengths = 5.4 ÷ 6 = 0.9 → 1 full length per truss (round up).
(For the full block — multiply by number of trusses found in (b).)

(b) Number of trusses:
Number of spaces = 20.1 ÷ 2.1 = 9.57...
Number of trusses = number of spaces + 1 = 9.57 + 1
Since spaces must be whole: 20.1 ÷ 2.1 = 9.571 → 10 spaces → 10 + 1 = 11 trusses.
(Alternatively: trusses at each end plus intermediate: ⌊20.1/2.1⌋ + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10 trusses if end truss counted once; accept 10 or 11 with correct working shown. Award full marks for correct method and rounding justification.)

questions.topic: Structural Analysis – Reactions and Force Diagrams
questions.diagramNote: Figure 5(a): A bridge beam of 10 m span supported at P and Q, carrying a UDL/self-weight of 100 kN and a point load of 12 kN from a car at 3 m from one support. Figure 5(b): Space diagram of a wall-mounted crane with a tie, strut at 30°, and a 1 000 N vertical load; the crane arm is shown with relevant geometry.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Taking span = 10 m, bridge self-weight 100 kN (UDL, so acts at centre = 5 m), car load 12 kN at 3 m from P:

Taking moments about P:
RQ × 10 = (100 × 5) + (12 × 3)
RQ × 10 = 500 + 36 = 536
RQ = 53.6 kN

RP = Total load − RQ = (100 + 12) − 53.6 = 112 − 53.6 = 58.4 kN

Mark scheme:
- Correct free body diagram/setup [1]
- Correct moment equation [1]
- RQ = 53.6 kN [1]
- RP = 58.4 kN [1]
- Correct units and equilibrium check [1]

(b) Wall-mounted crane with strut at 30° to wall, tie horizontal, 1 000 N vertical load:
Using resolution of forces (Lami's theorem or triangle of forces):
- Force in strut (F_strut): F_strut × sin30° = 1 000 N → F_strut = 1 000/sin30° = 2 000 N (compression)
- Force in tie (F_tie): F_tie = F_strut × cos30° = 2 000 × cos30° = 2 000 × 0.866 = 1 732 N (tension)

Mark scheme:
- Correct diagram/force triangle [1]
- Correct equilibrium equations [1]
- Force in strut = 2 000 N [1]
- Force in tie = 1 732 N [1]
- Correct identification of tension/compression [1]

questions.diagramNote: Figure 11(a): A simply supported beam of 6 m span carrying a uniformly distributed load (UDL) of 10 kN/m. Table 11(b): Compaction factor test results table showing partially compacted weight = 20.5 kg and fully compacted weight = 24.5 kg.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Simply supported beam, span L = 6 m, UDL w = 10 kN/m:
Total load W = 10 × 6 = 60 kN
Reactions: RA = RB = 60/2 = 30 kN (by symmetry)

(i) Shear Force Diagram (SFD):
- At A (x=0): SF = +30 kN
- At midspan (x=3): SF = 30 − (10×3) = 0 kN
- At B (x=6): SF = −30 kN

[5 marks: reactions correct [1], SFD shape correct [2], values at key points [2]]

(ii) Bending Moment Diagram (BMD):
- At A: BM = 0
- At midspan (x=3): BM = RA×3 − w×3×(3/2) = 30×3 − 10×3×1.5 = 90 − 45 = 45 kNm (maximum)
- At B: BM = 0
BMD is parabolic, maximum at midspan = 45 kNm.
Formula: M_max = wL²/8 = 10×36/8 = 45 kNm ✓
[5 marks: correct formula [1], correct working [2], M_max = 45 kNm [1], parabolic shape [1]]

(b) Compaction Factor = Weight of partially compacted concrete / Weight of fully compacted concrete
= 20.5 / 24.5
= 0.837 (≈ 0.84)

- Correct formula [1]

- Correct answer = 0.84 [1]
