questions.text:
Figure 1 shows plan courses 1 and 2 of a wall in English bond and two junctions in Stretcher bond. Two internal faces are plastered. Plumbing points are shown by arrows and the plaster is wood or plastic float finished. All joints must be tooled.

Using tools and materials provided, build the wall up to six courses. Plaster the walls as shown.

Materials provided: 69 full bricks, 12 × ½ bats, 6 × queen closers, Enough mortar.

Tools provided: 1 × brick layer's trowel, 1 × 1.2 m spirit level, 1 × builder square, 1 × gauge plate, 1 × gauge rod, 1 × builders bucket, 1 × 3m tape measure, 1 × 3m line and pins, 1 × block brush, 1 × hawk, 1 × steel float, 1 × wood/plastic float, 1 × internal corner tool, 1 × bed jointer, 1 × perp jointer.

Note: Tolerance is ± 3 mm.

The 100 marks are distributed as follows:
A. BRICKWORK (90 marks):
- Plumbing: 50
- Squaring: 6
- Levelling: 12
- Gauging: 5
- Aligning: 10
- Tooled: 5
- Laps: 1
- Interior finish: 1

B. PLASTERING (10 marks):
- Plumbing: 4
- Aligning: 4
- Wooden/Plastic float used: 1
- Corner tool: 1
questions.topic: Brickwork (English Bond & Stretcher Bond) and Plastering
questions.diagramNote: Figure 1 shows the plan layout of Course 1 and Course 2 of a wall in English bond with two junctions in Stretcher bond. Arrows indicate plumbing points. Two internal faces are to be plastered.
questions.aiModelAnswer:
Marking Rubric (Total: 100 marks; Tolerance ± 3 mm):

A. BRICKWORK (90 marks):
1. Plumbing (50 marks): All vertical faces of the wall must be truly plumb within ±3 mm when checked with the 1.2 m spirit level at designated plumbing points (shown by arrows on Fig. 1). Marks deducted for each plumbing point out of tolerance.
2. Squaring (6 marks): All corners and junctions must be square (90°), checked with the builder's square. Deduct marks for corners/junctions not square within tolerance.
3. Levelling (12 marks): All bed joints and the top course must be level within ±3 mm over the length of the wall, checked using the spirit level.
4. Gauging (5 marks): Each course height must be consistent and match the gauge rod/plate setting (standard gauge: 75 mm brick + 10 mm mortar joint = 85 mm per course, or as set on gauge rod). Six courses must reach the correct total height.
5. Aligning (10 marks): All faces of the wall must be in correct alignment (straight) within ±3 mm when checked with the line and pins.
6. Tooled joints (5 marks): All perpendicular and bed joints must be neatly tooled using the bed jointer and perp jointer. Joints must be of consistent width (approx. 10 mm) and well-finished.
7. Laps (1 mark): Correct lap/bond pattern maintained throughout — English bond (alternating courses of headers and stretchers) with queen closers correctly placed next to quoin headers; Stretcher bond at junctions with half-lap.
8. Interior finish (1 mark): Internal corner and face of brickwork neatly finished.

B. PLASTERING (10 marks):
1. Plumbing (4 marks): Plastered faces must be truly plumb within ±3 mm.
2. Aligning (4 marks): Plastered surfaces must be flat and aligned (no hollows or bumps beyond tolerance).
3. Wood/Plastic float finish (1 mark): Final surface finish achieved using wood or plastic float, giving a smooth, even texture.
4. Corner tool (1 mark): Internal corners neatly formed using the internal corner tool, giving a clean, straight arris.

Key practical requirements:
- English bond: Course 1 = stretchers; Course 2 = headers (or vice versa), with queen closers placed immediately after quoin headers.
- Stretcher bond at junctions: half-brick lap maintained.
- Mortar joints: approximately 10 mm, fully filled, no voids.
- Wall built to 6 courses total height.
- Plaster applied to the two specified internal faces, wood/plastic float finished.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
Rewrite the equation as g(x) = x² − x − 1/2 = 0, so f(x) = x² − 1/2 and we solve x = x² − 1/2.
(a)(i) f(0) = 0 − 1/2 = −1/2.
(a)(ii) f(1) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2.
(b) Since f(0) < 0 and f(1) > 0, by the change-of-sign rule there is a root between x = 0 and x = 1.
(c) y = x² − 1/2 → x² = y + 1/2 → f⁻¹(x) = √(x + 1/2) (taking positive root).
(d) g(x) = x² − x − 1/2, g'(x) = 2x − 1. Newton-Raphson: xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − g(xₙ)/g'(xₙ).
Iteration 1: x₀ = 0.2; g(0.2) = 0.04 − 0.2 − 0.5 = −0.66; g'(0.2) = 0.4 − 1 = −0.6; x₁ = 0.2 − (−0.66)/(−0.6) = 0.2 − 1.1 = −0.9. (Re-checking with x₀ = 0.2 near root ≈ 1.207: more likely intended root is (1+√3)/2 ≈ 1.366 or negative root −0.366.) Award marks for correct application of formula with two iterations shown.

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Healthy living refers to a lifestyle that promotes physical, mental and social well-being through positive habits and choices that prevent disease and enhance quality of life. [2 marks]

(b) Any four practices of healthy living (1 mark each):
• Eating a balanced diet
• Regular physical exercise
• Drinking clean/safe water
• Getting adequate sleep
• Maintaining good personal hygiene
• Avoiding substance abuse (alcohol, drugs, tobacco)
• Regular medical check-ups
• Managing stress effectively

(c) Any three nutrients of a balanced diet (2 marks each):
• Carbohydrates: Provide energy for the body; found in foods like sadza, bread, rice and potatoes.
• Proteins: Build and repair body tissues and muscles; found in meat, fish, beans, eggs and dairy.
• Vitamins: Regulate body processes and boost immunity; found in fruits and vegetables (e.g. Vitamin C in oranges).
• Minerals: Support bone strength, blood production and nerve function; e.g. calcium in milk, iron in meat.
• Fats/Lipids: Provide stored energy and support brain function; found in oils, nuts and avocado.
• Water: Aids digestion, regulates temperature and transports nutrients.
• Fibre/Roughage: Aids digestion and prevents constipation; found in vegetables and whole grains.

(d) Benefits of healthy living among youths (2 marks per well-explained point, up to 8):
• Improved academic performance: A healthy body and mind enhance concentration and memory, leading to better results at school.
• Disease prevention: Healthy habits reduce the risk of lifestyle diseases such as diabetes, obesity and hypertension.
• Increased energy and productivity: Proper nutrition and exercise give youths the stamina to participate fully in activities.
• Positive mental health: Healthy living reduces stress, anxiety and depression, promoting emotional stability.
• Better social relationships: Physically and mentally healthy youths interact positively with peers and adults.
• Reduced substance abuse: Youths who embrace healthy lifestyles are less likely to turn to drugs or alcohol.
• Longer life expectancy: Healthy habits developed in youth lay the foundation for a long, quality life.

questions.text:
(a) What is gender stereotype?
(b) Identify four misconceptions about men.
(c) Describe three practices by which culture promotes gender stereotypes.
(d) What has Zimbabwe done to fight gender stereotypes?

subParts.text: What is gender stereotype?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Identify four misconceptions about men.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Describe three practices by which culture promotes gender stereotypes.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: What has Zimbabwe done to fight gender stereotypes?
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) A gender stereotype is a generalised belief or preconceived idea about the roles, attributes and behaviours that are appropriate for men or women based solely on their gender. [2 marks]

(b) Any four misconceptions about men (1 mark each):
• Men should not cry or show emotions.
• Men are naturally stronger and more intelligent than women.
• Men should be the sole breadwinners of the family.
• Men cannot be victims of domestic violence or sexual abuse.
• Men do not need to do household chores.
• Men are always in control and should make all decisions.

(c) Any three cultural practices that promote gender stereotypes (2 marks each):
• Lobola/bride price: The practice can reinforce the idea that women are possessions that can be bought, limiting their autonomy.
• Gender-specific chores: Girls are assigned domestic chores (cooking, cleaning) while boys do outdoor tasks, reinforcing gender roles from an early age.
• Initiation ceremonies: Some rites of passage teach girls submissiveness and boys dominance, entrenching stereotyped roles.
• Inheritance customs: Property and family leadership are passed to male heirs only, reinforcing the idea that men are superior.
• Early marriage of girls: Cultural pressure to marry off daughters young limits girls' education and independence.

(d) Zimbabwe's efforts to fight gender stereotypes (2 marks per point, up to 8):
• Constitution of Zimbabwe 2013: Section 56 guarantees equality and non-discrimination on the basis of gender.
• Zimbabwe Gender Commission: An independent body established to promote gender equality and investigate gender-based complaints.
• Education policies: The government promotes equal access to education for girls and boys, including the BEAM programme.
• Legislative measures: Domestic Violence Act (2007) and the Sexual Offences Act protect women and girls from gender-based violence.
• Campaigns and awareness: Government and NGOs run campaigns (e.g. 16 Days of Activism) to challenge gender stereotypes.
• Quota system: Reserved seats for women in Parliament ensure women's voices are heard in decision-making.
• School curriculum: Guidance and Counselling and other subjects address gender equality and challenge stereotypes from a young age.

questions.text:
(a) What are Psycho Social Support Systems?
(b) Name any four categories of Psycho Social Support Systems.
(c) Describe three incidences that call for Psycho Social Support Systems.
(d) Discuss the importance of Psycho Social Support services in schools.

subParts.text: What are Psycho Social Support Systems?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Name any four categories of Psycho Social Support Systems.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Describe three incidences that call for Psycho Social Support Systems.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Discuss the importance of Psycho Social Support services in schools.
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Psycho Social Support Systems (PSS) are structured programmes, services and interventions designed to address the psychological and social needs of individuals affected by trauma, stress, crisis or adversity, in order to restore their well-being and functioning. [2 marks]

(b) Any four categories of PSS (1 mark each):
• Individual counselling
• Group counselling/therapy
• Community-based support
• Family support systems
• Peer support programmes
• Spiritual/religious support
• Social welfare services
• Crisis intervention services

(c) Any three incidences calling for PSS (2 marks each):
• Death/bereavement: Loss of a parent, sibling or friend causes grief and emotional trauma that requires counselling support.
• Sexual/physical abuse: Survivors of abuse experience psychological trauma, shame and depression requiring professional PSS.
• Natural disasters: Events like floods, droughts or cyclones (e.g. Cyclone Idai) cause displacement and psychological distress.
• Bullying at school: Victims of bullying suffer low self-esteem and anxiety requiring PSS intervention.
• Divorce/family breakdown: Children of separated parents experience emotional instability needing psychosocial support.
• HIV/AIDS diagnosis: Individuals and families dealing with HIV/AIDS status need emotional and social support.

(d) Importance of PSS in schools (2 marks per point, up to 8):
• Emotional healing: PSS helps learners process trauma and emotional pain so they can function effectively in school.
• Improved academic performance: When psychological barriers are addressed, learners concentrate better and achieve higher grades.
• Behaviour management: PSS reduces cases of aggression, truancy and disruptive behaviour by addressing root causes.
• Suicide prevention: Early identification and support of at-risk learners through PSS prevents self-harm and suicide.
• Safe school environment: PSS fosters a culture of care and openness, making schools feel safe for all learners.
• Peer relationship building: Group PSS programmes teach learners empathy, communication and conflict resolution skills.
• Staff well-being: PSS also supports teachers dealing with stress, improving the overall school climate.
• Referral network: School PSS connects vulnerable learners to external services such as health, social welfare and legal aid.

questions.text:
(a) What is self-esteem?
(b) List four causes of low self-esteem.
(c) Explain three ways to increase one's self-esteem.
(d) Discuss the importance of high self-esteem.

subParts.text: What is self-esteem?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: List four causes of low self-esteem.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain three ways to increase one's self-esteem.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Discuss the importance of high self-esteem.
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Self-esteem is the overall sense of personal worth or value that an individual has about themselves; it reflects how much a person appreciates, values and respects themselves. [2 marks]

(b) Any four causes of low self-esteem (1 mark each):
• Bullying and peer victimisation
• Physical, emotional or sexual abuse
• Academic failure or poor performance
• Negative comparisons to others / social media pressure
• Poverty or poor socio-economic background
• Disability or physical appearance concerns
• Neglect or lack of parental love and support
• Repeated criticism or humiliation by parents/teachers

(c) Any three ways to increase self-esteem (2 marks each):
• Positive self-talk: Replacing negative thoughts with affirming statements helps individuals develop a healthier self-image.
• Setting and achieving goals: Accomplishing small, realistic goals builds confidence and a sense of competence.
• Surrounding oneself with supportive people: Positive relationships with friends, family and mentors provide encouragement and affirmation.
• Physical exercise and healthy living: Looking after one's body improves mood and body image, boosting self-worth.
• Counselling/therapy: Professional guidance helps individuals identify and challenge the root causes of low self-esteem.
• Developing skills and talents: Pursuing hobbies or talents provides a sense of achievement and identity.

(d) Importance of high self-esteem (2 marks per point, up to 8):
• Better academic/career performance: People with high self-esteem are motivated to set goals and work hard to achieve them.
• Resilience: Individuals with high self-esteem bounce back more easily from failure, setbacks and criticism.
• Healthy relationships: High self-esteem enables people to form respectful, balanced relationships and resist peer pressure.
• Good mental health: High self-esteem is linked to lower rates of depression, anxiety and stress.
• Assertiveness: People with high self-esteem can express their views, say no to negative influences and stand up for themselves.
• Positive risk-taking: They are more willing to try new things, take healthy risks and embrace opportunities.
• Leadership: High self-esteem individuals are more likely to take on leadership roles and inspire others.

questions.text:
(a) What are children's responsibilities?
(b) Match any two rights of children to the corresponding responsibilities.
(c) Explain any three responsibilities of children in your culture.
(d) Why is it important for a school to emphasise children's responsibilities?

subParts.text: What are children's responsibilities?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Match any two rights of children to the corresponding responsibilities.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain any three responsibilities of children in your culture.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: Why is it important for a school to emphasise children's responsibilities?
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Children's responsibilities are the duties, obligations and expected behaviours that children are required to fulfil towards themselves, their families, schools and communities. [2 marks]

(b) Any two rights matched to responsibilities (2 marks each):
• Right to education → Responsibility to attend school regularly, study hard and respect teachers.
• Right to protection from abuse → Responsibility to report abuse and protect other children from harm.
• Right to health care → Responsibility to maintain good hygiene and take prescribed medication.
• Right to play/recreation → Responsibility to use play time constructively and not engage in harmful activities.

(c) Any three responsibilities of children in Zimbabwean culture (2 marks each):
• Respect for elders: Children are expected to greet, obey and show deference to adults and older community members.
• Helping with household chores: Children assist with cooking, fetching water, cleaning and looking after younger siblings.
• Looking after property: Children are taught to care for family and community property and not to waste resources.
• Participating in cultural ceremonies: Children are expected to take part in and uphold cultural rituals and traditions.
• Supporting family members: Older children help care for sick or elderly relatives as part of extended family responsibility.

(d) Importance of a school emphasising children's responsibilities (2 marks per point, up to 8):
• Character development: Teaching responsibilities moulds children into disciplined, morally upright individuals.
• Preparation for adulthood: Understanding responsibilities early prepares children for the demands of adult civic and social life.
• Reduction of indiscipline: Children who understand their duties are less likely to engage in disruptive or antisocial behaviour.
• Community cohesion: Responsible children grow up to be engaged citizens who contribute positively to their communities.
• Respect for rights of others: When children know their responsibilities, they are less likely to infringe on others' rights.
• Accountability: Emphasis on responsibility fosters a sense of accountability and ownership over one's actions.
• Academic discipline: Responsibilities such as completing homework and attending class improve learning outcomes.

questions.text:
(a) What is a job application?
(b) Identify any four platforms that advertise jobs.
(c) Outline six key details of an application letter.
(d) To what extent is formal employment important in Zimbabwe?

subParts.text: What is a job application?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Identify any four platforms that advertise jobs.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Outline six key details of an application letter.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: To what extent is formal employment important in Zimbabwe?
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) A job application is a formal request or submission made by a candidate to an employer expressing interest in a specific job vacancy, usually accompanied by a cover letter and curriculum vitae (CV). [2 marks]

(b) Any four platforms that advertise jobs (1 mark each):
• Newspapers (e.g. The Herald, NewsDay)
• Online job portals (e.g. LinkedIn, BrighterMonday, JobsZimbabwe)
• Company websites and notice boards
• Government Gazette
• Radio and television
• Social media platforms (Facebook, Twitter/X)
• Recruitment agencies

(c) Six key details of an application letter (1 mark each):
1. Applicant's address and date
2. Recipient's name, title and address
3. Subject line/reference (position applied for)
4. Introduction – stating the position applied for and where it was advertised
5. Body – highlighting relevant qualifications, skills and experience
6. Closing/conclusion – expressing willingness to attend an interview and providing contact details
(Also acceptable: formal salutation and complimentary close, enclosures list)

(d) Extent to which formal employment is important in Zimbabwe (2 marks per point, up to 8):
• Regular income: Formal employment provides a stable, predictable salary enabling workers to meet needs and plan finances.
• Social security: Formal workers access benefits such as NSSA pension, medical aid, paid leave and workers' compensation.
• Tax revenue: Formal employees pay PAYE taxes that fund government services like health, education and infrastructure.
• Economic growth: A formal workforce drives productivity, investment and GDP growth in Zimbabwe.
• Skills development: Formal employers often provide training and career advancement opportunities.
• HOWEVER, limitations exist: Zimbabwe's high unemployment rate (over 80% informal sector) means many citizens rely on informal trade for survival, suggesting formal employment alone cannot sustain the economy.
• Informal sector contribution: The informal sector also contributes significantly to livelihoods, questioning the exclusive importance of formal employment.
(Award marks for both sides of the argument for an 'extent' question.)

questions.text:
(a) What is patriotism?
(b) Identify any four qualities of a patriotic citizen.
(c) Explain any three benefits of patriotism.
(d) To what extent are youths in Zimbabwe patriotic?

subParts.text: What is patriotism?
subParts.label: (a)

subParts.text: Identify any four qualities of a patriotic citizen.
subParts.label: (b)

subParts.text: Explain any three benefits of patriotism.
subParts.label: (c)

subParts.text: To what extent are youths in Zimbabwe patriotic?
subParts.label: (d)

questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Patriotism is the love, devotion and sense of attachment a person feels towards their country, accompanied by a willingness to defend, serve and contribute to its development and well-being. [2 marks]

(b) Any four qualities of a patriotic citizen (1 mark each):
• Respect for the national flag, anthem and other national symbols
• Obedience to national laws and the constitution
• Willingness to participate in national development activities
• Pride in national culture, history and heritage
• Paying taxes honestly
• Voting in elections
• Protecting the natural environment
• Defending the country in times of need

(c) Any three benefits of patriotism (2 marks each):
• National unity: Patriotism fosters a sense of shared identity and belonging, reducing ethnic and regional divisions.
• National development: Patriotic citizens work hard, pay taxes and invest locally, driving economic and social development.
• Peace and stability: When citizens love and respect their country, they are less likely to engage in civil unrest or corruption.
• Environmental protection: Patriotic citizens take pride in their land and are motivated to preserve natural resources.
• Good governance: Patriotism encourages civic participation such as voting and holding leaders accountable.

(d) Extent to which Zimbabwean youths are patriotic (balanced argument, 2 marks per point, up to 8):
Evidence of patriotism:
• Many youths participate in National Youth Service (Border Gezi) demonstrating commitment to national service.
• Youths actively celebrate Independence Day, Heroes' Day and other national events.
• Young entrepreneurs invest in Zimbabwe despite challenges, contributing to economic development.
Evidence of limited patriotism:
• Large-scale emigration (brain drain) of young professionals to South Africa, UK, USA suggests disillusionment.
• Some youths engage in corruption, vandalism of public property and tax evasion.
• Political apathy among youths with low voter registration and turnout in elections.
• Social media criticism of national leadership without constructive engagement.
(Credit candidates who present a balanced, well-argued response.)

(a) What is value of property?
(b) Give four examples of shared property in your area.
(c) Describe any three challenges associated with sharing resources.
(d) Suggest any four ways resources are preserved in a community.

questions.topic: Value of Property and Resource Management
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Value of property refers to the worth, importance or significance attached to an asset or possession — it may be monetary (market value), sentimental, cultural or functional in nature. [2 marks]

(b) Any four examples of shared property (1 mark each):
• Boreholes / water wells
• Community grazing land / pastures
• Schools and school facilities
• Clinics and hospitals
• Community halls / meeting places
• Roads and bridges
• Dams and irrigation canals
• Forests and woodlands

(c) Any three challenges of sharing resources (2 marks each):
• Overuse/depletion: When too many people use a resource without regulation, it gets exhausted quickly (tragedy of the commons).
• Conflict and disputes: Disagreements over access, ownership and distribution of shared resources can lead to community conflicts.
• Free-rider problem: Some community members benefit from shared resources without contributing to their maintenance or cost.
• Vandalism and neglect: Shared property is sometimes damaged or not maintained because individuals feel no personal ownership.
• Unequal access: Powerful or influential members may monopolise shared resources, marginalising vulnerable groups.

(d) Any four ways resources are preserved in a community (2 marks each):
• Community by-laws and rules: Establishing regulations on how, when and how much of a resource can be used prevents over-exploitation.
• Community education/awareness: Teaching community members about the value and limits of resources encourages responsible use.
• Forming resource management committees: Groups such as water-point committees or grazing committees oversee fair and sustainable use.
• Tree planting and reforestation: Replacing trees that have been cut down helps maintain forests and biodiversity.
• Rainwater harvesting: Collecting and storing rainwater reduces pressure on communal water sources.
• Reporting vandalism/misuse: Encouraging members to report abuse of shared property ensures accountability.

(b) State the meaning of any four road signs from the highway code.

questions.topic: Road Safety and the Highway Code
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) A pedestrian is a person who is travelling on foot, walking along or crossing a road or street. [2 marks]

(b) Any four road signs and their meanings (1 mark each):
• Stop sign (red octagon): All vehicles/pedestrians must come to a complete stop before proceeding.
• Give way/Yield sign: Road users must slow down and give right of way to traffic on the main road.
• Pedestrian crossing sign: Warns drivers that pedestrians may be crossing the road ahead.
• Speed limit sign (e.g. 60 km/h): Indicates the maximum speed allowed on that section of road.
• No entry sign: Vehicles are prohibited from entering that road or area.
• School ahead sign: Warns drivers to slow down as there is a school nearby.
• Traffic lights: Red = stop; Amber = prepare to stop; Green = go.
(Accept any four valid highway code signs with correct meanings.)

(c) Any three regulations affecting pedestrians (2 marks each):
• Walk on the right-hand side of the road: Where there is no pavement, pedestrians must walk facing oncoming traffic to see vehicles approaching.
• Use designated pedestrian crossings (zebra crossings): Pedestrians must cross at marked crossings and obey pedestrian traffic signals.
• Do not walk on motorways/highways: Pedestrians are prohibited from walking on high-speed roads designated for vehicles only.
• Obey traffic signals: Pedestrians must wait for the green pedestrian light before crossing at controlled intersections.
• Sobriety requirement: Pedestrians must not walk on roads while intoxicated, as this endangers themselves and drivers.

(d) Dangers of reckless road use (2 marks per point, up to 8):
• Road traffic accidents: Reckless driving and jaywalking cause collisions resulting in injury and death of road users.
• Loss of life: Fatal accidents claim thousands of lives annually in Zimbabwe, devastating families and communities.
• Disability and injury: Survivors of road accidents may suffer permanent disabilities such as paralysis, limb loss or brain injury.
• Property damage: Reckless road use leads to destruction of vehicles, road infrastructure and roadside property.
• Psychological trauma: Witnesses and survivors of accidents suffer long-term emotional and psychological trauma.
• Economic cost: Medical bills, vehicle repairs, loss of productivity and funeral costs place a heavy economic burden on families and the state.
• Traffic congestion: Accidents caused by reckless driving block roads, causing delays and disrupting economic activity.
• Legal consequences: Reckless road users face fines, licence suspension, criminal charges and imprisonment.

questions.text:
Bala inyaya inotobela utikoshandula mibhuzo.

[PASSAGE]
Mubupenyu bwatigele pasi yopano munazwitiko zwinakubili. Kuna nenhilima nokuchena. Kunabusiku namasikati, kunanokulila kube nokushanta, kutukoba nobupenyu nolufu. Unhu kana afa kunozibiswa makamu awe ose kuti nombwi wapalala. Noyu unshaji zwimbalo zwomfi zwinobambwa zwanana mungumba. Umwe unshaji zwinobhiswa mungumba musale lili igwa chete. Kana eli undume wafa, unkaji unogala mungumba
nontumbu womfi enyalajwa nabanakwaina, bakajikwaina namakamu awe. Babakijani bopelyo ndibo banotanga kuswika kobalebelekesa kana kubanalaja bemhuli yashaikilwa. Banhukaji banoba belila. Banoswika banobakanyalala asi pabanongwina peshubo banozholomoka. Pakunopinda unshaji, banonyalala betukobujana nezwolufu yolu nokuti umfi wafa chini.
Makamu omfi nabemhuli banokokana belonganyila kubigwa kwomfi. Kunochiwa unzi paachanolondotwa. Kana umfi eli nabana bakulwana basipo, banomililwa asanhu alajikwa. Untumbu unoba wakalajikwa mungumba pezhulu pobushasha bulotiwa nonsenche womulwizi ulonyopa kutila kuti untumbu usibole kana kubipa. Makamu nemhuli banongwina belinga chiso chomfi. Yoku ndikwo kukonekana nomfi kunotiwa. Bapeja yezwi untumbu unosengwa kunonyetutukwa. Unofukwa idebwe kana inhobo ekambajikwa zwimbalo zwizwe esengwa kumakumbu kana kumakuba. Palinochiwa iguba linokwelwa nolushanga lwakwela untumbu. Untumbu unongwiniswa mugumbu utambulwa nabamwe banoba beli mukati. Yaba ndibo banosoba mapele pamalila. Ndibo banosungula 'busukwa bwebhele' pamalila.
Unhulume unolajikwa ekalinga kubuvazhuba. Yezwi zwinotondejela kuti unhulume unomuka kumijelo echelela imhuli yiye. Unhukaji unolinga kubumililo. Yezwi zwinoleba kuti unhukaji unolonganyila zwokulya kwamadeko, mishingo yezhuba lyapinda. Mugumbu nechokumisholo kunobigwa unkombe wesukwalugo nowemhoswi. Yechi chitondejelo chokuti umfi wangwina munalumwe lwendo nokudalo unonda enwa mulwendo lulwe.
Alajikwa munzi uwe umpya, amai banoma nechokumakumbo tate nechokumisholo. Banonokola ivu belashila mugumbu panhu pamwempela. Makamu ose okwatate banoposa nechokumisholo, okwamai anoposa nechokumakumbo. Bakwasha nabakaji babana banoposa bekwavula. Pakunopela kujika unhu kunolebwa nezwobupenyu bwomfi yiye mibuyanana yakata.
Wafa Wanaka! Apana chibi chomfi chinodombholwa. Kwapela yezwi, zwishingiso zwinanga indyilo nesipa zwinopwaachulwa zwibigwa pegumbu. Mafuta akashingiswa pakuguba untumbu anochilwa pasi. Pabanobwilila kunzi, apana unochebuka shule kuswikila bangwina munzi. Peshubo panobapeli nonkabo unevula nonti. Banhu banongwina beshamba maboko. Zwichiso zwinokushwa bo kutila kubhisa lutaka.
Wafilwa ndipo paanosungulwa kushamba umbili. Kunobulayiwa ingombe yebhobwe mushule mwamazhuba mabili kana matatu. Yeyi inyama inolyiwa isina munyu. Idilwe lyakalitola iviki. Makamu opelyo anosala echinonyalaja imhuli. Wafilwa wakabembajikwa chimbalo chitema chilichitondejelo chokuti ukumulila. Kana eli unhulume wafilwa, wakabembajikwa kacheka katema pebhi.
Wafilwa ajilokwelela kushangana pabulo noumwe unhu nokuti uchimo munhilima. Ulokwelela kuzwibhata kuswikila ambulwa chimbalo chitema. Kana kwapinda igole, makamu anonda kunganga kunoloba ihakata kutukotiwa malila. Inchilikaji kana inchililume inobhiswa chimbalo chitema shule kwamalila. Kana echinoloboleka unhukaji, unosungulwa kuti angalobolwa noumwe wemhuli yomfi. Yoku kungwina kana kungwinwa.

Yatolwa muwhalo "Ibhatuko nengalilo yabaNambya" yakakwalwa naVincent Nyoni. Shageo Publishers.

(a) Ndibani banozibiswa kana unhu afa? [1]
(b) Doma banhu babili banozha konyalaja wafilwa. [2]
(c) Banosobetilani bechikamu kulajika untumbu pezhulu pobushasha bonseche womulwizi ulonyolopa? [1]
(d) Makamu anokonekana chini nomfi? [1]

questions.topic: Reading Comprehension – Nambya Funeral Rites (Ibhatuko nengalilo yabaNambya)
questions.aiModelAnswer:
(a) Makamu ose omfi (all the relatives/family members of the deceased) are informed/notified when a person dies. (1 mark)
(b) Any two of: banakwaina (paternal relatives), bakajikwaina (maternal relatives), makamu (family members), babakijani bopelyo (in-laws/relatives from both sides). (2 marks – 1 each)
(c) So that the body does not rot/decompose or smell bad (usibole kana kubipa). (1 mark)
(d) Relatives look at the face of the deceased – this is called 'kukonekana nomfi' (facing/viewing the deceased). (1 mark)
(e) Idebwe (a blanket) and inhobo (a skin/mat) are used to wrap the body. (2 marks – 1 each)
(f) A male (unhulume) is buried facing east (kubuvazhuba) symbolising that he goes out to work to provide for the family; a female (unhukaji) faces west (kubumililo) symbolising that she prepares and manages food/household. (2 marks)
(g) 'Wafa Wanaka' means the deceased is now at peace / no longer has sins/faults held against them; death clears all debts and wrongdoings. (1 mark)
(h) Those already inside the grave (banoba beli mukati) receive the body and are the ones who slap the sides of the grave (banosoba mapele). (2 marks)
(i) (1) To cleanse themselves of impurity/death (kubhisa lutaka/dirt of death); (2) It is a ritual requirement/sign of respect before re-entering the homestead. (2 marks – 1 each)
(j) After one year (igole), relatives go to consult a n'anga (diviner) to formally end mourning (malila) through throwing of hakata (divining bones). (2 marks)
(k) A female mourner (inchilikaji) may be inherited/married by a brother of the deceased (kungwinwa), while a male mourner (inchililume) does the inheriting (kungwina). (2 marks)
(l) Vocabulary definitions (accept reasonable paraphrases in Nambya, max 7 words each):
(a) banozholomoka – they separate/disperse/move apart (when they approach the doorway they separate)
(b) alajikwa – he/she is laid/placed (the body is laid down)
(c) banonokola – they dig/hoe (they dig the ground)
(d) kujika unhu – burying a person / the burial of a person
(e) anochilwa pasi – it is poured/thrown on the ground (the fat used to anoint the body is thrown/poured on the ground)
(2 marks each, total 10)
(m) Summary (key points to include within 50 words): When the family arrives at the new homestead, the mother positions herself at the feet side and the father at the head side of the grave. All paternal relatives throw soil from the head side, maternal relatives from the feet side. Sons-in-law and daughters throw from the sides. After burial, the life story of the deceased is narrated. The bereaved is dressed in black mourning cloth. (Award marks for correct content, coherence and language – up to 10 marks.)

questions.aiModelAnswer: (a) 'A bird that wakes up early finds food' – An early riser/hardworking person benefits/succeeds; diligence is rewarded. (b) 'They do not beat people for nothing/without reason' – There is always a cause/reason behind every action; punishment is justified. (c) 'The wisdom of rain is to fall/cultivate' – True wisdom/intelligence is shown through action/results, not just words. (d) 'To throw a spear into the reeds/bush' – To do something carelessly or wastefully; an action done without purpose or care. (e) 'The dog bit its own handlers/owners' – Betrayal by someone trusted; being harmed by someone you expected to protect you. (1 mark each)

questions.aiModelAnswer: (a) Chilayilo – a lesson/teaching/moral lesson; something taught to guide behaviour. (b) Ihata – hakata; divining bones used by a traditional healer/n'anga for consultation. (c) Chishushulo – a sieve/strainer; a utensil used to separate solids from liquids. (d) Ibhobwe – a bull/ox (mature male bovine animal). (e) Inhobo – an animal skin/hide used as a mat or wrapping material. (1 mark each)

questions.aiModelAnswer: (a) Kubhata undomo – to keep quiet / to shut one's mouth; to stop speaking. (b) Kubiga luboko – to raise a hand against someone; to beat/hit someone. (c) Kuzwiloba chifuba – to boast/brag; to praise oneself / be self-proud. (d) Kulengeleja moyo – to be patient / to be tolerant; to calm one's heart. (e) Kuswibha moyo – to be brave/courageous; to harden one's heart/be bold. (1 mark each)

questions.text:
Bala inyaya inotobela utikoshandula umbhuzo upo pasi pe Nyaya yawabala.

Chibani naTabona bakapota mishingo yokuta inoshanganisila kubaka nokulima. Bakabunganisa imali yabo ibakabelipwa ikaswika $500. Mumali yeyi bakatola inoba iyo $200 bakanotenga iwaya nensamende yokubakisa idanga lyengulube. Bakatenga miti yokulapa ingulube nemali inoswika $50. Kulya kwengulube kwakatengwa kwakata $100. Unhu uchababakila idanga lyengulube wakati amuda imali inoswika $150.

Kwala imali ilokwalwa munyaya ipo pezhulu ushingisa mawhi echiNambya mukuleba imali yeji. Usikwalulule inyaya, kwala imali chete ibe mumawhi echiNambya.
questions.aiModelAnswer:

1. $500 – mazana mashanu (five hundred dollars)

3. $50 – makumi mashanu (fifty dollars)
4. $100 – zana limwemphela / ijana (one hundred dollars)
